text: I am against the repeal or weakening of the current language in the endangered species act that allows for designation of endangered species habitat. The only thing that should be considered when it comes to designating habitat is the following: does this endangered animal thrive in this area? And "if there is no other habitat that can mimic or suitably replace the habitat in question, then it needs to be maintained and preserved for the endangered animal." The point of the act is to preserve crucial habitats for animals and plants that will go extinct. If a habitat area is in question and and endangered or threatened animal or plant lives in the area, then it should remain off limits and protected for the sake of the endangered animal. It really is that simple.
title: Comment from Birkland, Caitlin

text:
I am a Chicago resident living beside Lake Michigan and a bird sanctuary — places that depend on critical habitat protections. Strong critical habitat designations are essential for maintaining the ecosystems that support healthy wildlife populations. Year after year, I can see the decline in migratory wildlife, and fewer fish being pulled up by anglers along the waterfront. This is just a small microcosm of what is going on in fisheries around the great lakes, and it is having huge economic impacts along the lakefront from Chicago all the way up to our norther border. Commercial fisherman are all but extinct, and even recreational fishing is a drying up industry throughout the region. It is because we have not protected the habitats needed for healthy wildlife populations.

I oppose the proposed changes in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 that would tilt decisions on excluding areas from critical habitat toward economic considerations at the expense of science and species survival.

Habitat loss is the leading cause of species decline, and giving greater weight to economic harms weakens the intent of the ESA. I urge you to prioritize ecological necessity and scientific data in critical habitat decisions rather than short-term economic goals. Once this habitat is gone it's gone, and it is much cheaper to save it than to try to restore it.
title: Comment from Alvarado, Daniel

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text: Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 represents a proposed rule that would fundamentally undermine protections for endangered and threatened species by altering how critical habitat exclusions are determined under the Endangered Species Act. The proposed revisions would expand the circumstances under which critical habitat designations can be excluded, prioritizing economic considerations and political factors over science-based conservation requirements that are essential for species recovery. By introducing greater flexibility in exclusion analyses and determining when "benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating the area as critical habitat," this rule creates dangerous loopholes that could allow development interests and short-term economic gains to supersede the fundamental purpose of the ESA: preventing species extinction. Critical habitat designations have proven essential for protecting both occupied and unoccupied areas necessary for species conservation, yet this proposed rule would make it easier for federal agencies to withhold these vital protections at a time when biodiversity loss and climate change threats are accelerating.

I, as a citizen of the United States of America oppose and am appalled by the current Administration’s decision to weaken the Endangered Species Act, stripping away protections for thousands of endangered plant and animal species across the country, in the name of exploiting their vulnerable habitats for resource mining and drilling.

With the weakening of these species’ protections will come devastating impacts on America’s natural environment, including increased loss of keystone animal species such as sea otters and red wolves, who play a vital role in keeping their ecosystems in balance. title: Comment from Genther, Caroline

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I respectfully request the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service retract these regulatory changes as well as any further reductions in ESA protections and instead advocate for stronger, more comprehensive conservation policies.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Nanninga, Roxanne

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th, 2025. I urge the reconsideration of these changes, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this authority increases risk for species that already live on the edge. Habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory billed woodpecker, the Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021). These losses demonstrate the irreversible consequences of weakening habitat protections.

My own field experience underscores what is at stake. This summer, I documented habitat for the federally endangered Karner blue butterfly and the declining monarch butterfly, and I conducted a bumblebee survey alongside the monarch survey. These species rely on highly specific and increasingly rare habitats. Karner blues depend entirely on wild lupine, monarchs require milkweed for breeding and larval development, and bumblebees rely on diverse native flowering plants throughout the season. Even small reductions in habitat quality or availability can cause immediate declines in their populations. Allowing broader exclusions from critical habitat designations would place these species at even greater risk, especially as their ecosystems continue to shrink.

For species already pushed to the brink, critical habitat is not optional. It is the foundation of their survival and recovery.

I am Rebecca Stefoff, a resident of Oregon and the author of many nonfiction books for young people, including books about wildlife and environmental science. The wonder, interest, and even joy I see in kids' faces and hear in their questions during school visits to talk about my books is one reason I'm writing to urge the Department of Interior to abandon its proposed rule change to the Endangered Species Act.

Another reason is basic science. If plant and animal species are to be protected, to survive at all, they require protection for their essential habitats and against "accidental" harms. Altering the definition of "harm" to give economic concerns priority over preserving the habitats that species require to survive would make a mockery of the Act. No species can survive without a safe place to live and reproduce.

Since its passage in 1973, more than half a century ago, the Endangered Species Act has fulfilled its purpose of giving our threatened and endangered animals and plants--including iconic species such as the Bald Eagle and the Florida Panther--a chance, if not a guarantee, of surviving into the future. To reduce protection under the Act at a time when all wildlife and wild habitats face threats from a changing climate and large-scale habitat destruction would be to sign a death warrant for species large and small.

I urge the Department of Interior to maintain the Endangered Species Act as currently written and to enforce its provisions.
title: Comment from Stefoff, Rebecca

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Riggen, Matthew

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Turska, Mary

text:
To those considering the weakening or dismantling of the Endangered Species Act:
I ask you to consider not just ideology, but practicality. The ESA is not an obstacle to prosperity, it is a safeguard of the natural capital upon which the American economy fundamentally depends.
Wildlife protections support agriculture by preserving pollinators, predators of crop pests, and clean water sources. They benefit the fishing industry by maintaining viable aquatic ecosystems. They sustain tourism, outdoor recreation, and environmental research, sectors that collectively contribute billions annually.
The ESA is not a burden; it is an investment. It prevents ecological collapses that would cost orders of magnitude more to repair, if they can be repaired at all.
Weakening this act for the sake of immediate industrial expansion would be a choice to mortgage the future for a fleeting fiscal bump. It would prioritize quarterly earnings over generational security.
American values include both innovation and respect for the land. The ESA embodies this duality, using science to inform policy, and ensuring that technological progress does not bulldoze biological heritage.
The extinction of species is not merely a symbolic loss, it removes genetic diversity, medical potential, ecosystem functionality, and the natural resilience that has allowed humans to thrive.
A species lost is a resource lost. A species lost is also a debt incurred, paid by those who follow us.
We must not define our national legacy as one of wasteful eradication. We must not boast about deregulation while ecosystems unravel.
I compel you:
Do not treat nature as expendable.
Do not destroy wealth that cannot be recreated.
Do not confuse destructiveness with efficiency.
Strengthen the Endangered Species Act. Let it continue to serve as evidence that America is capable not only of growth, but of wisdom.
Let's not sell the future for short term gains and stubbornness, please. This isn't about you or your need to see big number go up, this is about the future! Please!
title: Comment from Burrtoncini, Claire

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. title: Comment from Stillwell, Kennedy

text:
Endangered and Threatened Species: Critical Habitat

Docket ID: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001

I am a Texas native who has spent the majority of my life outdoors with family members hunting and fishing along the Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast. Regressing to allow exclusions in favor of industry and private landowners would be a mistake because it would allow further habitat fragmentation, habitat degradation, and would reduce both the physical size and actual effectiveness of critical habitat. Scientists from NOAA, USFWS, and other organizations spend months to years researching, reviewing, getting public input, and pursuing formal rulemaking in order to designate critical habitat for a single species. Economic and political interests should not be valued over raw data. Data has shown us that habitat loss is one of the leading reasons why plants and animals are listed as threatened or endangered in the U.S. Weakening protections for critical habitat would hinder or worsen ongoing efforts to protect plants and animals in danger of extinction, impacting the ecosystem as a whole. These changes must be rejected and either stronger protections must be pursued or the 2016 policy reinstated to allow threatened and endangered species to recover. American people, American land and waters, and American wildlife should always come first before private or industry profit.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Sabol, Sailor

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA has been one of the most effective conservation laws in the world precisely because it is precautionary, science-based, and focused on preventing irreversible harm to species and ecosystems.
Protecting endangered species matters deeply to me because extinction is irreversible, and laws like the ESA are among the few tools society has that place long-term ecological responsibility above short-term gain.
The proposed changes risk weakening these core protections at a time when biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation are accelerating. Once a species is pushed beyond a recovery threshold, legal or economic efficiencies become irrelevant—the loss is permanent. The ESA was explicitly designed to act before such tipping points are reached, even where scientific uncertainty remains.
Several aspects of the proposal are particularly concerning:
Erosion of precautionary decision-making.
The ESA’s strength lies in requiring protective action when credible risk is identified, not when absolute certainty is achieved. Weakening this standard increases the probability of irreversible extinction events.
Reduced protection for habitat and recovery.
Species do not survive in isolation. Any narrowing of habitat protections or recovery-focused interpretation undermines the biological reality that species persistence depends on intact, functioning ecosystems.
Increased discretion at the expense of science.
The ESA was intentionally structured to insulate species protection from short-term political or economic pressures. Shifting the balance away from independent scientific assessment risks decisions that favour expedience over long-term ecological stability.
It is also important to recognise that the ESA has consistently enjoyed strong, bipartisan public support over many decades. Its durability reflects a widely shared understanding that preventing extinction and protecting ecosystems are core societal responsibilities, not niche or partisan concerns. Weakening the Act risks undermining both its conservation effectiveness and its public legitimacy.
The ESA is not merely a regulatory tool—it is a safeguard against irreversible loss. Its success should not be measured by how easily it accommodates development, but by how effectively it prevents extinction and enables recovery. Weakening its protections now will externalise costs to future generations who will inherit diminished ecosystems and fewer options for recovery.
I urge you to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed changes and to reaffirm the original intent of the ESA: to protect imperilled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend, using the best available science and a precautionary approach.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical issue.
Sincerely,
Andy Hope, London, England

Knowing Southern Resident Killer Whales and those who work to research them or conserve their species (as well as the area salmon they rely on) has been the privilege of my life. These creatures have their own culture. Being around them completely resets my nervous system. They give me hope, community, understanding, joy, and are constantly evolving my scientific understanding. Before altering the ESA you should spend time with people who deeply know these impacted species. In my area for the species I care about that would be Orca Conservancy, Orca Behavior Institute, Center for Whale Research, and Seadoc society. Anyone from these orgs would be happy to help you understand why these pieces of the ESA matter and even show you these habitats and animals we put at risk by changing it. We as humans rely on these complicated ecosystems far more than we realize. This is why we should follow the science and not the money. These whales have made it thousands of years and now have less than 75 remaining because of what humans have done (captures, pollution, vessel disturbance, shore disturbance, overfishing, trawling, climate change). Don't we want to be better than the generations before us? Don't we want to leave and even restore nature for our kids? title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Southerland, Larisa

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Gangware , Elizabeth

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed amendment to Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) on the basis that the ESA currently has sufficient legal framework to prioritize habitat exclusion when the benefits of habitat exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, and that the amendment would critically weaken the mechanisms by which the ESA has saved 99% of listed species during its more than 50-year tenure. I am a biologist and I hold a PhD in biology. I work with animals protected under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including leatherback, Kemp’s ridley, loggerhead, and green sea turtles.

We know that protecting habitat reduces and mitigates harm to species across their environments. In the marine environment, Finkbeiner et al. (2011) found that sea turtle deaths in the waters of the United States Exclusive Economic Zone as a result of fisheries bycatch was reduced by 94% upon the implementation of mitigation measures, including spatial and temporal closures of critical habitat to fishing. In the terrestrial realm, Ehrhart et al. (2014) demonstrated the importance of protected nesting habitat for the reproductive success of loggerhead sea turtles at the Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge. These two studies and many others demonstrate the importance of habitat protection to the direct survival of protected organisms.

The planned amendment to the ESA will give disproportionate consideration to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. If this amendment passes, the exclusion process would become a mechanism for regulated entities and private industry to overrule scientific consensus, which is something that Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process. This proposed amendment is not based upon scientific consensus, and placed corporate greed and lobbyism before science.

References cited
Finkbeiner, Elena M., et al. "Cumulative estimates of sea turtle bycatch and mortality in USA fisheries between 1990 and 2007." Biological Conservation 144.11 (2011): 2719-2727.

Ehrhart, Llewellyn, et al. "Long-term trends in loggerhead (Caretta caretta) nesting and reproductive success at an important western Atlantic rookery." Chelonian Conservation and Biology 13.2 (2014): 173-181.

title: Comment from KING, TONI

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

title: Comment from Carl, Bruce

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from Parks, Leslie

text:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule “Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat” (Federal Register Document No. 2025 20550). The proposal would revise how the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service conducts exclusion analyses under Section 4(b)(2), which requires the agency to consider economic, national security, and other impacts when designating critical habitat.

While economic considerations are already required by statute, the proposed rule expands and formalizes the role of these impacts in ways that risk elevating non biological factors over the scientific needs of listed species. The notice states that the revisions are meant to articulate how the agency determines whether the benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating it as critical habitat. In practice, this could lead to more frequent exclusions, reducing habitat protections essential for species recovery.

Critical habitat is one of the ESA’s most effective tools. Scientific evidence consistently shows that habitat loss is the primary driver of species endangerment, and Section 4(b)(2) designations are intended to safeguard the physical and biological features species rely on. Increasing flexibility to exclude areas introduces additional uncertainty and may undermine protections at a time when intact habitat is already limited.

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of the proposed rule and the maintenance of a precautionary, science first approach to critical habitat designation under Section 4(b)(2).
Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida (the “Tribe”) submits this comment in response to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively, the “Services”) proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”) implementing regulations published in the Federal Register on November 21, 2025, Docket Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

The Tribe has been at home in the Everglades since time immemorial. It maintains deep cultural and spiritual connections to the land, water, and wildlife of the region. Numerous species protected under the ESA—including the Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi), the wood stork (Mycteria americana), and the Everglade snail kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis plumbeus)—are culturally significant to the Tribe and play an important role in the ecosystems that encompass the Tribe’s lands and waters. The proposed regulatory changes would significantly weaken protections for these species and their habitats, contrary to the ESA’s statutory purpose and the federal government’s trust responsibilities to Tribal Nations. The Tribe therefore opposes their implementation for numerous reasons, detailed below.

First, the proposal to eliminate the longstanding “blanket rule” protections for threatened species under ESA Section 4(d) would delay or deny essential safeguards for species listed as threatened under the ESA. Requiring species-specific rules before ESA protections may apply to species listed as threatened creates regulatory gaps, during which development or other federal actions may proceed without precautionary, science-based safeguards. For Tribal communities, such delays risk harming culturally important species and the ecosystems they rely on.

Second, several of the proposed revisions introduce new limitations that discourage or preclude critical habitat designation. For example, the proposed addition to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(1)(ii), allowing the Secretary to forgo designation where threats to habitat “stem solely from causes that cannot be addressed through management actions resulting from consultations under section 7(a)(2),” risks creating a broad exemption to critical habitat designation for actions that do not trigger section 7 consultation. If an action does not require section 7 consultation (because it is not solely tied to a federal agency, require federal authorization, or receive federal funds), important critical habitat designations will not be made, increasing the risk that listed species’ habitat, and therefore the species themselves, will be negatively impacted, in areas prone to development like south Florida. It is the Tribe’s opinion that this phrase be entirely omitted from the provision.

Third, the proposed revisions to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(b)(2) governing designation of unoccupied critical habitat constrain the Secretary’s ability to protect listed species in ways inconsistent with the ESA’s Congressional mandate. The requirement that the Secretary determine with “reasonable certainty” that an unoccupied area will contribute to species conservation introduces a level of confidence that is unachievable in prospective conservation decisions. Species recovery often depends on protecting habitat before it is occupied, particularly in dynamic ecosystems such as the Everglades. Replacing a precautionary, science-informed approach with a de facto requirement for near certainty risks excluding areas that are essential for long-term species survival and adaptation. It is the Tribe’s opinion that “reasonable certainty” be exchanged with “likelihood.”

Fourth, these proposed regulatory changes collectively shift ESA implementation away from its preventative and recovery-oriented purpose and toward a framework that prioritizes economic and development interests. As written, the proposed regulations increase the likelihood that large-scale land use and energy development will proceed at the expense of imperiled species and Tribal interests. At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss, they weaken science-based species protections and increase the risk of irreversible harm to species and ecosystems that are culturally and spiritually significant to the Tribe, rather than strengthen them.

The Tribe respectfully requests that the Services withdraw or substantially revise its proposed regulation revisions, remove provisions that unduly restrict critical habitat designation, elevate conservation considerations rather than economic interests, and preserve science-based decision-making in ESA implementation.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Bousquet, Cathryn

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Davidson, Lori

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I live in the Puget Sound region and am a devoted citizen (amateur) scientist for critical PNW species, including Pacific salmon and Southern Resident Killer Whales (SRKW). For many, these species are an integral part of our lives here in the PNW, and we are emotionally and culturally connected to them. In fact, this connection was THE reason I moved back to the area upon retirement.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the best wildlife conservation laws in the world, and a law Americans should be proud of. The habitat protection it provides is among the Act’s most effective tools. This proposal to expand exclusion authority turns the purpose of the Act on its head by prioritizing short-term economic interests over long-term species survival and recovery. It is undisputed that habitat loss is the leading driver of extinction, and once eroded, habitat restoration becomes difficult, expensive, and sometimes impossible.

The SRKWs and Pacific salmon depend on connected habitats that support prey availability, migration, and ecosystem function. Given their tenuous status, it is just too risky to exclude areas from critical habitat without adequate safeguards. Excluding habitat can fragment river, estuary, and nearshore systems that are essential for salmon spawning, rearing, and migration. And of course further loss of the salmon population directly impacts the SRKWs due to even more reduced prey availability. Sadly, we are in a time when species are being forced to adapt to global changes. Narrowing habitat protections will reduce the ability of these species to adapt, further limit their resilience, and undermine recovery efforts that depend on healthy, functioning ecosystems.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.
The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.
I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Irons, Bridget

text:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed reinstatement of the 2020 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) rule governing exclusions of critical habitat under section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). I am a coastal and marine conservation scientist with over 15 years of professional experience working on endangered species recovery, habitat protection, fisheries bycatch, climate vulnerability, and collaborative conservation partnerships, including work with Indigenous communities and Federal agencies. From this perspective, I am deeply concerned that this proposal weakens one of the ESA’s most effective and scientifically grounded tools for species recovery.

The ESA’s purpose is not merely procedural efficiency or impact minimization; it is to conserve ecosystems upon which listed species depend and to prevent extinction. Critical habitat designation is central to that mandate. The proposed rule re-centers discretionary exclusions in a way that elevates economic and administrative considerations over biological necessity, contrary to the Act’s precautionary intent and decades of conservation science.

As written, the proposal creates a framework that encourages exclusion of ecologically essential areas—including unoccupied and Federal lands—based on speculative or short-term impacts, while discounting long-term conservation value. This is particularly troubling for coastal, marine, and anadromous species, whose habitats are dynamic, spatially extensive, and increasingly threatened by climate-driven sea-level rise, ocean warming, habitat compression, and cumulative development pressures. For such species, protecting only currently occupied habitat is insufficient and scientifically indefensible.

The proposed “credible information” standard for initiating an exclusion analysis risks skewing the process toward exclusion by lowering the threshold for considering non-biological impacts, while no comparable standard is applied to ensure full consideration of climate resilience, ecosystem connectivity, or future habitat needs. In my professional experience, impacts to species often become irreversible well before they meet narrow or short-term thresholds of “meaningful” economic concern.

I am particularly alarmed by the proposal’s treatment of Federal lands. Federal ownership has historically been a cornerstone of species recovery precisely because it allows for landscape-scale conservation and long-term planning insulated from market volatility. Explicitly treating administrative and transactional consultation costs as a benefit of exclusion, even on Federal lands, undermines Congress’s clear directive that all Federal agencies must use their authorities to further the purposes of the ESA. Section 7 consultation is not an undue burden; it is a foundational safeguard that improves outcomes for species and ecosystems.

The proposal’s stated reliance on Executive Order 14154 further underscores the problem. Energy policy objectives—however framed—do not override statutory obligations under the ESA. Reinstating the 2020 rule in response to energy directives risks converting section 4(b)(2) from a narrow safety valve into a routine mechanism for avoiding habitat protection, particularly in coastal and marine-adjacent areas where energy, infrastructure, and development pressures are already intense.

In practice, this rule would likely result in fewer, smaller, and less ecologically coherent critical habitat designations, increasing extinction risk and undermining recovery—especially for species facing climate-driven range shifts. That outcome is inconsistent with the ESA’s text, purpose, and demonstrated success.

I urge the Service to withdraw this proposal and instead retain a regulatory framework that prioritizes biological necessity, climate adaptation, and ecosystem-scale conservation. The ESA has prevented extinction precisely because it requires foresight, precaution, and restraint in the face of uncertainty. This rule moves in the opposite direction.

Sincerely,
Allison Anholt

Removal of this habitat will allow the extinction of many of these species without having an explicit public conversation about individual species being “too expensive” to save.  It would be more transparent to have a “god squad” where the public weighs in on which species are saved or allowed to go extinct rather than this quiet and shielded way for political bureaucrats to decide behind closed doors.  The reason we don’t have these types of conversations, and there is no law for it, is the American public don’t want ANY species to go extinct.  If this administration thinks this has changed, they can introduce legislation rather than try to circumvent the will of the American people through rule changes.  Frankly, if ecosystem services were fully considered as suggested here critical habitat would almost never be removed based on economics, since extractive economics provide money one time or intermittently, but ecosystem services like flood and fire preventions, water filtration, ect are ongoing in perpetuity.  In fact, one might wonder why instead of removing critical habitat for bogus reasons they might get more economic bang for their buck by focusing more on habitat restoration.  Finally, any rule that includes the words “national security” by this administration is not to be taken seriously.  They claimed that remodeling the white house and deporting American citizens can be done under the guise of national security.  Anything they want to do that is not popular they claim is a national security issue.  Appropriate critical habitat will never be set aside again if the “national security” lever is available for them to pull.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under discussion. These potential amendments would severely compromise the ESA’s critical role in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems for wildlife and human communities alike.

1. **Eliminating default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)**

The ESA’s design is to act promptly before species face crisis levels. The 4(d) rule is backed by abundant scientific evidence indicating that early, precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and avert further declines. Ending these automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays, necessitating protections on a case-by-case basis, which could expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This runs counter to the ESA’s preventive goals, likely resulting in increased ecological and financial burdens.

2. **Complicating species listing by incorporating economic factors and weakening future-threat assessments**

ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Incorporating economic considerations would contradict this mandate, undermine scientific integrity, and risk delays until species are critically endangered. Additionally, limiting climate-related threat assessments ignores current conservation science that shows habitat loss, temperature changes, and ocean acidification already put species at risk. Weakening criteria for future threats reduces timely listings and heightens the chances of preventable extinctions.

3. **Diminishing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”**

Habitat loss is a leading cause of global biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially for unoccupied or climate-refuge areas, undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, redefining “harm” to exclude habitat degradation would reverse legal and scientific precedents. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. Weakening these definitions diminishes inter-agency collaboration, increases biological risks, and contradicts the ESA’s recovery objectives.

4. **Creating new loopholes enabling agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction risks, contradicts the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes would incentivize exemptions on a case-by-case basis, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. Such changes would disproportionately affect imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating the decline of already pressured species.

**Cumulative Impact**

Collectively, these proposals would:
- Weaken the scientific basis of the ESA,
- Delay or block necessary protections for species,
- Reduce habitat conservation amidst climate change,
- Increase extinction risks for domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- Inflate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, a testament to its grounding in science, precaution, and early intervention. These proposed changes undermine those core principles.

As global biodiversity faces unparalleled threats, the U.S. should strengthen, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and maintain the existing regulatory framework rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
DO MORE TO PROTECT CRITICAL HABITAT FOR ENDANGERED SPECIES!
The Endangered Species Act is one of the most beloved act's in American history. Americans want to see threatened and endangered species protected under the Endangered Species Act. I'm outraged that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle this beloved American conservation law. Americans demand that the Endangered Species Act be strengthened, not weakened, and this proposal will absolutely weaken the ability of the Endangered Species Act to protect threatened and endangered species. Don't let more species go extinct on YOUR watch! If the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries weaken the Endangered Species Act, it will because of YOU that more species go extinct and you will have to live with that. It is now or never for species on the brink, species that Americans love and hold dear to their hearts. In my area, it is Northern spotted owls, Gentner's fritillary, salmon, whitebark pine, and so many more that deserve protection under the ESA, that I am so concerned about. As a country we need to band together to protect these species, not let them go extinct while we sit by and do very little to help.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted.
