text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, Endangered and Threatened Species: Critical Habitat, and Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation. Collectively, these proposals undermine the ESA’s core purpose and place threatened and endangered species at heightened risk of extinction. Taken together with related proposed rules (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048), they dismantle longstanding conservation regulations that have proven both effective and widely supported.

First, the proposed changes to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, including the elimination of the blanket 4(d) rule, would significantly weaken protections for threatened species. The blanket 4(d) rule provides a clear, effective, and legally defensible conservation framework while still allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to tailor species-specific rules where appropriate. Removing this baseline protection increases the risk of population declines and places unnecessary administrative burdens on the agency by requiring individual 4(d) rules for every newly listed threatened species—delaying protections when they are most urgently needed.

Second, the proposed rule titled Endangered and Threatened Species: Critical Habitat would substantially erode the designation and protection of habitat essential to species recovery. Allowing federally managed public lands to be excluded from critical habitat designation based on economic considerations prioritizes short-term development over long-term conservation. This approach would enable energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial activities in areas that threatened and endangered species rely upon for survival. Given that most imperiled species now occupy only small fractions of their historical range, weakening critical habitat protections represents a serious setback to recovery efforts and a clear concession to industry interests.

Third, the proposed changes introduce economic considerations into decisions about whether to list a species as threatened or endangered. This shift contradicts a foundational principle of the ESA: that listing decisions must be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. Injecting economic analyses at this stage risks politicizing a science-driven process and delaying or denying protections to species facing imminent threats.

Fourth, the proposed rule Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation would weaken the interagency consultation process with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service. Framed as an effort to “streamline” consultations, this proposal would instead reduce expert oversight and allow federal agencies to move forward with projects without fully accounting for their impacts on imperiled species. Such changes threaten the effectiveness of one of the ESA’s most important safeguards against federal actions that jeopardize listed species and their habitat.

Together, these proposals revive regulatory rollbacks similar to those advanced during the first Trump administration—measures that are inconsistent with both the ESA’s proven record of success and public support. Since its enactment, the ESA has prevented extinction for 99 percent of the species it protects, and recent polling shows that more than four out of five Americans support the law across political and geographic boundaries.

The need for strong species protections has only grown. Accelerating habitat loss, expanding development, and climate change demand robust implementation and enforcement of the ESA—not its erosion.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed rules on Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, Critical Habitat, and Interagency Cooperation, and to uphold the full protections of the Endangered Species Act for the benefit of America’s wildlife and the ecosystems on which they depend.

text: This rule risks putting short term, short-sighted viewpoints about perceived or imagined economic and security benefits above the long-term health of ecosystems. text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to how critical habitat is designated under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), particularly the addition of non-biological factors such as economic impacts and national security considerations that could prevent areas from being protected.

Critical habitat designation is one of the most important tools under the ESA for preventing extinction and supporting species recovery. The purpose of critical habitat is to identify and protect the physical and biological features essential to the conservation of imperiled species. Introducing new discretionary factors unrelated to species survival undermines this core function and weakens the Act’s science-based framework.

The ESA already allows for limited consideration of economic impacts at specific implementation stages. Expanding the role of economic or national security factors at the habitat designation stage risks excluding ecologically essential areas, fragmenting habitats, and reducing the likelihood of recovery—particularly for wide-ranging, migratory, and climate-sensitive species.

Allowing such exclusions sets a dangerous precedent by prioritizing short-term or speculative concerns over long-term ecological resilience and biodiversity protection. Once habitat is lost or degraded, it is often impossible or extremely costly to restore. Preventing protection at the outset increases extinction risk and shifts greater costs to future generations.

Additionally, weakening critical habitat protections reduces regulatory clarity, limits interagency accountability, and undermines public confidence in federal conservation efforts. Strong, clearly defined habitat protections are essential for effective planning, enforcement, and recovery.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA to reject these proposed changes and to ensure that critical habitat designations remain grounded in the best available science and focused squarely on species conservation and recovery.

Please uphold the full intent and effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act and preserve strong protections for the habitats upon which endangered and threatened species depend.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

text:
My name is Patrick Freeman and I am a wildlife ecologist from California. As a member of the scientific community, I write to reaffirm my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the United States’ enduring commitment to preventing the extinction of species. The ESA remains one of the most vital and effective tools we have to halt the accelerating loss of life on Earth. For over 50 years, the ESA has served as a bedrock environmental statute, grounded in scientific rigor and ecological understanding. Its success is measurable: nearly all species listed under the ESA have been prevented from going extinct, thanks to careful evaluation, habitat protection, and recovery planning based on the best available science. The law’s principles of early intervention, critical habitat designation, interagency cooperation, and science-driven listing decisions reflect decades of consensus in the biological sciences about how to halt and reverse species declines.

Scientific consensus is clear: species are disappearing faster than at any time in human history, and in the U.S. alone, thousands of species are imperiled.
Science also makes clear that early interventions like those provided by the ESA are cost-effective and lead to better recovery outcomes. Delays in listing and inadequate habitat protections reduce the likelihood of recovery and increase the long-term costs of conservation. The ESA, developed by scientists and policymakers together, already recognizes that development initiatives must be designed to coexist with, not override, our dependence on nature. Weakening the ESA would not only undermine decades of conservation progress, but also jeopardize the future resilience of our planet in the face of accelerating climate and ecological disruption.

The proposed policy change ("requires consideration of the economic impact, the impact on national security, and any other relevant impact of designating any particular area as critical habitat; and authorizes the exclusion of areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating it as critical habitat.") undermines the ESA’s science-based decision framework by injecting politics and short-term economics into what should be evidence-driven processes. It runs the risk of excluding entire species or ecosystems from protection based on short-sighted convenience, not conservation need. And further, it ignores basic science principles related to species survival and limits our own ability to respond to long-term threats.

As a scientist, I stress that the loss of species is not only a moral tragedy, but also a practical threat. These species and their connections to each other and the world around us underpin ecosystem services essential to human well-being: clean water, pollination, disease regulation, carbon storage, and climate resilience, to name a few. The ESA does not just protect wildlife; it protects the systems that support agriculture, economies, and communities. The maintenance of Critical Habitat designations are integral to the Act's success.

To this end, I implore you to rescind this proposed rule change. Thank you for your consideration.

Best,
Patrick Freeman

title: Comment from Simon, Katy

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss and climate change, we should be strengthening, not dismantling science-based protections for wildlife. text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
RE: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 Endangered Species Act/Narrowing interpretation of Critical Habitat

The Board of the Idaho Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited (PCTU) has reviewed the proposed rule to narrow the interpretation of “Critical Habitat” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). PCTU has over 275 members, and our mission and values align with those of the national organization Trout Unlimited; namely the conservation of trout and salmon and the habitats they reside in, to ensure their enjoyment by current and future generations.

According the information provided by USFWS, a change in the rule is necessary to ensure other federal actions, and in particular mineral and energy extraction projects, can be permitted in an expedient fashion. The information also suggests the proposed rule changes will provide higher degree of clarity in determining whether actions that will occur in the presence of listed species are under Federal purview, and a process for determining if those actions will negatively affect conservation and recovery of the species being considered.

PCTU members, and thousands of other anglers, have benefitted enormously from protections provided to bull trout, a “threatened” species which is widely distributed in our geographic area. Recovery efforts in our area have not only produced a state record (catch and release) bull trout, but have facilitated benefits for westslope cutthroat trout, kokanee, and other fisheries. In our part of Idaho, collaborative efforts to restore bull trout have engaged anglers, businesses, industries, Tribes and others to implement conservation measures made available through the nexus of listed bull trout. Bull trout are recovering, and petitions for ESA listing of westslope cutthroat trout early this century were obviated, in part because bull trout conservation helped bolster cutthroat trout populations.

We are concerned narrowing the definition of Critical Habitat will result in important habitat needed for the recovery of listed species being subjected to habitat modifications that will impair or prevent recovery. In the case of potential listings for native trout and salmon, that would eventually result in not only the loss of species, but the loss of fishing and other valuable (to include economically valuable) aspects of healthy native salmonid populations. This proposed change has the potential to severely compromise the ability to effectively implement the letter and intent of the ESA. Thus, we oppose the rule as proposed.

In Idaho and elsewhere, there are numerous examples of collaborative efforts to effectively implement ESA , to include working in designated Critical Habitat, while finding paths forward for other land and water uses to occur in ways that are economically viable for those stakeholders looking to extract, develop, or otherwise modify natural resources. We strongly encourage any modifications to rules be focused on facilitating effective collaboration amongst stakeholders, and to do so in a timely manner. Doing so will allow appropriate designations while creating opportunities to address other natural resource needs while meeting the intent of the ESA.

Thank you for considering these comments.
Charles E. Corsi, President
Panhandle Chapter Trout Unlimited
title: Comment from (Idaho) Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Gianni, Nicole

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Malone, Rachel

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to submit a public comment expressing concern regarding the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations governing critical habitat exclusions.

As a physician, I am trained to evaluate risk not only by what is immediately visible, but by what may unfold over time if early warning signs are ignored. In much the same way, critical habitat protections are a preventative measure—designed to preserve the ecological conditions necessary for species survival and recovery before irreversible decline occurs.

The proposed addition of a formal “exclusion analysis” lowers the threshold for omitting areas from critical habitat designations and shifts the balance away from conservation. By encouraging exclusions based on economic, national security, or other competing considerations, the rule risks transforming critical habitat from a science-based recovery tool into a negotiable outcome driven by short-term interests.

Habitat loss remains the primary driver of species decline. Critical habitat is not a theoretical designation—it identifies the physical and biological features species require to survive, reproduce, and adapt to changing environmental conditions. Weakening these protections undermines recovery efforts and increases the likelihood that species will remain imperiled indefinitely.

Weighing economic or development pressures against conservation benefits at the exclusion stage also fails to account for the long-term costs of ecosystem degradation. Healthy ecosystems provide services essential to human health and economic stability, including flood mitigation, water filtration, climate regulation, and food security. Excluding habitat today may yield temporary economic benefit, but it often results in far greater ecological and public health costs tomorrow.

The ESA was deliberately crafted to prioritize conservation when extinction is at stake. Introducing a formalized pathway to exclude critical habitat risks eroding this foundational principle and diminishes the law’s effectiveness as a preventative safeguard.

I respectfully urge the agency to reconsider these proposed changes and to maintain strong, science-based critical habitat protections that reflect the interconnectedness of ecosystems, wildlife, and human health. Protecting habitat is essential not only for species recovery, but for the resilience of the natural systems upon which we all depend.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for your continued consideration of policies that safeguard our shared environmental future.

Sincerely,
A concerned physician and conservation advocate

text:
With respect to the aforementioned proposed rule, the Captain Paul Watson Foundation (CPWF) Chapter for Chicago and Illinois is opposed to the adoption of the proposed rule by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service titled "Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat" (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, RIN 1018-B176) of November 21, 2025 in any way, shape, or form.

We will further emphasize we oppose even the slightest adoption and implantation of this short sighted proposed rule by the Federal Government. Already it is clear that the 1982 addition to the U.S. Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973, Section 4(b)(2) has had unintended, negative effects on the Act’s effective of preventing species extinction and ensuring species recovery. That negative effect being allowing more harmful, unnecessary economic activities within the proposed critical habitat of an Endangered or Threatened species protected by the act and only preserving the bare minimum area required to prevent the extinction of the aforementioned species.

In essence preventing a species’ extinction but not preserving enough habitat to ensure full population recovery overtime.

This proposed rule by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Department of the Interior will only make this problem exponentially worse. It will make the problem worse by allowing the Secretary of the Interior greater ability (without proper federal oversight to prevent potential corruption) to exclude areas from critical habitat designation considerations, potentially excluding consideration (in proposed paragraph paragraph (d)(1)(iv) of the proposed rule) of already designated Federal Lands as lands to also add to designated critical habitat for Endangered and Threatened Species, and allow for greater and necessary consideration (even more than before) of even relatively minimal long term economic impacts on whether to even designate certain areas as critical habitat for endangered and threatened species.

This will hamper the long term ability of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to implement meaningful recovery programs for ESA listed species and designate enough critical habitat for them to achieve population recovery in the long term.

This proposed rule can be best described by us as ecologically destructive, unnecessary, and extremely short sighted.

We strongly recommend this proposed rule is not implemented in any way, shape, or form. Instead, we recommend several alternative steps to improve the Endangered Species Act in the immediate. These steps are ensuring the “2020 rule” (85 FR 82376) of December 18, 2020 is not revived in any way, shape or form, to convince Congress to repeal the 1982 addition to the ESA known as Section 4(b)(2) alongside reverting to the previous Federal stance regarding the importance of protection of species habitat as emphasized in the Supreme Court decision Tennessee Valley Authority v. Hill (437 U.S. 153) of June 15, 1978, to ensure any of 2019 federal rules changing implementation of the ESA are not revived, to repeal all federal Executive and Agency orders that promote the weakening of bedrock environmental laws like the ESA, and to improve funding, implementation, and enforcement of the ESA.

Bedrock Environmental Laws like the U.S. Endangered Species Act of 1973 have been instrumental in protecting the unique species of animals, plants, and wild spaces Americans have enjoyed and benefited from for generations. They are true national treasures, priceless and worth more than any short term economic gains that could be gained by destroying them. We must protect them no matter the short term costs.

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

text:
As a concerned citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to change the long-standing definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The current definition, supported by sound science and legal interpretation, appropriately recognizes that habitat modification and destruction can cause harm to threatened and endangered species. Excluding habitat modification from the definition of harm could drastically weaken one of the ESA’s most effective and widely used protections. Without question, this change could threaten the survival and recovery of endangered species, and could inadvertently fast track many species onto the list. Species we cannot afford to lose. Additionally, the recovery of listed species could become much more difficult and costly as more essential habitat could be impacted or lost. Protecting habitat is essential to avoid future ESA listings. 
There is long-standing scientific documentation that habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the leading cause of species declines in the US and globally. It is not only over-harvesting or direct impacts to individual plants and animals that result in the decline of a species. The greatest threats – the degradation and loss of their habitat, critical feeding, sheltering, breeding, and/or nesting grounds –  bring species to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, the current interpretation of the definition of harm, to include impacts to habitats, has been utilized by the USFWS for decades. This interpretation has even been upheld in a case before the US Supreme Court.

title: Comment from Chedsey, Deanna

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Goodman, Arthur

text:
To whom it may concern,

I’m writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would severely weaken the ESA's ability to prevent extinctions, aid in species recovery, and protect critical ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA aims to act before species reach critical levels. The 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early protections lower recovery costs and prevent declines. Removing these protections would lead to unnecessary delays, needing individual rulemaking, and would expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive goals and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would undermine scientific objectivity and delay necessary protections. Limiting the consideration of future threats disregards current conservation science, which acknowledges that issues like habitat loss and climate change threaten species long before population declines become evident. Weakening these criteria makes timely protection less probable and increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, while narrowing the definition of “harm” would undo years of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife, a fact long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations and increase biological risks.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decision-making away from science-based analysis, disproportionately impacting species like the Florida panther and gray wolves.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Collectively, these changes would:
• weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• delay or block necessary protections,
• reduce habitat conservation,
• increase extinction risk,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• and raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has historically prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, proving its effectiveness through science, precaution, and early action. These proposals conflict with those principles.

In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all four proposed rule changes and retaining the current regulatory framework, grounded in science and successful implementation.

text:
I am appalled by the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, and I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. This proposed rule will destroy the government’s ability to designate critical habitat. If an endangered species doesn’t currently occupy an area, even if it historically lived there, even if it must return there for its recovery, this area will be ruled out. This is handing over a species’ ability to recovery to industry, and is absolutely counter to the intent of the ESA.

Congress intended the authority to exclude habitat to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

In addition, the rule would give private industry more weight than biological researchers by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This dangerous change to the ESA will allow corporations the ability to exclude areas that need habitat protections, including areas that already currently have protection as deemed by the USFWS as part of a species’ necessary recovery. This is absolutely not what the ESA was intended for.

I urge the Service to abandon this proposed rule and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

The threat to wildlife and habitat has not decreased since the introduction of the ESA; rather, it has increased due to habitat loss, destruction, and climate change. Weakening the ESA will only drive species further toward extinction. Not only that, but weakening the Act is counter to what most Americans want. Recent polls, such as the one conducted by Atomik Research before the 2024 election on behalf of the Indianapolis Zoological Society, showed that 87% of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, believe that the federal government should do more to strengthen the Endangered Species Act.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Hunter, Dani

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

It’s why these protections have been in place. Stop overstepping. Protections need to remain as they are.
title: Comment from Daugherty, Jennifer

text:
Under the ESA, the government designates critical habitat to protect threatened and endangered wildlife. But this rule change would allow the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to prioritize economic interests over habitat conservation needs for newly listed species. That’s a major setback for wildlife like wolverines, which depend on large, connected landscapes that are easily fragmented by development, drilling and mining.

I urge the government to take a stand and continue to protect our most vulnerable neighbors
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Prottas, Jenny

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Orr, Taylor

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Lynch, Rachel

text:
Hello;

I am writing to urge you to NOT adopt Revision FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, which would require economic and national security impacts to be taken into consideration in designation of critical habitat. This has not been the case since the inception of the Endangered Species Act in 1973, and there have been no serious instances of impact in either area. In addition, the phrase "any other relevant impacts" is very broad and has the potential for abuse. This measure should not be passed. Thank you for the opportunity to express my opinion on this important matter.

Sincerely,

Ellen M. Lawler
title: Comment from Lawler , Ellen

text:
§ 424.19 Impact analysis and exclusions from critical habitat., bullet (c):
"The Secretary, however, will not exclude any particular area if, based on the best scientific and commercial data available, the Secretary determines that the failure to designate that area as critical habitat will result in the extinction of the species concerned."

The goal of ESA is not simply to protect endangered species from extinction but also to promote their recovery. This sentence is overly restrictive. While it is important to understand and consider economic, security and other consequences as outlined in this section, areas that are critical to the recovery of a species should also be covered.

Proposed change:

The Secretary, however, will not exclude any particular area if, based on the best scientific and commercial data available, the Secretary determines that the failure to designate that area as critical habitat will result in the extinction of the species concerned, or will prevent, hinder or obstruct the recovery of that species.

title: Comment from Williams, Meredith

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Angel Valkolilja

text:
What are we doing here, other than giving in to corporate lobbyists?

I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.
The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.
Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.
The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.
title: Comment from Ehlert, Karl

text:
I am reaching out today to express my opposition to the proposed rule regarding critical habitat exclusions. The revised framework the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has introduced would ultimately make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat, authorizing exclusions if the potential national security and economic benefits outweigh the benefits associated with protection.

This poses a particular threat to currently unoccupied historic habitat. Even if these areas are unoccupied now, they have the potential to support species survival, recovery, and longevity in the future. Paving the way for their destruction and degradation would be a massive mistake—one that inevitably drives future extinction and biodiversity loss.

Please protect these lands and the species they support by abandoning this harmful rule.

title: Comment from Shuler, Jyoni

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival

text: I live in the Breezy Point Cooperative, private property on the western tip of the Rockaway Peninsula.  For years, the Coop and USFW have been working hand in hand and fencing off areas for nesting piping plovers.  The beach can get very crowded in the summer with upwards of 3000 people on a mile long strip of beach.  Fortunately it is a wide beach and the Coop fences off part to protect the plovers.  As an amateur birder and  member of NYC Plover Project, I have observed how effective the fencing installed by the Coop and monitored by USFW has positively impacted plover populations.  This past summer we had 14 fledglings!  I am sure that if the designation for critical habitat is weakened or rescinded there would be NO fledglings from this critical strip of beach and within a generation, the plovers would be gone.  Forever.  In addition, the area set aside for the plovers also protects, common and least terns, black skimmers, American oystercatchers, killdeer and other birds.  My estimate is over 1000 baby birds fledged on this beach in each of the past two summers!  I also have no doubt that without USFW protecting this area, the Coop would face pressure from residents to develop the land for playgrounds, food stands, volleyball courts all of which exist already elsewhere on the property.  In addition, by preserving and protecting this area, we are protecting ourselves.  Keeping this area undeveloped protects us from storm surge, which we learned the hard way from Sandy, potentially saving billions of dollars.  Please keep protecting critical areas and endangered species so my grandkids can someday see a piping plover.
