I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Comment on Blanket 4(d) Rule Removal (2025-20552)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Interagency Consultation (Section 7) Rule (2025-20551)

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Book, Ashley

text:
I submit this comment to oppose the proposed revisions to the section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework for critical habitat designation.

Congressional intent limits exclusion authority. Section 4(b)(2) permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat after weighing benefits, provided exclusion will not result in extinction. This provision was intended as a narrow safety valve, not a broad license to subordinate biological needs to economic preferences. Legislative history makes clear that Congress expected exclusions to be exceptional and carefully justified. The proposed rule distorts this balance. By creating a framework that presumes exclusion unless the agency can affirmatively demonstrate extinction risk, the rule transforms the exception into the default. This reversal is inconsistent with statutory structure. The ESA places the burden on those seeking to reduce protections, not on the agency to justify maintaining them.

The extinction standard is insufficient. The proposed rule's reliance on extinction risk misunderstands the ESA's purpose. The statute aims at conservation and recovery, not merely staving off extinction. A species hovering at the brink of extinction is not a conservation success—it is a conservation failure. Moreover, the extinction standard is scientifically unworkable. Extinction risk often becomes clear only when it is too late to intervene. Small populations face genetic and demographic stochasticity that can drive rapid collapse. The ESA's precautionary approach exists precisely because of these uncertainties and because the costs of error are irreversible.

This proposal inappropriately elevates speculative economic impacts. The proposed rule permits exclusions based on economic "concerns" that need not meet the evidentiary standards applied to biological data. This asymmetry is indefensible. If the agency must use "best available science" for biological determinations, economic assertions should meet equivalent standards. The rule also fails to account for the economic value of intact ecosystems. Wetland species maintain water filtration and flood control. Forest species support watershed protection. Grassland species maintain soil health and carbon sequestration. Marine species underpin fisheries. When critical habitat is excluded based on narrow calculations ignoring these ecosystem services, the analysis is fundamentally misleading.

There are real-world consequences of weakened habitat protection. Critical habitat designations identify areas necessary for recovery, focus conservation resources, and inform land-use planning. Weakening these through expanded exclusions degrades all these functions. Consider a migratory species depending on stopover sites—excluding even one critical site can break the chain and render the entire migration route unviable. Consider an aquatic species requiring cold, clean water—excluding upstream habitat may doom the species even if downstream habitat remains designated. These reflect real conservation challenges where habitat connectivity is decisive.

The proposed expansion of section 4(b)(2) exclusion authority is inconsistent with the ESA's text, purpose, and conservation mandate. I urge the Service to withdraw these revisions and maintain an exclusion framework that treats exclusions as rare, carefully justified departures from the default requirement of habitat designation based on biological need.

We live in a time of accelerating biodiversity loss. The species we are legally obligated to protect are often the same species whose ecological functions sustain the landscapes we depend upon for clean air and water, productive soils, and climate stability. When we compromise their habitat, we compromise the resilience of natural systems that provide essential services. The choice to exclude critical habitat is not merely administrative—it is a choice about what kind of world we will leave to those who come after us, and whether we will honor our commitment to share this planet with the other forms of life that have as much right to be here as we do.

title: Comment from White , Sarah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Frangioni, Liana

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Almendral, Desiree

text:
Rule 0048-0001, regarding: critical habitat analysis

I strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule, as it runs counter to Congress’s original intension for the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Should this proposed rule be implemented, it would further weaken the ESA, with the likely result being many more species being unnecessarily pushed into extinction, which in turn will lead to a further unraveling of the already-frazzled web of life.

The proposed rule would change the way that critical habitat for threatened and endangered species is determined. It would allow, in some cases, for the economic cost of proposed protections to outweigh the ecological benefits of preserving species and the ecosystems of which they are a part, resulting in denial of areas for critical habitat designation. This proposed rule clearly allows decision makers to give more weight to economic considerations than to the protection of species and our environment. It will allow corporations to put pressure on the Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service to exclude areas from critical habitat designation that are in fact critical to the survival of species. Seeing as habitat loss is the foremost reason species are driven to extinction, this proposed rule would severely weaken the ESA if implemented.

It seems unnecessary to say it, but protecting the habitat that threatened and endangered species occupy, or have occupied in the past and may well occupy in the future, is essential for the specie’s survival. We all need a place that provides what we need to live. If this habitat is no longer habitable due to its degradation or destruction, there may not be other habitats available that would allow for the specie’s survival. Even in cases where there is other habitat that might provide for the specie’s needs, the species may not be able to successfully relocate. It should go without saying that critical habitat protections are absolutely indispensable if the goal is to protect threatened and endangered species. The ESA as it stands is clear on this. If anything, critical habitat protections should be strengthened.

The failure of the Trump Administration to see that in prioritizing corporate profits over a healthy and sustainable environment, it actually reduces America’s national security. Without a healthy and sustainable environment, which is inseparable from a healthy biodiversity, this country can never be secure, as we, and future generations, are all absolutely dependent upon this environment for our survival. Any further destruction of our environment ultimately threatens our national security. Beyond that, it is simply immoral to allow other species to be pushed by humans into extinction. Other species have as much right to exist as do humans.

For these reasons, I very strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule. Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Russell Wray

Future generations counting on you, including the children you know. One never knows what each species can teach us, our unique nation must be protected. I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.
title: Comment from Schlott, Jo Ann

text:
I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change regarding critical habitat criteria.

​​This revision would prioritize resource development over species protection, which is in direct contrast to the intent of the Endangered Species Act.

​​Weakening the critical habitat designation procedure would make it easier to exclude key habitats and avoid the requirement to mitigate impacts for activities that occur in these areas.

​​Critical habitat designations should be based on science and not special interests.

​​Habitat protection is key to species recovery.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA §4(b)(2) framework for excluding areas from critical habitat.

Section 4(b)(2) authorizes exclusions only as a narrow exception. Habitat may be excluded only when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, and only when exclusion will not result in extinction. The statute does not treat exclusion as a preferred outcome.

The proposed rule alters that balance. In effect, it shifts the governing premise from “critical habitat is designated unless exclusion is clearly justified” to “critical habitat should be excluded unless extinction can be proven likely.” That is a burden shift. It elevates economic concerns while reducing recovery to a secondary consideration.

By framing extinction avoidance as the operative threshold, the rule treats recovery as optional. Yet recovery — not persistence at the brink — is the ESA’s conservation mandate. Habitat that supports long-term viability, resilience, and adaptation is exactly what critical habitat is meant to protect.

The rule also invites economic objections without requiring comparable scientific rigor, risking a process in which speculative impacts outweigh biological evidence. I urge the Service to withdraw this proposal and retain a §4(b)(2) framework in which exclusions remain rare, carefully justified, and subordinate to the biological needs and recovery of listed species.
title: Comment from Larrea, J.J.

text:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule that would reinstate the 2020 regulations for designating critical habitat under Section 4 of the Endangered Species Act. I have professional experience implementing the ESA, including service with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service working on Endangered Species Act and CITES matters. I currently lead a nature technology company focused on nature-based risk analytics.

The proposed rule would reinstate regulations making it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat designations for economic reasons. This change contradicts the ESA's statutory text and would harm imperiled species by reducing protected areas essential for survival and recovery.

ESA Section 4(b)(2) allows exclusions based on economic impacts only if benefits outweigh conservation value and exclusion will not lead to extinction. The proposed rule expands discretion to favor exclusions without rigorous analysis, contradicting congressional intent to designate habitat based on science. The 1978 amendments emphasized that habitat protection is fundamental to preventing extinction.

Under FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009), and DHS v. Regents, 140 S. Ct. 1891 (2020), policy changes require good reasons and consideration of reliance interests. This rule reverses the 2022 rescission of the 2020 regulations without new evidence, disregarding habitat conservation plans and recovery efforts developed under the current framework.

Congress defined critical habitat to include unoccupied areas essential for conservation because species often require expanded ranges for recovery, as demonstrated by red wolf and gray wolf reintroductions. Broader exclusions would restrict protections for range shifts needed amid climate change.

Executive Order 14154's burden-reduction premise is unsupported. Critical habitat designations minimally impact development. The 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation estimates wildlife-related activities contribute approximately $395 billion annually to the U.S. economy.

I urge the Service to withdraw this proposed rule.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Saladino, Susan

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act has stood as a promise that we would not allow our most vulnerable wildlife to disappear on our watch. Because of this law, 99% of listed species have been saved from extinction. As someone who deeply loves and cares about America’s wildlife, I am heartbroken by this proposed rule change and urge you to withdraw it. It turns its back on decades of legal precedent, ignores the best available science, and opens dangerous loopholes that strip critical habitat from species still fighting to survive.

The Endangered Species Act is about more than individual animals; it reflects our moral responsibility to protect the living systems that sustain all life, including our own. Weakening these protections will accelerate species decline, unravel fragile ecosystems, and permanently damage the conservation legacy generations have worked to build.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this rule and honor the original promise of the Endangered Species Act: that we will do everything in our power to protect endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are not optional; they are essential if we want wildlife to have a real chance to recover, for the sake of future generations and the planet we share.

title: Comment from Riordan, Rory

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of listed species. Reinstating it would contradict the core purpose of the Endangered Species Act, which is to conserve ecosystems and promote species recovery—not to reduce protections for industry convenience.

Exclusions from critical habitat designation must be grounded in clear scientific evidence, not speculative or generalized economic concerns. Because habitat loss is the primary driver of species decline and extinction, weakening critical habitat protections directly undermines recovery prospects. The Fish & Wildlife Service should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger, science-forward framework.
title: Comment from Pagay, Amanda

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Zukas, Alex

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.

title: Comment from Mulligan, William

text:
Some say that the "cost" of maintaining conditions of environment -- particularly for those in which endangered species now live -- is related only to monetary burdens for development or extraction of resources. What about the costs of chain effects within the ecology of that environment? What about the as yet not fully comprehended links between any living member of such an environment on the continuance of other forms of life and their population regulation.

In the same way that non-native species often upset the balances of native ecologies, overlooking small (sometimes seemingly insignificant) effects (as this rule change suggests) can permanently alter environments and make them uninhabitable for species presently found within them. It is our due responsibility to ensure that these unwitting changes do not happen.

With climate change -- brought on by heavy use of fossil fuels during the last century and a half -- vigorously under way, we must be even more rigorous in our efforts to curtail loss of further species. Ultimately, we humans too are part of the network of life. We damage our future prospects by recklessly forging into delicate regions of life. In the long run, we will gain no benefit from this profligacy.

I oppose this rule change for the above reasons.

Diego Gonzalez
Springvale, ME

title: Comment from Terada, Justin

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to all four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under consideration. These proposals would severely weaken the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and preserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and humans.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA's design is proactive, aiming to protect species before they reach crisis levels. The 4(d) rule has been a cornerstone of preventive action, supported by decades of scientific evidence showing that early protective measures reduce recovery costs and avert further declines. Removing these protections would lead to unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm, contradicting the ESA's preventive goals and leading to higher ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific evidence, excluding economic impacts. Allowing economic considerations undermines statutory language, scientific integrity, and could delay necessary protections until species are near extinction. Additionally, ignoring future or climate-driven threats contradicts current conservation science, which shows that gradual pressures like habitat loss and climate change already endanger species long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria will hinder timely listings and increase preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline, both globally and in the U.S. Limiting critical habitat designations, especially unoccupied or climate-refugia habitats crucial for recovery, undermines conservation efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation disregards long-standing legal and scientific precedent, which recognizes the indirect harm habitat destruction causes to wildlife. This would weaken inter-agency consultations, increase biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections, even when extinction is a possible outcome, contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes would encourage project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analysis. This disproportionately affects wide-ranging and imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines in already pressured species.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Individually, these changes are concerning, but collectively, they would:
- Undermine the scientific basis of the ESA,
- Delay or obstruct protections for vulnerable species,
- Diminish habitat conservation amid climate change,
- Heighten extinction risks for domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- Increase taxpayer costs for long-term recovery.

The ESA has succeeded in preventing 99% of listed species from extinction due to its foundation in science, precaution, and early intervention. These proposed changes run counter to these principles. Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be bolstering—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is grounded in science, legal precedent, and successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Auerbach, Julian

text:
I am deeply concerned about proposals to roll back lifesaving Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections for endangered wildlife and their habitats and oppose any effort to weaken the ESA.

The proposed rules/ changes to the ESA ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. They attack imperiled species and the places they live by:
(1) Depriving newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.
(3) Loosening compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.
(4) Violating the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.
(5) Altering the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous, absolutely unacceptable, and must not be allowed.

Protections under the ESA are our most effective tool for combating the appalling decline of wildlife across the nation. Hundreds of species were on a path to extinction until they were saved by this law’s protections, including bald eagles and gray wolves. And a million species are at risk of extinction in the coming decades, including grizzly bears, Florida panthers, and manatees. Right now, we have a choice between bringing endangered wildlife back from the brink, or losing them forever. We must act while we still can.

More than four out of five Americans support the ESA. Please uphold this essential law and protect imperiled wildlife.

Thank you for your consideration.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to convey my firm opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both individually and as a collective whole, would severely weaken the ESA’s capability to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and preserve the ecosystems that both wildlife and human communities rely on.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)**

The ESA was crafted to intervene before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default protections for threatened species would cause unnecessary delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking for protections currently automatic, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm or death. This contradicts the ESA’s preventative purpose and will result in greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations would contradict statutory language, undermine scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species face extinction. Additionally, limiting the use of projected threats ignores conservation science, which shows that pressures like habitat loss and climate change place species at risk long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listing less likely, increasing the likelihood of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”**

Habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery planning. Narrowing the definition of “harm” so habitat degradation no longer qualifies would reverse decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often kills wildlife indirectly, and this has long been recognized in law. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations, increase biological risk, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. **Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Creating or expanding mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections—even where extinction is foreseeable—conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would promote project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This disproportionately affects imperiled species like Florida panthers and gray wolves, accelerating declines in species already under pressure.

**The cumulative impact of these proposals**

Though each proposal is concerning, together they would:
- Undermine the scientific basis of the ESA
- Delay or block protections for species in need
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change
- Increase extinction risks for both domestic and international species
- Weaken inter-agency cooperation
- Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers

The ESA has averted extinction for 99% of listed species. It’s one of the most successful conservation laws due to its grounding in science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes run counter to those principles. Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be bolstering, not diluting, its key wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and retain the existing regulatory framework, grounded in science, legal precedent, and successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Rollins, Shelley

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

I strongly oppose the Docket Document FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001 and the other three proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under review.

The ESA was passed into law in 1973 with overwhelming bipartisan support.
Fifty years later, support is still overwhelming.
84% of Americans support the ESA.
Half of Americans participate in wildlife-watching.
One third of Americans participate in birdwatching.

From an economic standpoint, birdwatching is big business. Lose birds, lose dollars. According to the Rachel Carson Council, "Birding is a major driver of tourist, retail, and conservation funding. The $107.6 billion spent by birders in 2022 was divided between $14 billion for trip-related expenses, and $93 billion for gear. Additionally, these expenses generated $7 billion in county taxes, $9 billion in state taxes, and $22 billion in federal taxes. All of this birdwatching activity produced $90.2 billion in labor income and supported 1.4 million jobs. text:
I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

Thank you for your consideration.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever.
Thank you.

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Hill, Kathleen

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, Lisa Sanchez
title: Comment from Sanchez, Lisa

text:
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

The proposal to allow economic considerations in listing decisions reverses the ESA’s science-only standard, which has served our nation well for 50 years. Allowing economic costs to influence listings could delay or prevent the protection of species at the edge of extinction.
Species like the bald eagle, whooping crane, and American alligator recovered because they were listed based solely on science, not economic tradeoffs. America would be very different today if our proud and patriotic bird the American Bald eagle was only a memory. On the other hand, 21 species were recently declared extinct because protection came too late, often due to inaction or regulatory delay. (https://www.fws.gov/press-release/2023-10/21-species-delisted-endangered-species-act-due-extinction)

Critical habitat designations are essential for recovery. Species such as the northern spotted owl and the snail darter survived because their habitat received legal protection. Many species also depend on protected areas for safe nesting and breeding, and disruptions can cause immediate and severe harm. The Piping Plover and the Florida Scrub-Jay are clear examples where disturbance or loss of nesting habitat leads directly to nest failure and population decline. Even species that are not currently listed depend on these protections. Even species not in the Endangered Species Act such as the Horned Lark, for example, is experiencing steep declines due to habitat loss and benefits when natural areas are preserved. Weakening the habitat designation process, including allowing exclusions of unoccupied habitat, would remove the very places species need to survive, recover, and adapt to a changing climate.

text:
I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

Comment on Critical Habitat Exclusions Rule (2025-20550)

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

The Endangered Species Act clearly states “ (1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation.

This is why the ESA gives priority to endangered and threatened species that are or may be in conflict with construction or other development projects or other forms of economic activity which threatened critical habitat. These species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the nation and its people.

The proposed rules work against these goals.
