title: Comment from Mansulla, Marlene

text:
I am writing this comment to oppose all four proposed changed to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Each change threatens the ability of the ESA to not only conserve and support species populations and habitats, but also conserves habitats that function for human benefit as well.

1. Removing the the blanket rule and striping default protections for threatened species would make the recovery for when those species inevitably end up endangered much more expensive and difficult. By turning to a case-by-case basis for threatened species leaves many vulnerable to steep declines while waiting for cases to make their way through the already busy court system. Allowing this rule to be repealed would only create more work for the future and increase the cost of protecting the species.

2. Allowing listing decisions to be influenced by economic decisions is illogical and avaricious. This would hinder the ESA's ability to protect newly listed species that may require large and connected landscapes. Habitat loss and fragmentation are the biggest threats to any endangered or threatened species. Many species utilize different ecosystems to carry out their life cycles and by allowing listings to be influenced and weakened due to economic interest defeats the very purpose of this well supported piece of legislation.

3. Reducing the critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of "harm" would destroy one of the major foundations of the ESA. As stated in the prior reasoning, habitat loss is the number one threat to biodiversity. It is much easier and more effective to preserve critical habitat as is rather than try and replicate said ecological conditions for preservation in the future. The protection of critical habitat not only allows for a greater chance of species to rebound from low numbers but also saves money and time. It is much more expensive to recreate conditions for these species than to protect the habitat they rely on.

4. Allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections is a disastrous decision and makes it much harder to protect listed species. Fragmenting the ability of the ESA to protect species and allow certain agencies to do immense harm to listed species and weakens the strength of the ESA as a whole. Many of the species that would be affected are large predators that are often keystone species and play a large role in maintaining the balance in their ecosystems. Allowing species such as the gray wolf and grizzly bear to be vulnerable to bypasses in the ESA will lead to catastrophic consequences for not only these species but others as well.

Each change undermines the purpose of the ESA and raises the costs of conservation in the future. Save taxpayer money and keep the ESA as is. This act as prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct because it is based on science, not economics, and prioritizes early action.

One of the main draws of the United States to the rest of the world is the incredible biodiversity and ecosystems all located within one country. We should be strengthening the ESA and be proud of the natural wonders of our country.

I urge these proposed changes to be withdrawn and for the ESA to be kept grounded in science.

I urge you to do the right thing.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

RE: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
The proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act would put threatened and endangered species in danger. Many species have specific environmental needs in order to thrive, the designation of critical habitat through the Endangered Species Act protects these environments so that threatened and endangered species can bounce back. This rule change would create loopholes to allow the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species, putting short term economic interests over habitat conservation needs for newly listed species.

The rescinding of the "blanket rule" for newly listed species as is expressed in the proposed rule change would withhold protections such as restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing, to species added to the threatened/endangered species list. Getting rid of these automatic protections would do nothing more than hasten their demise by making it much more difficult to obtain species specific protections.

The introduction of ambiguity in the definition of "recovery" opens the door to species being taken off of the endangered species list before they are truly recovered. The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. There is no reason for this change as it only puts species in danger of having their protections removed before they are ready.

This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. This change would completely undermine the ESA's purpose by allowing projects to be approved before evaluating the potentially negative environmental affects.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our responsibility to care for the creatures who we share this planet with. It also reflects a responsibility we have to ourselves, to preserve the beauty of our natural world, and start reconciling our relationships with the creatures we have lived with side by side for millenia. The changes proposed to the Endangered Species Act serve as a way of avoiding these responsibilities out of convenience for ourselves, the same mindset that has lead to the necessity of the endangered species act in the first place. I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent, to show to the American people a dedication to uphold our responsibilities instead of skirting them.
title: Comment from Wittrock, Kailyn

text:
I’m writing to express my complete opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

title: Comment from Egan, Kimberly

text:
I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under review. Each proposal would, individually and collectively, undermine the ESA’s capacity to avert extinctions, facilitate species recovery, and conserve essential ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA is designed to take preventive action before species crises occur. The 4(d) rule, backed by decades of scientific research, proves that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating these automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, requiring individual rulemaking and exposing vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the preventive intent of the ESA and will result in higher ecological and financial costs long-term.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Factoring in economic considerations would undermine the law’s intent, delay protections, and place species on the brink of extinction. Ignoring projected threats, like habitat loss and climate change, disregards conservation science, threatening species before declines become evident. Weakening these criteria will likely result in preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a primary cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” excludes habitat degradation, reversing legal and scientific precedents. This weakens inter-agency consultations, increases biological risks, and conflicts with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, conflicts with the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analysis, disproportionately impacting imperiled species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

The collective impact of these proposals:

These rules, if enacted, would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs. The ESA, preventing 99% of listed species from extinction, is effective due to its grounding in science and early action. These proposals contradict those principles.

In a time of significant global biodiversity loss, the United States should reinforce, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to rescind all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing, scientifically grounded regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the proposed changes to the regulations for excluding areas from critical habitat. This proposal shifts the Fish and Wildlife Service's focus away from its core mission of species recovery and toward the mitigation of economic inconvenience for private and industrial interests.

1. Mandatory Exclusions Undermine Conservation By making exclusions mandatory when "benefits of exclusion" outweigh the "benefits of inclusion," the Service is abdicating its discretionary authority to prioritize biology. Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction. A rigid cost-benefit analysis—which often struggles to put a dollar value on the "benefit" of a species existing—will almost always favor immediate, quantifiable economic gains over the long-term, "invisible" value of a healthy ecosystem.

2. The Danger of Excluding Federal Lands Federal lands are often the last strongholds for endangered species. The proposal to facilitate the exclusion of Federal lands from critical habitat is a violation of the spirit of the ESA, which mandates that Federal agencies use their authorities to further the purposes of the Act. Excluding these lands to "Unleash American Energy" (per E.O. 14154) creates a fragmented landscape where species have no safe harbor, even on public property.

3. Elevating Administrative Costs over Biological Survival Allowing "administrative and transactional costs" to serve as a primary justification for excluding habitat is a dangerous precedent. The "cost" of filing paperwork or attending a consultation should never be weighed against the permanent loss of a species' home. This change creates an incentive for stakeholders to inflate the perceived "burden" of regulation to avoid conservation obligations.

4. Fragmenting Habitat through Stakeholder Influence By giving significant weight to economic data provided by outside stakeholders, the Service invites biased data into the decision-making process. Critical habitat works best when it is contiguous and scientifically determined. Allowing "piecemeal" exclusions based on the complaints of individual landowners or industries will result in "swiss-cheese" habitat that is insufficient for species migration and recovery.

Conclusion The Endangered Species Act was designed to prevent extinction "whatever the cost." This proposed rule flips that mandate, seeking to avoid costs "whatever the risk to the species." I urge the Service to maintain the 2022 standards and ensure that habitat protection remains a biological priority, not an economic negotiation.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 that expand or clarify exclusions from critical habitat based on economic or other considerations. Habitat loss and fragmentation are the leading drivers of species decline, and critical habitat protections are fundamental to long-term recovery.
Ecosystems function as interconnected systems, not isolated parcels. Excluding areas that appear economically burdensome in the short term often leads to long-term ecological degradation, reduced species viability, and increased future costs for recovery efforts. Scientific evidence consistently shows that protecting intact habitat is more effective and more economical than attempting restoration after degradation occurs.
I urge the Service to prioritize ecological function, connectivity, and resilience when designating critical habitat and to apply exclusions sparingly and cautiously. Conservation decisions should reflect long-term biological outcomes rather than short-term economic pressures.

title: Comment from Stobie, Shawna

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I'm writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under consideration. Each proposal—individually and as a whole—would significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and preserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)

The ESA was crafted to act before species face crises. The longstanding 4(d) rule, based on decades of scientific evidence, shows that early protections cut recovery costs and prevent declines. Ending these automatic protections will cause unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive intent and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making It Harder to List Species by Allowing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors contradicts statutory language, undermines scientific objectivity, and risks delaying protections until species are nearly extinct. Ignoring projected or climate-driven threats overlooks conservation science showing that pressures like habitat loss and climate change endanger species long before population declines are apparent. Weakening future-threat criteria lessens the likelihood of timely listing, increasing preventable extinction risks.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Limiting the Definition of “Harm”

Habitat loss is a key driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Cutting critical habitat designations, especially unoccupied or climate-refugia habitats crucial for recovery, undermines planning. Narrowing “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific precedent, as habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife. Weakening these definitions reduces inter-agency consultation effectiveness, increases biological risk, and conflicts with the ESA's recovery mandate.

4. Opening New Loopholes Allowing Agencies or Special Committees to Bypass ESA Protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, conflicts with the ESA’s purpose. Such loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making from science-based analysis. This disproportionately affects species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines under pressure.

Cumulative Impact of Proposals

Collectively, these rules would:
- Weaken the ESA's scientific foundation,
- Delay or block needed species protections,
- Reduce habitat conservation during accelerating climate change,
- Heighten extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- Increase taxpayer recovery costs.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction because it’s rooted in science, precaution, and early action. These changes oppose these principles.

Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening its most effective wildlife protection law, not weakening it.

Request

For the reasons outlined above, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes entirely and retain the current framework based on science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I am writing to urge that these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act not be made. Every one of these proposed changes will meaningfully weaken the protections that should be afforded to threatened and endangered species, creating loopholes that will only benefit people seeking to exploit our natural world for their own short term profit. The creation of different rules for “newly listed” species is a transparent attempt to weaken the Endangered Species Act as a whole.

When I was a kid in the late 80’s the appearance of a single bald eagle at our local lake was unusual enough to warrant a series of articles in our local newspaper. Now bald eagles are regularly seen at the same lake.

The appearance of that bald eagles was the outcome of a series of changes, which were mostly invisible to the average person. We all hear about how banning DDT led to increased eagle populations, but we hear less about how improved protections for lakes and streams resulted (slowly) in the return of life to poisoned rivers. When I was a kid, I never remember seeing a fish bigger than a minnow in that local lake, but now every time I am there I see at least a few that are larger than my hand. The fish needed their own food sources to rebound, and those insects needed their own habitat to once again be habitable, and etc. and at any point in that chain one could write an article (as I’m sure that many were) about the economic waste and bother that was being created by attempting to preserve the habitat of “this bug” or “that water weed” but each one was necessary for the return of the bald eagle (and the loons, which have thankfully also returned).

Attempting to separate species protection from habitat protection cannot be done, and anyone suggesting it clearly does not care about protecting either.

Of course newly listed species should receive “blanket-rule” protections to buy time for the development of more tailored species specific protections. This is just plane sense.

But if we are going to talk in purely economic terms, when I was a kid that lake had a fine town beach and a few camps. It did not have many fish. People from away had no reason to go there and so they didn’t. Nowadays, with “the bugs”, and “the waterweeds”, and the bald eagles, and the loons, it is a beloved local spot for fishing and recreation, and property values around the lake have increased accordingly.

The proposed rule improperly prioritizes economic interests over biological imperatives, compelling the agency to favor economic impacts—even when such impacts are uncertain or minor.

Additionally, the rule sets an unreasonably high bar for retaining habitat, insisting that areas be excluded unless the agency can prove that such exclusion would cause extinction. This approach runs counter to the ESA’s precautionary spirit and protective objectives. Judicial decisions have repeatedly affirmed that the purpose of designating critical habitat is to promote recovery, not merely to prevent extinction.

Furthermore, the proposed changes appear to give outsized influence to non-scientific stakeholders, including private businesses, by inviting economic “concerns” that do not meet the same standards of scientific evidence. This risks turning the exclusion process into a tool for regulated parties to override biological expertise—precisely the outcome Congress aimed to avoid when it removed economic factors from the species listing process.

I strongly encourage the Service to withdraw these proposed revisions and preserve a 4(b)(2) exclusion policy that keeps exclusions rare, firmly justified, and always subordinate to the biological needs of threatened and endangered species.

Dear Members of the Government,

I am submitting this comment as someone who cares deeply for biodiversity, healthy ecosystems, and protecting our future on our one true home planet. The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has always been a safeguard that works to protect species by centering around science and public interest, placing the values of biological need and scientific reality above outside pressures. It outweighs industrial considerations for protections that guarantee the safety of not only biodiversity but also our own well-being.

The proposed changes to narrow the criteria for critical habitats would be massively detrimental to wildlife species, ecosystem health, and the well-being of our societies. These changes could lead to widespread loss of biological function that can be critical for wildlife species and different environments to survive, and nearby human settlements would feel these effects in areas such as agricultural productivity loss and the spread of disease. These oversights could result in a loss of accountability for those responsible for environmental harm and public accountability for those who strongly support these protections for environmental and public safety. This is why I urge many of you to uphold the strong intent of the ESA: protecting biodiversity and ensuring that human society can have a future on a thriving, healthy planet.

title: Comment from Martin, Samantha

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Pearson, Nancy

text:
I strongly object to the proposed changes for listing endangered and threatened species and designated critical habitat. These proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act do not “clarify” the ESA.
Instead, they would essentially disable the statute from fulfilling the intentions of Congress,
intentions that have been well served by the agencies’ lawful enforcement of this act for over 50
years. They enhance the likelihood that threatened species will become extinct before they even
attained “endangered” status under the act; fail to protect endangered species from the fatal
consequences of past habitat destruction; permit fast-track approvals of destructive projects
without adequate consideration of their consequences for endangered and threatened species; and
erode the scientific foundations of this law, by prioritizing corporate finances over science in
decisions about species' survival. As we homogenize the habitats in which these plants and animals evolved, and as we
increase the pressure for products that they are in a position to supply (usually unwillingly),
we threaten their — and our own — genetic heritage. The value of this genetic heritage is,
quite literally, incalculable....
From the most narrow possible point of view, it is in the best interests of mankind to
minimize the losses of genetic variations. The reason is simple: they are potential resources.
They are keys to puzzles which we cannot solve, and may provide answers to questions
which we have not yet learned to ask.
To take a homely, but apt, example: one of the critical chemicals in the regulation of
ovulations in humans was found in a common plant. Once discovered, and analyzed,
humans could duplicate it synthetically, but had it never existed — or had it been driven out
of existence before we knew its potentialities — we would never have tried to synthesize it in
the first place.
Who knows, or can say, what potential cures for cancer or other scourges, present or future,
may lie locked up in the structures of plants which may yet be undiscovered, much less
analyzed? … Sheer self-interest impels us to be cautious. “Extinction is forever,” says Katherine Miller, Country Director for FOUR PAWS USA. “If we allow the ESA to be weakened and species’ habitats to be destroyed for profit, the consequences of these decisions will reverberate for generations. Science has shown that protecting a listed species’ habitat is vital to their survival and recovery. This is why I urge FWS and NMFS to withdraw their proposed rule and uphold America’s commitment to save endangered species, ensuring a livable planet for all of us.
title: Comment from Voss, Jean

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text: I DISAGREE WITH THIS PROPOSAL BECAUSE altering portions of Section 4 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) would have serious negative impacts on Gray Wolves. Under the proposed rule, these changes would make it easier to delist and harder to relist Gray Wolves, opening the door for increased vulnerability, more fragile populations, and inadequate recovery that is driven by political decisions rather than best available science. In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

title: Comment from Botchman, Tenley

text:
I am absolutely disgusted by the U.S. House’s decision to pass H.R. 845! This bill strips wolves gray wolves of federal protection by politics, not science, and block court review! This will silence one of the last checks meant to protect wildlife from reckless decisions! We already know what happens when wolves lose protections! Look at Wyoming, where extreme anti-wolf rhetoric and weak oversight have normalized cruelty and violence against wolves! Or take a glance at when 218 wolves were slaughtered in Wisconsin when protections were removed for a brief period! Congress is making decisions that will weaken the Endangered Species Act and put wolves back in the crosshairs! It is time to listen to the people and keep protections as they are!

This absurd behavior and reckless decisions won’t stop here either! I know that the reason we have to do these public comments, and tell you all basic common sense, is because there are plans to designate crucial land that endangered animals need to survive. The reason you want these habitats is for money, for the valuable resources that the area may contain. What you don’t know though is that when that land is gone, those animals will die out. If extinction wipes our keystone species, humans will eventually fall to the same fate. It is outrageous that businesses and corporations are set on making the most money, feeding their greed, but don’t realize that when we run out of these resources: we won’t be able to eat or drink money. Please realize that money has no value if we destroy all that we need to survive on this planet!

In terms of reviewing the endangered species list and designating which animals need to be on said list, I ask you: Why fix something that isn’t broken? The Endangered Species Act began in 1973, and since then has saved 291 species from extinction. The act has a 99% percent success rate and has saved millions of animals because of regulations that prevent their downfall! By protecting vulnerable wildlife with the Endangered Species Act, we also make progress in other areas of sustainability. Wildlife play an important role in the carbon cycle by capturing and storing carbon. But once we lose a species, we also lose its ability to contribute to the biodiversity of the area and keep heat-trapping carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere! The Endangered Species Act is key in addressing the challenges of climate change and biodiversity loss because it provides comprehensive protection for species and their habitats, has a science-based approach, includes citizen engagement and interagency cooperation, and requires the development of recovery plans and programs. It is essential that there aren’t ANY changes to the act, and that we maintain these beautiful creatures and their homes for future generations to enjoy and for their survival because if the animals go, then humans do as well. Don’t forget that.

Be careful of the change you create, because it is not always good. Our world, its climate, and its natural disasters are on a slippery slope already. If we tip the scale towards negative impacts, then humans won’t stand a chance. This decision doesn’t just affect your wallets, it affects your livelihoods as well. Please make the right decision and keep the Endangered Species Act protected, without any changes. Thank you for taking the time to listen to what I have to say, and I hope me saying this has led you to making the right decision.

title: Comment from Godfrey, Jennifer

text:
The ESA is one of if not the most important conservation laws in our country due to its function as a safety net against species extinction from human and environmental impacts. It is essential that additional efforts to prevent the need for federal listing in the first place be incorporated into any proposed regulations involving updates to the ESA. Central to this effort should be to highlight and strengthen the section 7(a) (1) requirements for federal agencies to implement and carry-out programs that promote the conservation of listed species, not just recover them.
I encourage the FWS to recognize and evaluate the numerous efforts that have occurred for at least the past 20 years to “streamline” consultation and other regulatory requirements of the ESA to make it more effective and user-friendly. The vast majority of the American public cares deeply about the conservation and recovery endangered species and the definitions and processes associated with the ESA currently work better than many recognize.
Currently, listing, delisting and reclassification relies on the long-standing foundation that the best scientific and commercial data available is used “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination.” The proposed rule would alter this remove the term “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination,” and therefore alter an essential pillar for species protection under the ESA. I strongly oppose this proposed change as it has the potential to impair the goals and intent of the ESA. Science-based evaluations must be maintained to gauge how well species are meeting the stated recovery criteria before being proposed for delisting. To alter any of this with political interference and/or perceived importance of economic considerations may significantly impact species listing processes or their recovery. I would argue that this proposal is not needed because there are already numerous ESA related tools available to address potential conflicts between human uses and species recovery.
Science-based evaluations involving appropriate critical habitat designations are essential to recovery of listed species. The ESA currently requires that critical habitat be designated to the “maximum extent prudent and determinable”. The proposed rule seeks to expand the circumstances under which critical habitat might not be designated. The proposed rule also states that exclusion analysis will be performed either when a proponent of such exclusion presents credible information in support of the request or when the Secretary exercises discretion over the matter. As a former ESA practitioner, I strongly oppose these proposed changes for the following reasons – first, project proponents already have ample opportunity to provide comment and evidence for or against proposals involving critical habitat designations through established processes for public input. This input often results in adjustments to the initial proposals put forth by FWS. There is no need to further dilute and extend the evaluation process with additional input that, frankly, could be easily biased and inaccurate rather than science based. There is also no need to have the Secretary weigh in on critical habitat if qualified professionals are free to do their job. I encourage FWS to evaluate this aspect of the proposed rule closely as it may very well prohibit recovery rather than promote it.
The current regulation for this determination states that “the foreseeable future extends as far into the future as the Services can make reasonably reliable predictions about the threats to the species and the species' responses to those threats.” The proposed change for this determination appears to be similar but notes that “the term foreseeable future extends only so far into the future as the Services can reasonably determine that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are likely.” I oppose this proposed change primarily because there is no need for it. In my experience the current term has worked well and the agencies understand it. The impact of cumulative effects can be very real, and evaluating the foreseeable future can already be a complicated undertaking and inexact science. Furthermore, cumulative effects evaluations can vary by activity or influence and promoting a “reasonably reliable prediction regarding threats and species responses” is the appropriate way to address it because determinations can be impossible to arrive at even with the best available science. This is an important distinction and the proposal will further complicate analysis and recovery efforts and likely result in some important future threats being disregarded because they really can’t be “determined” with any reliability. But they can be predicted based on models and other science-based information and professional knowledge.

title: Comment from Scarborough, Belinda

text:
I write to oppose the the amendment of section 4(b)(2) to the Endangered Species Act of 1973 as amended.

I am particularly concerned that the amendment of this section allows: “…Secretary would exercise the broad discretion given under section 4(b)(2) by establishing as a principle that the FWS will exclude areas whenever it determines that the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, as long as exclusion will not result in the extinction of the species.”

There are no guarantees in this amendment that the Secretary’s discretion must continue protection for imperiled species (threatened or endangered species). Further, there is no explicit stipulations that, if this amendment goes through, that the Secretary will clearly take into account keys aspects of the species’s natural history, such as life history including trends in species recovery, critical population sizes, behavior, generation time, temporal use of critical habitat, and essential resources. (This is a non-exhaustive list officers that likely are relevant).

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from S, Justin

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Please do not jeopardize Florida’s rich natural and cultural resources for future generations.

Sincerely,

Ryan Horvath

title: Comment from Klawitter, Emily

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Selvaggio, Raffaella

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the ESA’s 4(b)(2) exclusion rules. While the ESA allows the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat if the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress made it clear that this should only happen in narrow cases where exclusion won’t push a species to extinction. The new rule wrongly puts economic concerns ahead of the biological needs of species, and even worse, it forces the agency to prioritize economic impacts—even when those impacts are uncertain or secondary.

The proposed rule also sets an unfairly high bar for keeping habitat designated, by requiring proof that excluding it would directly lead to extinction. This flips the ESA’s focus, which has always been on protecting species and supporting recovery, not just preventing extinction.

Additionally, the rule seems to give too much weight to economic interests, like private industry, by allowing them to submit “concerns” without requiring solid scientific evidence. This could turn the exclusion process into a tool for industries to push aside scientific facts, which is exactly what Congress wanted to avoid when it removed economic factors from the listing process.

I urge the Service to scrap these changes and stick with a 4(b)(2) framework that keeps exclusions rare, fully justified, and focused on the biological needs of species.
title: Comment from Saul, Leif

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:
Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.
Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.
Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.
Respectfully submitted,

text:
Public Comment Opposing Proposed Changes to the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule (ESA Section 4(b)(2))

My name is Ron Goodwin, and I am submitting this comment to oppose the proposed changes to the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule under Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act. This comment should be considered together with my prior submissions opposing the proposed elimination of the threatened species blanket 4(d) rule and the proposed changes to the Listing and Critical Habitat Rules (50 CFR part 424). Taken as a whole, these rulemakings represent a coordinated weakening of the ESA’s core conservation safeguards.

The 2020 exclusion rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations above the biological needs of imperiled species. Reinstating this approach contradicts the fundamental purpose of the ESA: to conserve ecosystems and recover species—not to reduce protections for the convenience or profitability of industry and special interests. The Act does not exist to maximize short-term economic gains; it exists to prevent extinction and promote recovery using science-based decision-making.

Exclusions of critical habitat must be grounded in clear, demonstrable scientific evidence. Allowing speculative or exaggerated economic concerns to justify exclusions invites undue political pressure and shifts the balance away from conservation. As I noted in my previous comments, weakening science-based standards—whether in listing decisions, habitat designations, or threatened species protections—undermines the integrity and effectiveness of the ESA.

Habitat loss remains the primary driver of extinction in the United States and globally. Any regulatory change that weakens critical habitat protections directly harms species’ recovery prospects. When combined with the rollback of the blanket 4(d) rule and constraints on habitat designation under Part 424, expanded exclusions would create compounding gaps that favor development interests at the expense of wildlife and wild places.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt an even stronger, science-forward framework that clearly prioritizes ecological necessity over economic lobbying. Protecting wildlife and the wild areas they depend on must take precedence over fattening the pockets of industry and special interests.

Consistent with my prior public comments, I urge the Service to reject these proposed changes and reaffirm its commitment to the Endangered Species Act’s conservation mission.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,
Ron Goodwin

title: Comment from Duarte , Cynthia

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
