text:
The State of Utah (“State”), through the Utah Public Lands Policy Coordinating Office (“PLPCO”) and in coordination with the Utah Department of Wildlife Resources (“DWR”), has reviewed the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (referred to herein as the “Service”) Proposed Rule titled Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat (“Proposed Rule”). Under State law, the DWR has jurisdictional authority and public trust responsibilities for the management of state fish and wildlife resources within the State, Utah Code Ann. § 23-14-1. The State, through the DWR, works closely with the Service to coordinate management efforts for federally listed threatened and endangered species throughout the State, while also striving to delist recovered species and avoid the future listing of state-managed species under the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”).

The State generally supports the Proposed Rule because it provides structure for when and how the Service analyzes the exclusion of critical habitat and increases the clarity and certainty in the critical habitat designation process. The State provides the following specific comments based on statutory authorities, public trust responsibilities, and special expertise related to wildlife resources, recreation, social, and political considerations.

Regulations for designating critical habitat

The Proposed Rule seeks to amend portions of the Service’s regulations for Section 4 of the ESA. Specifically, Section 4(b)(2) requires consideration of the economic impact, the impact on national security, and any other relevant impact of designating any particular area as critical habitat; and authorizes the exclusion of areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating it as critical habitat, so long as excluding will not result in the extinction of the species. The Proposed Rule would provide structure and clarity for when and how the Service conducts this analysis.

First, the State generally supports the effort to provide structure and clarity to this process. The rules governing critical habitat designations often have significant impacts on local economies. It is therefore imperative for the Service to solicit and consider local information. Structuring this involvement will ensure the best available information informs critical habitat designations.

Second, the State appreciates and supports the Service’s recognition of conservation agreements and plans permitted under Section 10 of the ESA. These agreements often provide tremendous conservation benefits for species while allowing management flexibility to account for local conditions. As noted in the Proposed Rule, one benefit of excluding an area from critical habitat can be “the unhindered, continued ability to maintain existing partnerships, as well as the opportunity to seek new partnerships with potential [conservation] plan participants, including States, counties, local jurisdictions, conservation organizations, and private landowners,” who, together, “can implement conservation actions that the FWS would be unable to accomplish without their participation.” See 90 Fed. Reg. at 52,596. The State strongly supports the Service’s recognition of these benefits and seeks continued coordination with State and local governments and stakeholders in the development and evaluation of critical habitat designations.

Thank you for considering the State’s comments on the Service’s proposal to amend portions of regulations for section 4 of the Endangered Species Act. The State looks forward to working with the Service to improve wildlife and endangered species management and practices in the State and Nation.

Please contact me to discuss any questions or concerns.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me—not only as a citizen, but as someone who has always felt a strong connection to nature and all the animals we share this planet with. I believe deeply that the health of wildlife and ecosystems is inseparable from our own well-being. There is a balance between nature and humanity; without healthy environments, we cannot expect healthy communities or futures.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest, not political pressure or short-term economic influence. Science can tell us what species need to survive; our values determine whether we choose to protect them. The proposed rule changes move decision-making away from both science and shared public responsibility.

Allowing industry considerations to outweigh biological need and scientific reality undermines the very purpose of the ESA. In particular, the proposed changes to the Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)) would narrow the criteria for excluding critical habitat, allowing economic interests to override essential habitat protections. When economic considerations are given more weight than the protection of critical habitat, entire ecosystems—not just individual wildlife species—are placed at risk, threatening the ecological balance that sustains us all.

These rollbacks also reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections. A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful public review, not weakened safeguards.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the Endangered Species Act’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, rather than weaken, federal safeguards so that states and industry cannot sidestep their responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.

I ask you to uphold the original intent of the ESA: to prevent extinction and ensure that future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems—where wildlife, natural habitats, and people can all continue to exist in balance.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
Stacy Bos

title: Comment from Neuman, Larry

text:
Dear Secretaries Burgum and Lutnik
I write as a citizen, gravely concerned about the future of livability on Earth, to oppose the proposed rule to amend the Endangered Species Act’s (“ESA”) section 4 implementing regulations (“the 2025 Proposed Rule”).
We live in a complex web of interrelationships. Biodiversity is what sustains that web and, necessarily, us. Yet biodiversity is in crisis. We are living through what has been called the Sixth Great Extinction: approximately one million species are currently at risk of extinction, and as populations of wild species decline, crucial ecosystems are at risk of collapse.
The ESA stands as a powerful protection against this process. Congress passed the ESA 50 years ago to prevent extinction, recover imperiled species, and protect the habitats and ecosystems in which they live. The ESA’s current framework allows for efficient, flexible, science-informed decision making. And it has a strong track record: about 99% of U.S. species listed under the ESA—including some of America’s most iconic species, like the bald eagle—are still with us, and hundreds of those species are recovering their vitality. Also, importantly, the ESA’s protections have slowed the loss of habitat for imperiled species on federal lands.
Now is the time to strengthen the ESA, but the recently proposed rules go in exactly the wrong direction. If finalized, the proposed revisions would:
•Curtail the designation of critical habitat and weaken the listing process for imperiled species, narrowing the definition of “foreseeable future”;
•By removing the so-called “blanket rule” they would make it more difficult to extend protections to “threatened” species (i.e., before they are technically “imperiled”), which would delay lifesaving action until a species' population is so small it may be challenging to save;
•Allow economic interests to block habitat protections. This is specifically prohibited by the ESA, which unambiguously requires that listing and delisting determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available.” 16 U.S.C. §1533(b)(1)(A); and
•Weaken the interagency consultation process designed to prevent harm to endangered species and their habitats from the activities of federal agencies.

These proposed changes aren’t simply modified implementations of the ESA; they undercut its original Congressional intent. Taken together, the proposed regulations if finalized would prioritize green-lighting destructive projects over protecting species that are at risk of extinction. They would make it easier for federal agencies to approve roads, pipelines, mines, and logging projects without fully assessing their impact on threatened and endangered species or their habitats. Additionally, the proposed regulations would allow economic interests to influence decisions about which species and critical habitats warrant federal protection.
Recent decisions of the Supreme Court do not change the bedrock principals of the Administrative Procedure Act. Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), affirmed that it is ultimately the province of the courts to determine the meaning of a statute and to ensure that agency interpretations of statutory text conform to the best meaning. It does not clear the way or require that agencies embark on new regulatory revisions of the statute. Any ESA-implementing regulation must conform to Congress’ original intent that the Services list species and designate critical habitat in accordance with the ESA’s requirements, that they conserve and recover listed species, and that they establish procedures for federal agencies to ensure that agency actions don’t jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify their designated critical habitat. 16 U.S.C. § §1531(b), 1532(3), 1536(a)(2).
Preserving a robust ESA is not just about a moral imperative to protect life: Weakening the ESA recklessly endangers all of us. Forests protected under the Act crucially absorb carbon dioxide and transfer it to fungi for storage in the soil. Wetlands don’t just provide safe havens for countless species: they act as buffers during storm surges and against rising sea levels.
Decades of polling have shown strong bipartisan support for the ESA with approximately 84% of Americans supporting it. That includes me, and that’s why I oppose these damaging rollbacks and urge the Trump administration to withdraw these proposals. We must prioritize our cherished wildlife and work to strengthen, not weaken, our nation’s best tool for helping to prevent extinction and putting species on the road to recovery.
title: Comment from Mascioli, William

text:
I, Amie Dodd, strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Please don't cause more harm than has already been done! Please don't make these changes!!!

Thank you.

title: Comment from Canay, Ashley

text:
As a citizen of the United States, I take tremendous pride in our unique, awe-inspiring native wildlife species. My home would not be the same without the calls of the golden-cheeked warbler (Setophaga chrysoparia, listed Endangered) ringing out, or the blooms of the bracted twistflower (Streptanthus bracteatus, listed Threatened) dotting the landscape. These species are an integral part of my state and national identity, both for me and many others. Additionally, I hold a Bachelor’s of Science in Biology and a Master’s of Science in Wildlife Biology. I am deeply familiar with the species, ecosystems, and human communities which are affected by the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act is a critical piece of legislation that has a proven track record of success for ensuring the protection of these species both for current citizens of the U.S. and for posterity, having prevented an estimated 291 species’ extinction and saved an estimated 99% of listed species (Greenwald et al. 2019 “Extinction and the U.S. Endangered Species Act”). The success of the Endangered Species Act has been seen in population recoveries of the red-cockaded woodpecker (Dryobates borealis, downlisted to Threatened in 2024) and the Kirtland’s warbler (Setophaga kirtlandii, delisted in 2019), and this Act is recognized internationally as a premier example of effective biodiversity conservation legislation.

I am commenting in regards to the proposed changes to Section 4(b)(2) as outlined in FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048. I strongly oppose these changes and I ask the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to NOT enact these changes.

Designating critical habitat has been shown to be a crucial aspect contributing to the Endangered Species Act’s success (see Martin et al. 2005 “The Effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act: A Quantitative Analysis”). This is because habitat loss is one of the most common causes of population decline, and protecting habitat is therefore one of the most effective methods to protect and recover species. The science and information about a species itself should be the only factors allowed in designating what habitat is necessary for a species survival. Allowing for explicit consideration of economic factors in excluding areas of critical habitat is not aligned with best practices for effective species conservation and goes against the goals of population recovery. Additionally, allowing for the entry of nonbiological knowledge into decisions around critical habitat opens the door for undue influence by profit-driven entities that, unlike the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, do not have the good of the species or the American people at heart. Changing the interpretation of critical habitat in the ways proposed would lead to irreversible habitat loss and ultimately, the decline of these species.

In summary, the proposed changes would hinder the Endangered Species Act’s proven effectiveness and lead to population declines of our beloved native species. Keep the Endangered Species Act strong and keep the tools to protect nature in the hands of the communities who live among and care for these rare, native species.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Congress designed the ESA to err on the side of preventing irreversible harm. These proposed changes move in the opposite direction and are inconsistent with the statute’s purpose, scientific consensus, and public interest.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw these proposals in full and maintain robust, science-driven ESA regulations that prioritize species recovery and habitat protection.

Weakening ESA protections is particularly dangerous in fast-growing states like Florida, where development pressure already outpaces conservation and recovery efforts

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Bucher, Jeannine

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from D, Jennifer

text:
I am a conservation ecologist, and I am writing to express concern about the proposed revisions to the regulations governing how critical habitat exclusions are evaluated under Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act.

Critical habitat is one of the most important tools the ESA provides—not just to prevent extinction, but to support recovery. Identifying and protecting the areas that species depend on throughout their life cycles helps guide federal decision-making, reduces conflict over time, and creates clarity about what species need to persist. Weakening this tool has real consequences for species already under significant pressure.

While the ESA allows the Service to consider economic and other impacts when designating critical habitat, it also sets a clear standard: areas should only be excluded when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, and when exclusion will not increase extinction risk. The proposed rule appears to expand and formalize exclusion analyses in ways that could make it easier to leave out biologically important habitat, even when that habitat is essential for long-term conservation.

From an ecological perspective, this is deeply concerning. Many species rely on habitats that are not consistently occupied, are used only during certain life stages, or may become increasingly important as conditions change. These realities are well documented across taxa and ecosystems. Excluding such areas based on short-term or speculative considerations does not reflect how species actually survive and recover.

I am also concerned that this proposal further shifts the balance of critical habitat decisions toward non-biological factors. Congress was explicit that the ESA’s purpose is to conserve species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. When economic or other considerations are allowed to outweigh sound biological judgment, the result is often delayed action, fragmented habitat protection, and increased risk to already vulnerable species.

At a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating and environmental conditions are changing rapidly, we need regulatory approaches that strengthen the role of science in conservation decisions, not weaken it or remove it entirely. This proposal moves in the opposite direction.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to revise or withdraw the proposed rule and to ensure that critical habitat designations remain firmly grounded in biological need and the best available science.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Montes , Karen

text:
My name is Brandi Griffin. I have lived and worked in Georgia and Florida my whole life, and I am proud to be from a region with extraordinary biological diversity. I grew up alongside wild lands and endangered species, and I have seen firsthand that the Endangered Species Act (ESA) works.
I am now an ecologist, and my work includes supporting the conservation of protected plants such as the federally listed Schwalbea americana. Over my lifetime, I have also witnessed the number of bald eagles in Georgia increase from 2 mating pairs to hundreds an example of how strong protections, combined with habitat conservation and improved environmental conditions, can bring species back from the brink. I have also witnessed the rampant development of Florida and the devastation that has cause to native species endangered and common alike.
For these reasons, I am deeply concerned about proposals that would weaken ESA provisions that support recovery by protecting the habitat species depend on. The science is clear: habitat loss and land use change are among the leading drivers of species declines because they disrupt life histories, reproduction, and the ecological relationships species need to persist. If automatic protections are reduced or delayed after a species is listed, we risk losing populations and irreplaceable genetic diversity during the critical period before recovery planning is completed.
I urge the government to keep these rules in place and to ensure that any changes to ESA implementation are preceded by a scientifically rigorous, transparent review that fully evaluates ecological consequences. If we prioritize short-term economic considerations over ecological integrity, we risk losing entire ecosystems, not just individual species.
Please withdraw these proposed rule changes and continue to support science-based protections that have repeatedly proven effective in preventing extinctions and promoting recovery.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Sincerely,
Brandi Griffin

text: When Teddy Roosevelt was a young man he had a dream about what the American West would be based on stories. He was greatly disappointed to find that what he had dreamed of was not what he got when he finally went West. He discovered that the Bison had dwindled due to unchecked hunting by men who came before him - and all the wildlife he wanted to see had suffered for it. This was the start of a turning point for him in terms of conservation. If I recall correctly, all of this occurred in part due to the expansion of the railroads. I understand that we as humans will always be "progressing" forward - but I don't agree that we should do that at the cost of habitat to the other species of this world. We likely will never get back what we destroy in haste toward "progress". And while many try to convince me that we need more in order to survive, or be safe, or something to do with the economy - I don't believe that's true. I think the most dangerous thing we can do to ourselves as a species is to destroy the natural world around us. And someone somewhere might think to themselves "I don't need this or that creature or plant in the world. It will be fine if it's gone". But that person clearly doesn't understand the importance of ecosystems and how they affect their own personal existence. Honestly, I'm less concerned about the humans of this world - and more concerned about the rest of the species on this planet. We need to protect critical habitats for them without question. But I will always appeal to the human need to survive - and as a species we would be lost without a natural world. We haven't quiet figured that out yet - and I fear the day we do discover it - because it will probably be too late for us and the rest of the species of this planet when we do learn that lesson finally.

title: Comment from Litton, Alison

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

As an environmental scientist who has helped write a 5 Year Review for the ESA, I care deeply about science-informed policy and stewardship of the wildlife in this country. The ESA is still taught as a triumph of science-backed legislation, and was lauded internationally as a groundbreaking framework with bipartisan support at the time of its enactment. The proposed changes greatly undermine the ESA, and undermine the protections that species depend upon to survive. The proposed rules shift decision making away from scientists with the expertise to make informed decisions, and prioritizes industry considerations instead. Make no mistake, this will lead to extinctions which, it seems worth saying explicitly, are irreversible.

The Endangered Species Act is not meant to center political or economic interest, but instead uplift the public interest. We as a people decided to value our wildlife, for ourselves and future generations, and most Americans still strongly support strong environmental conservation protections. As a Georgia resident, I’ve seen the peoples’ environmental support first-hand in protecting the Okefenokee Swamp, and I know this is not an isolated sentiment.

Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions threatens the health of entire ecosystems. The point of the ESA is to prioritize public interest over economic interest, and this proposal would let economic interests override any other considerations. These species need the fullest protections we can provide in order to continue to exist. I urge you to uphold the intent of ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations benefit from healthy ecosystems. Do not weaken one of the United States’ best examples of bipartisan protection for our wildlife. I ask the agency to withdraw these proposed rules to maintain strong, science-based protections for endangered species.
title: Comment from McCrum, Kelly

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life. This has been a long-fought protection of precious life and life cycles that are essential to our understanding of environment and balance of nature. Commerce can be entered but only with the knowledge of its affect and effect on heritage. This is not a sentimental wish but one of science and common sense.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I have made it my career and life goal to do my part in conservation efforts and exploring the balance of anthropomorphic infrastructure and preservation of our natural world. Therefore, I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

Until there is an way for human expansion without further destruction and risk of extinction the most we can do is make sure what habitat and populations these species have left are protected. I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As someone who lives on the East Coast and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.
The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed. Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide. My specific concerns are detailed below:
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.

If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests.
These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.
I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections.
Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

We should be working to strengthen the ESA. However, the recently proposed rules do the opposite.If finalized, those revisions would:

I also oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0044) concerning interagency cooperation under Section 7 of the ESA. Weakening the consultation process between federal agencies would allow actions that harm listed species and critical habitat to proceed without adequate review. Section 7 consultation is one of the most effective tools for preventing irreversible damage and ensuring that federal actions do not push species closer to extinction. These changes would undermine a framework that has protected hundreds of species for decades.
—
I object to the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0029) that would eliminate the longstanding “blanket” protections for threatened species under Section 4(d) and replace them with case-by-case regulations. This approach would create dangerous gaps in protection for newly listed species and delay conservation actions at a critical time. The ESA’s success depends on early, consistent protections, and removing them increases the risk of further decline before recovery measures are implemented.
—
Finally, I strongly oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0048) regarding exclusions from critical habitat designations under Section 4(b)(2). Allowing economic or other non-conservation factors to outweigh the survival needs of species contradicts the ESA’s recovery mission. Critical habitat protections are essential to preventing extinction and supporting species recovery, and weakening them would reverse decades of conservation progress.u
For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act’s science-based mandate to prevent extinction and promote recovery.
Thank you for your consideration and for protecting vulnerable wildlife and the ecosystems on which they depend.

title: Comment from Collins, Elizabeth

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I am submitting this comment to oppose the proposed rollbacks to protections under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws in U.S. history and has prevented the extinction of hundreds of species by requiring decisions to be based on the best available science. Weakening these protections undermines the core purpose of the Act and disregards decades of scientific evidence demonstrating the importance of strong, enforceable safeguards for threatened and endangered species.

These proposed changes would increase the risk of extinction for vulnerable species by limiting habitat protections and weakening interagency responsibilities. Healthy ecosystems are essential not only for wildlife, but also for clean water, food security, climate resilience, and community well-being. The loss of biodiversity has long-term consequences that cannot be reversed.

At a time of accelerating climate change and habitat loss, the federal government should be strengthening, not weakening, protections for imperiled species. Economic or political considerations must not override scientific findings or the legal mandate of the ESA.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rollbacks and to uphold the full protections of the Endangered Species Act in accordance with its original intent and the best available science.

title: Comment from Bailey, Ann

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text:
We must retain Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) as currently written to protect the habitats threatened and endangered species require to survive now and into the future. Habitat protection is essential for ensuring the survival of every species, and how the government designates habitats has a direct impact on the ability of a species to recover and thrive.
Currently Section 4(b)(2) focuses on what the “threatened” or “endangered” species requires to thrive, not just the few individuals present now but also the habitat required for the population to grow enough to stabilize. Specifically, critical habitat is not just space, it includes all of the elements necessary for that species such as food sources, symbiotic relationships with other species, hazard free environment, etc. The rule change seeks to shift the focus away from the needs of “threatened” or “endangered” species to the desires of potential exploiters. This is a shameful attempt to shift policy away from habitat protections that are so desperately needed.
The proposed changes include a very specific change in language from “may exclude” to “shall exclude” that will deny situational discretion. The list of reasons for excluding an area’s potential to be identified as “critical habitat” will be extended to include vague categories such as economic impact, to which “shall” will be applied. It is clear these changes are intended to give broad leeway to those who put profit over environmental stewardship.
Species must have critical habitat to survive. We have to be their voice, when they have none. Designating critical habitat under the current Section 4(b)(2) is already a challenging process, but the proposed changes would nearly eliminate all possibility of critical habitat protection.
Please, do not make the proposed changes to Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act.

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. Nature, wilderness, and wild species are a defining part of what makes the United States such a remarkable place to live. These landscapes are not just scenic backdrops—they are living systems that support our physical health, emotional well-being, local economies, and cultural identity. When we protect wildlife and intact habitats, we are protecting something fundamental about who we are as a nation.

Humans are not separate from nature; we are part of it. Science is clear that healthy, diverse ecosystems provide clean water, stable soils, pollination, climate resilience, and countless other benefits that communities rely on every day. Just as importantly, access to thriving natural places supports mental health and quality of life. When species decline and ecosystems are fragmented, the impacts ripple outward, ultimately affecting people as well as wildlife.

The Endangered Species Act works because it is grounded in science and the public interest, not short-term political or economic pressure. Species play essential roles in maintaining the balance and function of ecosystems, and protecting them is often key to protecting the habitats that sustain many other forms of life. Weakening core provisions of the ESA—such as protections for threatened species, critical habitat, and federal consultation—risks delaying recovery and allowing preventable harm to occur before science can guide effective action.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule, which would reinstate the 2020 exclusion framework and make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat designations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Critical habitat designation is often the only mechanism that ensures species retain the physical and biological features essential for recovery. For many imperiled species, particularly those facing habitat loss, fragmentation, and climate-driven stressors, these designations are not redundant protections—-they are foundational. Weakening them directly undermines the ESA’s recovery mandate.

Reinstating the 2020 exclusion rule would shift decision-making away from science and conservation need and toward short-term economic and political pressure. By expanding the circumstances under which areas may be excluded, this rule would make it easier for industry interests to influence the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to remove habitat critical for species survival and recovery, even when exclusion increases extinction risk.

This approach contradicts the intent of the ESA, which prioritizes the conservation of ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend. Economic impacts are already considered through existing consultation and implementation processes. Elevating economic considerations at the exclusion stage disproportionately weakens habitat protections and creates an imbalance that favors development over biodiversity conservation.

The practical effects of this rule would be severe. It would reduce the size, connectivity, and effectiveness of critical habitat designations, leading to increased habitat fragmentation. Fragmentation is a well-established driver of species decline and directly undermines recovery planning by isolating populations, limiting dispersal, and reducing resilience to climate change, disease, and other cumulative threats.

Recovery requires intact, connected, and functional habitats—often across broad landscapes and sometimes in areas not currently occupied by the species. Making exclusions easier compromises the long-term viability of species and increases the likelihood that emergency listings and costly interventions will be needed later.

Bringing back the 2020 exclusion rule would erode public trust in the scientific integrity of the ESA, increase litigation risk, and weaken one of the most effective conservation tools available. Once critical habitat is excluded and degraded, it may never be restored, permanently foreclosing recovery options.

I urge the agency to reject this proposed rule and maintain a science-based, precautionary approach to critical habitat designation that prioritizes species recovery and ecosystem integrity over short-term economic interests.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering the long-term consequences of this proposal for wildlife, ecosystems, and future generations.

Comment on Blanket 4(d) Rule Removal (2025-20552)
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
As a born and raised Texan, I feel very protective of our country's natural spaces and the creatures that live in them. We have a shared fondness for our deer, fowl, and fish, certainly, but also the creatures big and small that have lived here as long as we have, if not longer. Part of good environmental stewardship is understanding that ecosystems are complex and intricately woven. To that end we should take the preservation of each of its component parts very seriously. Experience has shown us, both in our own country and across the world, that loss of even just a few keystone species can cause a cascade of environmental damage that is much harder to fix than it is to prevent. We must be proactive, we must be cautious, we must be zealous in maintaining our natural spaces.
The Endangered Species Act, environmental protection policies broadly, are expressly premised on the notion that our natural resources are an innate good and of an innate value that is worth preserving so that future generations may all have a chance to experience the unique grandeur and bounty of America's wilderness. This premise is directly undercut by such proposals among these 4 bills like allowing for the consideration of economic costs or benefits when determining listing status or protections for potentially Endangered or Threatened species. If such considerations are to be allowed we then resign ourselves to the inevitability of losing our natural spaces as the projected cost of leaving land undeveloped, resources unextracted, becomes greater and greater.
Other sections claim changes for clarity, or to put more specific bounds on terms like "foreseeable future." Others seemingly seek to allow greater autonomy among states in presiding over the protection of their own ecosystems and species. In principle I don't disagree, but in my estimation these are not arguments made in good faith, but rather nicely painted words that intend to obfuscate a desire to side-step federal protections and, again, undermine the efficacy of the Endangered Species Act.
To my eyes, all 4 of these bills disagree with the foundational premise of Environmental Protection as a legal concept, as stated before: the natural bounty of America is inherently valuable to the degree that it should be preserved indefinitely for each subsequent generation. To loosen and "clarify" sections of the relevant rules as in these proposals, to me, shows a willingness to instead consume more than our fair share of our country as it becomes convenient to do so, leaving less to use and less to experience for those who come after us. I personally find this unacceptable and contemptible.
I strongly urge all 4 proposals be rejected.
