If economic analysis is allowed, it must be optional and never influence determinations.
I also oppose reinstating the 2019 definition of “foreseeable future,” which emphasizes “determining” rather than “predicting.” Predictive models, including climate and habitat projections, are essential tools and must remain part of best available science.

For delisting, objective, measurable criteria must remain flexible and species-specific. Language changes that imply error in original listings or restrict consideration of future habitat needs undermine recovery.

Critical habitat designations are vital for species survival. The proposed “not-prudent” framework lacks clarity and risks becoming a broad exemption. Unoccupied habitat must remain part of recovery planning, especially under climate-driven range shifts. Imposing higher evidentiary standards for unoccupied areas ignores ecological realities and detection challenges, limiting conservation tools.

Thank you for considering these comments. I urge the Services to retain the 2024 rule and reject changes that weaken ESA protections.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed regulatory revisions concerning critical habitat designation under section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The proposed rule would revise how the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) determines when and how areas can be excluded from critical habitat by weighing economic and other impacts.

I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change. The revisions, as written, would shift emphasis toward prioritizing resource development and other special interests over scientifically necessary species protections — a direction that is fundamentally inconsistent with the clear conservation goals of the ESA.

Critical habitat designation is a science-based conservation tool. Critical habitat identifies specific areas that contain physical or biological features essential to the conservation of a species and which may require special management or protection. It guides federal agencies in ensuring their actions do not “destroy or adversely modify” habitat that species need to survive and recover.

Habitat loss and degradation are among the primary drivers of species extinction. Across terrestrial and marine ecosystems, habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the most widespread threats to biodiversity, making habitat protection indispensable for recovery. Scientific evaluations show that species with designated critical habitat are more than twice as likely to exhibit population improvements than species lacking such protections.

Weakening the criteria for designation and creating broader avenues to exclude areas from critical habitat — especially where economic considerations outweigh ecological needs — will erode key safeguards that help prevent further declines in imperiled plants and animals. Habitat protections based on robust science are essential because many imperiled species already occupy only small fractions of their historical ranges, and unoccupied but ecologically suitable habitats are crucial for supporting resilient populations and facilitating adaptation to environmental change.

Furthermore, decisions about critical habitat should not be driven by short-term economic interests or special interests when the best available science demonstrates that certain areas are essential for conservation. The ESA was designed to conserve the ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend, not to subordinate those conservation needs to competing non-ecological priorities.

In summary, weakening the critical habitat designation process undermines the scientific foundation of species recovery, reduces protections for areas essential to survival and recovery, and would ultimately make it easier to exclude key habitats to avoid mitigation for harmful activities. Habitat protection remains one of the linchpins of effective species recovery, and it must be based on science — not on privileging resource development or special interests. For these reasons, I strongly urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change.

title: Comment from Standish, Adelina

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species. We, The People, disapprove of your efforts to weaken the ESA.

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act’s Section 4(b)(2) critical habitat exclusion framework. My perspective is informed by hands-on experience in animal science, wildlife rehabilitation, field research, and rescue work, where the availability and integrity of habitat directly determines whether species decline, persist, or recover.

While the ESA allows for limited habitat exclusions, Congress clearly intended this authority to be narrow and subordinate to species conservation. In practice, I have seen that habitat loss is one of the most consistent drivers of injury, displacement, and population decline in wildlife. Elevating economic considerations above biological need reverses the ESA’s precautionary and recovery-focused purpose.

The proposed rule sets an unlawfully high bar for retaining critical habitat by requiring proof that exclusion would cause extinction, rather than evaluating if habitat is needed for survival or recovery. From both a scientific and practical standpoint, this framework ignores how species actually respond to environmental pressure. Wildlife rarely collapses abruptly; declines occur gradually as habitat quality is eroded over time, most beyond the point where recovery is possible.

By encouraging speculative economic claims without requiring comparable scientific rigor, the proposal risks allowing short-term economic interests to override well-established biological evidence. In research/rehabilitation contexts, decisions unsupported by ecological data result in increased mortality, reduced reproductive success, and long-term population instability.

Based on my experience working directly with wildlife and using conservation science in real-world settings, I believe these revisions would substantially weaken the ESA’s protective function. Critical habitat is not a theoretical designation, it is a safeguard that determines whether species have a future. I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and retain a framework that prioritizes science, habitat protection, and species recovery as Congress intended.

Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am strongly against the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework, which is Congress's intention.

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

Furthermore, the rule creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am a biologist with over 40 years of global field experience on mammals including endangered species for which I bear witness to the human destruction of the natural world that surpasses levels of past mass extinction events. The proposed changes to the ESA are clearly meant to take us back to a time when far less knowledge and understanding of how critical biodiversity losses are occurring. The United Nations Intergovernmental Science Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services 2019 report states that one million of the Earth’s 8 million species are threatened with extinction. This is being caused by direct and indirect destruction of the natural world by out-of-control human populations and over-consumption. Indeed, human existence on Earth has reached a pinnacle of influence. We have manipulated the natural world to be barely recognizable as a functional living planet. Scientists recently calculated that humans and our domesticated fur-bearers compose 96% of global mammal biomass (dry weight), with only 4% accounting for wildlife that is disappearing at accelerating rates.
The U.S. Agricultural Department alone in 2017 killed 357 gray wolves; 69,041 adult coyotes, plus an unknown number of coyote pups in 393 destroyed dens; 624,845 red-winged blackbirds; 552 black bears; 319 mountain lions; 1,000 bobcats; 675 river otters, including 587 killed “unintentionally”; 3,827 foxes, plus an unknown number of fox pups in 128 dens; and 23,646 beavers. Bird collisions with skyscrapers cause 100 million to 1 billion bird deaths in the US each year. Hunters kill 200 million game animals and vehicles collisions kill another 400 million per annum. Due to human pollution and spraying of pesticides insect populations have plummeted 75% in some areas.
Globally humans kill 51 billion sea animals and 8.3 billion land animals for food annually. In addition, the number of animals killed by deforestation, mining, pollution, by-catch and other means is incalculable. Recent studies predict collapse of some tropical rain forest ecosystems within the next few years. These areas hold 56% of all biodiversity and generate global climates that support all life but are being destroyed at record rates. Seventy-five percent of Amazonian rain forest loss is due to destructive forest clearing for cattle grazing. The meat industry alone emits more global warming gases than the entire transportation sector, including every car, bus, truck, airplane, motorcycle and train on Earth combined.
We are currently in a Sixth Mass Extinction, as humans have decimated wildlife populations on average by 60% in just 40 years. In the time it took me to write this, 230,000 more humans have been added to the already overburdened planet. According to the Global Footprint Network, in 2017 humans began consuming more than the Earth can physically produce. A study by MIT scientists looking at human consumptive trends and population growth have predicted both industrial and ecological collapse around the year 2030, reducing human populations from 7.4 billion to just 500 million globally. Although it is anticipated the Earth will survive the Sixth Mass Extinction as it has all others, will this include humans? With the previous five mass extinctions the extermination pace occurred over thousands to millions of years, but the Sixth Mass Extinction is happening between 1,000 and 10,000 times faster. Thus, we are in uncharted territory as to how devastating this accelerated extermination will be and what the aftermath will hold.
With the massive increases in human populations, we are driving many of the other 10 million species to extinction at accelerating rate. Common sense and logic dictates that the more people using resources the tighter the regulations are required to prevent catastrophic breakdown of natural systems. I would strongly suggest that each one making these decisions read the 1968 essay entitled Tragedy of the Commons by Garret Hardin. The rolling back of the ESA is foolhardy and not based on the scientific literature or reality of what is occurring in the natural world on which we all depend on for survival.

title: Comment from Kellogg, Anastasia

text:
Hills For Everyone (HFE) writes to oppose the proposed change to section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act would make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat designations based on economic and other nonbiological factors, and therefore is harmful to biodiversity across the nation. By reinstating and strengthening the 2020 exclusions framework, the rule shifts the balance away from conserving “the ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend” and toward avoiding perceived regulatory burdens on development, including energy and infrastructure projects prioritized in recent executive orders. This change elevates short‑term economic and political considerations over the long‑term ecological integrity this landscape requires.

First, broadening and formalizing the circumstances under which the Service will conduct exclusion analyses—and establishing a principle that areas will be excluded whenever the benefits of exclusion are found to outweigh the benefits of inclusion, so long as extinction is avoided—effectively lowers the standard for maintaining critical habitat on the ground. Critical habitat is already narrowly defined and often under‑designated relative to species’ full ecological needs; carving out additional areas for economic, national security, or other “relevant” impacts will further fragment the habitat base needed for recovery, particularly in regions like the Puente–Chino Hills where remaining natural areas are limited, highly connected, and irreplaceable. Treating extinction as the only hard backstop ignores the ESA’s core purpose of recovery and invites incremental degradation that pushes species toward chronic jeopardy without technically crossing an extinction threshold.

Second, the proposal explicitly encourages consideration of exclusions on Federal lands and elevates nonbiological “benefits of exclusion,” such as avoiding consultation costs or facilitating development, even where those lands provide essential habitat functions. In a multi‑jurisdictional landscape like the Puente–Chino Hills, federal and other public lands often anchor regional connectivity, fire‑resilient refugia, and core habitats for state and federally listed species; their designation as critical habitat is a key tool for coordinating conservation across boundaries. Making it easier to exclude such areas will reduce the scope and effectiveness of section 7 consultations, weaken incentives for strong conservation partnerships and conservation plans, and erode the landscape‑scale protections our organization relies on to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem function for current and succeeding generations.

We urge reconsideration of the proposed amendments and do not support the modifications as they will harm ESA listed species and the habitats they depend on to survive.

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As someone who lives in Ohio and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4):
Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)):Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule.
The proposed rule is significantly flawed procedurally. The comment period for this proposed rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and Executive Order (EO) 12866 on regulatory planning and review. The APA requires federal agencies to "give interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rule making through submission of written data, views, or arguments with or without opportunity for oral presentation." 5 U.S.C. § 553(c).
Section 6(a)(1) of EO 12866, which implements the rulemaking provisions in the APA, states that federal agencies "should afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases should include a comment period of not less than 60 days."
The comment period for this proposed rule is only 31 days, from November 21 through December 22, 2025. A proposed rule of this importance should have a comment period of at least 60 days. The comment period for the proposed rule should be extended at least 29 days to comply with the rulemaking requirements in the APA and EO 12866. If the comment period is not extended, the proposed rule will be in violation of the APA, which prohibits federal agency actions that are arbitrary and capricious and otherwise not in accordance with legal requirements.
I strongly oppose the substance of this proposed rule, which would revise § 17.90 and reinstate § 17.90(a). The proposed revisions would give the agency unbridled discretion based on a vague standard (“economic, national security, and other relevant impacts”), and with insufficient transparency, to exclude areas from critical habitat designations, thereby allowing the Secretary to skirt implementation of necessary protection for threatened and endangered species. Although the proposed rule touts transparency in the consideration of relevant impacts in deciding whether to exclude areas from critical habitat, no concrete details are given.

Reinstated § 17.90(a) states: “Based on the best information available regarding economic, national security, and other relevant impacts, the proposed designation of critical habitat will identify the areas that the Secretary has reason to consider for exclusion and explain why.” The proposed language further states that “impacts may be qualitatively or quantitatively described.” There is no requirement to provide associated supporting data and analysis.

Proposed § 17.90(b) states, “Prior to finalizing the designation of critical habitat, the Secretary will consider the probable economic, national security, and other relevant impacts of the designation upon proposed or ongoing activities,” but does not mention publication of any supporting data or analysis for the final decision.  

Proposed § 17.90(c)(2)(i) uses vague and ill-defined or undefined terms for the decision-making process regarding a discretionary exclusion analysis. The terms “credible,” “meaningful,” and “relevant” are not subject to standards or metrics. Further, and the Secretary is given uncircumscribed discretion in proposed § 17.90(c)(2)(ii), which states that the Secretary may otherwise decide to exercise discretion to evaluate any particular area for possible exclusion without giving any rationale.

Proposed § 17.90(d) includes a list of “principles” that the Secretary must apply in conducting a discretionary exclusion analysis, but because they are non-exhaustive, almost anything could serve as a principle to justify exclusion. Further, the discussion on weighing impacts provides no guidance on how weights are to be assigned. There is also no guidance on consideration of factors in analyzing the benefits of including or excluding particular areas covered by conservation plans, agreements, or partnerships that have been authorized by a permit.

For the foregoing reasons, the proposed rule would result in a faulty process for excluding areas from critical habitat designations, thereby undermining protection of threatened and endangered species and their habitat. The proposed rule should not be adopted.

title: Comment from Gold, Joanne

text:
The United States should seek to maintain and increase current protections rather than spend taxpayer dollars trying to dismantle them.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose proposed changes that expand or encourage exclusions of critical habitat under Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Critical habitat designation is a cornerstone of the ESA, ensuring that the areas essential to the recovery and survival of listed species are identified and protected from federal actions that could cause irreversible harm.

Section 4(b)(2) was intended to allow limited, carefully justified exclusions only when the benefits of exclusion clearly outweigh the benefits of designation—and only when exclusion will not result in the extinction of a species. Expanding the use of exclusions, or weakening the standards for determining them, undermines the statutory purpose of critical habitat and shifts the balance away from science-based conservation toward short-term economic or political considerations.

Critical habitat protections are especially important in the context of climate change, as species increasingly depend on habitat connectivity, refugia, and the ability to shift ranges in response to changing conditions. Excluding areas that are currently unoccupied or perceived as less critical ignores the dynamic nature of ecosystems and compromises species’ chances of recovery in a rapidly changing environment.

Moreover, broad or poorly justified exclusions reduce transparency and public trust. Decisions to exclude habitat should be rare, well-documented, and subject to meaningful public scrutiny. Without clear standards and robust analysis, exclusions risk becoming the default rather than the exception, eroding the ESA’s effectiveness and increasing legal uncertainty.

The ESA has consistently been upheld by the courts as prioritizing the conservation of endangered and threatened species. Weakening critical habitat protections through expanded exclusions is inconsistent with congressional intent and the Act’s plain language. I urge the agency to reject any revisions that dilute Section 4(b)(2) safeguards and to ensure that critical habitat designations remain grounded in the best available science and focused on species recovery.

title: Comment from Mohler, Erykah

text:
I oppose and effort to weaken the Endangered Species Act and, therefore, strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Colbert, Amanda

text:
I spend much of my life outdoors, teaching, studying, and working within California’s ecosystems. I see firsthand how fragile many of these systems already are and how quickly damage compounds when protections are weakened. Because of this lived experience, I strongly oppose any effort to dilute the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is not abstract policy to me. It is one of the few tools that has consistently slowed biodiversity loss in real places, with real consequences.

The strength of the Endangered Species Act lies in its refusal to treat extinction as negotiable. It places biological reality ahead of convenience and recognizes that once species and habitats are lost, they cannot be recovered through economic compromise. Proposals that insert industry flexibility or political discretion into decisions meant to be guided by ecological science fundamentally misunderstand how ecosystems function. Nature does not respond to timelines, markets, or lobbying pressure.

Removing automatic protections for newly listed species creates an unnecessary and dangerous gap at the very moment when intervention matters most. Species are often listed only after years of decline. Any delay in protection increases the likelihood that recovery becomes impossible. Similarly, weakening protections for threatened species ignores decades of conservation science showing that early, consistent safeguards are far more effective than reactive measures taken after populations collapse.

Critical habitat protections are equally nonnegotiable. Habitat is the foundation of survival. Allowing economic considerations to outweigh the preservation of essential habitat does not merely threaten individual species but destabilizes entire ecological networks. These losses ripple outward, affecting pollination, water quality, soil stability, and climate resilience. As an educator, I teach that ecosystems are interconnected systems, not isolated assets that can be selectively compromised.

Limiting federal consultation and oversight further erodes accountability. In many cases, federal review is the only mechanism ensuring that wildlife protection is not subordinated to local or industrial interests. title: Comment from Voight, Carly

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Miller, Debra

text:
1. Threatened Species Protections – Elimination of the Blanket 4(d) Rule

The blanket 4(d) rule is a long-standing, science-based policy that ensures newly listed threatened species receive immediate protections when they are most vulnerable. Eliminating this rule would create dangerous regulatory gaps, leaving species exposed to harm while species-specific rules are developed. These individualized rules are slow, resource-intensive, and highly susceptible to political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

Species-specific 4(d) rules cannot replace broad baseline protections. The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive actions aimed at weakening environmental safeguards. The Fish and Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent unnecessary delays and further species decline.

2. ESA Section 7 Interagency Consultation Regulations

Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA. It ensures that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. Rolling back the stronger 2024 regulations and reinstating the weaker 2019 framework significantly undermines this essential safeguard.

The proposal raises the threshold for impacts considered “reasonably certain to occur,” excluding indirect, cumulative, and climate-driven effects that are well-supported by science. It also narrows the definition of the environmental baseline and limits the evaluation of cumulative and landscape-scale harms. These changes would allow harmful federal projects—such as oil and gas development, pipelines, dams, grazing permits, and timber sales—to proceed without a full and honest assessment of their impacts.

Climate change, habitat fragmentation, and cumulative loss are primary drivers of extinction risk and must be considered in Section 7 consultations. The proposed rollback reinstates provisions widely criticized by courts and scientists as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. The Service should withdraw this rule and restore the stronger 2024 protections.

3. Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule – ESA Section 4(b)(2)

Reinstating the 2020 Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule improperly elevates economic and political considerations over the biological needs of imperiled species. The framework is biased toward excluding habitat, particularly for industry, energy development, ranching, and private landowners, even when scientific benefits of designation are substantial.

Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction. Weakening critical habitat protections directly harms recovery prospects and contradicts the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems upon which listed species depend. Exclusions must be based on clear scientific evidence, not speculative or inflated economic concerns. The Service should reject this proposal and ensure critical habitat decisions prioritize long-term conservation outcomes.

4. Listing and Critical Habitat Rules – 50 CFR Part 424

The proposed rollback of the 2024 Listing and Critical Habitat rules would narrow how the “foreseeable future” is interpreted for threatened species, make it harder to designate unoccupied critical habitat, and complicate listing, delisting, and climate impact considerations.

The ESA requires use of the best scientific and commercial data available. Many species threatened by climate change depend on future-oriented science. Artificially narrowing the foreseeable future restricts the ability to act before populations collapse, undermining the preventative intent of the ESA. Recovery often requires habitat beyond the small areas species currently occupy; restricting unoccupied critical habitat contradicts the Act’s recovery mandate.

Reinstating the 2019 regulations moves ESA implementation backward, not forward. The Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries should retain the 2024 improvements and uphold science-based, forward-looking protections.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Jensen, David

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Weitzner, Michael

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am appalled and horrified that this proposal would essentially gut and totally rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it, for the sake of our children and grandchildren and the world as we know it. The ESA is one of the most successful wildlife laws in the world, with more than 99% of species under the ESA's care getting either saved or are on the path to recovery. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

When we harm wildlife to the point of extinction, the ecosystems they tend and live in change, and that impacts whole communities and biomes in ways we can't predict even when we are just thinking on a selfish, immediate, economic basis. I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The Endangered Species Act should be preserved as it is. Wildlife and wild places should not be victims of punitive partisan politics.

Protecting critical habitat is essential not only for the species and ecosystems we aim to save, but also for humankind. We are part of these ecosystems and rely on them.

This rule would reinstate the 2020 exclusion rule (a Trump-era rule) that makes it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat designations. It reintroduced several ill conceived concepts, such as a framework biased toward exclusion, especially for industry, energy development, ranching and private landowners, requirements that the US Fish and Wildlife Service assign weight to economic impacts in ways that reduce habitat designations, and a more rigid process that can force exclusion even when scientific benefits of designation are high. All of these concepts are in opposition to the mandate of the ESA as enacted, the protection of threatened and endangered species.

The proposed changes are significant. Critical habitat is often the only way species retain the physical and biological features essential for recovery. A return to the 2020 rule would remove discretion by the Secretary of the Interior in designating critical habitat. Currently, the language states the Secretary may exclude critical habitat from protection; however, the new rule states the Secretary shall exclude habitat protections if there are economic interests at stake. I highly disagree with excluding habitat protections due to non-scientific factors. ESA requires decisions based on the best available science. The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species. Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose of conserving ecosystems and recovering species, and not reducing protections for industry convenience.
The changes would also make it easier for industry to pressure FWS into excluding habitat. Any exclusions must be based on lear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns. This would also reduce the size and effectiveness of critical habitat designations, with increased fragmentation. Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction so weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects.

Essentially, the proposed changes shift decisions away from science and toward economic consideration. All of this would undermine recovery planning.

At the very least, FWS should restore the more balanced 2016 policy. But especially as development continues to infringe on habitat, FWS actually should adopt a stronger science-forward framework to more effectively preserve species.

title: Comment from Owen, Garrett

text:
America's wildlife is a gem in both our natural and cultural history. I have lived coast to coast across the mainland United States, and have seen much of our nature first-hand. I am deeply proud of not only our wild places and species, but our dedication to protecting them. Which is why I am writing to urge the Department of the Interior Fish and Wildlife Service to reject the FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029 proposal, and to not remove vital regulations within the Endangered Species Act, including the 'blanket' rule.

As it stands today, the Endangered Species Act has saved ninety-nine percent of species listed under its protection. All of them shielded from extinction with the rules in place. Repealing any of the current regulations will only result in loss no force on our earth can ever replace.

As an example, we can look towards the blanket rule, which directs that any new threatened species will have the same baseline of protections applied as soon as they are listed. Removing that rule will only delay safeguarding any future proposed species and will place these already vulnerable species in harm's way. The blanket rule is not only a stopgap meassure during new listings, but an immediate way to protect a species at risk and lay down early guidelines prior to more specific assessments. Removing the blanket rule will create more strain on agency systems, raise administrative costs, and delay the process of listing future threatened species as a whole. Slowing down protection to a species on the brink might mean the line between existence itself.

Our Endangered Species Act is a powerful tool to save species, in and out of America. I have lived across the mainland US, and have seen so much beauty in nature all across our nation. I do not want to imagine a world in which many of our country's fragile ecosystems and species were gutted by bureaucratic hurdles. I do not want to imagine our world under such loss.

So I ask the Administration to maintain the protection that America has extended to threatened and endangered species for over fifty years now. I urge the Administration to rescind this proposed rule that would harm our ability to guard vulnerable species through the tried and proven blanket rule. Thank you.

text: I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act’s critical habitat exclusion analysis under Section 4(b)(2) (Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001). While transparency and public understanding are important objectives, the substance of this rule would substantially weaken one of the most crucial protections for endangered and threatened species by prioritizing economic considerations over biological necessity. Critical habitat designations are not merely administrative exercises — they are rooted in ecological science as a preventive conservation tool that secures the physical and biological features necessary for species survival and recovery. Scientific research consistently shows that species at risk face multiple interlinked threats, including habitat loss, fragmentation, climate change, and increased edge effects. By identifying and protecting critical habitat, agencies can help maintain viable populations and genetic connectivity across a species’ range — fundamental principles in conservation biology. Section 4(b)(2) already allows consideration of economic and other non-biological impacts after identifying biologically essential habitat. However, the proposed rule would fundamentally elevate economic analyses and potentially exclude large swaths of habitat that are scientifically necessary for species persistence. A scientific consensus holds that habitat loss and degradation are among the most significant drivers of extinction — far more directly linked to species declines than generalized economic indicators. Prioritizing economic metrics at the exclusion stage would shift ESA decisions away from biological science toward a cost-benefit framework inappropriate for a statute focused on preventing extinction. Ecological and population viability research shows that even small reductions in habitat quantity, quality, or connectivity can sharply increase extinction risk, particularly for small, isolated, or already declining species. Excluding key areas — especially unoccupied or marginal habitats that support dispersal, climate refugia, or life-stage-specific needs — would make recovery more difficult and recovery plans less effective. These areas are often critical for species’ adaptive responses to changing environmental conditions, including climate change — a driver of species loss that cannot be ignored in 21st-century conservation.The ESA’s primary objective is to protect and recover imperiled species — and it explicitly prohibits considering economic factors in listing decisions. While Section 4(b)(2) allows weighing economic impacts after identifying habitat essential for conservation, it never intended to subordinate biological needs to economics in a way that could eliminate protections that science demonstrates are necessary. Embedding economic priorities into the biological determination of habitat needs sets a dangerous precedent that could be exploited to exclude nearly all habitat in regions with high development value.Conservation science endorses a precautionary approach when dealing with species on the brink of extinction. Because extinction is irreversible and because ecological systems are complex and interconnected, regulatory decisions should err on the side of protection, not exclusion. The proposed rule risks imposing arbitrary economic thresholds that could delay or prevent the safeguards species need long before they recover — if they recover at all. Climate change, invasive species, pollution, and other anthropogenic pressures interact with habitat loss to elevate extinction risks. A scientifically valid habitat analysis must consider cumulative impacts, not just direct, immediate effects. Excluding areas because the short-term economic benefits of development or extraction appear to outweigh immediate mitigation costs ignores the broader ecological consequences that are often delayed, synergistic, and difficult to reverse. For these scientific and legal reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Section 4(b)(2) critical habitat exclusions in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001. Any final rule must uphold the ESA’s foundational mission — to prevent extinction and promote recovery based on the best available science, not economic expediency.
