title: Comment from SCHNEIDER, GREG

text:
I do not support reinstatement of the 2020 rule that made it easier to exempt areas from critical habitat designations. The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species.
Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to reduce protections for industry convenience.
The Service must base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns.
Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction; weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects.
FWS should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger science-forward framework. They should not prioritize the economic gain of a few for the detriment of the many, human, environment, and animal alike.
title: Comment from Von Plinsky, Autumn

text:
This comment has been submitted to the following dockets:
FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029
FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039
FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048
FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044

As a physician-scientist (MD-PhD) in Wisconsin, I recognize the importance of protecting biodiversity both to protect the health of ecosystems, for human health, and to preserve ecosystems for generations to come. In Wisconsin, we have seen a dramatic resurgence of certain wildlife populations including cranes and wolves with intensive protections and efforts to bring back these important members of our local and regional ecosystems. These gains are fragile and depend on ongoing protection. Newly listed species should be protected until species-specific rules are written.

Please maintain and expand interagency efforts to protect species that are endangered by human interventions including habitat loss, climate change, and inappropriate hunting.

Sincerely,
Kaitlin Sundling, MD, PhD
title: Comment from Sundling, Kaitlin

text: I strongly oppose this proposal! We the people believe in protecting the earth we have been given and all the creatures that live upon it. Life is more important that profit. We will not accept less! Please do not allow Trump and his wicked corporate conglomerates to destroy the ESA. The ESA is one thing the country can unite over!
title: Comment from Davis, Matthew

text:
We need to keep the ESA protections strong. If these rules go through, they would:
-Strip automatic protections from newly listed species, leaving them vulnerable while politicians argue over whether they “deserve” protection.
-Shrink what counts as “critical habitat,” excluding areas species need to recover — especially as climate change accelerates.
-Let economic and corporate interests outweigh science in decisions about whether species live or die.
-Limit federal oversight, making it easier for logging, drilling, mining, and development projects to move forward even when they harm endangered wildlife.

We need science to prevail over political bias. Do not give in to corporations and let science and coexistence the mark of success.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text: Please do not weaken the Endangered Species Act. Protecting our country’s animals and habitats Makes America Great.
title: Comment from Walker, Emma

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful conservation tools in our nation’s history. Weakening it now, when so many species are on the brink, is simply unacceptable. Critical habitat is the lifeline for species like the Southern Resident orcas and endangered salmon who are keystone species. If we start removing protections, we will push these species to extinction.

This rule prioritizes short-term industry gains over long-term ecological stability, cultural values, and the health of communities that depend on thriving ecosystems. We cannot afford to lose salmon. We cannot afford to lose orcas or any other endangered animal. And we cannot afford to weaken the very protections meant to save them. Our environment is in crisis, the very home we all rely on.

Please reject this rule and uphold the ESA’s original promise to prevent extinction, and to recover endangered species, not sacrifice them.

title: Comment from Alger, Dylan

text:
I strongly oppose FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048. The proposed action would weaken federal protections at a time when habitat loss, fragmentation, & human encroachment are accelerating across the West & Great Lakes, placing Grizzlies and Wolves at renewed & foreseeable risk of decline. Thus proposal fails to account for real-world landscape conditions, cumulative development pressures, & the biological requirements of wide-ranging keystone species whose survival depends on connectivity, dispersal & low levels of human-caused mortality. Weakening federal safeguards while habitat is actively being degraded undermines decades of recovery work achieved under the ESA & risks permanent population fragmentation.

Grizzly Bears are long-lived, slow reproducing mammals whose population stability is governed primarily by adult female survival & access to secure habitat. Even modest increases in human-caused mortality or chronic disturbance can halt or reverse population growth. Grizzly recovery in the lower 48 states has never depended on short-term numerical gains or isolated population centers; it has depended on large, connected landscapes that allow bears to forage, den, disperse, & recolonize suitable habitat. Fragmentation is the dominant long-term threat to Grizzlies, particularly for females, whose dispersal is essential for connectivity & genetic health. Once landscapes are subdivided by roads, extractive development, ag & urban expansion, habitat quickly becomes a mortality sink rather than a recovery asset.

In Wyoming Grizzly habitat is already under intense pressure from mining, energy development, ag expansion & associated infrastructure. These activities introduce chronic disturbance through road building, heavy equipment traffic, increased human presence, & attractants that elevate conflict risk. Ag landscapes further constrain movement through fencing, irrigation systems, m livestock operations, & conflict-driven removals. Grizzlies navigating these altered environments face increased risk of displacement & death, particularly when food availability is reduced or redistributed. Weakening federal protection in this context assumes that habitat conditions are static or improving when the opposite is true.

In southwest MT in the Paradise Valley & Bozeman region, development pressure has reached a tipping point. Rapid population growth, subdivision expansion, increased traffic, & year round recreation are transforming what were once functional linkage areas into barriers. This region is crucial for connectivity btwn the GYE & N Continental Divide Ecosystem. Bears moving through this corridor must contend with dense development, attractants, road mortality, & conflict risk. Each subdivision or access road narrows the margin for successful dispersal, particularly, for females. Grizzlies do not adapt to this level of encroachment by simply coexisting, they are displaced, killed or prevented from dispersing altogether. Once these linkage zones are lost, they are gone for generations.

Connectivity is not optional for Grizzly recovery. Isolated populations suffer from genetic bottlenecks, demographic instability & increased vulnerability to stochastic evens such as disease, wildfire or food failures. The Service's own scientific anslyese have repeatedly acknowledged that linkage btwn. ecosystems is necessary for long-term viability. Weakening federal protections in this context assumes that habitat conditions are static or improving when the opposite is true.

Climate change further magnifies these risks. Altered food availability, shifting denning conditions, drought & wildfire force bears to travel farther & use lower quality habitat, increasing encounters w humans. Fragmented landscapes leave no room for adaptive movement. Any rule making that weakens habitat protections w/o fully accounting for climate-driven cumulative stressors fails the requirement to rely on the best available science.

Gray Wolves face parallel but distinct risks. Forested landscapes provide cover, prey stability, denning security & movement pathways essential for dispersal. When forest are heavily logged, fragmented or converted into industrialized landscapes, dispersing Wolves are forced into exposed routes where mortality risk increases sharply. Roads are among the strongest predictors of Wolf death. Logging also alters prey distributions & increases overlap w livestock leading to more conflict & lethal control. If Fix Our Forest Act advances the consequences for Wolves would be severe. In the N Rockies Grizzlies & Wolves share the same landscapes & face the same structural threats; expanding road networks & human encroachment. WY & MT already pursue wildlife policies that prioritize development & lethal control over long-term conservation. For Grizzlies & Wolves habitat loss outpaces recovery. 0048 abandons principles & replaces them w regulatory shortcuts that ignore impacts & biological reality. I urge USFWS to withdraw this proposal.
title: Comment from hersey, rene

text:
We are currently losing species at a rate 1,000 times greater than the natural extinction rate. This is a sixth great extinction and it's being caused by habitat loss and degradation, climate change, pollution, overexploitation, and invasive species. And we, human beings, are responsible or partially responsible for all these causes. We therefore have a responsibility to limit the damage we do and more importantly, mitigate the effects. We rely on a healthy, thriving environment for clean water, pollination of crops, sources of medicines, and a livable climate.
Now is the time to strengthen and expand the Endangered Species Act, not limit and undermine it. As there are fewer and fewer areas with native species in a thriving ecosystem, those areas need more protection and not less. We need all the protection and mitigation we can get.
Please reject this proposed rule change.

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

text:

Another component of the current Endangered Species Act (ESA) is species-specific rules, which are necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created so the blanket rule provides needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. The broad baseline protections of the ESA ensure that species don’t fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups. Each of these components aids in the protection of all the species in North America. Taking care of natural resources and protecting the species that dwell therein should not be contingent upon economic interest and politics. Protecting the environment and all species is part of our role as stewards of the planet. We cannot allow economic costs to interfere with stewardship over North American species. Under the proposed rules, section 4(b)(2), efforts to save a species can occur if the price is right. The potential changes put an economic cost on preserving a species. The proposed regulations call for a prioritization of economic impact analysis, despite the law forbidding anything except science from influencing such a decision. The designation of critical habitat should be guided by science and species conservation, rather than politics or money interests. The main cause of extinction is habitat loss. This proposed rule would weaken essential habitat protection tools and propel more species towards extinction. 

An important element of the ESA is the listing requirements and conditions for protecting critical habitats. The proposed rule regarding listing and critical habitat regulations would narrow the interpretation of listing requirements and make it more difficult to list species as endangered or threatened. It would also be easier to delist a species. These proposed changes would make it more challenging to grant ESA protections for species that are affected by changes in the climate, such as drought, disease, and other effects. This new rule would limit the USFWS in designating currently unoccupied wolf habitat as critical, even if those areas are necessary for future wolf expansion and recovery. Proper endangered species conservation requires forward-thinking and science-based predictions. By removing the ability to list species, as the current Act allows, it would hinder our ability to proactively save species before they are on the brink of extinction. Proper recovery looks at all areas a species once roamed, and could roam in the future. For example, gray wolves only occupy about 10-12% of their historical range. If the species is going to truly recover from the harm humankind inflicted, they must rely on unoccupied areas in addition to the areas where they are currently found. The USFWS and the NMFS must reject these proposed rules in order to safeguard North American species. Instead of accepting these proposed rules the USFWS should focus on real scientific results such as the improvements made in 2024.

The majority of Americans are in favor of the current rules surrounding the ESA and reject the proposed rules put forth by the Trump administration. North America is home to a variety of amazing species and we must safeguard them and their habitats. By rejecting the proposed rules, we can guarantee the species alive today will continue to live on and thrive for future generations to enjoy. We have an obligation to steward this planet in a way that allows all life to flourish. We only have one planet, which means we need to take extra care of the resources we have, including all life-forms. We have already lost too many to extinction. The current ESA is one of many laws which help us steward our planet properly. Please protect our beautiful planet by rejecting the proposals that would alter the Endangered Species Act.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Metzloff, Paul

text:
Docket Number FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I urge USFWS and NMFS to withdraw the proposed rule changes regarding designations of critical habitat.

Habitat loss is the main cause of extinction. The proposed rule changes would weaken one of the ESA's most essential habitat protection tools. The changes improperly and illegally elevate resource development and administrative burden over species conservation.

Inherent in the success of the Act is the condition that economic costs not be a factor in deciding whether to protect a species. However, the new regulations call for greater emphasis on economic impact analysis, despite the law forbidding anything except "good science" from influencing a listing decision.

Critical Habitat Must Be Science-Based, Not Burden-Based

The proposal would allow critical habitat to be excluded where designation is deemed an “undue burden” on activities such as energy development and resource extraction. This approach directly conflicts with the intent of the ESA, which prioritizes species protection and recovery based on the best available science—not short-term economic or political interests.

Weakening the critical habitat designation process would make it easier to exclude ecologically essential areas, avoid mitigation requirements, and allow harmful activities to proceed without adequate safeguards. Habitat protection is fundamental to species recovery; without sufficient habitat, listed species cannot survive or recover, regardless of other conservation measures.

Concerns with Section 4 and Critical Habitat Designation Criteria

The ESA requires that critical habitat be designated at the time of listing “to the maximum extent prudent and determinable." The proposed expansion of “not prudent” determinations is overly broad and risks excluding habitat that could meaningfully contribute to species conservation, including by buffering against climate change and other cumulative threats.

Designation may still temper impacts from threats that are not fully addressable through discrete management actions and may play an important role in long-term recovery, connectivity, and adaptation.

Improper Weight Given to Administrative and Economic Burdens

The proposed rule allows administrative burden, anticipated consultation frequency, or transactional costs to drive exclusions from critical habitat designation. Administrative inconvenience alone should never justify excluding areas essential to species conservation.

The proposal also risks expanding exclusions of federally managed lands, which is especially concerning in my own state of New Mexico, where roughly one-third of the land is federally managed and the majority of listed species depend on federal lands. Broad exclusion authority could eliminate protection for large portions of species’ ranges.

Critical Habitat Provides Broad Ecological and Economic Benefits

The proposed rule undervalues the full benefits of critical habitat designation. Protecting habitat supports ecosystem productivity, biodiversity, clean water, carbon sequestration, pollination, and climate resilience. Wildlife itself has substantial economic value: in 2022, wildlife-related recreation contributed hundreds of billions of dollars to the U.S. economy. Healthy ecosystems also reduce long-term regulatory burdens by enabling species recovery.

Limiting the recognized benefits of critical habitat to narrow “conservation value” or framing productivity only as an economic cost ignores these broader, well-documented benefits.

Specific Regulatory Recommendations
I urge the Services to:
a) Reject exclusions based on “undue burden” to development interests;
b) Ensure critical habitat designations and exclusions are grounded solely in the best available scientific data, consistent with ESA Section 4;
c) Retain strong protections for unoccupied habitat necessary for future recovery, climate adaptation, and connectivity;
d) Avoid expanded exclusion of federally managed lands from critical habitat designation;
e) Recognize intrinsic, ecological, cultural, and economic values of wildlife and habitat as benefits of designation; and
f) Maintain transparent, documented standards when weighing inclusion versus exclusion decisions.

Conclusion

Critical habitat designation is a cornerstone of the ESA’s success. The proposed rule would devalue habitat, weaken recovery prospects, and grant excessive discretion to exclude essential areas based on economic or administrative considerations. These changes are inconsistent with the ESA’s purpose, statutory text, and scientific understanding of species recovery.

I respectfully request that the Services withdraw the proposed rule and uphold strong, science-based critical habitat criteria that ensure the long-term survival and recovery of endangered and threatened species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the ESA's section 4(b)(2) critical habitat exclusion guidelines. I am concerned this change would lead to more habitat loss, which is the main driver of species extinction. It is a mandatory requirement that the Secretaries consider economic impacts, impacts to national security, and any other relevant impacts prior to designating an area as part of a critical habitat designation. The Secretary has rather broad discretion when determining if the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion. There is essentially no limit to the perceived benefits of excluding an area from critical habitat designation. While the proposed changes seek to provide more transparency on how the Secretary plans to exercise this discretion, the only criteria by which the Secretary may exclude an area is if the exclusion will result in extinction. The ESA states that it is the policy of Congress that the Federal Government will seek to conserve threatened and endangered species and use its authorities to further the purposes of the Act. 16 U.S.C. 1531(c)(1). Logically, extinction is not in line with conservation; conservation entails consulting and utilizing the best available science to preserve and protect a species and the habitat crucial to its viability into the future (recovery).
The proposed modifications to the language in 50 CFR 424.19(c) appear to codify and make binding an endless number of “relevant impacts” that would “prompt” the Secretary to enter into the discretionary exclusion analysis under section 4(2)(b). It appears that the presentation by proponents of exclusion or inclusion of “credible information” could trigger the discretionary exclusion analysis. This opens the door to consideration of speculative and secondary effects. Furthermore, proposed paragraph (e) would establish as a principle that FWS will exclude areas whenever it determines that the innumerable possibility of broad benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, as long as exclusion will not result in the extinction of the species.
Of great concern is the proposed consideration of avoidance of administrative and transactional costs as a benefit of exclusion of a particular area of Federal land combined with the reversal of the 2016 Policy’s prior position of generally not excluding Federal lands from critical habitat designation. This places economic concerns above scientific research and guidance and completely overrides the intent of the ESA.
Critical habitat designation decisions should prioritize science over economic considerations, and I urge you to withdraw this proposal.

title: Comment from Hunhoff, Lindsey

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.
First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

In the face of increasing threats, I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes. These changes will only accelerate the decline of these species and dismantle the very core of the ESA that has saved 99% of species that have been listed from extinction. There is a good track record- why change a good thing and lose the species that make the US such a wonderful place to call home. We must listen to the science-backed research and recommendations not the whims of an administration.

What will we tell future generations if we do not take the necessary actions today to protect these vulnerable species. Species that provide benefits to human and healthy ecosystems.

title: Comment from Doyle, Tammis

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As someone who lives in New Mexico and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.
The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed. Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

title: Comment from Smith, Greg

text:
I am concerned about how the proposed revisions to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s regulations implementing section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act risks weakening the protection of critical habitat.

The ESA is a recovery statute whose purpose is to conserve ecosystems essential to endangered and threatened species. Critical habitat designation is one of the Act’s most important tools. While transparency in how exclusions are considered is valuable, the proposed rule appears to lower the threshold for conducting exclusion analyses and expand the circumstances under which habitat may be excluded based on economic, administrative, or speculative nonbiological impacts.

In particular:
• The “credible information” standard is vague and may allow relatively modest or short-term impacts to trigger exclusion analyses, even for areas of high conservation value.
• Granting broad discretion in weighting benefits risks undervaluing habitat essential for recovery, climate resilience, and connectivity.
• Treating administrative and consultation costs on Federal lands as a benefit of exclusion undermines the conservation purpose of section 7 and risks excluding some of the most ecologically important lands.
• Economic analyses often undervalue ecosystem services and long-term public benefits provided by intact habitat.
• The prohibition on exclusions that cause extinction is not an adequate safeguard; the ESA is intended to promote recovery, not merely avoid extinction.

I urge the Service to revise the proposed rule to more clearly prioritize biological and ecological value, limit exclusions to truly exceptional circumstances, and ensure that critical habitat designations remain a strong, science-driven conservation tool.

Thank you for considering these comments.

title: Comment from Lybarger, Lisa

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act regulations under Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001, which would change how the Fish and Wildlife Service determines whether to exclude areas from designation as critical habitat under section 4(b)(2) of the ESA.
Critical habitat is foundational to species conservation. Scientific evidence shows that habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation are the primary drivers of species decline and extinction worldwide. Protecting the geographic areas essential for recovery — including those not currently occupied but necessary for long-term resilience — is vital to prevent more species from disappearing. The ESA was designed to rely on biological criteria to define these areas and identify threats to species survival, not on short-term economic considerations.
The proposed rule aims to clarify when the benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating that area as critical habitat. However, any framework that privileges economic or development interests at the expense of biological necessity risks undercutting the science-based protections that have enabled many species to persist. Experts in ecology and conservation biology have repeatedly documented that protecting connected, intact, and climate-resilient habitats increases the likelihood of recovery well beyond protecting only current populations.
The statute itself requires consideration of economic impacts, national security, and other relevant impacts when deciding on exclusions. Yet this consideration is meant to be weighed against the biological importance of habitat for a species’ survival and recovery. Excluding areas that serve as movement corridors, climate refugia, or future range under changing environmental conditions could fragment populations and impair recovery potential, particularly for wide-ranging species and those facing shifting habitats due to climate change.
Real world cases have shown that designation of critical habitat can help guide federal and non-federal conservation efforts, inform land management practices, and prioritize habitat restoration. These designations do not automatically prohibit development. Rather, they ensure that federal agencies take into account the biological needs of species when authorizing, funding, or carrying out actions that may affect protected species and their habitats. Weakening this process by narrowing the scope of what counts as necessary habitat or by tipping the balance too far toward economic impacts can delay or reduce meaningful protections, ultimately undermining species recovery.
The Endangered Species Act has a strong track record of preventing extinctions and enabling recoveries when applied with scientific rigor. A regulatory framework for critical habitat exclusions should retain the emphasis on biological criteria and transparency so that decisions are grounded in the best available science and consistent with the law’s purpose of conserving imperiled wildlife and plants.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to ensure that any final rule maintains robust standards for identifying and protecting habitat essential to species’ survival and recovery. Critical habitat protections should be strengthened — not weakened — to reflect the ongoing biodiversity crisis and the urgent need for ecological resilience.
Thank you for considering my comments.
title: Comment from Pilipow , Marsha

text:
I’m a US citizen concerned by the additional limits being suggested for the endangered species act—an act which is already quite limited in scope and conservative in what it impacts. Individual citizens overwhelmingly support the ESA as it exists today—how it protects land critical to the success of threatened and endangered species from human development. A lot of what these species need for continued existence requires habitat protection of key areas and pesticides regulations. It is imperative that we continue protecting critical habitat for endangered species and also those listed as threatened, continuing the blanket rule for the most expedient action to protect threatened as well as endangered species.

Take the complex life process of the monarch butterfly. It is not the same monarch that returns to its overwintering grounds, but one 4 generations later. Failure can happen at any step during its life process—the development from egg to butterfly to overwintering ground—an egg can be unfertilized or eaten, a caterpillar can be eaten or parasitized or taken over by fungus or pesticides, it can fall while forming its chrysalis, it can die while in a chrysalis state, its wings can be wrinkled and unable to fly, it can be hit by cars or pesticides while flying south, and it could find its overwintering habitat gone and be unable to survive the cold winter months. That last step is the most critical for governments to step in and protect because average citizens do not have the power to protect their overwintering grounds—areas of critically important undeveloped land.

It is possible for average citizens to plant milkweed, protect them from pesticides and plant nectaring flowers—to help monarchs grow their numbers during the summer months so they have enough to survive the winter. Average citizens have helped stabilize their plummeting populations by doing just that. But without protecting their overwintering habitat, their life process fails—their species’ future disappears.

I am so thankful for the ESA and its ability to protect threatened and endangered species. Let’s protect and defend the ESA’s ability to protect endangered and threatened species—to fulfill its very purpose—not strip away its ability to do so. Protecting a small amount of land to protect an endangered or threatened species is priceless. Think of what we’ve already lost and what we would give to get them back if we could. But that’s just it, once we lose a species, it is gone forever. We cannot trade entire species for short-term, temporary, short-sighted development interests.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. Although the ESA allows the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not risk extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations over biological needs, effectively giving economic impacts—often speculative—priority in the analysis.
The rule also imposes an unreasonably high evidentiary standard by suggesting that habitat should be excluded unless the agency can prove that exclusion would cause extinction. This approach reverses the ESA’s precautionary framework and conflicts with the statute’s recovery-focused purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must support species recovery, not merely prevent extinction.
In addition, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non‑biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic concerns without requiring comparable scientific rigor. This risks turning the exclusion process into a tool for regulated entities to override scientific judgment—precisely the outcome Congress sought to prevent when it removed economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to withdraw these revisions and maintain a section 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, scientifically justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

I grew up in Florida, inspired by the Everglades and impact is the BO oil spill had on my community. Seeing the way humans interact with our environment, how we have the ability to both protect it and harm it simultaneously. Learning about the Everglades throughout my next graduate and graduates studies I learned how the Everglades and the species that call it home are a true American success story. Once on the brink of complete habitat destruction, many of the species that are unique to the Everglades once on the verge of extinction, were protected and revived by the action of a strong public interest and democratic processes. The action taken to protect one of America’s most unique and important ecosystems was a success story of environmental protection through federal oversight and public interest. However, the Everglades is not the only ecosystem that makes America beautiful, the American alligator isn’t the only species that needs protection. There are so many ecosystems, habitats, and species that rely on a strong ESA. It is our duty as stewards of this land to do what we can to protect it for all.

As someone who grew up in Florida, a state heavily impacted by overdevelopment and habitat loss I’ve seen firsthand of the destruction of critical habitat can lead to species decline, synurbization, and eventual extinction. As environmental scientist who has completed section 7 consultations, EAs and EISs, I understand how vital it is to consider critical habitat has a factor when determining the impacts of a project. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.

If a species no longer has a home, a habitat that their lively and health relies on, the ability for that species to exist diminishes. If there are no wetlands, no old growth forest, mangrove forest, MPAs, or cypress swamps where will endangered species like the American crocodile, grizzly bear, Florida Panther, West Indians manatee, or right whale. Not protecting critical habitats leads to species decline and eventually extinction. Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
Americans don’t agree on much lately as a nation, but most Americans love our natural lands and the species that call them home.

As someone who loves our environment, loves all species that rely on a strong ESA and consultation periods, and as an American, proud of our democratic republic, I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA. I urge the legislature to stand with its constituents and fellow Americans, not lobbyists and corporations. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I urge you to continue to work towards preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. The democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.


Thank you

text:
I do not support this revision to the Endangered Species Act for several reasons as outlined below:

1) Weakened Habitat Protections -> Narrower criteria for designating unoccupied critical habitat and increased exclusions may leave species without sufficient space to recover, especially under climate change.

2) Delays in Safeguards -> Requiring species-specific rules for threatened species could slow down implementation, leaving species vulnerable during the rulemaking process.

3) Economic Considerations in Conservation can be risky -> Introducing economic factors—even if not decisive—risks shifting focus away from biological needs toward development priorities.

4) Potential for Increased Litigation -> More complex rules and exclusions could lead to legal challenges, diverting resources from conservation efforts and spending more of the taxpayers money.

These proposed changes could potentially cause imperiled species to face extinction at a time when we should be strengthening protections!

title: Comment from Jensen, Susie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Shaw, John

text:
Also see the attached file, which includes references.

Modification of habitat by humans often results in degradation; i.e., a reduction in the fitness (survival and reproductive potential) of individuals and a reduction in the viability of populations. Wilcove et al. (1998) demonstrated that habitat loss is the single biggest threat to endangered species in the United States. Although there are many other factors that impact endangered species, this consensus remains among wildlife biologists and conservation biologists today. As an example, the textbook I use for the Environmental Science course I teach states quite clearly that habitat destruction is the greatest threat to endangered species (Friedland and Relyea, 2023, p. 701).

The Service in the proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) claims that the first sentence of section 4(b)(2) of the ESA mandates that economic and national security impacts of critical habitat designation be considered and that an exclusion analysis should be undertaken whenever such impacts are thought to exist (unless habitat exclusion is likely to lead to the extinction of the Threatened or Endangered Species). I believe that this is an incorrect interpretation of the statutory language. The Secretary of the Interior and staff members to whom the responsibility is delegated (“Secretary”) have broad discretion to determine whether an exclusion analysis is warranted. The Secretary should not undertake an exclusion analysis when it is not warranted; to do so would undermine government efficiency. Furthermore, it would increase the probability that exclusions would be made and thus undermine the recovery of Threatened and Endangered Species. It is an incorrect reading of the statute to elevate economic and security considerations to equal footing with the principle purpose of the Act, which is to conserve Threatened and Endangered Species. If there is reason to exclude land from critical habitat designation to mitigate impacts on economics and security, the Secretary has broad discretion to do so (as long as it is not likely to lead to the extinction of the Threatened or Endangered Species). However, the Secretary is not under statutory obligation to search for such impacts.

I object to the proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) because it would mandate the consideration of economic and security impacts for every critical habitat designation and thus undermine both government efficiency and the recovery of Threatened and Endangered Species. I also object to the proposed rule because it would include a list of different types of impacts and mandate that the Secretary consider each of these and potentially more (since it is termed an “inexhaustive list”). Again, this would undermine both government efficiency and the recovery of Threatened and Endangered Species.

I also object to the proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) because it would mandate that every final determination regarding critical habitat include exclusion analyses and/or the basis for deciding not to undertake an exclusion analysis. If the Secretary had to document the rationale for not doing an analysis, it would be necessary to do an analysis to show that there is no reason for an analysis. This is clearly counter to the goal of government efficiency. It would also slow the process of designating critical habitat, which would imperil the recovery of Threatened and Endangered Species.

I object to the proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) because it would allow the exclusion of federal land from critical habitat designations and thus mandate that the Secretary consider whether to conduct an exclusion analysis even on federal lands. This would undermine government efficiency and the recovery of Threatened and Endangered Species.

I object to the proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) because it would include as a benefit of exclusion the costs avoided from not conducting section 7 consultation with federal agencies. Section 7 of the Act describes the process intended by Congress to be used to resolve conflicts between species conservation and other land management goals. Section 7 should not be thrown out just because of two sentences in section 4(b)(2) that allude to the consideration of costs. Congress would not have included section 7 in the Act if it had not been the intent of Congress for this process to be followed. To include the avoidance of section 7 consultation costs as a benefit of exclusion would unnecessarily complicate exclusion analysis and might necessitate undertaking exclusion analysis where it would not have been necessary otherwise. Such an approach is clearly counter to government efficiency and the conservation of Threatened and Endangered Species.

This proposed rule (USFWS, 2025) would have a significant effect on the human environment if adopted and requires the preparation of an Environmental Impact Statement under the National Environmental Protection Act to describe the potential impacts on the human environment.

•[Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048; FXES11110900000-256-FF09E23000] Critical Habitat

Dear USFWS and NMFS
I am writing as your constituent to express strong opposition to current proposals that would weaken the Endangered Species Act, including the weakening of the Blanket Rule that will reduce or eliminate protection for threatened species including the Critically endangered Oceanic Whitetip, Scalloped Hammerhead and Soupfin (Tope) sharks all desperately need this rule to allow for their recovery and fend of imminent extinction in US waters.
The ESA has saved species like humpback whales, gray whales, sea turtles, and sea otters by safeguarding their habitat and requiring strict consultation and evaluation of threats. Weakening these protections would open the door to unchecked habitat destruction and put vulnerable species at grave risk.
For over 50 years the ESA has successfully protected 99% of the nearly 3000 species listed under the Act.

We urge you to:
1.Support efforts to strengthen and modernize the ESA rulemaking process, not freeze it.
2.Speak publicly in favor of robust habitat protections, strong consultation triggers, and full scientific integrity in ESA decisions.
3.Eliminate any language weakening the Blanket Rule and other ESA proposed changes regarding critical habitat, the definition of “Harm” and interagency coordination implementing the ESA.

Thank you for representing our district. I hope you will act to defend America’s wildlife legacy. On behalf of over 10,000 members and volunteers we also submit this petition with over 2800 members of the US public urging you to leave the ESA intact.

Sincerely,
David McGuire, Director

text:
In trying to understand why anyone would want to strangle the Endangered Species Act, I realized it is in a very, VERY short-term goal of gaining the approval of one man and one industry with no thought of the profound consequences of doing so.
Extinction of various species unbalances the ecosystem of the planet; if predator species go extinct, the prey species will multiply until they, too have been eradicated also, and so on.
You are burdening not just the people that are alive now, but the future inhabitants of our world.
Drop this effort now. Ask yourself? What are you afraid of if you don’t? Are you “just following orders?”
The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.
I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The ESA provides critical federal oversight to an assessment process that select industries would otherwise weaken, but this oversight is necessary to protect America's iconic wild species.

I grew up in Alaska, where having wild animals at your doorstep is a given. I've had the benefit of growing up witnessing major triumphs of the Endangered Species Act. Here, bald eagles seem as common as pigeons do in a city; they are a flagship success story of the Endangered Species Act helping an American icon recover to the point of no longer requiring the Act's protections. I grew up with a resident bald eagle pair that nested in our backyard, and every return to my childhood home is guaranteed several eagle sightings. In the summertime, my family alongside hordes of other of tourists would gasp over humpback whales in the Kenai Fjords and gray wolves in Denali National Park, two other iconic species that I might never have seen without the protections of the Endangered Species Act. Thus, first and foremost I speak as a concerned American about the negative cultural and economic impacts of weakening the Endangered Species Act.

Furthermore, as a professional ecologist, I know the scientific importance that the Endangered Species Act carries for protecting our country's beautiful plants and animals. As a scientist, I understand the data necessary for listing species for protection by the Endangered Species Act. We also know that the Endangered Species Act works—it has helped prevent the extinction of 99% of listed species. However, the proposed rules eschew science to the detriment of American values by allowing industrial desires to outweigh the biological realities that this country needs to ensure the cultural, economic, and innumerable ecological benefits of protecting endangered species.

Specifically, I am concerned that the Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)) will prevent habitat protection and instead allow short-term economic interests to override scientific understanding, to the detriment of not only protected species but entire ecosystems, which themselves are critical for American cultural values, recreation and economic growth, and the innumerable ecosystem services they provide.

The proposed rule change threatens democratic processes by reducing public accountability and ignoring science. Thus, as a concerned American citizen and as a concerned scientist, I urge the agency to maintain the Endangered Species Act's science-based protections and current successes by withdrawing this proposed rule.

See attached file for full comment and footnotes.

Attorneys for Animals, Inc. (AFA) is a Michigan non-profit and 501(c)(3) organization of legal professionals and animal advocates. Founded in the 1990s, we have actively followed legislation and agency actions in Michigan and on the federal level for many years. We carefully observe how the Endangered Species Act (ESA) provides protection to many species in the state.

We frequently attend the Michigan Natural Resources Commission monthly meetings and participate in public comments. As the animal welfare representative to the state’s statutorily mandated 7-member Wolf Management Advisory Council (2021-2022), we observed first-hand the outright hostility of some toward the ESA and toward the state’s Department of Natural Resources.

This is one of four proposed rules published by the Services on the same date. A complete discussion of our opposition to all four can be found in AFA’s Comment on the proposal to remove the “blanket rule”, Rule Docket Number FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, Comment Tracking Number mjh-tz3z-z6u5.

We oppose the proposed modification of the interagency cooperation rules because it:

•is prompted by political considerations rather than best available science
•does not meet Regulatory Planning and Review Standards

Politics not science:
The current administration’s Executive Orders and the Agency Order of Secretary Burgum put the agency in the unenviable position of being given a required outcome and then having to work backward to justify the proposed rule. This is made clear in the Service’s description of two Executive Orders and a Secretary’s Order under which guidance this proposed rule was formulated. What chance does a thorough and straightforward review of science have when the Service is taking its marching orders from an Executive Order titled “Unleashing America’s Energy"; another EO citing the (now dismantled) Department of Government Efficiency whose ideology is deregulation fn; and the Secretary’s blatant directive to “take steps, as appropriate, to suspend, revise, or rescind multiple actions that had been finalized under the prior Administration” fn

Not Consistent with Regulatory Planning and Review standards
The proposed rule states: E.O. 13563 emphasizes further that regulations must be based on the best available science and that the rulemaking process must allow for public participation and an open exchange of ideas. We have developed this proposed rule in a manner consistent with these requirements.(emphasis added)
We disagree with the conclusion. E.O. 13563 emphasizes that regulations must be based on the best available science and that the rulemaking process must allow for public participation and an open exchange of ideas. The Services state: “We have developed this proposed rule in a manner consistent with these requirements.” The process for developing the proposed rule, as discussed in the first section above, calls into question whether it “allow[s] for public participation and an open exchange of ideas,” (emphasis added) given that the Secretary has effectively dictated the outcome.

Conclusion
Critical habitat designation is crucial to the recovery of species listed under the ESA. Yet the proposed rule, under the guise of making the process more transparent, instead re-opens the door to prioritizing economic and political considerations over the biological needs, while contradicting the ESA’s purpose of conserving ecosystems and recovering species. The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species.
Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose of conserving ecosystems and species recovery.
For the reasons stated, we urge the Service to withdraw the Proposed Rule and restore the 2016 rule.
