Re: Comments on Proposed Rulemaking Regarding Designation of Critical Habitat Under the Endangered Species Act, Docket Number FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048

Dear Director Nesvik:

The Animal Welfare Institute (“AWI”), on behalf of our members and supporters nationwide, submits the following comments in strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (“USFWS” or “Service”) proposed rulemaking that would revise the Service’s regulations related to implementation of section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”), 15 U.S.C. §§ 1531, et seq. See 90 Fed. Reg. 52,592 (Nov. 21, 2025). The proposed rulemaking arbitrarily and capriciously reduces the conservation of habitat that is critical to species’ survival, which is contrary to the mandate and purpose of the ESA.

AWI is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to alleviate animal suffering caused by people. We seek to improve the welfare of animals everywhere: in agriculture, in commerce, in our homes and communities, in research, and in the wild. Since 1951, AWI has advanced its mission through strategically crafted policy and legal advocacy, educational programs, research and analysis, litigation, and engagement with policymakers, scientists, industry, educators, other NGOs, the media, and the public. We seek scientifically-grounded protections for animals in all settings, and robust enforcement of those protections.

Through this rulemaking, USFWS proposes to reinstate the “critical habitat exclusion rule” at 50 C.F.R. § 17.90, which was added to the ESA’s implementing regulations on December 18, 2020, and became effective in January 2021 (“Final Rule”). 85 Fed. Reg. 82,376 (Dec. 18, 2020); 86 Fed. Reg. 59,346 (Oct. 27, 2021). USFWS subsequently rescinded the rule in July 2022. 87 Fed. Reg. 43,433 (July 21, 2022). The Final Rule created non-discretionary procedures for undertaking critical habitat exclusion analyses under Section 4(b)(2) of the ESA. The Final Rule superseded the joint regulation on critical habitat exclusions contained in 50 C.F.R. § 424.19, and also superseded a 2016 policy (“2016 Policy”) issued jointly by USFWS and the National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively “the Services”).

The 2016 Policy articulated criteria for designating critical habitat for threatened and endangered species, and had broad implications for species’ recovery under the Act. Reports on the unprecedented rate of biodiversity loss in the United States and globally, which is primarily driven by habitat destruction,2 makes it clear that the areas the Services choose to protect, and the nature of those protections, are essential to preventing extinction and to ensuring the long-term security of species.

The Final Rule left areas that are essential to species’ recovery unprotected, undermining implementation of the goals and purposes of the ESA, and placing listed species in peril. AWI therefore strongly opposes USFWS’s proposed rule, which would reinstate the Final Rule, and urges USFWS to withdraw it. AWI opposes the proposed rule for four primary reasons: (1) the proposed language is less protective than the plain language of the ESA requires and reduces conservation of species’ habitat; (2) the proposed rule is arbitrary and capricious; (3) the proposed rule provides extractive industries with undue influence in the critical habitat designation process; and (4) critical habitat designations do not significantly reduce private development.

AWI specifically endorses and incorporates by reference the comments filed by the Southern Environmental Law Center on behalf of itself and numerous other public interest organizations, including AWI, on USFWS’s proposed rulemakings, Docket Numbers FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, as well as the comments filed by the Natural Resources Defense Council (“NRDC”) on behalf of itself and numerous other public interest organizations, including AWI, on USFWS’s proposed 4(b)(2) rulemaking, Docket Number FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048. We also incorporate by reference the comments AWI submitted on the proposed rulemaking that led to the Final Rule, 85 Fed. Reg. at 55,398.3.

For a full discussion of our opposition to the proposed rulemaking, please see the attached comments.

If you have any questions or if there is any additional information we can provide, please do not hesitate to contact us.

text: I have attached a peer-reviewed paper demonstrating the ESA's economic benefits prior to these rule changes. If the administration's rule change insists on presenting economic data alongside listing decisions, it must be a full accounting. It cannot just list the 'costs' to developers. It must also list the 'revenue' generated by the species through ecosystem services, tourism, recreation, water filtration, pest control, storm buffering, etc, etc. Presenting only the cost of protection without the Return on Investment (ROI) of preservation is financially illiterate and misleading to the public. The ESA has a fantastic return on investment by keeping animals and plants from going extinct. This not only provides long-term ecosystem services valued at trillions of dollars that compound like interest, but also drives tourism, from fishing and birding to nature photography and more. The rule that considers the short-term economic value of a commodity alongside scientific data, without the value stated above, when deciding whether to develop a habitat, is not well thought out, as it will allow the destruction of many other small economies surrounding a protected natural area. I am mostly retired from a long, demanding career in the business world and I enjoy spending time in nature. Going out into nature is getting harder and harder in my state of Florida, where habitats that should have been protected have been developed instead, and smaller businesses lose out from more failed habitats. Allowing habitat to be developed where endangered species temporarily live is the worst business decision you can make, and it shows very little regard for our future.

title: Comment from Converse County, Wyoming

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Linn County Oregon comments in support of this proposed rule. The Endangered Species Act requires the consideration of the economic impact and other relevant impacts of designating any particular area as critical habitat, and allowing for the exclusion of areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating an area critical habitat.

The proposed revision of the regulations to articulate when and how a determination is made whether the benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating the area as critical habitat, would better allow the appropriate consideration of the impacts on local economies and other impacts for rural jurisdictions such as Linn County.

Re: Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat.

The Museum of Life and Science respectfully submits the following comments on Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat. Since the enactment of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the Museum of Life and Science has been a partner with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) in some of the most challenging and successful recovery efforts, including saving the American Red Wolf from extinction. We are concerned that this proposal will needlessly complicate and delay species protections.

The Museum of Life and Science is an accredited member/partner of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA), a 501(c) (3) nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing zoos and aquariums in animal care and welfare, conservation, education, science, and guest experience. AZA members, including the Museum of Life and Science, are the foremost authorities and practitioners of animal care, well-being, husbandry, conservation, and research.

Timing: On Friday, December 5, AZA requested an extension of time to submit comments on this proposal and the three additional proposals published by the USFWS, either individually or jointly with the National Marine Fisheries Service (Services), on the same day. These proposals, individually and collectively, represent potentially significant changes to ESA implementation and to the conservation of endangered and threatened species and the ecosystems on which they and we depend. Clearly, the Services have put substantial time and effort into considering these proposed changes. Your conservation partners deserve the same.

AZA requested an extension of the comment period to allow a total of 120 days for the public and your partners to consider these changes.

Process: We have two substantial process concerns regarding this proposal and the additional three proposals.

First, the timing issue described above. Thirty days during the holiday season to comment on a matter of this potential magnitude, especially when it is coterminous with three other potentially significant and related proposals, is concerning.

Second, publishing these proposals individually complicates and undermines the public's and your partners' ability to understand the comprehensive vision for and impact of these proposed changes. By proposing them individually, you have seemingly absolved yourselves of the responsibility to explain the vision and its impact thoroughly. This is concerning.

Purpose: The Endangered Species Act establishes the purpose of your work, and therefore, your obligation. Paraphrased, that purpose is to conserve endangered and threatened species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. Neither this proposal nor any of the three coterminous proposals provides any explanation of how they will forward that purpose. Absent such an explanation, we are concerned that the effect may be the opposite.

Regarding this specific proposal, we are concerned that the ongoing use of terms such as “foreseeable future” and the procedures for considering occupied and unoccupied habitats introduce unnecessary confusion and invite litigation that will ultimately frustrate species conservation. For example, is it significant for the agency to consider unoccupied habitat in a two-step process rather than a simultaneous one? It is difficult to argue with the logic that unoccupied habitat need not be considered if currently occupied habitat is “sufficient” to conserve the species. However, it seems incomplete and potentially detrimental to halt further analysis at a point when, based on current circumstances and knowledge, the occupied habitat is deemed sufficient.

We believe the better approach is to identify and consider all areas that contain the physical or biological features essential to the species' conservation.
We support your proposed language, which expands the Services’ flexibility in making “not prudent” determinations. Critical habitat designations are scientifically and legally complex. We think the agencies deserve appropriate discretion, and we support this aspect of your proposal.

To Whom It May Concern,

This comment is in reference to Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048.
We are firmly and unequivocally opposed to this regulatory change regarding critical habitat. We represent tens of thousands of supporters and donors who stand firmly against this regulatory change.

The NYC Plover Project is a non-profit organization founded in March 2021 to protect threatened and endangered species, preserve natural coastal ecosystems, and engage diverse New Yorkers to help safeguard these natural areas and the species that call them home. We are dedicated to the protection of the federally-threatened Atlantic Coast Piping Plover, the only federally-listed bird species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 to be found nesting in New York City. The mission of the NYC Plover Project is to protect endangered Piping Plovers and other fragile beach-nesting birds on New York City’s beaches through education, community engagement, and volunteer stewardship.

We have implemented a volunteer program with 500+ volunteers who have worked more than 18,000 hours of service in our city’s public green spaces. In 2022, the National Park Service and the National Park Foundation bestowed the George and Helen Hartzog Award for Outstanding Volunteer Service, “Volunteer Group of the Year” for the entire nation, to the NYC Plover Project.

With regard to this regulatory change, critical habitat is often the only way species retain the physical and biological features essential for recovery. When speaking of the species we know most, the Piping Plover, this species cannot survive without the unequivocal protection of its habitat.

Bringing this rule back from the past will give extractive and environmentally-damaging industries a pass to exclude habitat and make dollars and cents, not science, what drives the decision. What’s more is that this will greatly reduce the size of critical habitat designations and undermine the entire planning process.

This regulatory change, as you well know, goes against the will of the American people. With nine out of ten Americans supporting a strong and intact ESA, across the political spectrum, this runs contrary to the fundamental American ideal of protecting wildlife and open spaces.

The ESA was signed into law in 1973 to protect ecosystems and our most fragile species, not to create a highway of convenience for big industry to run roughshod over our laws. It is the Service’s role to base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns.

As wildlife biologists and scientists, we all know that habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction; weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects. The rule must be withdrawn from consideration.

Sincerely,

Chris Allieri
Executive Director
NYC Plover Project

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Re: Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat

The Oregon Zoo respectfully submits these comments in opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (USFWS) proposed revisions to the Secretary of the Interior’s process for designating critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As a leader in wildlife conservation and a long-standing partner in species recovery and conservation with the USFWS, the Oregon Zoo is concerned that the proposed rule directly undermines the statutory purpose and Congressional intent of the ESA by expanding the Secretary of Interior’s discretion to weigh economic interests in different ways than biological and conservation criteria when designating critical habitat for newly listed species.

For over 30 years, the Oregon Zoo has collaborated with USFWS and other partners to recover endangered species like the California condor through breeding programs. This recovery effort depends not only on direct species management as well as designating and protecting critical habitat that is essential for long-term species survival.

Congress recognized that habitat loss is the leading cause of species decline and for that reason, established critical habitat designations as a core mechanism to conserve the physical and biological features that are essential to species recovery. Decades of scientific research clearly demonstrates that critical habitat designations are an effective tool for recovering listed species by protecting the places where they live.

By introducing additional discretion and allowing economic interests to be weighed more heavily than biological and physical considerations during the critical habitat designation process, the proposed rule risks delaying, narrowing, or preventing critical habitat designations at the very moment when newly listed species are most vulnerable to further habitat degradation.

For these reasons, the Oregon Zoo stands with the American conservation community and respectfully urges the USFWS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety and retain the existing framework for designating critical habitat, which appropriately centers the best available science and conservation-focused statutory purpose of the ESA. Critical habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled listed species a meaningful chance at recovery.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Heidi Rahn, Director, Oregon Zoo

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I am reaching out today to express my opposition to the proposed rule regarding critical habitat exclusions. The revised framework the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has introduced would ultimately make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat, authorizing exclusions if the potential national security and economic benefits outweigh the benefits associated with protection.

This poses a particular threat to currently unoccupied historic habitat. Even if these areas are unoccupied now, they have the potential to support species survival, recovery, and longevity in the future. Paving the way for their destruction and degradation would be a massive mistake—one that inevitably drives future extinction and biodiversity loss.

Please protect these lands and the species they support by abandoning this harmful rule.

title: Comment from Cardile, Rebecca

text:
The Services should not reinstate 17.90(a) and the Services and Secretaries should not consider economic or "other relevant impact" when designating Critical Habitat. Critical Habitat is, as it is named and defined, critical to the ongoing survival of the listed species. The entire point of the Act is to preserve species as a long-term goal of Congress as a priority over short-term economic gain. The allowance of consideration of economic or other impacts is antithetical to the purpose of the Act. There will always be some economic or other impact of Critical Habitat designation. It is irrelevant to the main Act objective of ensuring the continued existence of listed species. Including exclusions for national security reasons is prudent because it may be a human life or death consideration, where economic and other relevant impacts are not critical or urgent to human life.

Proposed paragraph (c)(2) opens the Act to individual interference by including circumstance (1) "when a proponent of excluding the area has presented credible information in support of the request." This appears to allow any individual or organization to require the Services to reevaluation designation decisions. This could lead to well-known obstructive practices as regularly observed in abusive uses of the California Environmental Quality Act. Proposed paragraph (c)(2) also confers too much discretion to a single person, the Secretary, to decide if an exclusion analysis is warranted. The decision should be made based on a defined process based on the best available science and not at the sole discretion of a single person. The Services should not reinstate 17.90(c).

Consistent with my comment not to reinstate 17.90(c), the Services should not reinstate paragraph (d). Particularly counter to the purposes of the Act is the proposal to consider exclusion based on economic or other relevant considerations. The administrative or transactional costs associated with consultation should have no bearing on decisions and designations made pursuant to the Act, though the Services should seek to minimize costs and streamline processes. Similarly, project modifications necessary to avoid destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat is essential to the purposes of and definitions in the Act and cannot be excluded or avoided based on costs. The necessary modifications reflect the true cost of the action when ongoing survival of a listed species is accounted for, as required by the Act. If the action becomes too costly by avoiding causing the extinction of a species, then the Act is fulfilling its intent and purpose. Although the paragraph discussing these considerations states that the costs "can be divided into two types," a third type is stated discussing the "opportunity cost associated with projects and activities." Opportunity costs is not defined and I presume it to mean that designation of critical habitat may preclude exploitation of a resource for economic gain, such as inability to construct a mine or conduct logging operations due to critical habitat designation. The idea that economic exploitation of resources should trump the continuing existence of a listed species runs entirely counter the intent and purposes of the Act and should not be included. Similarly, the concept of avoiding the costs of going through consultation process required by the Act being grounds for exclusion from designation of Critical Habitat is entirely antithetical to the intent and purposes of the Act and should not be reinstated.

The Services should not reinstate paragraph (e) that again gives too much discretionary power to one person, the Secretary, rather than the process and scientific evidence and, as commented above, the Secretary should not consider economic and other relevant impacts when making critical habitat designation decisions.

title: Comment from Murphy, Stephen

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.
title: Comment from Herd, Dani

text:
The Endangered Species Act is a landmark piece of legislation that protects wildlife in the United States. Hundreds of species have been saved from the brink of extinction, many ecosystems have been restored with the work of conservationists, and the economy has benefited from the initiation of projects and an increase in job opportunities for those invested in saving the animals that they love.

The proposed changes will not only put thousands of species at risk for extinction, but they are also not based on significant scientific evidence. While the economic impact of certain projects or developments may be considered, they should not be placed over the lives of thousands of individuals who depend on the current resources they have available. This proposal can lead to fewer critical-habitat designations, reduce protections of habitats, and shift the framework of land management in the wrong direction.

I implore the Fish & Wildlife Service to reconsider its decision and not go through with the proposals that have been put forward. We need to continue preserving wildlife to maintain healthy ecosystems and facilitate the influential processes on this Earth; these proposals are clearly not what will help us move in that direction.

For more than five decades, the Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation’s most effective conservation tools, preventing 99% of listed species from disappearing forever. I am deeply concerned that the proposed rule change—allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to prioritize economic interests over habitat conservation—would undermine the ESA’s legacy and jeopardize the future of vulnerable species.

Critical habitat designations are grounded in science, not economics. Species like wolverines, which rely on large, connected landscapes, cannot recover if their habitats are carved up by development, drilling, and mining. Opening the door for economic considerations to override biological needs abandons established legal precedent and weakens the very purpose of the ESA.

Protecting imperiled species means protecting the ecosystems they depend on. This proposed rule would create unnecessary loopholes, accelerate habitat loss, and put countless species at greater risk.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this rule change and reaffirm its commitment to strong, science-based habitat protections. The ESA’s original mandate—conserving endangered species and the ecosystems essential to their survival—must remain intact if we are serious about safeguarding America’s wildlife for future generations.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

text:

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Smith, Emily

text:
I am reaching out today to express my opposition to the proposed rule regarding critical habitat exclusions. The revised framework the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has introduced would ultimately make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat, authorizing exclusions if the potential national security and economic benefits outweigh the benefits associated with protection.

This poses a particular threat to currently unoccupied historic habitat. Even if these areas are unoccupied now, they have the potential to support species survival, recovery, and longevity in the future. Paving the way for their destruction and degradation would be a massive mistake—one that inevitably drives future extinction and biodiversity loss.

Please protect these lands and the species they support by abandoning this harmful rule.

title: Comment from Brown, Pat

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Canessa, Laura

text:
The Endangered Species Act of 1973 has been protecting critical habitats and species for 50+ years and in that time it has been integral in maintaining and protecting species that actually help with our economic prosperity. It has been proven over and over in scientific studies and ongoing research that when we protect critical species and their ecosystems, the benefits are far-reaching when it comes to the sustainability of overall regions and bigger picture land management, including commercial needs. For example, research that was fomented by ESA protects has come to reveal that endangered southern sea otters (which were over hunted for commerce) are keystone species. Their ability to garden kelp forests and estuaries means they keep the balance of the ecosystems in check. Invasive and voracious green crabs have ruined commercial fishing areas from Washington state and are heading south; with a potentially devastating financial impact on local fishermen, their communities and local economies.
But studies done on introduced otters and their feeding on green crabs revealed them to be the only effective deterrent to the species growth of these damaging crabs. With otters introducing them into their normal feeding routines, green crabs infestation finally had a nature-based management system that humans can’t replicate.
When the ESA protects species, it can wholesale save human industries, restore eco-balance by allowing natural species to correct what humans have done, and continue to do, to disrupt in nature. Green crabs came with human fishing and accidental transplanting of this invasive species.
And there are thousands of other examples where nature can correct major problems, but that’s IF we protect ESA species and keep them vital. Rampant deregulation and business first models are good for the 1% only and temporarily. In the end, the resources taken from nature without care for impact will ruin those businesses too. Thoughtless commercial leaders can’t take their wealth with them. Their corporate shareholder gains-first legacies ruin what they leave behind so they can’t be trusted to not have guardrails like the ESA. It’s only because of ESA protections that entire ecosystems remain, that there are beautiful spaces for rich people to build homes with views or unspoiled wilderness to appreciate.
The designation of critical habitat has the word “critical” in it for a reason. There’s a red line we can’t cross with these species. When we didn’t have the ESL, we created mass extinction situations that continue to have negative impacts. Protection laws like these were passed to make sure we sustain balance and protect the smallest species even when it’s financially inconvenient. Our world is on the precipice of monumental decline with climate change and corporate deregulation so the ESA is not only critical for the USA to remain competitive through its managed resources, but it’s a moral necessity for a human world with less and less conscience about creating and maintaining environmental balance.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Farr, Andrew

text:
I am reaching out today to express my opposition to the proposed rule regarding critical habitat exclusions. The revised framework the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has introduced would ultimately make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat, authorizing exclusions if the potential national security and economic benefits outweigh the benefits associated with protection.

This poses a particular threat to currently unoccupied historic habitat. Even if these areas are unoccupied now, they have the potential to support species survival, recovery, and longevity in the future. Paving the way for their destruction and degradation would be a massive mistake—one that inevitably drives future extinction and biodiversity loss.

Please protect these lands and the species they support by abandoning this harmful rule.

title: Comment from Woodman, Jennifer

text: I strongly oppose this proposed rule change. It would ensure that political influence and economic gains bypass both scientific reality and biological need. This document would impede federal oversight of agency actions and allow destructive projects to be green-lighted before all data is assessed and the comprehensive impact presented. Since 1978, the ESA has automatically given threatened species the same protections as endangered species unless tailored rules are in place. This blanket protection was how species were prevented from sliding off the cliff into extinction while the Fish & Wildlife Service figured out the specific protections the species needed. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans and it needs to remain intact!
title: Comment from Larson, Kurt

text:
For more than half a century, the Endangered Species Act has stood as one of our nation’s most successful conservation laws—protecting 99% of listed species from extinction. As a committed advocate for America’s wildlife and the irreplaceable ecosystems they call home, I strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change. It disregards decades of legal precedent, contradicts the best available science, and undermines Congress’s original intent by creating dangerous loopholes that would allow critical habitat to be excluded when species need it most.

The Endangered Species Act is more than a policy—it is a promise. A promise that we will safeguard not only vulnerable species, but the habitats and ecological systems that support life across our country. Weakening this commitment threatens to accelerate species decline and compromises the very foundation of the ESA.

I respectfully call on the Administration to withdraw the proposed rule and reaffirm its dedication to the ESA’s core mission: protecting endangered species and preserving the ecosystems essential to their recovery. Robust, science-driven habitat protections are indispensable if we are to give imperiled wildlife a meaningful chance to survive and thrive.

title: Comment from Brown, Olivia

text:
strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: As a citizen of the US, I oppose this rewrite of the Endangered and Threatened Species Act. Affording protections to species deemed endangered or threatened not only saves species from extinction, but creates great success stories in the world of conservation. To repeal or rewrite the act in a way that affords less protections would go against the wishes of the majority of voters, and is an insult to conservationists and anyone who has felt encouraged by recent conservation success stories. Furthermore, rushing these changes with such a short comment period is unfair and undemocratic, and will deny many voting citizens the right to read and comment on the proposal. Please listen to voters, both professionals working in conservation, and citizens with an interest in nature, and give us a say in our own country's rules and regulations.

title: Comment from Danner, Annette

text:
I am submitting my two cents as biodiversity and a healthy ecosystem is not only just important to me on a fundamental level but substantially so for the world we live and breathe today.

As someone who lives in Georgia and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss due to constructions and other human blights, we do not need to weaken our already in place environment laws for the good of industry influence.

The Endangered Species Act works it centers around science and public interest at heart- not political influence or economic pressure. The scientific values determine whether we chose to protect said species and what they need to survive and thrive... these rules that are trying to be implemented take away the decision-making from both subjects and would allow industry considerations outweigh both biological needs and scientific reality.

Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed that could ultimately lessen the diversity of this country.

Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.

Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests.

With all this in mind, A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.

Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems that will continue on and leave a lasting legacy for the kids.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Lehman, Nanette

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. Although the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress meant for this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an unreasonably high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This directly contradicts the ESA’s intentional precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, such as private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Landry, Hayley

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Staby, Paul

text:
Protecting threatened species is not optional—it is a core promise built into the Endangered Species Act, and the blanket rule is essential to upholding Congress’s original intent. Weakening this safeguard would leave already-vulnerable species exposed to avoidable decline. Likewise, the proposed interagency cooperation rule would undermine the very heart of the ESA by shifting its focus from conservation to convenience, allowing commercial interests to overshadow the urgent needs of imperiled wildlife.
Critical habitat is the foundation of species recovery, especially as climate change accelerates habitat loss through drought, fires, shrinking snowpack, and vanishing rivers. Reducing habitat protections or narrowing the definition of “harm” ignores the reality that species cannot rebound without the space and resources to survive. With hundreds of species still waiting for protection—and many having already endured years of delay—now is the time to strengthen safeguards, not weaken them.
Excluding habitat to accommodate profit-driven development disregards both ecological science and public support. Americans overwhelmingly back strong wildlife protections because extinction is permanent; once a species disappears, it is gone forever. To hollow out the ESA is to unravel the biological foundations of a healthy planet. We must defend critical habitat, reject rollbacks, and honor our responsibility to protect the species that depend on us for their very survival.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Honorable officials,

The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.  

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.  

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Respectfully,
Caleb Merendino

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Stauffer, Ellen

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
