title: Comment from Pierce, Kathleen

text:
Subject: Protect Our Wildlife—Do Not Weaken the Endangered Species Act

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

As a concerned citizen, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, (and signed into law by a Republican) the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

I staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: I oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: I reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: I oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: I oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for this country's iconic species.

I call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,
Brett Ochs, Boulder, CO

title: Comment from Starr, Danielle

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Vollmer, Terry

text: The proposed Endangered Species Act rulemakings will dramatically weaken protections for the nation’s most vulnerable species. These changes undermine the ESA’s core requirement that the designation of critical habitat be based on best available science. Congress enacted the ESA to provide a comprehensive, science-based framework for protecting imperiled species and the ecosystems they depend on. It is unacceptable to prioritize economic interests over science when extinction and ecosystems are on the line. We need to fight the exploitation of our ecosystems. Habitat loss is the leading driver of species declines worldwide. Habitat protection must be strengthened, not restricted! The ESA’s greatest successes — the recovery or down-listing of species like the bald eagle, peregrine falcon, and many others — have come through strong habitat protection, restoration, and conservation, not merely preventing direct killing. As habitat loss accelerates in the U.S. and globally, weakening habitat protections will push more species toward extinction. I urge the agencies to withdraw these changes and retain the science-based regulations that have helped prevent extinctions for more than 50 years. Thank you for your attention.‌‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿‍ ‍﻿‍ ﻿ ‍ ﻿

Additionally, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Jones, Jaden

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was NOT to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I strongly oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction.  Protection of a species that is struggling to survive is NOT debatable.
With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes, both individually and collectively, will significantly weaken the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.

1. **Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule**: The ESA is intended to preempt severe species decline. The 4(d) rule, grounded in scientific evidence, shows that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent species decline. Removing these default protections will cause harmful delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking, and expose species to unnecessary risks. This opposes the ESA’s preventive nature, leading to increased ecological and financial burdens over time.

2. **Incorporating Economic Considerations**: Listing decisions under the ESA must rely solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors undermines scientific integrity and risks delaying protections until species face extinction. Ignoring future threats like climate change contradicts conservation science, making timely listings less likely and increasing extinction risks.

3. **Reducing Habitat Protections**: Habitat loss is the primary cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations and narrowing the definition of “harm” reverses legal and scientific precedents. These changes risk ineffective inter-agency consultations and contradict the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Creating Loopholes for ESA Protection Bypass**: Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is possible, conflicts with the ESA’s purpose. Such loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from scientific analysis, adversely affecting vulnerable species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

**Cumulative Impact**: If implemented, these proposals would undermine the scientific basis of the ESA, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation amid climate change, heighten extinction risks, weaken agency cooperation, and increase long-term taxpayer costs.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, driven by science, precaution, and early action. At a time of global biodiversity loss, we should be strengthening, not weakening, this crucial wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all proposed rule changes and the maintenance of the current regulatory framework, which is rooted in science, legal precedent, and proven success.

Thank you for considering my comments.
title: Comment from Gutierrez, Betty

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being reviewed. Each proposal—both individually and collectively—would significantly undermine the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and preserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA is intended to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and avert further declines. Eliminating automatic protections would create unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to greater ecological and financial costs in the future.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA clearly states that listing decisions should be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Including economic factors—either directly or indirectly—would contradict statutory language, undermine scientific integrity, and risk delaying necessary protections. Restricting the use of projected threats disregards conservation science, showing that slow-burn pressures like habitat loss and climate change put species at risk before population declines are visible. Weakening these criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listings and increases preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a primary driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations—especially for unoccupied areas essential for recovery—undermines planning efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” so habitat degradation isn’t recognized would reverse long-standing scientific and legal precedent. Weakening these definitions would hinder inter-agency consultations, increase biological risk, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections—even with potential extinction outcomes—contradicts the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines in already vulnerable species.

Cumulative Impact of These Proposals

Collectively, these proposals would:
- Weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay protections for species in need,
- Reduce habitat conservation during accelerating climate change,
- Increase extinction risks,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction and is successful due to its foundation in science and early action. At a time of biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening—not weakening—its most effective conservation law.

Request

Based on these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and retain the current framework grounded in science and legal precedent.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Porfiri, Dave

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Subject:Strong Opposition to Proposed Rule Modifying Exclusionary Authority for Designating Critical Habitat (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries,
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would modify the process for excluding areas from critical habitat designation based on economic impact (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048).
My opposition is rooted in conservation biology, economic principles related to ecosystem services valuation, and the mandate of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) to make decisions based fundamentally on the best available science, not economic expediency.
Arguments & Analysis: Prioritizing Economic Impact Over Biological Necessity
The core of my argument focuses on how the proposed change would elevate short-term economic costs above the long-term, irreversible biological necessity of preserving critical habitat.

Undermining the Biological Mandate: The ESA is designed to conserve ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend. Decisions regarding what constitutes critical habitat must be based solely on scientific data about species needs and recovery potential. The current framework allows for exclusions, but the proposed rule seeks to broaden and prioritize the consideration of economic impacts, effectively allowing economic concerns to override biological imperatives. This contradicts the scientific mandate of the Act.
The Incalculable Value of Ecosystem Services: Standard economic analyses often struggle to quantify the full value of ecosystem services (e.g., clean water filtration, pollination, flood control) provided by healthy, conserved habitats. By prioritizing direct, localized economic costs (e.g., development revenue) over these holistic ecosystem values, the Service risks making decisions that are net negative for society in the long run. Statistics consistently show that the economic value of preserved ecosystem services often exceeds the short-term development value they replace.
Statistical Risk of Irreversible Harm: The designation of critical habitat is strongly correlated with species recovery. A meta-analysis of listed species recoveries has shown that species with designated critical habitat are more than twice as likely to be recovering than those without it. Increasing the ease with which essential habitat can be excluded for development significantly increases the statistical risk of habitat fragmentation and species decline, leading to irreversible biodiversity loss.
Creating a Precedent for Habitat Loss: The proposed rule creates a dangerous precedent that financial interests can consistently bypass scientific recommendations for vital conservation areas. This is poor public policy and a misuse of economic analysis that fails to account for the catastrophic cost of extinction.

Conclusion & Recommendation
The proposed changes to the critical habitat exclusion process prioritize incomplete short-term economic metrics over robust, long-term biological necessities and ecosystem function. This rule is fundamentally inconsistent with the scientific principles required to protect species from extinction.
I respectfully request that you withdraw the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) and maintain the rigorous, science-first standard for designating critical habitat, ensuring that the biological needs of imperiled species remain the paramount consideration.
Sincerely,
Lisa Conner
Concerned Citizen & Conservationist
Gig Harbor WA 98335

text:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment because healthy ecosystems and strong wildlife protections matter deeply to me. The continued decline in genetic diversity among Mexican gray wolves is only one example of how urgently imperiled species need science-based safeguards.

The proposed rule changes weaken the Endangered Species Act by undermining the scientific standards and democratic accountability that have made the law effective. The ESA works because decisions are grounded in evidence and insulated from political or economic pressure. These proposals shift decision-making away from that foundation.

Removing automatic protections for newly listed species would leave vulnerable wildlife exposed at the moment they most need support. Ending the blanket 4(d) rule risks inconsistent and delayed protections for threatened species. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to outweigh biological necessity, putting entire ecosystems at risk. Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
Certainly! Here's a rephrased version:

---

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my firm opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both individually and as a whole, threatens to notably weaken the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding in species recovery, and preserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA's intent is to act before species reach critical danger. The longstanding 4(d) rule, supported by extensive scientific research, shows that proactive protection reduces overall recovery costs and prevents further declines. Removing these default protections will cause undue delays, necessitating individual rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, exposing vulnerable species to unnecessary harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose, leading to greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Complicating species listing by incorporating economic considerations and weakening future threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best scientific data available, excluding economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations, even indirectly, would contradict the law’s language, compromise scientific impartiality, and risk postponing protections until species are nearly extinct. Additionally, ignoring projected or climate-driven threats overlooks conservation science, which indicates slow-burn pressures like habitat loss and rising temperatures pose risks long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria decreases the likelihood of timely listings, increasing the risk of avoidable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline in both the U.S. and globally. Limiting critical habitat designations, especially those crucial for long-term recovery, undermines recovery strategies. Similarly, redefining “harm” to exclude habitat degradation would overturn decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. Narrowing these definitions would weaken inter-agency consultations, heighten biological risk, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Introducing loopholes for agencies or committees to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, contradicts the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes encourage case-by-case exemptions, reduce transparency, and remove decision-making from a science-based approach. This could have a disproportionate impact on species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines in already threatened species.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

While each proposal is concerning on its own, collectively they would:
• Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• Delay or block necessary species protections,
• Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
• Heighten extinction risks for both domestic and international species,
• Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• Increase taxpayer recovery costs in the long run.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, highlighting its success as a science-based, precautionary law. These proposed changes contradict these principles.

In this era of rapid biodiversity loss, strengthening, rather than weakening, our most effective wildlife protection law is imperative.

Request

Given these reasons, I strongly urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing, scientifically and legally grounded regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from M, Phoebe

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from S., Jithendra

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to all four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under consideration. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, threatens to significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and conserve the vital ecosystems upon which both wildlife and human communities depend.

1. **Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species**

The ESA was designed to intervene before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule, backed by decades of scientific evidence, has proven that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending these default protections would cause delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking for protections currently automatic, and expose threatened species to unnecessary risks. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose, leading to higher ecological and financial costs long-term.

2. **Introducing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations undermines scientific objectivity and risks delaying protections until species are nearly extinct. Ignoring future or climate-related threats disregards current conservation science indicating that issues like habitat loss and climate change elevate species risk well before population declines are evident. Weakening criteria for future threats reduces timely listings, increasing preventable extinction risks.

3. **Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Narrowing the Definition of “Harm”**

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Limiting critical habitat designations—especially for essential unoccupied or climate-refugia areas—weakens recovery efforts. Narrowing “harm” definitions so habitat degradation isn’t included reverses established legal and scientific standards, as habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife. This would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations, heightening biological risks and conflicting with the ESA’s recovery objectives.

4. **Creating Loopholes Allowing Bypasses of ESA Protections**

Expanding agencies’ abilities to override ESA protections—even with potential extinction risks—conflicts with the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes encourage exemptions on a project-by-project basis, reduce transparency, and divert decision-making from science-based analyses. Such changes disproportionately impact species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, further threatening already vulnerable populations.

**Cumulative Impact of the Proposals**

Together, these proposals threaten to:
- Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation.
- Delay or block crucial species protections.
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change.
- Increase extinction risk for both domestic and international species.
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation.
- Inflate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, grounded in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes oppose those foundational principles. Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening, not weakening, its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes entirely and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is rooted in science, legal precedents, and decades of effective implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Futrell, Sherrill

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes would significantly weaken protections for endangered and threatened species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA created strong, science-based safeguards, including the prohibition on “take,” the requirement that federal agencies ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species, and the development of recovery plans for at-risk species.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum has stated that these revisions “restore the Endangered Species Act to its original intent” by providing “clear, consistent and lawful standards” that respect the livelihoods of Americans. However, the purposes of the ESA, as written in the statute, do not support weakening core protections. Congress explicitly stated that the Act exists to conserve ecosystems upon which species depend; to provide programs for the conservation of endangered and threatened species; and to implement relevant treaties for species protection.

Congress also made clear findings when passing the ESA:

Many species in the United States have already been rendered extinct due to economic growth and development carried out without adequate conservation;

Other species have been so depleted that they are now endangered or threatened; and

These species hold esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value for the nation.

The original legislative intent was not to lessen regulatory burdens on industries whose activities jeopardize biodiversity. Instead, it was to ensure that economic activity is tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” The proposed rules contradict this intent by undermining basic protections for threatened and endangered species and by narrowing the definition and use of critical habitat.

I oppose these rule changes, which would deprive newly listed threatened species of automatic protections against killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species currently being considered for listing—such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage-grouse, and Monarch butterfly—could remain unprotected for years even after federal listing decisions. The impacts extend to species not yet identified, including the roughly 80% of insect species still unnamed.

The Earth is experiencing an accelerating extinction crisis. Addressing this crisis requires strong, science-based ESA regulations, not weakened ones. I urge the agency to withdraw the proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s longstanding, effective protections.

title: Comment from Creighton, Kayleigh

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Paddock, Cheryl

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Davis, Patti

text:
I strongly object to the proposed changes to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. Although the ESA allows for the exclusion of areas from critical habitat when the benefits of doing so outweigh the benefits of their designation, Congress intended this authority to be rarely used and only when exclusion wouldn’t lead to extinction. The new rule wrongly places economic considerations above biological needs, demanding that economic impacts be prioritized even when they are speculative or secondary.

The rule also sets an unacceptably high standard for retaining habitat by suggesting areas should be excluded unless it can be proven that this would cause extinction. This change undermines the ESA’s precautionary approach and contradicts its protective goals. Courts have consistently interpreted that critical habitat designations should focus on recovery, not just preventing extinction.

Additionally, the rule seems to disproportionately favor non-biological interests, like those of private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring the same scientific rigor. This risks turning the exclusion process into a means for regulated entities to overturn scientific judgment—a result Congress explicitly intended to prevent by removing economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to discard these revisions and uphold a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions are rare, justified, and secondary to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text: I oppose these proposed changes that would weaken critical habitat designations for threatened and endangered species.  Biodiversity, wildlife, and healthy ecosystems have value in and of themselves to myself and many Americans, who overwhelmingly support the ESA and oppose weakening it.  Protecting large areas of suitable habitat from development and extraction is vital for the survival of many threatened and endangered species.  For example, wolverines, a recently listed threatened species, have specific habitat requirements (high elevations, deep snowpack in winter and early spring, boreal/coniferous forest) and are vulnerable to changing seasonal and climate conditions.   Prioritizing industry in the critical habitat decision-making process is problematic because the interests of extractive industry can be at odds with the based available science (such as science that tells us wolverines are vulnerable to climate change and need large areas of connected habitat).  Habitat designations and recovery programs should also not be limited to the minimum viable populations necessary to prevent extinction of a species.  True recovery means that wolverines, Mexican gray wolves, hellbenders and other rare species can thrive and allow landscapes to benefit from the ecosystem services these species provide.  The ecological and environmental benefits of biodiversity should not be overlooked or sidelined in favor of corporate interests.  Democracy and the best available science, not industry or corporate interest, should guide protections for the wildlife who are in the public trust and enjoyed by all Americans.  The US Fish and Wildlife Service should uphold the intent of the ESA and strengthen, not weaken critical habitat protections for imperiled species.

title: Comment from CHERRY, JANE

text:
I am submitting this comment because our environment is extremely important. Health ecosystems and biodiversity matter deeply to me. It is our duty to protect all living creatures. The Endangered Species Act works because it is science based and it centers around those scientific findings and public interest. The proposed changes would be detrimental and it would allow considerations to outweigh biological need and scientific reality.
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
I urge to to please withdraw these proposed rules. We need to maintain the ESA's strong, science-based protections. Those protections need to be strengthen so federal safeguards will not allow states and industries to sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
Science must guide the decisions that are made about our wildlife. Corporations have to abide to those regulations and should not be allowed to influence.
title: Comment from Roman, Azucena

text:

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. title: Comment from cox, lanie

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.
I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.
We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Tess-Navarro, Jessica

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fulton, Stacey

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As an avid supporter of America’s wildlife (wildlife that makes our country healthy, beautiful, and magnificent), I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the current Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The ESA reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken (something President Theodore Roosevelt stood for). This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

This rule would only damage our country and the beautiful animals and spaces that make up our landscapes.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Kunc, Patrick

text:
I am submitting these comments because healthy and well-balanced biodiversity and ecosystems matter deeply to me. I live in the beautiful state of Montana and regularly see the effects of habitat loss, and I am extremely concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. This is the time to incorporate science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country and not allow your politics to drive the decisions.
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) works because it centers both science and the public interest, as it should, and NOT political pressure or economic influence. The science tells us what species need to survive, and values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
Proposals:
1)Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly-listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin; newly-listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed;
2)Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide;
3)Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species; and
4)Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

The only check on state wildlife systems is, oftentimes, on the federal level, which is already heavily shaped by industry interests. At a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections, which is evident in my state of Montana, these rollbacks reduce public accountability. Transparency is required for a science-backed and democratic science-based process, on which the ESA is founded.

In closing, I fervently encourage you to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections, post haste. It is my strong hope you will strengthen and not weaken the federal safeguards so states and the industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect endangered wildlife. Please uphold the intent of the ESA, which is to prevent extinction and ensure future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The repeated use of “national security” as a blanket justification for dismantling environmental safeguards is unacceptable. These proposed changes do not reflect sound science or the precautionary principles embedded in the Endangered Species Act; instead, they prioritize short-term political and economic agendas over the long-term health of ecosystems that sustain all life. The rationales offered—such as reducing “regulatory burdens” and increasing “efficiency”—mask the reality that these revisions will narrow critical habitat protections, allow economic considerations to influence listing decisions, and weaken interagency consultation standards, all of which undermine species recovery and ecosystem resilience. [fws.gov], [publicceo.com]
If adopted, this rule will accelerate habitat fragmentation, ignore cumulative impacts of authorized harm, and normalize incidental take as routine rather than exceptional, eroding accountability and conservation standards. Agencies appear to be functioning as conduits for political projects rather than independent stewards of wildlife and habitat. Species and ecosystems cannot defend themselves—our laws were designed to do that. Weakening them under vague pretexts like “national security” is not only contrary to congressional intent but also a direct threat to biodiversity and the ecological systems upon which we all depend.
title: Comment from Steward, Deborah

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Tucker, Holly

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

To whom it may concern:

As a board member of the Oregon Zoo Foundation, I write to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA has been our nation’s most effective tool to safeguard imperiled species and the ecosystems they depend on — protecting not only animals, but the interconnected habitats that sustain them.

Sincerely,

text: I am writing to strongly oppose the agency's proposed changes to section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act. Congress enacted the ESA to provide a comprehensive, science-based framework for protecting imperiled species and the ecosystems they depend on. It is unacceptable to prioritize economic interests over science when extinction is on the line. Habitat loss is the leading driver of species declines worldwide. Habitat protection must be strengthened and expanded, not restricted! The ESA's greatest successes -- the recovery or down-listing of species like the bald eagle, peregrine falcon, and many others -- have come through strong habitat protection, restoration, and conservation, not merely preventing direct killing. As habitat loss accelerates in the U.S. and globally, weakening habitat protections will push more species toward extinction. I urge the agencies to withdraw these changes and retain the science-based regulations that have helped prevent extinctions for more than 50 years.​​​​
title: Comment from Jenkins, Noah

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed revisions to Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Section 4(b)(2) ensures that decisions about designating critical habitat are guided by the best available science while also considering economic and other relevant impacts. This balanced, science-centered approach is essential for protecting species that are already at risk of extinction.

The proposed changes threaten to weaken the ability of federal agencies to designate critical habitat effectively. By expanding discretion to exclude areas from critical habitat or by placing greater weight on non-biological factors, these revisions risk prioritizing short-term economic considerations over the long-term survival and recovery of species. Such an approach contradicts the intent of the ESA, which was designed to prevent the loss of irreplaceable biodiversity and to ensure that species have the habitat they need to recover and thrive.

Critical habitat designation is one of the strongest and most effective tools for preventing extinction. Limiting or complicating the process undermines decades of conservation progress and places vulnerable species at even greater risk. Decisions about critical habitat must remain grounded in sound science, not in pressure to minimize protections.

For these reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed changes to ESA Section 4(b)(2). Protecting and restoring habitat is fundamental to species survival, and any revisions that weaken these safeguards are contrary to the purpose and success of the Endangered Species Act. I urge the agency to uphold the integrity of Section 4(b)(2) and maintain the strong, science-based protections that are essential for conserving our nation’s biodiversity.
