First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from ladnier, Jean

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from vandermeid, callie

text:
Section 4(b)(2): Critical habitat exclusion rule (only applies to FWS)  
Inherent in the success of the Act, is the condition that economic costs not be a factor in deciding whether to protect an animal.  
Under the new rules, efforts to save a species can occur if the price is right.

• Science and species conservation, not politics or money interests, should steer the designation of critical habitat.

We've already entered the 6th Mass Extinction and sadly humans have gone beyond the tipping point and are now included without regard for wildlife, future generations or the environment/mother earth.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from ODonnell, Lisa

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

My concern is twofold. First an foremost we are charged with the stewardship of the Earth and the creatures that live here. The reason that many of these species are endangered in the first place is that humanity has proven to be such a poor steward in the past. The second is that these recommended changes are obviously from the point of view of people who do not understand or care about the natural world and the people and animals who live here. They care about removing accountability to and making billionaires happy. This is not in the best interest of the people, only those in power who don't want to answer to the very people they are meant to serve.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Evan Niewoehner
Affiliation: Mystic Aquarium

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from E Michalak, Tina

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Heidi Hart-Zorin

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Respectfully submitted,

Pat Cheney

text:
Re: Critical Habitat Exclusions Rule (2025-20550)

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior,

I am a physician, wife and mother. I am an active hiker, mountain biker, and skier. Being in the outdoors – shared with plants and animals - has always been a vital part of my routine, for both physical and mental health. I believe strongly in advocacy for wild spaces and wildlife, as the creatures of this world do not have a voice at the political table. Sadly the biodiversity of our world is ever shrinking and many species of both plants and animals are threatened or endangered. The little biodiversity that remains relies fundamentally on protections such as the ESA.

I strongly oppose the revisions to ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above scientific and biological needs.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high threshold for protecting habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

Stop being so near-sighted and selfish! Do not give our future generations monocultures void of biodiversity. Do the right thing and oppose the revisions and maintain the 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified in science, and supportive of biodiversity.

Sincerely,
Robin Brown

title: Comment from Arens, Gina

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes would dramatically expand the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s ability to exclude areas from critical habitat designations—particularly in response to economic objections, energy-development pressures, or federal land user requests. Such a shift poses serious risks to the future of Gray Wolves and other imperiled species whose recovery depends on the protection of essential habitat.

Altering Section 4(b)(2) in this way would have significant negative implications for Gray Wolves. By removing or weakening key provisions that safeguard critical habitats from development or other disruptive uses, the proposed rule would sharply reduce the availability of the landscapes wolves need to thrive. Critical habitat is not optional for species survival—it provides the prey base, shelter, and space required for packs to establish territories, reproduce successfully, and maintain healthy population structures. Without these protected areas, wolves are far more vulnerable to human activity, habitat fragmentation, and ecological instability.

Gray Wolves are a keystone species, playing an indispensable role in maintaining the health, balance, and function of natural ecosystems. Their presence supports biodiversity, regulates prey populations, and helps preserve the ecological integrity of vast landscapes. Weakening protections for their habitat would not only jeopardize wolf recovery but also create cascading harm across entire ecosystems.

For these reasons, I urge you to reject the proposed revisions to Section 4(b)(2). Decisions regarding critical habitat must prioritize science, ecological need, and species recovery—not economic pressure or development interests. Maintaining strong, consistent habitat protections is essential to ensuring the long-term survival of Gray Wolves and the stability of the ecosystems they support.

Thank you for considering this comment and for your commitment to safeguarding our nation’s wildlife.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes that would weaken or narrow the designation of critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Critical habitat is foundational to recovery, not a regulatory afterthought.
Many threatened and endangered species are already restricted to small, degraded, or fire‑altered landscapes. Limiting critical habitat to areas currently occupied ignores ecological reality: species must be able to shift ranges in response to climate change, altered fire regimes, and human land use. In fire‑prone regions like California, recovery often depends on unoccupied but suitable habitat that supports post‑fire regeneration, refugia, and recolonization.

Excluding areas based on short‑term economic considerations undermines long‑term resilience.
Healthy ecosystems provide public benefits—fire mitigation, watershed protection, carbon storage, and pollinator support—that far outweigh narrow development gains. As someone engaged in wildfire education and native landscaping outreach, I have seen how intact habitats reduce risk to communities while supporting biodiversity.

Science and data support broader, forward‑looking habitat protection.
Advances in ecological modeling, remote sensing, and community science data allow us to identify areas essential for species recovery with increasing accuracy. Regulatory changes that constrain the use of best available science, or that prioritize current occupancy over ecological function, move policy in the opposite direction of where science clearly points.

The ESA has been successful precisely because it recognizes that species cannot survive without functioning ecosystems. Weakening critical habitat protections would erode one of the Act’s most effective tools at a time when biodiversity loss and climate stress are accelerating.

I respectfully urge the agency to maintain strong, science‑based criteria for designating critical habitat, including protection of unoccupied but suitable areas necessary for recovery and climate adaptation.

text:
“I am writing this comment because I strongly oppose the proposed regulatory changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA). For more than 50 years, the ESA has served as one of our nation’s most effective environmental laws, preventing the extinction of 99% of the species under its protection and helping recover iconic wildlife such as the bald eagle, gray whale, and American alligator. Weakening these safeguards now would put vulnerable species and the ecosystems we all depend on at serious risk.
The proposed rollbacks—such as reducing protections for newly listed threatened species, limiting the consideration of long-term climate impacts, and altering critical habitat rules—would undermine science-based decision-making. These changes prioritize short-term economic interests over the long-term health and stability of our environment. Endangered species protections are not just about wildlife; they safeguard clean water, healthy forests, resilient coastlines, and overall biodiversity that supports human wellbeing.
I urge the agency to reject these changes and maintain the full strength of the ESA. Instead of weakening protections, we should be improving science-based conservation strategies, supporting habitat restoration, and ensuring that federal decision-making fully reflects the best available evidence.
Please uphold the integrity of the ESA and protect our nation’s irreplaceable wildlife for future generations.
Thank you for your time,
Janna Bock

title: Comment from Callison, Mary

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.
I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.
We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from Burns, Amanda

text:
As a concerned citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to change the long-standing definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The current definition, supported by sound science and legal interpretation, appropriately recognizes that habitat modification and destruction can cause harm to threatened and endangered species. Excluding habitat modification from the definition of harm could drastically weaken one of the ESA’s most effective and widely used protections. Without question, this change could threaten the survival and recovery of endangered species, and could inadvertently fast track many species onto the list. Species we cannot afford to lose. Additionally, the recovery of listed species could become much more difficult and costly as more essential habitat could be impacted or lost. Protecting habitat is essential to avoid future ESA listings.

There is long-standing scientific documentation that habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the leading cause of species declines in the US and globally. It is not only over-harvesting or direct impacts to individual plants and animals that result in the decline of a species. The greatest threats – the degradation and loss of their habitat, critical feeding, sheltering, breeding, and/or nesting grounds – bring species to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, the current interpretation of the definition of harm, to include impacts to habitats, has been utilized by the USFWS for decades. This interpretation has even been upheld in a case before the US Supreme Court.

In Illinois, the survival of federally endangered species, like the Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), over a dozen mussel species, the Indiana (Myotis sodalis) and Northern Long-Eared Bat (Myotis septentrionalis), and the Rusty Patched Bumble Bee (Bombus affinis), are dependent on the ESA protections offered to these species, including protections to the habitats on which they depend. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the current definition of “harm” to ensure the continued protection of our nation’s most vulnerable wildlife.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Rush, Rebecca

text:
For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our nation’s most effective conservation laws, preventing the extinction of 99% of listed species. Central to that success is the designation of critical habitat based on the best available science.

The proposed rule change would undermine this foundation by allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to prioritize economic interests over the conservation needs of newly listed species. This represents a significant departure from longstanding legal precedent and Congressional intent. Species such as the wolverine, which depend on large, connected landscapes, are particularly vulnerable to habitat fragmentation caused by development, drilling, and mining. Weakening habitat protections will only accelerate their decline.

The ESA reflects our collective responsibility to protect not only imperiled species, but the ecosystems that sustain them. This proposed rule would erode that responsibility by creating loopholes that allow critical habitat to be excluded, even when such habitat is essential for species recovery.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and reaffirm its commitment to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered and threatened species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential if we are to give wildlife a real chance at recovery and uphold the intent of one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.
title: Comment from Chaffin, J

text:
I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under review. These changes, both individually and collectively, would dramatically weaken the ESA’s capacity to avert extinction, aid species recovery, and protect ecosystems essential for both wildlife and human communities.

The ESA is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.
Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S. In addition, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction and this is something to be proud of. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly support the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the continued protection of grizzly bears as a listed endangered species. The ESA is one of our nation’s most important and effective conservation laws, grounded in sound science and a responsibility to protect wildlife from irreversible harm. Weakening or circumventing its protections puts vulnerable species and ecosystems at unacceptable risk.

Grizzly bears remain threatened by habitat loss, fragmentation, climate impacts, and increased human conflict. Population recovery is fragile and uneven, and delisting would expose these iconic animals to greater danger before long-term, connected, and genetically healthy populations are secured. Decisions regarding their status must be based on rigorous science—not political or economic pressure.

Public lands play a critical role in the survival of grizzly bears and countless other species. These lands belong to all Americans and must be protected at all times and at all costs. Conservation, habitat connectivity, and responsible land management are essential not only for wildlife but for clean water, climate resilience, recreation, and future generations.

I urge decision-makers to uphold the Endangered Species Act, keep grizzly bears listed as an endangered species, and prioritize the permanent protection of public lands. Our natural heritage depends on strong, enforceable protections now and in the future.

title: Comment from Ackerman, Judith

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I request that you reject the proposed rules, which would:

**Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

**Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

**Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

**Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

Thank you.

Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

title: Comment from Chernak, Debi

text: I’m writing to ask our government to oppose any efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinction of 99 percent of listed species. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.

FWS should revert to the balanced 2016 policy or adopt an even stronger science-based approach.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Schmittauer, John

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Stephanie Hoban

title: Comment from STEFANIC, SHELLEY

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinction of 99 percent of listed species. As a devoted supporter of wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which would prioritize economic interests over the habitat protections imperiled species urgently need.

Critical habitat designations are fundamental to species recovery. Weakening these protections abandons decades of legal precedent, ignores the best available science, and undermines Congress’s original intent.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment not only to protecting imperiled species but also to conserving the ecosystems that sustain them. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
​​I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change regarding critical habitat criteria.

​​This revision would prioritize resource development over species protection, which is in direct contrast to the intent of the Endangered Species Act.

​​Weakening the critical habitat designation procedure would make it easier to exclude key habitats and avoid the requirement to mitigate impacts for activities that occur in these areas.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Loucks, Cynthia

text:
The proposed rule improperly prioritizes economic and political considerations over the biological needs of imperiled species. Reinstating this approach directly conflicts with the Endangered Species Act’s fundamental purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover endangered and threatened species to the point where the protections of the Act are no longer necessary.

Any exclusions or limitations under the ESA must be grounded in rigorous, peer-reviewed science—not economic speculation or political convenience. Habitat loss remains the primary driver of extinction worldwide, and weakening habitat protections undermines species recovery, ecosystem stability, and the long-term effectiveness of the Act.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should abandon this flawed rule and instead revert to the more balanced and scientifically sound 2016 policy, or adopt an even stronger, science-based framework that fully reflects the best available science. The ESA was designed to place conservation first, and its implementation must remain faithful to that mandate.
title: Comment from Families, Beal

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

title: Comment from Andary, Eric

text:
To Whom it may Concern,

I am in strong opposition to the suite of proposed rulemakings that would significantly weaken implementation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA)—one of our nation’s most effective and widely supported conservation laws. Collectively, these proposed changes would shift the ESA away from science-based, precautionary conservation and toward increasingly discretionary, economically driven decision-making.

I oppose the elimination of Threatened Species Protections (the Blanket 4(d) Rule)
The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk. Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

I oppose revising Section 7 Interagency Consultation Regulation
Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA; any weakening puts species survival at risk. Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review. Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy. The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. The rule should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections instead of narrowing them.

I oppose reinstating the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2))
The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species. Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to reduce protections for industry convenience. The US Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS) must base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns. Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction; weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects. FWS should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger science-forward framework.

I oppose changes to the Listing & Critical Habitat Rules (50 CFR Part 424)
Reinstating the 2019 rule moves ESA implementation backward, not forward. FWS and National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) should keep the 2024 improvements rather than revert to weaker, outdated language. The ESA requires using the best scientific and commercial data available; weakening listing criteria undermines that legal standard. Species threatened by climate change rely on future-oriented science, narrowing “foreseeable future” restricts the ability to act before collapse. Recovery often requires habitat beyond the small areas species currently occupy; restricting unoccupied critical habitat contradicts the purpose of the ESA.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.
title: Comment from Graygor, Robyn

text:

The proposed rule states it will identify known national security and other relevant impacts of the proposed designation and identify any areas that the Secretary has reason to consider for exclusion and explain why. You also propose to include a non-exhaustive list of categories of potential impacts that the Secretary will identify.
It is clear the purpose of this new proposal is to write in exclusions and reduce endangered species protections for activities that will generate a lot of money for big donor companies
The purpose of this new regulation is to take into account ‘economic hardship’, of personal profit and ‘Homeland Security’, which is a farce to exploit resource products from our public lands. Our public lands and the species that live there need to be protected above all personal profit. Profit should not be considered when protecting endangered species and habitats.

There is no ‘energy crisis’ and this EO is a perfect example of why placing ‘national security’ or economic interests over ESA or CH. Our public lands are ours, not just rich peoples. If rich people want to use our land for their profit, then they must go through a rigorous examination on the effects their activities may have on ESA species and Critical Habitat, without exception!

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Meyer, Jerry

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am compelled to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, individually and collectively, threatens to undermine the ESA’s crucial role in preventing extinctions, fostering species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems.

1. Eliminating Default Protections for Threatened Species
The ESA was crafted to take action before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule, backed by decades of scientific evidence, highlights that early protections reduce recovery costs and stave off declines. Ending these automatic safeguards would lead to unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive spirit and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Incorporating Economic Considerations in Listing Decisions
The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic factors. Introducing economic considerations undermines statutory language and scientific integrity, risking protection delays until species are near extinction. Future-threat analysis is crucial, as habitat loss and climate change pressures already heighten extinction risks. Weakening these criteria diminishes timely listings and increases preventable extinction likelihoods.

3. Curtailing Critical Habitat Protections
Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially climate-refugia areas, hampers recovery. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses years of legal and scientific precedent. Weakened definitions render inter-agency consultations less effective and compromise the ESA’s recovery mission.

4. Creating Loopholes to Bypass ESA Protections
Loopholes allowing agencies to sidestep ESA protections, even at extinction’s risk, clash with the ESA’s core goals. Such mechanisms encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from scientific analysis. This would severely impact wide-ranging species like Florida panthers and gray wolves, accelerating declines for many at-risk species.

Cumulative Impact
Together, these proposals threaten to weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and hike recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species’ extinctions, thanks to its scientific, precautionary, and proactive foundations. Weakening this law amid a global biodiversity crisis is counterproductive.

Request
I urge the complete withdrawal of these four proposed rule changes and the preservation of the current science-based regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering my perspective.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The public and god know the names of the people bulldozing the land we love. You will be held accountable.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
