title: Comment from Love, Rodney

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. I am in 100% agreement with the following statement authored by Mr. Jim Pattiz:

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:

As a devoted supporter of wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which would prioritize economic interests over the habitat protections imperiled species urgently need.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Karpinski , Elizabeth

text:
The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

title: Comment from Johnston, Sue

text:
To Whom, it may Concern,
I am in strong opposition to the suite of proposed rulemakings that would significantly weaken implementation of the Endangered Species Act (ESA)—one of our nation’s most effective and widely supported conservation laws. Collectively, these proposed changes would shift the ESA away from science-based, precautionary conservation and toward increasingly discretionary, economically driven decision-making.

I OPPOSE REINSTATING THE CRITICAL HABITAT EXCLUSION RULE (SECTION 4(B)(2))
THE 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species. Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to reduce protections for industry convenience. The US Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS) must base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns. Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction; weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects. FWS should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger science-forward framework.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

Protect the Endangered Species Act. Do not weaken it.

title: Comment from Johnson, barbara

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposed rule would undermine the ESA's requirement that critical habitat designations be based on "the best scientific data available." It would give undue weight to economic or non-biological criteria at the expense of the species' recovery.

I am concerned that this proposal will lead to extinctions because it would exclude too much area from critical habitat designations. Habitat loss is the top driver of species extinction. In the United States, species proposed for listing such as the Monarch butterfly and the Bethany Beach firefly will need critical habitat protections. Science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.

I have taken every opportunity since childhood to explore our public lands and the species these house, all across the country. I visit National Wildlife Refuges, National Monuments and Parks, State parks and wildlife refuges, National Forests. These are our national treasures and cannot be what they are today if all threatened and endangered species are not protected. Economic growth does not require us to pollute, eliminate, or otherwise waste habitat. We can develop technologies that protect species and allow us to grow without eliminating the species we ourselves need to survive.

title: Comment from Felts, M

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process. To emphasize, economic factors should not be the paramount factor, or any factor, for that matter in determining whether habitat and species are protected. The proposed revisions are logically fundamentally at odds with the purpose of the ESA.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: “I’m writing to ask our government to oppose any efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act. This landmark law protects southern sea otters. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Weaver, Elaine

text:
Support the Endangered Species Act (ESA) because of its role in preventing extinction, maintaining biodiversity, protecting ecosystem health (clean air/water), and safeguarding human benefits like potential medicines.
The ESA also prevents irreversible loss and upholds moral responsibility to nature, with successes like saving the Bald Eagle. It is a critical safety net against habitat destruction, its ecological benefits, and its value for future generations, despite criticisms about economic impacts that are exaggerated for the further enrichment of big money interests over the importance of a balanced healthy environment.

Importance of the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

• Prevents Irreversible Extinction: The ESA is the last line of defense, stopping species from vanishing forever, as extinction is permanent.
• Protects Biodiversity: Each species plays a role; losing one weakens the whole ecosystem, impacting nature's balance.
• Maintains Ecosystem Health: Healthy ecosystems provide clean air, water, and fertile land, essential for human survival and health.
• Economic & Medical Benefits: Biodiversity offers potential cures for diseases and supports industries like tourism and recreation.
• Proactive Conservation: It stops habitat destruction (the #1 driver of extinction) before it's too late, safeguarding critical habitats.
• Success Stories: The ESA has successfully recovered iconic species like the Bald Eagle, American Alligator, and Gray Wolf.
• Moral & Ethical Duty: We have a responsibility to protect other species for future generations and for their intrinsic value. 

Addressing Common Criticisms:
• "It hurts businesses/jobs": The ESA's focus on habitat protection ultimately safeguards the natural resources industries rely on.
• "It's too restrictive": The definition of "harm" (habitat destruction) is crucial for proactive conservation, not just preventing physical harm. 
How It Works:
• Identifies species at risk (endangered/threatened).
• Prohibits killing, harming, or trading them.
• Protects their "critical habitat" (places they need to live).
title: Comment from Griffin , Gregory

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Reamer, Crystal

text:
I submit this comment in opposition to HQ-ES-2025-0048 based on my professional experience working in threatened and endangered species recovery in Hawaiʻi. My work requires applying conservation science in real-world conditions to prevent extinctions and advance recovery for some of the most imperiled species in the United States.
Hawaiʻi’s endangered species face extraordinary and compounding threats, including invasive species, habitat loss, disease, and accelerating climate impacts. Successful recovery depends on strong, clear, and enforceable implementation of the Endangered Species Act. Any regulatory change that reduces protective standards, increases procedural uncertainty, or limits the use of best available science directly undermines recovery outcomes in Hawaiʻi, where population sizes are often critically small and the margin for error is effectively zero.
From an implementation perspective, HQ-ES-2025-0048 would make it more difficult to carry out timely and effective conservation actions. In practice, recovery programs rely on predictable regulatory processes to plan habitat management, species translocations, and long-term monitoring. Policies that introduce ambiguity or weaken conservation requirements shift limited staff and funding away from recovery actions and toward administrative compliance, reducing overall effectiveness and increasing extinction risk.
For Hawaiʻi, the consequences of weakened protections are immediate and irreversible. Once an endemic species is lost, it cannot be restored. Federal policies governing endangered species conservation must recognize Hawaiʻi’s unique biological context and uphold the strongest possible application of the ESA. I urge the agency to withdraw or substantially revise HQ-ES-2025-0048 to ensure that it supports science-based recovery and fulfills the federal responsibility to prevent further extinctions in Hawaiʻi.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide this comment.
title: Comment from Goodale, Kelly

text: I’m writing to ask our government to oppose any efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act. This landmark law has protected Hawaiian monk seals, Guadalupe fur seals, southern sea otters and other animals and their ecosystems for more than 50 years. The proposed changes would seriously undermine these protections and threaten decades of progress. Please reject these reckless changes and stand up for endangered species and the ecosystems we all depend on.

title: Comment from Evert, Matthew

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment not only to protecting imperiled species but also to conserving the ecosystems that sustain them. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Nascimento, Bianca

text:

text:
I am concerned that these proposed revisions to section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act would make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat designation. While the proposal is framed as increasing “transparency and certainty,” the practical effect appears to be a shift toward prioritizing economic and other considerations over the core purpose of the Act: protecting imperiled species and the habitats they need to survive.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the updated Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat (2025) rule because it weakens the core intent of the Endangered Species Act and prioritizes short-term economic and political interests over science, biodiversity, and long-term public good.
The Endangered Species Act was created to prevent extinction using the best available science, not to make conservation conditional on convenience or cost. Rolling back protections, narrowing habitat designations, or raising barriers to listing species ignores decades of ecological research showing that habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction. Protecting species without protecting the ecosystems they depend on is ineffective and performative.
These changes also undermine climate resilience. Healthy ecosystems protect communities from wildfire, flooding, drought, and extreme heat. Weakening habitat protections today increases environmental and economic costs tomorrow—costs that will be borne by taxpayers, local communities, and future generations.
Importantly, this rule disregards Indigenous knowledge, public trust responsibility, and the moral obligation to preserve irreplaceable species. Once a species is lost, it is lost forever. Conservation delayed is conservation denied.
The Endangered Species Act has a proven success record, preventing the extinction of over 99% of species under its protection. Weakening it is not modernization—it is regression.
I urge decision-makers to reject these changes and uphold strong, science-based protections for endangered and threatened species and the critical habitats that sustain them.

title: Comment from Marquez, Rachel

text:
I strongly disagree with the proposed changes to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA allows the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat if the benefits of exclusion outweigh those of designation, Congress intended this power to be limited and only used when exclusion wouldn’t lead to extinction. The proposed changes improperly prioritize economic factors over biological needs, pushing the agency to favor economic impacts even when they’re speculative or secondary.

Additionally, the rule imposes an unreasonably high standard for maintaining habitat by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can prove exclusion would result in extinction. This undermines the ESA’s precautionary approach and contradicts its protective purpose. Courts have consistently emphasized that critical habitat should be designated with recovery, not just extinction avoidance, in mind.

Furthermore, the rule seems to disproportionately favor non-biological interests, such as private industry, by promoting the submission of economic "concerns" without demanding the same scientific rigor. This risks turning the exclusion process into a tool for regulated entities to override scientific judgment, contrary to Congress's intent when it removed economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to reject these revisions and uphold a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and prioritize the biological needs of listed species.

text:
Human beings, contrary to popular belief, are merely one part of the entire ecosystem; we share that environment with the countless other species upon whose welfare we depend. The species identified as ‘endangered’ are at the greatest risk of extinction; human existence goes the way they do. text:

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. title: Comment from GRETZ, BONNIE

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my strong objection to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. These proposals, both individually and collectively, would greatly undermine the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and preserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA is designed to act before species reach crisis levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is grounded in decades of scientific evidence that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing default protections for threatened species will cause unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations contradicts this, undermining scientific objectivity and risking delays until species are near extinction. Additionally, restricting future-threat analysis ignores current conservation science, which shows slow-burn pressures like habitat loss and climate change increase risk before population declines are evident. Weakening these criteria reduces the chance of timely listings and increases preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and within the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery planning, particularly for essential unoccupied or climate-refuge areas. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses longstanding legal and scientific precedents, ignoring the indirect harm habitat destruction causes. Weakening these definitions reduces inter-agency consultation effectiveness, increases biological risks, and contradicts the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Opening new loopholes allowing agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes for agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, conflicts with the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and divert decision-making from science-based analysis. This disproportionately impacts wide-ranging and imperiled species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, and could hasten declines in many already pressured species.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Individually concerning, collectively these rules would:
• weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
• delay or block protections for species in need,
• reduce habitat conservation amidst accelerating climate change,
• increase extinction risks for both domestic and international species,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• and increase taxpayer-funded recovery costs.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct. As one of the most effective conservation laws, it succeeds through science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes contradict those principles.

During this time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be enhancing—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes in full and maintain the current regulatory framework, rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from v Br, Mickey

text: Wildlife and the ecosystem means a lot to me and my community, we want our environment to be protected and regulated by informed scientists. The Endangered Species Act is important because it values science, research, and public wellbeing, rather than bending to the wills of political pressure. These proposed changes would allow industry to override and scientific reason and respect for the public. The Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows criteria for critical habitats which would allow economic interest to easily override habitat protection and threaten the environment. With more weight on economic interest than environmental health this could easily put entire ecosystems and communities at risk, not just endangered species. This also ties to the Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7) which limits federal review of agency actions and would make it easier for destructive projects to come to fruition without having its impacts on endangered wildlife regulated or reviewed. These changes would undermine the democratic nature of governance and the reduction of federal oversight would allow industry to trample on public accountability and wellbeing. The health of our wildlife and our community means everything to us, I urge you to uphold the principles of the ESA and withdraw these proposed rules to support protections backed by scientific research and save protect our ecosystems for our future generations to inherit.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Behl Whiting, Kathy

text:
Re: Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Service’s regulations implementing ESA section 4(b)(2). I am submitting this comment as a career environmental educator, Washington State Master Naturalist, and conservation professional who works closely with the public on issues of habitat protection, wildlife recovery, and public lands stewardship.

I appreciate the Service’s stated goal of increasing transparency around how exclusion decisions are made. That said, I am concerned about the direction this proposal could take in practice, particularly with respect to Federal public lands. Critical habitat has always played an important role not only in preventing extinction, but in supporting long-term recovery, resilience, and connectivity. In my experience, Federal public lands often contain some of the most intact and ecologically important habitat remaining for listed species, and they also serve as places where the public expects strong conservation leadership from the Federal government.

I am especially concerned that the proposed framework could make exclusions more routine by placing greater emphasis on administrative burden and transactional costs associated with consultation. Consultation under section 7 is a core feature of the Endangered Species Act, not an unintended side effect, and avoiding that process should not, on its own, outweigh the conservation value of habitat that is important for recovery.

I also encourage the Service to clearly define what qualifies as “credible information” and “meaningful impacts” when determining whether to initiate an exclusion analysis. Without clear guardrails, there is a risk that speculative or incomplete claims could drive decisions that gradually erode habitat protections, even where biological value is high and recovery needs are significant.

I urge the Service to ensure that any final rule keeps conservation value central, clearly distinguishes between survival and recovery, and treats Federal public lands as essential components of species recovery rather than as candidates for routine exclusion. Thank you for considering these comments and for the Service’s ongoing work to steward the nation’s wildlife and public lands for present and future generations.

Sincerely, Christina Woolf, Bainbridge Island, WA 98110

title: Comment from Kelly, Michelle

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Malsan, Brian

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Animals are awesome. Please continue to protect them :)

title: Comment from Savino, Heather

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

My colleagues and I work every day to preserve and protect these keystone species and the environments in which they live. By lessening protections for these habitats and their inhabitants, it would create a ripple effect that many of the more vulnerable species may not be able to recover from.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Ian Dorsey
Assistant Trainer of Pinnipeds, Mystic Aquarium

title: Comment from Wagner, Priscilla

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Mark Clifford

text:

text:
To Whomever it May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Humans seem to think that we are separate from the environment, when in truth we play just as critical a role in these ecosystems as other organisms. Endangered species are the “canaries in the coal mine”; what harms them harms us just as much. We should take care to protect endangered species because what causes their demise will come for us too, sooner or later.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Audrae Seladi Roberts
Water Quality Manager
Mystic Aquarium

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Maguire, Paul

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from gouge, Gerald

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Thomas Kruse, Barbara

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I object to the promulgation of these proposed revisions, which will unduly constrain the Fish and Wildlife Service's discretion to administer the Endangered Species Act. The FWS has developed expertise over the decades since the enactment of the ESA. Now, the current Administration is limiting or undermining altogether, FWS’s role as the expert agency in this regard — especially with regard to Federal lands — and its ability to further the conservation of threatened species, per the statutory mandate of the ESA, by forcing outside “expertise” into the equation for determining designation exclusions.

The FWS must remain in the driver’s seat to make appropriate designations of critical habitats to protect threatened species, and to authorize any exclusions. The FWS has boots on the ground, often with roots in local communities, to better understand the most appropriate balance of competing ecosystems (human versus wildlife), and how best to balance nature’s need to thrive against human’s need to act. The use of outside “experts” in this proposed regulatory scheme is vague and overbroad, and permits reliance on so-called experts, outside FWS, to decide the interests of “national security,” “homeland security,” and “economic impact.” There is no need for outside expertise, as the current scheme allows FWS to conduct the appropriate balance between transparency and predictability against flexibility and discretion, with an avenue for judicial review by proponents/opponents of a particular designation. There is no compelling reason to revise this framework.

Let’s admit. Executive Order 14154 is a precursor for a Federal land-grab by private stakeholders, with limited or non-existent regulatory and judicial review, all while hiding behind the banner of “national security” or “economic impact.” These proposed revisions are simply the next step in the process. You show your hand by acknowledging in the text: “while Federal lands are important areas to the conservation of species habitat, we do not wish to foreclose the potential to exclude areas under Federal ownership.”

Since the enactment of the ESA, the Secretary has not been hampered to act on Federal lands when there have been true, bona-fide emergencies for a designation exception. Therefore, there is no reason to thwart the current regulatory scheme and negatively impact Federal lands in these regards. But now, this Administration seeks to cement a streamlined pathway, in writing, to encumber Federal lands per the proposed revisions, by compelling the agency’s reliance on alleged “expertise” of private stakeholders.

Finally, these provisions are vague, as the exclusion analysis does not account for or require any undertaking of downwind responsibilities of private stakeholders accessing excluded Federal lands, pursuant to Section 4(b)(2) of the ESA. The revisions’ proposed balancing test — whether the benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating the area as critical habitat — completely ignore any analysis of land-use responsibility. Who must pay the costs for environmental harm - including the destruction of wildlife habitat - committed by stakeholders on excluded Federal lands? Who will be responsible for repairing any damage to Federal lands, if such should occur? Who will pay the bill? Will taxpayers get a substantial cut of any profits derived from private land-use on public lands? If not, why not? Proponents of designation exclusion should be required to make a sufficient showing. Without a regulatory scheme in place to hold private stakeholders responsible for their actions on excluded Federal lands, the proposed revisions are deficient, because they do not require these factors during the exclusion analysis.

One of the crown jewels of the United States has been our century-long protection and preservation of Public Lands, to the envy of the rest of the world. No one has done this better than the USA. Over the last half century, the FWS has performed its mandate under the ESA, by protecting Federal (and other) lands, without curtailing our nation’s military, security, or economic prowess to any significant degree. The proposed revisions now seek to undermine the agency’s long-held expertise in designating critical areas and in balancing appropriate exceptions to these designations, by letting private stakeholders and profit motives put their fingers on the scales to determine public outcome.

The Secretary has presented insufficient revisions, without requiring proponents of designation exceptions to justify their impact on Federal lands, and has shown no compelling reason to implement these proposals.

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s Section 4(b)(2) critical habitat exclusion framework. Although the ESA allows the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress clearly intended this authority to be exercised sparingly and only where exclusion would not jeopardize the species’ survival. For these reasons, I urge the Service to abandon the proposed revisions and retain a Section 4(b)(2) framework in which exclusions are rare, well-justified, and clearly subordinate to the biological needs and recovery of listed species.
