text: I am writing today in protest of the proposal to require the consideration economic and national security impacts when giving species ESA designation. This is just meaningless red tape. No species listed so far has ever caused significant economic or national security harm. In fact, it’s done the opposite. Conservation programs for the Kirtland’s Warbler have maintained a thriving logging sector in Michigan. The warbler can only breed im Jack pine forests between the ages of 6 and 20 years. Loggers have been able to maintain and expand Kirtland’s Warbler populations by clear-cutting and replanting a few chunks of Jack pine forest every year, ensuring that there is always suitable breeding habitat for the warbler while also creating dependable income for logging communities. National security interests can also help endangered species. Fort Benning is a major stronghold for the Red-cockaded Woodpecker. The woodpecker can only breed in old-growth Longleaf pine woodlands, which need regular burning to stay healthy. Fort Benning is located in Longleaf pine country, and their regular gunnery exercises start the low-intensity fires needed to maintain the forest. So in all, this proposed rule is meaningless red tape that solves a problem that never existed in the first place.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Mary Keeler

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. If applied loosely, at risk species could lose ESA protection before populations are truly stable and resilient. The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival

text:
To those it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed modifications to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being considered. Each proposal, on its own and collectively, threatens to significantly diminish the ESA's effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and preserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Eliminating Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repealing the Blanket 4(d) Rule)**

The ESA's purpose is to act before species face critical threats. The longstanding 4(d) rule, supported by decades of scientific evidence, shows that early safeguards lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing these default protections would lead to unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and place vulnerable species at risk of harm or extinction. This contradicts the ESA's preventive intent and will lead to increased ecological and financial burdens over time.

2. **Complicating Species Listing by Allowing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Considering economic factors would undermine scientific objectivity and risk deferring protections until species are near extinction. Limiting the consideration of projected or climate-driven threats ignores essential conservation science, as slow-burn factors like habitat loss and climate changes put species at risk long before population declines are apparent. Weakening future-threat criteria hinders timely listing and raises the chance of avoidable extinctions.

3. **Diminishing Critical Habitat Protections and Redefining “Harm”**

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and nationally. Reducing critical habitat designations, particularly for unoccupied or climate-refuge areas essential for recovery, undermines conservation efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses legal and scientific precedents, as habitat destruction can indirectly lead to wildlife deaths. Weakening these definitions diminishes inter-agency consultation effectiveness, heightens biological risk, and violates the ESA's recovery mandate.

4. **Creating Loopholes for Agencies or Committees to Bypass ESA Protections**

Expanding mechanisms allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, conflicts with the ESA's purpose. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analysis. This disproportionally affects imperiled species such as Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating their decline.

**Cumulative Impact of These Proposals**

Individually concerning, these rules collectively:
- Undermine the ESA's scientific foundation,
- Delay or block essential protection for species,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- Increase extinction risk for domestic and international species,
- Weaken inter-agency cooperation,
- Raise recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, making it one of the most successful conservation laws, based on science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes oppose its foundational principles.

In an era of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should enhance—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to fully withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, grounded in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful application.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
HELP STOP THE REPEAL OF THE ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT. Basically, the new rules will value economic development over habitat preservation. This could possibly affect the Balcones Canyonlands Endangered Species Habitat and others opening them up to development.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service seeks to reverse Biden era Endangered Species Act rules which reversed Trump's first administration's rules so the old Trump rules will again be effective.

I urgently ask that you comment. Below is a concise comment already posted if you would like to use it. https://www.regulations.gov/comment/FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039-7480. Almost 2,000 comments have been posted.
See the Federal Register: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/21/2025-20550/endangered-and-threatened-wildlife-and-plants-regulations-for-designating-critical-habitat).
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DO NOT CHANGE OR WEAKEN the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to risk further extinction. The 4 proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of inter-agency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the inter-agency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA is supported by more than 4 out of 5 Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades but rather increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitating strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

DO NOT RETRACT these regulatory changes, each species was created to balance nature. With each species lost a domino affect occurs negatively affecting other species.
title: Comment from Philipson, Carol

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
To whom it may concern,
I am writing to firmly oppose all four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each of these changes, both individually and collectively, would greatly diminish the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and conserve the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)The ESA was crafted to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on scientific evidence that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default protections would result in unnecessary delays and case-by-case rulemaking, exposing vulnerable species to harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will increase long-term ecological and financial costs.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysisThe ESA mandates that listing decisions be based on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations would undermine objectivity and delay protections until species face extinction. Ignoring climate-driven threats disregards conservation science, which shows that habitat loss and climate change already heighten risks. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listing less likely and increases preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”Habitat loss is a leading driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery planning. Narrowing the “harm” definition so habitat degradation doesn’t qualify would reverse legal and scientific precedents. Habitat destruction often kills wildlife indirectly, and the law recognizes this. Weakening these definitions would make consultations less effective and risk biological harm.

4. Opening new loopholes allowing agencies to bypass ESA protectionsCreating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making from scientific to project-based analysis. This would disproportionately affect species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating their decline.The cumulative impact of these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay or block species protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs for taxpayers. The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct because it is based on science and early action. These changes oppose these principles.At a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening its most effective wildlife protection law, not weakening it.RequestFor these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and keep the existing framework grounded in science and successful implementation.
Thank you for considering my comment.

text:
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Changes to Endangered Species Act Critical Habitat Designations
FWS-ES-2025-0048_0001

To Whom It May Concern:

I submit the following comments in strong opposition to the proposed rule changes to critical habitat designations under the Endangered Species Act.

The proposed rule is fundamentally flawed for the following reasons:
1. Contradicts Scientific Evidence: The rule disregards the best available science regarding habitat requirements for species recovery, violating the ESA's statutory mandate to base decisions on scientific data.

2. Undermines Legal Precedent: This proposal abandons decades of established legal interpretation and case law surrounding critical habitat protections, creating uncertainty and weakening enforcement.

3. Compromises Congressional Intent: The rule creates broad loopholes allowing administrative exclusion of critical habitat, directly contradicting Congress's original purpose in enacting the ESA—to conserve endangered species and the ecosystems upon which they depend.

4. Threatens Conservation Success: For 51 years, the ESA has prevented extinction for 99% of listed species. Weakening critical habitat protections will reverse this progress and accelerate species decline.
Critical habitat designations are essential to species recovery, not optional considerations. The proposed rule prioritizes short-term economic or administrative convenience over the long-term survival of imperiled wildlife and the ecosystem services they provide.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and reaffirm its commitment to robust, science-based habitat protections as mandated by the Endangered Species Act.

Sincerely,
Tara Shade
Kenilworth, IL

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose. If an industry - any industry - is so promising, I promise, it will find another way. I do not want us to abandon the wildlife of tomorrow in favor of potential profits today, as in the long term, the costs to our wellbeing and the planet will be greater than can ever be recovered.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. title: Comment from Ryan, Anita

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinction of 99 percent of listed species. As a devoted supporter of wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which would prioritize economic interests over the habitat protections imperiled species urgently need.

Critical habitat designations are fundamental to species recovery. Weakening these protections abandons decades of legal precedent, ignores the best available science, and undermines Congress’s original intent.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment not only to protecting imperiled species but also to conserving the ecosystems that sustain them. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Cason, Regina

text:
To whom it may concern,

We are currently in a mass extinction crisis and protecting endangered species is crucial to saving species across the US. Humans have used large swaths of land for our own personal gain with little consideration to how it affects our native species. The ESA safeguards these species and takes their specific needs into consideration. Without this law or protections, humans unknowingly destroy habitat and valuable resources. Once a species is gone, it is gone forever. Please, you are able to stop the destruction of our beautiful resources here in the US. Endangered species do not have a voice, we are their voice. We need to artfully balance and manage the taking of resources to do so sustainability. Removing these protections is not sustainable, it is detrimental and allows loop holes that will see the end to the incredible flora and fauna we have in our country.

Thank you for your consideration,

Rachel Holland
Lafayette, CO

title: Comment from Mason, Rhonda

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

n the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
International Crane Foundation
North America
News
Whooping Crane
Stand up for Endangered Species
Stand up for endangered species, like the Whooping Crane, and submit your comment(s) on the proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 22, 2025.

Share
Last month, the Trump Administration proposed four new rule changes that would profoundly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the most important law for protecting and conserving threatened plants and animals in our country. We believe these changes would be catastrophic for Endangered Whooping Cranes, as well as countless other species, and their habitats.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

Signed into law in 1973—the same year as the International Crane Foundation was established—the ESA is a keystone of conservation success. It is credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, such as the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the first cohort protected by the law.

Click on the four proposed rule changes below to find the unique link for each to submit a comment. You may submit a comment for one or all four rule changes.

Since it was signed into law in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has been credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, including the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the very first cohort protected by the law.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

title: Comment from Garries, Debra

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule change, which undermines the original intent of Congress to safeguard species from future threats and support sustainable ecosystems through science-backed conservation.

Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Mackie, Amanda

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Protecting the Endangered Species Act is important because it prevents the extinction of plants and animals that are vital to healthy ecosystems. By preserving biodiversity, the ESA also supports clean air and water, food security, and a balanced environment for future generations.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Megan Cole
Mystic Aquarium

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Once a species becomes imperiled, it is much harder to safeguard them, so it is our job as stewards of the land to ensure we protect these species while we can.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Stacie Cole
Supervisor of Belugas- Mystic Aquarium

Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Hello My name is Aubrey Sawyer and I am very concerned about changing the designations of critical habitat. I understand that the goal of this proposed rule is to make the process more transparent and predictable for the public and stakeholders. While transparency is important, I am concerned that these changes could weaken protections for endangered and threatened species.
The Endangered Species Act was created to protect species at risk of extinction and to help them recover. Critical habitat designations are a key part of that goal because they protect the ecosystems species need to survive. Although the ESA allows the Service to consider economic and other impacts, this was meant to be done carefully and not in a way that prioritizes development over conservation. By making it easier to trigger an exclusion analysis—especially when “credible information” can come from landowners or developers—the proposed rule could lead to more land being excluded from critical habitat than Congress originally intended.
I am also concerned about how the rule defines the “benefits of exclusion.” Including things like administrative costs, permitting delays, or community opposition may place too much weight on short-term economic concerns. In contrast, the environmental impacts of losing critical habitat can be permanent and may seriously harm a species’ chances of recovery. Protecting a species from extinction is not the same as helping it fully recover, and the ESA clearly aims to do both.
Finally, the idea that areas would be automatically excluded whenever the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion—as long as extinction is not likely—sets the bar too low. Survival alone should not be the standard. If critical habitat is reduced too much, species may continue to struggle long-term, which goes against the purpose of the ESA.
In conclusion, while I support efforts to make the regulatory process more transparent, I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to ensure that conservation remains the top priority. Any final rule should limit exclusions and make sure that decisions are based primarily on protecting species and their habitats, not on convenience or economic pressure. Thank you for considering my comment.

text:
I recognize the Service’s responsibility to balance conservation needs with economic and community considerations. However, after reviewing the proposed rule, I have significant concerns that several revisions, especially when combined, pose risks to the effectiveness and integrity of critical habitat protections.

1. Mandatory economic and “other relevant” impact analysis risks overshadowing biological necessity.
The ESA’s core purpose is to prevent species extinction and promote recovery based on the best available scientific data. While economic and community impacts may be appropriate to consider under §4(b)(2), making these considerations mandatory in every designation risks shifting biological conservation from being the primary driver to just one factor among many. In practice, this could result in disproportionate weight being placed on short-term economic or administrative costs rather than long-term ecological benefits, ecosystem resilience, or species recovery needs.

Recommendation: Retain flexibility. The Service should preserve discretion to determine when an economic analysis is appropriate rather than requiring it for every designation. Biological necessity should remain the central determinant for critical habitat decisions.

2. Lowering the threshold for exclusion analyses significantly increases opportunities for strategic objections.
Under the proposed rule, any “credible information” submitted—often by landowners, developers, or industries—automatically triggers an exclusion analysis. This creates an incentive for stakeholders to submit minimal or selective evidence to delay or undermine proposed designations. It may also strain agency resources by forcing analyses on issues that are not scientifically meaningful.

Recommendation: The Service should clarify and strengthen the definition of “credible information” to ensure that only well-supported, scientifically grounded submissions compel exclusion analyses. Without this safeguard, exclusions may become too easily triggered and could impede timely habitat protections.

3. Automatic exclusion when benefits of exclusion outweigh benefits of inclusion may undercut long-term conservation goals.
Although the extinction threshold is an important safeguard, the proposed automatic-exclusion rule does not sufficiently consider species recovery needs beyond survival. Many species require habitat protection not only to avoid extinction, but to recover to stable, resilient populations. Allowing automatic exclusions whenever short-term economic or administrative benefits appear greater than conservation benefits could reduce the geographic scope of habitat protections essential for recovery.

Recommendation: The Service should weigh recovery needs, not just extinction risk, when comparing benefits of inclusion versus exclusion. The final rule should explicitly recognize that critical habitat is essential to both preventing extinction and achieving recovery.

4. Increased stakeholder influence risks creating an imbalance between scientific evidence and economic interests.
Expanding the role of third-party stakeholders can provide valuable local knowledge. However, in practice, those most likely to submit exclusion requests are entities with economic motives rather than ecological expertise. This may skew the process toward development interests unless the Service ensures rigorous scientific review of submitted claims.

Recommendation: The Service should reaffirm that decisions must be grounded in the best available science. Stakeholder-provided information should undergo clear standards for validity, transparency, and scientific reliability.

5. Potential impacts on climate resilience and long-term ecosystem function should be more explicitly considered.
Critical habitat designations increasingly intersect with climate-related shifts in species range, habitat fragmentation, and environmental stressors. Reducing the scope or frequency of designations—especially through streamlined exclusions—could leave species more vulnerable to climate change.

Recommendation: The rule should explicitly require consideration of long-term ecological and climate resilience when evaluating benefits of inclusion or exclusion.

While the proposed rule aims to increase transparency and consistency, several of its provisions could weaken the effectiveness of critical habitat designations by elevating economic considerations over biological imperatives. I respectfully urge the Service to revise the rule so that species recovery and long-term habitat integrity remain the central priorities of ESA implementation.

o whomever it may concern,

Mystic Aquarium

title: Comment from Suffoletta, Megan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Repensek, Gail

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Secrist, Wendy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Kerl, Alexandra

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

For over 25 years, the ESA has used science-based decision-making to assist in the recovery of many species, including sea otters and manatees. In today’s world, I believe we should be focused on increasing protections for the natural resources (both landscapes and species) we still have and not tearing down existing protections.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Danielle R. Lavoie, MS
Affiliation: Mystic Aquarium

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from McNamara, Anita

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, Melanie Bauer
