title: Comment from Arnold, Karlee

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts,and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

I believe deeply in individuals having large impacts on the world, hence why I chose to dedicate my career to protecting these amazing species. However, I recognize that some things are much bigger than what one individual can achieve, and for those issues we rely on our federal government. Not acting in the best interest of these species is detrimental to not only our own country, but our global community as well.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Kaitlyn Quirke

Senior Beluga Whale Trainer, Mystic Aquarium
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is a successful bipartisan piece of legislation that has saved hundreds of species from extinction and its current format provides optimum protections.

​​I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change regarding critical habitat criteria. This revision would prioritize resource development over species protection, which is in direct contrast to the intent of the Endangered Species Act.

​​Weakening the critical habitat designation procedure would make it easier to exclude key habitats and avoid the requirement to mitigate impacts for activities that occur in these areas. Without strong habitat protection endangered and threatened species have little hope of survival. We as humans deserve to let other species on this earth survive alongside us.

​​Critical habitat designations should be based on science and not special interests. The intent of the law is to prioritize species recovery rather than special interests. It has worked for decades and in a non-partisan manner. Special interests will degrade this functioning process. Habitat protection is key to species recovery and good science is the right way to make those designations.

I strongly urge you to leave the ESA as is. It is a successful, bipartisan success story.

Thank you for your consideration.

Lynn Quanstrom
title: Comment from Quanstrom, Lynn

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Baron, S

text:
Subject: Comment Opposing Proposed Changes to ESA Regulations (FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039, -0044, -0029, -0048)
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:
I strongly oppose all four proposed rules. Collectively, they would weaken key regulatory baselines by:
Narrowing the definition of critical habitat, especially currently unoccupied habitat, by expanding use of section 4(b)(2) exclusions and narrowing the criteria for including habitat necessary for recovery and climate-driven range shifts. Habitat currently considered “uninhabitable” for ESA listed species often includes significant portions of species’ historical ranges, and is of incredible conservation importance. If excluded from the definition of critical habitat, we will lose an important tool for reversing ecosystem harm and will likely see the further endangerment or extinction of vulnerable species. These changes increase risks to rare plants dependent on fragmented or specialized ecosystems like serpentine soils, vernal pools, dunes, riparian corridors, and coastal bluffs, many of which require unoccupied, climatically suitable refugia for long-term survival and migration .

Weakening interagency consultation (Section 7) by raising thresholds for “adverse modification” and narrowing the scope of conservation measures attached to federal actions and permits. In California, federal nexus projects, including infrastructure, energy development, and water management, have historically produced enforceable avoidance zones, seasonal restrictions, and habitat restoration requirements that protect sensitive plant populations. Narrowing consultation removes federal leverage to secure these critical protective measures.

Eliminating automatic take prohibitions for threatened species (4(d) blanket protections) and requiring species-specific 4(d) rules, creating regulatory gaps that could delay protections for newly listed plants and harm threatened species while species-specific rules are developed. Many rare California plant species are listed as threatened, not endangered, and are highly vulnerable to collection, grading, trampling, dumping, hydrological disruption, and invasive species introduction. Tailored rules do not offset the immediate loss of automatic protections and the uncertainty introduced during transition.

Elevating economic development considerations over ecological and climate-based recovery needs by making exclusions easier to justify, by limiting considerable future impacts to species, and by removing the prohibition of economic considerations in listing decisions. This favors short-term development interests at the expense of species persistence, recovery planning, and climate resilience– outcomes that directly conflict with the ESA’s purpose to prevent extinction and conserve ecosystems upon which species depend.

California’s rare flora is among the most climate-threatened in the nation. Effective conservation increasingly requires protecting future-suitable and unoccupied habitat that enables upslope, inland, and latitudinal migration, and maintaining strong consultation standards that mandate minimization of ecological harm. The proposed rules that narrow the definitions of “foreseeable impacts” and “critical habitat” would remove these tools, accelerating population decline and compounding climate stressors precisely when protections must expand, not contract.
California’s native plants depend on defensible critical habitat designations for land protection, funding eligibility, and conservation planning; robust consultation outcomes that yield enforceable, science-based minimization and mitigation measures; and immediate anti-take protections for threatened plants facing acute human and climate pressures.
The rules undermine each of these pillars, providing narrowed protections that cannot reliably prevent habitat loss or extinction risk.
Position
We urge the FWS to instead:
Retain automatic 4(d) take protections for threatened species unless expanded by stronger species-specific rules;

Maintain broad and conservation-inclusive criteria for unoccupied and peripheral habitat essential for future migration and recovery;

Preserve or strengthen the adverse-modification and jeopardy standards that ensure meaningful consultation outcomes; and

Apply section 4(b)(2) exclusions sparingly, ensuring economic analysis cannot override habitat necessary for species persistence and climate resilience.

Use the best available science to inform listing decisions, without the biases introduced by allowing economic considerations.

Thank you for considering this comment and the recovery of California’s endangered and threatened native flora.
Sincerely,
Matt Cronin

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife and former National Park Service Ranger, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Cannon, Aubrey

text:
While the ESA remains one of the most powerful conservation statutes globally, its procedural structure, citizen-suit provisions, and low standing thresholds have enabled systematic misuse by a subset of environmental NGOs and law firms. These abuses primarily take the form of litigation leverage rather than species recovery, often targeting landowners, developers, infrastructure providers, and public agencies.

The result is frequently:

Delay without biological benefit
Settlement-driven regulation without scientific rigor
Rent-seeking behavior by legal intermediaries
Weaponization of process rather than outcomes

1. Serial “Sue-and-Settle” Litigation Campaigns
Mechanism of Abuse

NGOs file procedural ESA lawsuits alleging agency failure to:
Meet listing deadlines
Update recovery plans
Designate critical habitat
Agencies settle quickly to avoid legal cost and risk
Settlements commit agencies to pre-negotiated regulatory outcomes

Why This Is Abusive
No adversarial testing of science
No economic balancing
Policy outcomes determined in private settlement negotiations
Courts never evaluate whether the action benefits the species

Practical Effect
ESA enforcement becomes NGO-driven rulemaking
Federal agencies lose discretion
Landowners and developers face downstream consequences without standing

2. Attorney-Fee Harvesting as a Business Model
Mechanism

ESA’s mandatory fee-shifting provision guarantees prevailing plaintiffs recover legal fees
Repeat filers target easy procedural violations
Cases often resolved quickly with minimal work

Why This Is Abusive
Incentive shifts from species recovery to litigation volume
Same firms file dozens or hundreds of nearly identical cases
Conservation outcomes are secondary or irrelevant

Empirical Pattern
Small number of firms account for a disproportionate share of ESA litigation
Many cases never involve habitat restoration, population recovery, or monitoring

3. “Paper Species” and Hyper-Granular Listings
Mechanism

Petitioning for listing of:
Sub-populations
Distinct population segments (DPS)
Taxonomically questionable variants

Why This Is Abusive
Expands ESA jurisdiction without meaningful conservation gain

Listings often based on:
Sparse data
Conservative modeling assumptions
Precautionary speculation

Practical Effect
ESA becomes a land-use veto tool
Species recovery metrics become irrelevant once restrictions are imposed

4. Critical Habitat Designation as a De Facto Land-Use Ban
Mechanism

Aggressive critical habitat mapping that includes:
Unoccupied habitat
Marginal or speculative habitat
Areas incapable of supporting the species

Why This Is Abusive
ESA does not require habitat to be currently suitable
Designations ignore:
Economic feasibility
Infrastructure constraints
Existing development

Outcome
Massive areas frozen for development
No obligation to fund or implement actual habitat improvements

5. Blocking Projects with No Species Nexus
Mechanism

ESA claims tied to:

Water permits
Federal loan guarantees
Minimal federal “touchpoints”

Used to halt:
Housing
Renewable energy
Transportation
Water infrastructure

Why This Is Abusive
Species impact is often:
De minimis
Theoretical
Fully mitigable

ESA invoked as procedural cudgel, not conservation tool

6. Weaponization of “Take” Liability
Mechanism

Broad interpretation of “harm” or “harassment”

Includes:
Habitat modification
Indirect impacts
Speculative future effects

Why This Is Abusive
Landowners face strict liability

Incentivizes:
Pre-emptive habitat destruction
Avoidance of conservation investments
Creates perverse incentives counter to ESA goals

7. Delay as the Actual Objective
Mechanism

Lawsuits filed late in entitlement or permitting process

Even weak claims cause:
Financing collapse
Investor withdrawal
Project abandonment

Why This Is Abusive
Plaintiff need not win on the merits
Delay alone achieves the goal
No accountability for economic or housing impacts

8. Class-Action Framing Without Real Classes
Mechanism

Styled as “public interest” or ecosystem-wide harm
No real class certification
Plaintiffs act as self-appointed representatives

Why This Is Abusive
No affected party consent
No balancing of competing public needs
Courts defer due to environmental framing

9. Anti-Housing and Anti-Infrastructure Leverage
Observed Pattern

ESA increasingly used to block:

Housing (especially in growth markets)
Transmission lines
Water storage
Wildfire mitigation
Renewable energy (ironically)

Why This Is Abusive
ESA becomes a proxy for anti-growth ideology
Species protection used to override democratically adopted plans

title: Comment from Brown, Winter

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Kravcov Malcolm, Karen

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Micki Locks

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to 50 Code of Federal Regulations, Part 424, regarding the listing of endangered and threatened species and the designation of critical habitat. These changes would significantly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and jeopardize the survival of vulnerable wildlife in several critical ways:

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation: By removing language that prevents agencies from considering “possible economic or other impacts,” the proposal opens the door for development projects to override habitat protections on federal lands. This shift would place short-term economic gains above the long-term health of ecosystems and species survival.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule: This rule has been a proven, legally sound, and efficient tool for protecting threatened species. Its removal would increase the risk of population declines and create unnecessary administrative burdens, requiring species-specific regulations for every threatened listing.

Introducing economic considerations into listing decisions: The ESA was designed to base listing decisions solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. Allowing cost-benefit analyses into this process undermines science-driven conservation and risks politicizing decisions that should remain objective and evidence-based.

Restricting critical habitat designations: Limiting consideration of “unoccupied areas” and narrowing the definition of “foreseeable future” would ignore essential factors such as climate change, habitat destruction, and species recovery needs. These changes would prevent proactive measures necessary for long-term survival.

For over 50 years, the ESA has been one of our most effective conservation laws, preventing extinction for 99% of listed species. At a time when climate change and development pressures are accelerating, we need stronger—not weaker—protections for wildlife and their habitats.
I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed regulatory changes to uphold the ESA’s original intent and safeguard America’s imperiled species and ecosystems. Thank you for considering my comments, and I look forward to your response on this critical issue.

Sincerely,

I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations published on November 21, 2025. These changes would significantly weaken protections for threatened and endangered species at a time when habitat loss and biodiversity decline are accelerating.

The proposal is driven by executive directives aimed at reducing regulatory “burdens,” not by conservation science. The ESA was created to prevent extinction and protect ecosystems, not to accommodate industry interests. Weakening its standards undermines that mission.

Reverting to the 2019 definition of “foreseeable future” restricts how far into the future agencies must consider threats. Many species face long‑term pressures — including habitat destruction, climate impacts, and ecosystem fragmentation — that unfold over decades. Narrowing this timeframe risks overlooking real, predictable dangers.

The proposed delisting framework would allow species to lose protections before they have truly recovered. Delisting should only occur when recovery is demonstrated, not when regulatory definitions are narrowed.

The rule also makes it harder to designate critical habitat by expanding “not‑prudent” exceptions and reinstating a restrictive two‑step process for unoccupied habitat. Habitat loss is one of the primary drivers of species decline. Limiting habitat protections — especially when large‑scale logging and land conversion continue — will only accelerate that decline.

For these reasons, I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and retain the stronger, clearer protections established in 2024. Weakening the ESA now would put vulnerable species and their ecosystems at even greater risk.

Thank you for considering my comment.

title: Comment from Bailey, Maryanne

text:
I very opposed to the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Please do the right thing!

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Lamb , Ashlee

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from Hemmelgarn, Griffin

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
We are a wildlife scientist and wildlife attorney based in Charlottesville, Virginia. We write to oppose implementation of 90 FR 52592-01, titled Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat. We request USFWS refrain from finalizing 90 FR 52592-01, Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat. In any further proceedings for this rulemaking, we ask that USFWS and NMFS address concerns that these changes make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” designation and thereby jeopardize the recovery of endangered species.

The ESA requires that USFWS designate ‘critical habitat’ for endangered species. Even if the Service determines habitat to be critical, it may, in its discretion, exclude habitat from designation. The proposed rule directs the Secretary to conduct exclusion analyses more frequently (i.e., by defining ‘credible information’ to include “a reasonably reliable indication regarding the existence of a meaningful economic or other relevant impact supporting a benefit of exclusion for a particular area.” ) The rule also changes the evidentiary standards for exclusion by allowing the prioritization of economic impacts as described by private interests (i.e., “The Secretary would give weight to benefits [of exclusion] consistent with…firsthand information”). These standards would result in greater scrutiny of critical habitat determinations when the areas affect privately held lands and, ultimately, lead to more habitat exclusions justified by economic considerations rather than ecologically-relevant reasoning. We request the Service clarify what would be considered ‘expert or firsthand information’ regarding nonbiological impacts if the regulation were finalized.

If USFWS is truly committed to “additional conservation efforts for listed species,” as the proposed rule states, it would prioritize robust protections for habitat critical to endangered species’ survival. Instead, the proposed rule would replace critical habitat designation with “‘conservation plans” that can be made with “no involvement of the FWS” without public comment, and which would allow incidental take of protected species (i.e., “[A] plan or agreement is developed in partnership with the FWS…to authorize any take of listed species caused incidentally by the activities described in the plan or agreement.”). Conservation agreements might achieve some conservation goals, but USFWS retains the duty to “make a determination whether such program is in accordance with [the ESA]” (Endangered Species Act, 16 U.S.C.A. § 1535 (1988)). The Service’s ability to perform its statutory duty to protect endangered species will be hindered if the proposed regulation is finalized. We ask the Service to clarify how it will oversee states and private entities’ “conservation plans” and ensure compliance with the ESA if the proposed regulation is finalized.

While the proposed rule will not apply retroactively, it makes no mention of how UFSWS will consider pending rules if it implements the proposed regulations. The rusty-patched bumble bee was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 2017. A proposed rule that would protect 1.6 million acres of bumblebee habitat has been pending since November 2024. We request the Service clarify how it will resolve actions pending at the time these proposed rules may be finalized. Applying 90 FR 52592-01 to earlier-filed proposed rules would thwart the reliance interests of stakeholders who have been seeking ESA protections for months or even years. If USFWS is truly committed to “making transparent” its ESA process, as the proposed rule states, we urge the Service to codify proposed rules in ESA actions based upon the regulations applicable at the time the proposed rules were published in the Federal Register.

For these reasons, we oppose 90 FR 52592-01.

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
DO NOT CHANGE OR WEAKEN the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to risk further extinction. The 4 proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of inter-agency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the inter-agency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA is supported by more than 4 out of 5 Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades but rather increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitating strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

DO NOT RETRACT these regulatory changes, each species was created to balance nature. With each species lost a domino affect occurs negatively affecting other species.

title: Comment from Arnold , Shay

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose this proposal because it weakens critical habitat protections under the Endangered Species Act and will directly harm real species that are already struggling to survive. Species like the northern spotted owl, Florida panther, and Mexican gray wolf depend on remaining habitat protections to recover. Making it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat puts these species at even greater risk.

Critical habitat is designated only after a species has already been found to be in serious trouble, usually because too much of its habitat has already been lost. For species like the Florida panther, which relies on shrinking habitat in south Florida, further exclusions could mean the difference between recovery and continued decline. These species do not have extra habitat to spare.

The Service says this rule is about transparency and certainty, but in practice it creates a clearer path to excluding habitat that species need to survive. Courts have allowed exclusions in limited cases, but they have never said habitat protections should be routinely traded away. Writing this approach into regulation risks turning an exception into the norm, especially when economic pressure is high.

The Endangered Species Act was passed because species like the bald eagle, gray wolf, and manatee were pushed toward extinction by unchecked development and economic priorities. Congress chose to protect habitat precisely because species cannot survive without it. This proposal moves the ESA backward and threatens species that are already hanging on. The Service should reject this rule and keep critical habitat protections strong and meaningful. I know this agency doesn't care about wildlife, but the American people do.
title: Comment from Carpenter, Morgan

text:
DO NOT CHANGE OR WEAKEN the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to risk further extinction. The 4 proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of inter-agency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the inter-agency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA is supported by more than 4 out of 5 Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades but rather increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitating strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

title: Comment from Marx, Lily

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.
Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021)

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from Zirinsky, Kenneth

text:
Dear USFWS,

As a wildlife biologist and environmental educator with a decade of experience, I strongly oppose all proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. The ESA should not be shaped by political pressure or economic influence. From my experience working in environmental consulting, I regularly see the effects of habitat loss from development and wildfire in California and am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. For example, I work with the threatened California spotted owl who would benefit immensely from being listed under the ESA, which would allow for sustainable timber management for the health of wildlife, the forest, and people.

The ESA has been one of our nation's most effective and popular conservation laws for over 50 years. It has saved species like the American bald eagle, California condor, peregrine falcon and the Florida manatee from extinction and put countless other species on the road to recovery. This would have far-reaching impacts, including exacerbating the biodiversity and extinction crisis, increasing the administrative burden on agencies, and undermining the conservation of habitat important for at-risk species.

I submit the following comments regarding the US Fish and Wildlife Service proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act, Docket Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039 (Section 4), FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 (Section 7), FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 (Section 4(d)), FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048 (Section 4(b)(2)).
•Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
•Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
•Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
•Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

These regulations would have major effects on ecosystem health and the genetic diversity of species. I strongly urge the Department of Interior and US Fish and Wildlife Service to keep in place critical components of the ESA like the blanket 4(d) rule which has saved countless threatened species from sliding toward extinction.

Additionally, the agencies must not move forward with changes improperly allowing economic concerns to bias the science-based decision making about which species warrant protection that has made the ESA one of the most effective conservation laws in the US. Nor should the Fish and Wildlife Service finalize the proposed changes that would pave the way for habitat-destroying industries to exclude areas from habitat protection. Once our wild spaces and endangered species are gone, they’re gone forever. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

Thank you,
Michelle Harris

text: I oppose the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act implementation. These rollbacks prioritize economic considerations over science-based conservation. text:
I beg of you, please recommit to the Endangered Species Act’s original mandate! Our natural resources and the animals that have no voice to save themselves are so important to protect.

Last month, the Trump Administration proposed four new rule changes that would profoundly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the most important law for protecting and conserving threatened plants and animals in our country. We believe these changes would be catastrophic for Endangered Whooping Cranes, as well as countless other species, and their habitats.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

Signed into law in 1973—the same year as the International Crane Foundation was established—the ESA is a keystone of conservation success. It is credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, such as the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the first cohort protected by the law.

Despite its overwhelming success and public support, the ESA has been sharply criticized by those who want to increase mining, drilling, and other land- and water-resource development that could negatively impact the habitat requirements of endangered species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
