text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Collectively, the proposed changes would make it far more difficult to designate the habitats birds need to survive and recover. Limiting designations to only those threats considered during Section 7 consultations disregards real-world drivers of decline, and raising barriers to designating unoccupied, but essential, recovery habitat undermines hope for long-term species recovery.

Without the opportunity to expand into currently unoccupied but critical habitats for survival, some endangered species may not survive. Alternatively, if species are not able to expand their range as they recover, full recovery and delisting may not be possible.
title: Comment from Mesmer, Karen

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am opposed to the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. It's crucial for consultations to ensure federal actions don't harm listed species or destroy critical habitats. These changes would greatly weaken the process.

By narrowing essential definitions, like “environmental baseline” and the criteria for effects “reasonably certain to occur,” the proposal risks allowing agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts, which are well-documented in ecological research. For many species, especially those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect impacts are major factors in their decline. Ignoring them contradicts the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Also, removing offsetting measures, which are crucial for reducing harm when incidental take can't be avoided, further weakens conservation efforts. Offsetting requirements aren't substitutes for avoidance, but they're essential to ensure that unavoidable impacts don't gradually harm populations.

The ESA mandates “conservation” to promote recovery, not just survival. These revisions stray from that legal requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and instead strengthen protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Gergerian, Edmund

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. These changes, both individually and collectively, would severely weaken the ESA's crucial role in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and maintaining the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Eliminating default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA was established to act before species reach crisis levels. The 4(d) rule, with its decades of scientific backing, shows that early, precautionary measures lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing automatic protections for threatened species introduces unnecessary delays and case-by-case rulemaking, exposing vulnerable species to preventable harm. This opposes the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to higher ecological and financial costs in the future.

2. Hindering species listing by considering economic factors and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations undermines scientific integrity and delays protections until species face extinction. Ignoring projected or climate-driven threats contradicts current conservation science, which recognizes that habitat loss, climate change, and other pressures endanger species long before population declines become evident. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listing less likely, increasing the risk of avoidable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations, essential for recovery, undermines planning efforts. Similarly, limiting the definition of “harm” so habitat degradation is excluded reverses longstanding legal and scientific precedents. Habitat destruction indirectly harms wildlife, long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions diminishes inter-agency consultations, increases biological risk, and disrupts the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections—where extinction is a possible outcome—contradicts the ESA’s core mission. Such loopholes encourage project-specific exemptions, decrease transparency, and shift decisions away from scientific analysis. This disproportionately affects species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, hastening declines in already pressured species.

Cumulative impact of these proposals

Individually concerning, collectively these changes would:
- Undermine the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay or block necessary species protections,
- Reduce habitat conservation amidst accelerating climate change,
- Heighten extinction risks for both domestic and international species,
- Weaken inter-agency cooperation, and
- Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, grounded in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes contradict those principles. At a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be bolstering—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection laws.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all proposed rule changes and maintain the existing framework based on science, legal precedent, and years of successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.
title: Comment from Di Trapani, Julia

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Young, Amanda

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Woodman, Renee

text:
I am commenting in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I implore the department to the reconsider changes to the following rules which would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021)  Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge.

text: Please do not let economic factors influence wildlife protections. Protect critical habitats.
title: Comment from Eberle, JoAnn

text:
As a devoted supporter of wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which would prioritize economic interests over the habitat protections imperiled species urgently need.

Critical habitat designations are fundamental to species recovery. Weakening these protections abandons decades of legal precedent, ignores the best available science, and undermines Congress’s original intent.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment not only to protecting imperiled species but also to conserving the ecosystems that sustain them. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving wildlife a real chance at recovery.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

text:
### Comment for Regulations.gov

I respectfully urge FWS to ensure that any revisions to ESA section 4(b)(2) implementing regulations do **not** expand exclusions from critical habitat in ways that weaken conservation outcomes. Critical habitat is a central ESA tool because habitat loss is a primary driver of extinction; the exclusion authority in section 4(b)(2) must remain a **narrow, carefully justified exception**, not a routine off-ramp.

**1) “Transparency and certainty” must not become a pathway to more exclusions.** Codifying procedures can be helpful, but the practical effect matters: if the framework increases the frequency or ease of exclusions—especially under economic or development pressure—it risks undermining the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems and prevent extinction.

**2) The “credible information” trigger risks biasing the process toward exclusion requests.** The proposal would initiate exclusion analyses when proponents provide “credible information” of “meaningful” impacts. In practice, well-resourced interests may generate extensive impact claims, while conservation benefits are harder to monetize. FWS should guard against a one-sided evidentiary dynamic by requiring equally rigorous, species-specific accounting of conservation value, ecological function, and climate resilience for each area proposed for exclusion.

**3) Counting consultation “transactional/administrative costs” as a benefit of exclusion is problematic.** Treating the basic section 7 process itself as an avoidable “cost” risks reframing core ESA compliance as a harm to be minimized. Consultation is the mechanism that prevents destruction/adverse modification and supports recovery; avoiding it should not be weighted heavily as a benefit of exclusion.

**4) Excluding Federal lands should be exceptionally rare and strongly justified.** Federal agencies have affirmative conservation duties under ESA section 7(a)(1) and must avoid jeopardy and adverse modification. The proposed shift to more readily consider excluding Federal lands—particularly where non-Federal permits/leases exist—creates a major risk of losing high-value habitat blocks that are often essential for connectivity, recovery, and climate adaptation.

**5) Economic and “other relevant impacts” must not outweigh biological necessity absent a compelling, science-based showing.** While section 4(b)(2) requires considering impacts, the ESA also requires designations be based on the best scientific data available. “Other relevant impacts” categories (e.g., community interests, wildfire risk, invasive species management) can be important, but they must be evaluated with transparent standards, and not used as vague grounds to exclude ecologically essential areas.

**6) The balancing and “weighting” approach needs safeguards against undervaluing conservation benefits.** FWS should explicitly account for: (a) ecosystem services and non-market benefits; (b) connectivity and metapopulation dynamics; (c) cumulative impacts and irreversible loss; and (d) climate-driven range shifts that make future habitat essential. Exclusions should not be based on speculative economic projections or short-term opportunity costs when the conservation value is high.

**7) The extinction backstop is not enough.** The statutory “no extinction” limitation sets a floor, not a conservation standard. The ESA’s goal is recovery and ecosystem conservation; exclusions that materially impair recovery, resilience, or critical habitat function should be rejected even if they do not immediately cause extinction.

For these reasons, I request that FWS revise the proposed rule to: keep exclusions rare; avoid treating consultation itself as a benefit to be avoided; apply heightened scrutiny to exclusion requests (especially for Federal lands); and require clear, science-based, species-specific documentation showing that any exclusion will not meaningfully reduce conservation and recovery outcomes.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Harris, Julia

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from McMillan, Laura

text:
I'm submitting this comment because I care about biodiversity and the long term survival of all species. I've learned a lot about these species through documentaries and classes at school. When I saw this proposal I thought about how it would influence the effectiveness of the ESA and further the abuse of federal lands that can negatively impact wildlife.

The proposed rules revises portions of the regulations concerning critical habitat and will allow them to put aside the rule of harm if economic and other impacts trump it. I believe that as another species of life we need to coexist and putting our wants first is selfish.

Studies have shown that protecting habitats is essential for feeding, breeding and migration significantly improves recovery for the animal. Habitats serve as the backbone for long term populations. Risking the extinction of these species for short term interest would be irresponsible. This would let companies be perverse in the use of land for monetary gain in high value areas despite them being important for species to recover.

This proposal also has a lot of unintended consequences. Fragmenting habitat networks reduce the area essential for population growth. This will also create uncertainty despite the proposal aiming for it. I see future disputes coming about because we then have to argue about what amount of economic benefit allows them to push aside critical habitat. Species recovery will also be delayed.

I recommend that they prioritize scientific reasoning and think of the biological necessity first and also enforce researched documentation of the habitat value especially for unoccupied essential habitats. I don't think economic benefit should be a deciding factor and it shouldn't override biological necessity unless it doesn't risk extinction. They need to be more transparent with the public, especially those near the area. I also think it shouldn't be a one time thing , it has to be monitored and reviewed as time goes on.

I don't support this because it undermines the ESA heavily but if it has to go through they need to prioritize sciences over money.

significantly improves recovery for the animal. Habitats serve as the backbone for long term

irresponsible. This would let companies be perverse in the use of land for monetary gain in high

title: Comment from C, Shawn

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to proposed Endangered Species Act changes which will alter decisions to exclude land from critical habitat designations. As a high school senior who has had the privilege of taking both environmental science and sustainable development classes, this is a matter that I care deeply about. In my future, I would also like to pursue journalism with a focus on the environment, and plan to spend my life bringing awareness to issues such as this. I fear that if harmful decisions are made with little environmental consideration, my generation will suffer, so it is imperative that these decisions are made carefully, as they will alter the environment that I will inherit. Such decisions disproportionately impact younger people, and will have long lasting consequences both environmentally and economically.
I am specifically commenting on the part of the regulation that has to do with automatic exclusion, regarding areas that yield greater overall benefit. I believe that this will allow for an increasing number of areas to be excluded from critical habitats, leading to less protection for both threatened and endangered species. Not only are these areas important for maintaining ecosystems, but they are foundational for protecting all kinds of species. As more area is taken away, the impacts of such habitat loss will accumulate and impact younger generations over decades, and it is very difficult to reserve once allowed.
Considering the long term impacts, this decision would create both environmental consequences and impact future generations. The gradual loss of habitat over time would lead to various losses such as biodiversity, ecosystem services, and climate resilience. An article by NOAA Fisheries titled “Threats to Habitat” notes how “habitat loss has been the most common cause of extinction for freshwater fish in the United States,” highlighting how losing habitat is one of the main drivers of species extinction, and is therefore a critical factor in species recovery (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). The protection of these habitats can protect multiple species as well as various ecosystem services at once, making it even more crucial. This decision will also impact future generations, as it will reduce access to natural spaces and create issues that younger people will have to bear.
I understand that there are also economic considerations involved in both this decision and in policymaking, but using monetary gain to justify land use will only create greater problems. The degradation of habitats may produce short term profits, but over time younger generations will have to pay the price of declining natural resources and a loss of ecosystem services, among other things. If money is an important factor in this decision, then there are more sustainable ways to redirect economic growth while still protecting habitats. Ecotourism, for example, is a sustainable source of revenue that helps local economies, and depends on habitats that are intact.
My recommendations for this issue would be, first and foremost, to strengthen science based criteria for habitat designation. Any decisions made should be driven by ecological needs and considerations, instead of financial interests. When analyzing costs, impacts on future generations should also be considered by looking at long term impacts both economically and environmentally. When possible, sustainable economic alternatives should always be considered, instead of narrower protections in favor of immediate economic benefits.
In conclusion, this decision about critical habitat designation is incredibly important, especially to groups like my generation. Each regulation created shapes both the environment and economic future that I will be living with. I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed changes, and adopt regulations that include long term habitat protection and are fair to future generations.
title: Comment from Doud, Charlotte

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Fiesler, Laurie

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the bipartisan Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change as it abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Pisani, Marisa

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Paltauf, Annalisa

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Duborg, Killian

text:
The Endangered Species Act is monumentally important, having saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Nature over profit!
title: Comment from Berner, Yvette

text: We don’t have to choose between the economy and the environment. Many jobs balance both, like the National Park Service and federal agencies that manage lands and bodies of water. Defunding those jobs isn’t the answer. Keeping those jobs maintains livelihoods and supports the economy in other ways by encouraging the public to visit parks and pay it forward.

title: Comment from Haynes, Elizabeth

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
YOUR MESSAGE:
(Copy and paste the text below into this portal.)

The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

title: Comment from Ibarra, Elizabeth

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Woodthorpe, Christopher

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from finker, Paul

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anderson, Sharon

text:
he Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.
