title: Comment from Monforte, Thomas

text: I don't support this regulation change. I believe there is inherent worth to biodiversity, and that economic impacts are a poor metric for its value. However were they to be used, I don't believe business or the current Administration would fairly tally the costs and benefits given the lack of science- and fact-based policymaking going on. The complex modeling necessary to project ecosystem services into the future, with the added complexity of accurate climate models and rigorous base data, is far beyond the scope of an Administration that is aggressively laying off its own workforce. Add to that the subjective leeway granted the agency to define habitat and species worth, and this regulation change is disastrous. It is in fact, from what I can see, a poorly masked attempt to gut the ESA and trample on public resources that should be preserved for future generations.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. title: Comment from Patterson, Patricia

text: I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rulemaking on the Endangered Species Act (ESA) by making it easier to destroy habitat. Habitat destruction is the number one cause of animal and plant decline and extinctions. The proposed law’s proponents claim the economic benefits to people will justify weakening it, but they fail to account for the tourism benefits and for the benefits of protecting lands for ecological quality and at-risk wildlife. People recognize this. More than four out of five Americans support the ESA and consider biodiversity to be a priority for future policy. title: Comment from Denker, Marcy

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Liburt, Nettie

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.
title: Comment from Laferriere, Evelyn

text:

text:
Dear Director Nesvik and Acting Director Menashes,

I am writing in opposition to the four proposed rules regarding the Endangered Species Act found in the following dockets:  

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

As someone concerned with the protection of birds across the United States, and someone who believes in the power and importance of the Endangered Species Act as a tool to boost recovery and prevent extinction, I request that these proposed rules be withdrawn and the current statutory language stay in place.  

Species like the Hawaiian Coot, Nene, Marbled Murrelet, and Eastern Black Rail are facing high pressure from invasive species, habitat loss, and climate change. Threatened species such as the Florida Scrub-Jay have long escaped being designated as “endangered” because of crucial protections in the blanket 4(d) rule. Additionally, birds such as the Whooping Crane and Streaked Horned Lark could be harmed by federal projects from other agencies, making clear inter-agency communication important.  

I believe that the proposed rules would weaken the Endangered Species Act for birds, making important tools such as critical habitat designations, inclusion of historical baselines in listing decisions, and blanket protections for threatened species inaccessible.

Please withdraw the proposed rules in dockets FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039. Given the ongoing declines of birds confirmed by scientific studies, now is not the time to weaken ESA protections. As a scientist who directly works to inform effective conservation and management strategies for animals protected by the Endangered Species Act, I must emphasize how important it is that the ESA remains unaltered. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely, 

Jonathan

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.
I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

title: Comment from Baucum, Darren

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

title: Comment from Zumchak, Elizabeth

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fortunak, Sharon

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Cafferty, Anita

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposed rule would undermine the ESA's requirement that critical habitat designations be based on "the best scientific data available." It would give undue weight to economic or non-biological criteria at the expense of the species' recovery.

I am concerned that this proposal will lead to extinctions because it would exclude too much area from critical habitat designations. Habitat loss is the top driver of species extinction. In the United States, species proposed for listing such as the Monarch butterfly and the Bethany Beach firefly will need critical habitat protections. Science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.
title: Comment from Helber, JENNIFER

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Statement Opposing the Fix Our Forests Act (H.R. 471 / S. 1462)
I strongly oppose the Fix Our Forests Act (H.R. 471 / S. 1462) because it undermines the very safeguards that protect our forests, wildlife, watersheds, and communities. While the bill is framed as a wildfire and forest‑health measure, its core provisions weaken environmental oversight, limit public participation, and open the door to large‑scale logging and development with minimal accountability.

The bill’s reliance on expedited National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews and broad new categorical exclusions is especially troubling. NEPA is one of the most important tools the public has to ensure that federal agencies fully evaluate environmental impacts before approving major actions. By exempting or fast‑tracking a wide range of forest management activities—including commercial logging—the bill strips away transparency and reduces opportunities for communities, scientists, and Tribal Nations to weigh in on decisions that affect their lands and resources.

The Act also introduces significant changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) consultation, a move that even wildfire‑focused organizations acknowledge falls outside the scope of legitimate fire‑risk reduction efforts. Weakening ESA review threatens imperiled species that depend on intact, mature, and old‑growth forests—habitats already under pressure from climate change, fragmentation, and past mismanagement.

Although the bill claims to “improve forest resilience,” it prioritizes increased logging, mechanical thinning, and industrial‑scale interventions while downplaying the well‑documented role of climate change, drought, and development patterns in driving catastrophic wildfire. True forest resilience requires science‑based, ecologically informed strategies—not shortcuts that bypass environmental review and favor extractive interests.

Finally, the bill centralizes decision‑making power within new federal “Fireshed” and “Wildland Fire Intelligence” structures without ensuring meaningful public oversight or safeguards against misuse. Forest management must be transparent, collaborative, and grounded in ecological science—not driven by speed at the expense of environmental integrity.

For these reasons, I urge Congress to reject the Fix Our Forests Act. We need legislation that strengthens—not weakens—our environmental laws, invests in climate‑smart forest restoration, supports Tribal stewardship, and protects the biodiversity and ecological functions that healthy forests provide. Our forests deserve solutions rooted in science, accountability, and long‑term resilience, not deregulation disguised as reform.
title: Comment from LaCombe, Marlene

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to oppose this proposed rule. Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat proposed rule change would allow industry the ability to block or shape habitat protections, which is preposterous given that this part of the Endangered Species Act exists precisely to prevent industry from determining what habitat should be protected and what shouldn’t. If we let industry determine land use instead of the people, industry is always going to choose extraction and development, because that’s what makes money.

But saving critical habitats literally saves lives, not just the lives of endangered plants and animals, but human lives, too. These critical habitats act as carbon sinks, which helps regulate Earth’s temperature. We’ve already done so much damage to our planet, and it’s resulted in more severe weather events that cause huge losses in human life and structural damage to dwellings and businesses.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most publicly popular pieces of legislation that exists. Protecting endangered species benefits everyone and everything. The Endangered Species Act brings together environmentalists, naturalists, hunters, outdoor recreation enthusiasts, and everyday people to stand for a common cause.

I say NO to this rule change. Keep the Endangered Species Act intact.
title: Comment from Voelkel, S

text:
The most chilling aspect of this rule change would be the expansion of circumstances under which Fish and Wildlife (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) could circumvent the designation of critical habitat. Some listed species might not have any designated critical habitat areas.

Preserving their habitat is essential to their recovery, which is the point of the law.

Habitat loss is the #1 threat driving more than 71% of threatened species toward extinction worldwide, according to a study that analyzed the major threats to IUCN Red List species, threatening more species than all other categories combined.1

This rule change ignores the extraordinary importance of habitat loss. If enacted, it would kneecap our ability to protect endangered and threatened species by removing one of the most essential mechanisms of the ESA, the ability to protect the habitats they need to survive.

The rule changes give too much discretion to the agencies.

One of the major prompts for this proposed revision was the Administration’s executive order, Unleashing American Energy, that directs agencies to review regulations that may slow domestic energy development or add hurdles to large federal projects. Ironically, by not designating all of the necessary critical habitat early in the recovery process, it might cause more uncertainty and disruption for development projects later on.

Predictable rulemaking that’s grounded in science and protected from political whims is essential for both conservation and development projects.

The agencies would also be able to exclude areas from critical habitat if they decided that economic or national security concerns outweigh the conservation benefits, as long as such exclusion doesn’t cause an extinction. This standard is contrary to the intent of the ESA, which is focused on improving outcomes for listed species.

And this a good moment to remember that the ESA exists because we consistently chose our interests over the survival needs of other species.

This cost/benefit analysis also violates the Public Trust Doctrine. Under federal and state laws and policies, fish and wildlife must be maintained for the public: “these resources are held in public trust by the Federal and State governments for the benefit of present and future generations of Americans” (43 CFR § 24.1(b)). The co-trustees are meant to protect the ecological, cultural, educational, historical, aesthetic, scientific, recreational, economic, and social values of wildlife for all Americans.

For all Americans, including future generations. Not merely for one group who would benefit economically if a particular parcel was not designated as critical habitat for a listed species.

I urge you to withdraw this rule change.
----
1: The greatest threats to species. https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/csp2.12670

Jill Shultz, M.S., Environmental Sciences, former land steward
title: Comment from Shultz, Jill

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I do not support the proposed rule changes, which would weaken protections for vulnerable and endangered species. Considering short-term economic effects such as the loss of potential revenue from oil-drilling bans alongside the best available environmental science is short-sighted and destructive.
Eliminating habitat protections for the sake of profit will not only harm important ecosystems, but will lead to further species being threatened and endangered. We need these ecosystems for a healthy planet and for a healthy people. We cannot endanger our natural environment like this if we expect to be able to grow food, live at habitable temperatures, and enjoy the outdoors.
Furthermore, I strongly urge the Department of Interior and US Fish and Wildlife Service to keep in place the blanket 4(d) rule which has saved countless threatened species from sliding toward extinction. This is an important rule for preventing endangerment before it occurs, which will ultimately save time, money, and effort. Prevention is the more efficient option and should not be undermined.

title: Comment from Stahura, Linnea

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Jarnstedt, Natalie

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
The NYC Biodiversity Alliance opposes the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that were published on November 21, 2025. For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act has successfully prevented extinctions through its commitment to science-based decision-making and the protection of imperiled species as a national priority. The proposed revisions would undermine these core principles by introducing uncertainty, weakening long-standing protections, and limiting pathways to conservation and recovery. These changes would further disadvantage invertebrates and plants, which are already underrepresented on the ESA list and often require swift action to prevent irreversible declines. Moreover, these revisions run counter to public sentiment, with over 80% of Americans supporting a strong, science-driven ESA.

Critical Habitat Exclusions (50 CFR Part 17; Section 4(b)(2)) The proposal would allow exclusion of critical habitat when proponents provide “credible evidence,” and would treat administrative costs, such as avoiding Section 7 consultations, as benefits of exclusion. It also expands the list of economic impacts, including “opportunity costs.”

This approach is flawed because:

USFWS biologists lack the expertise to quantify economic impacts, and economists lack the expertise to quantify ecological externalities.

The rule emphasizes economic costs but not ecological costs or long-term economic benefits (ecosystem services, tourism, fisheries, disaster mitigation), creating biased analyses.

The proposed rules collectively weaken science-based protections, delay action, discount ecosystem benefits, and limit agencies’ ability to consider future threats such as climate change. The NYC Biodiversity Alliance urges retention of existing ESA language and policies to ensure species receive timely and effective protections.

title: Comment from Fairfax, Krystal

text:
The most chilling aspect of this rule change would be the expansion of circumstances under which Fish and Wildlife (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) could circumvent the designation of critical habitat. Some listed species might not have any designated critical habitat areas.

Preserving their habitat is essential to their recovery, which is the point of the law.

Habitat loss is the #1 threat driving more than 71% of threatened species toward extinction worldwide, according to a study that analyzed the major threats to IUCN Red List species, threatening more species than all other categories combined (The greatest threats to species. https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/csp2.12670).

This rule change ignores the extraordinary importance of habitat loss. If enacted, it would kneecap our ability to protect endangered and threatened species by removing one of the most essential mechanisms of the ESA, the ability to protect the habitats they need to survive.

The rule changes give too much discretion to the agencies.

One of the major prompts for this proposed revision was the Administration’s executive order, Unleashing American Energy, that directs agencies to review regulations that may slow domestic energy development or add hurdles to large federal projects. Ironically, by not designating all of the necessary critical habitat early in the recovery process, it might cause more uncertainty and disruption for development projects later on.

Predictable rulemaking that’s grounded in science and protected from political whims is essential for both conservation and development projects.

The agencies would also be able to exclude areas from critical habitat if they decided that economic or national security concerns outweigh the conservation benefits, as long as such exclusion doesn’t cause an extinction. This standard is contrary to the intent of the ESA, which is focused on improving outcomes for listed species.

And this a good moment to remember that the ESA exists because we consistently chose our interests over the survival needs of other species.

This cost/benefit analysis also violates the Public Trust Doctrine. The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.
title: Comment from Frawley, Robert

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

The Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973 stands as one of the most successful pieces of environmental legislation in American history, boasting a 99% track record in preventing the extinction of listed species. By prioritizing rigorous scientific evaluation over political or economic interests, the Act has successfully brought iconic symbols of

American heritage-such as the bald eagle, the peregrine falcon, and the American alligator-back from the brink of disappearing forever. Allowing politicians to weaken these protections would undermine the Act's primary purpose: ensuring that decisions affecting our most vulnerable wildlife are guided by biology rather than short-term
Beyond its moral imperative, the ESA is essential for maintaining the health of the ecosystems that provide vital "services" to human society, including clean air, filtered water, and natural pest control. Biodiversity acts as a critical buffer against climate change and environmental stressors, meaning that every species protected by the Act plays a role in the stability of our own environment. For example, the protection of critical habitats not only saves wildlife but also prevents the destruction of lands that are vital for flood control and groundwater recharge.

Economically, the ESA provides immense value that far outweighs the costs of conservation through burgeoning wildlife tourism and stable property markets. A 2025 study found that wildlife tourism in just two national parks alone generates an estimated net economic value of $753 million annually. Furthermore, research as recent as 2025 indicates that home values near federally protected areas can rise by up to 10%, demonstrating that preserving our beautiful land is a sound financial investment for local
communities. Diluting the Act's power would not only risk an irreversible loss of biodiversity but also jeopardize the massive, multi-billion-dollar economic benefits lobbying.
derived from a healthy, untrammeled natural world.

title: Comment from McFarland, Alexie

text:
As a concerned citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to change the long-standing definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The current definition, supported by sound science and legal interpretation, appropriately recognizes that habitat modification and destruction can cause harm to threatened and endangered species. Excluding habitat modification from the definition of harm could drastically weaken one of the ESA’s most effective and widely used protections. Without question, this change could threaten the survival and recovery of endangered species, and could inadvertently fast track many species onto the list. Species we cannot afford to lose. Additionally, the recovery of listed species could become much more difficult and costly as more essential habitat could be impacted or lost. Protecting habitat is essential to avoid future ESA listings.

There is long-standing scientific documentation that habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the leading cause of species declines in the US and globally. It is not only over-harvesting or direct impacts to individual plants and animals that result in the decline of a species. The greatest threats – the degradation and loss of their habitat, critical feeding, sheltering, breeding, and/or nesting grounds – bring species to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, the current interpretation of the definition of harm, to include impacts to habitats, has been utilized by the USFWS for decades. This interpretation has even been upheld in a case before the US Supreme Court.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

title: Comment from Jacobs, Kathy

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

text:
I’m writing to ask the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to keep strong protections in place for endangered and threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

Strong, science-based ESA protections help safeguard wildlife and the habitats they depend on, while also supporting hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, and responsible land management on public lands. These protections matter not just for wildlife, but for the communities and traditions connected to healthy ecosystems.

Thank you for considering my comment and for the work you do to protect America’s wildlife for future generations.

title: Comment from Jacobs, Kathy

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
I’m writing to ask the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to keep strong protections in place for endangered and threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has protected America’s wildlife for more than 50 years. It was signed into law by President Richard Nixon with broad bipartisan support, reflecting a shared belief that preventing extinction and caring for our natural heritage is a responsibility we all share.

Strong, science-based ESA protections help safeguard wildlife and the habitats they depend on, while also supporting hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, and responsible land management on public lands. These protections matter not just for wildlife, but for the communities and traditions connected to healthy ecosystems.

Weakening how the law is implemented would make it harder to protect species already under stress and could undermine long-term conservation efforts. I urge the Service to uphold the intent of the Endangered Species Act and maintain clear, effective protections grounded in science.

Thank you for considering my comment and for the work you do to protect America’s wildlife for future generations.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I oppose your proposed changes to weaken the Endangered Species Act. Biodiversity is critical to ecosystem function, on which our lives and economy depends.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

You need to withdraw these dangerous proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Christina Batteate
93003
California

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:

My name is Benjamin LaBier, and I am an Environmental Studies major student at Keene State College. I am writing to you with concerns about the proposed rule for the Endangered and Threatened Species: Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat. My primary concern above all else is that this proposed rule places economic considerations in the forefront of the issue. I understand that preserving the economy is extraordinarily important, but I don’t believe that the endangered and threatened species protections are having a large negative impact on the economy. Even the Government Accountability Office has claimed that these protections have had no measurable negative impacts on the national GDP and that they have never created a broad slowdown of economic growth.
By including ruling that economic considerations must be taken into account before protecting species, you will be creating room for many critical species to not receive the protection they require over baseless concerns. Even in cases where economic considerations are important, how can you quantify the value of a species when it is so intricately involved with so many other parts of its ecosystem? My suggestion is to remove this from the proposed rule altogether.
title: Comment from LaBier, Benjamin

text:
It’s absolutely appalling that this administration is wasting its time destroying and dismantling the safeguards that have been in place for years not just regarding other people, but now animals as well. I have been asking, “Where is our humanity?” for the past year as we have watched in horror the selfishness and cruelty on full display by people in power. I don’t believe this should even be a conversation being had; it should just be known and universally understood that the ESA is incredibly important and vital to maintaining and regrowing endangered animal populations within our country. I would find it to be one of the highest ironies of our lifetime if we were to see the bald eagle, the biggest symbol of America’s freedom and what we stand for, become more endangered or worse, extinct, if this decision to roll back essential protections on endangered wildlife were to be approved.

I appeal to the humanity of any who must take this comment into consideration: whatever money, power, or prestige that you would gain from this is not worth it. You are enacting cruel and unusual legislation if you approve this decision, and the consequences could prove to be dire for hundreds of species that live within our country. I hope that this decision is not approved, and I hope that something so pointless and damaging for no reason other than selfishness is never brought forth again. As we see protections for fellow humans taken away one after another, it’s disheartening to see that the administration is not content with just that; they must go after our most vulnerable animals too.

I urge whoever reads this comment to NOT roll back protections granted by the ESA.

Thank you for your time.
