First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Pat Nunez
15100 SE 92nd Ct
Florida

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Riels, Annmarie

text:
The most chilling aspect of this rule change would be the expansion of circumstances under which Fish and Wildlife (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) could circumvent the designation of critical habitat. Some listed species might not have any designated critical habitat areas.
Preserving their habitat is essential to their recovery, which is the point of the law.
Habitat loss is the #1 threat driving more than 71% of threatened species toward extinction worldwide, according to a study that analyzed the major threats to IUCN Red List species, threatening more species than all other categories combined.1
This rule change ignores the extraordinary importance of habitat loss. If enacted, it would kneecap our ability to protect endangered and threatened species by removing one of the most essential mechanisms of the ESA, the ability to protect the habitats they need to survive.
The rule changes give too much discretion to the agencies.
One of the major prompts for this proposed revision was the Administration’s executive order, Unleashing American Energy, that directs agencies to review regulations that may slow domestic energy development or add hurdles to large federal projects. Ironically, by not designating all of the necessary critical habitat early in the recovery process, it might cause more uncertainty and disruption for development projects later on.
Predictable rulemaking that’s grounded in science and protected from political whims is essential for both conservation and development projects.
The agencies would also be able to exclude areas from critical habitat if they decided that economic or national security concerns outweigh the conservation benefits, as long as such exclusion doesn’t cause an extinction. This standard is contrary to the intent of the ESA, which is focused on improving outcomes for listed species.
And this a good moment to remember that the ESA exists because we consistently chose our interests over the survival needs of other species.
This cost/benefit analysis also violates the Public Trust Doctrine. Under federal and state laws and policies, fish and wildlife must be maintained for the public: “these resources are held in public trust by the Federal and State governments for the benefit of present and future generations of Americans” (43 CFR § 24.1(b)). The co-trustees are meant to protect the ecological, cultural, educational, historical, aesthetic, scientific, recreational, economic, and social values of wildlife for all Americans.
For all Americans, including future generations. Not merely for one group who would benefit economically if a particular parcel was not designated as critical habitat for a listed species.
I urge you to withdraw this rule change.
A Concerned Citizen
----
1: The greatest threats to species. https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/csp2.12670

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Foltz, Victoria

text:
I'm outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.
title: Comment from A, Nadya

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under consideration. These proposals, both individually and collectively, would significantly weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and preserve ecosystems crucial to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)**

The ESA is intended to act before species reach critical levels. The long-established 4(d) rule is based on years of scientific evidence indicating that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent declines. Removing default protections would cause unnecessary delays, necessitate individual rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive mission and will increase ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis**

Listing decisions must be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Including economic considerations would undermine objectivity and delay protections until species are nearly extinct. Ignoring projected or climate-related threats disregards conservation science that identifies ongoing pressures such as habitat loss and climate change. Weakening these criteria makes timely listing less likely and raises the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”**

Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline. Curtailing critical habitat designation undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing “harm” to exclude habitat degradation would overturn legal and scientific precedent. Such changes weaken inter-agency consultations, increase biological risk, and violate the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections conflicts with its core purpose. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from scientific analysis. This would harm wide-ranging and imperiled species like the Florida panther and gray wolf, accelerating declines for many species already under pressure.

**The cumulative impact of these proposals**

Taken together, these rules would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay or block necessary protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risk, undermine agency cooperation, and raise taxpayer recovery costs.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction because it is based on science, precaution, and early action. These changes run counter to these principles. In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening its wildlife protection laws.

**Request**

For the reasons stated, I urge the withdrawal of all proposed rule changes and the retention of the existing framework, which is rooted in science and legal precedent.

Thank you for considering this comment.
title: Comment from Foltz, Vicky

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act. It is appalling that federal agencies have become the servants of moneyed interests.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Brad Marston
02906
Rhode Island

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposed rule would undermine the ESA's requirement that critical habitat designations be based on "the best scientific data available." It would give undue weight to economic or non-biological criteria at the expense of the species' recovery.

title: Comment from Anderson, Jeff

text:
Hello Public Servants,

With great concern I implore you to uphold the current protections of habitats that shelter endangered species. Drilling, seismic surveys, commercial fishing, and deep sea mining have economic incentives that are outweighed by the need to preserve the finite resource that is wildlife. Many migratory mammals provide nutrients to the habitats they frequent, and are susceptible to sonic disruption. Even under the Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act, 70% of humpback whales and 82% of North Atlantic right whales have scars from entanglement in fishing gear and marine tackle in the Gulf of Maine. This is collateral echoes in marine sanctuaries and coastlines across the United States, and any alterations to the ESA and regulatory precautions could have cataclysmic impact on habitats. Consequences of industry are not always immediate, and changes made to policy are sometimes not observed in the ecosystem until years or decades later. Climactic shifts in the Alaska food chain caused a 34% decrease in North Pacific humpback populations between 2013-2021, and nonprofits like Whale Trust report that stock is still recovering. Please safeguard our already vulnerable wilderness and keep the protection of critical habitats as they are. How we treat our planet is a legacy of stewardship that will far outlive our economic and political agendas.

Thank You,

Richard Dolan
title: Comment from Dolan, Richard

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: I am against rolling back the protections for endangered (even if newly listed) wildlife and their climates. I don't believe we should prioritize economic interests over the welfare of our wildlife. Humans are creative - we can utilize space better, renovate existing property, work from home or otherwise find new ways of expanding and driving our economy without literally expanding the room we take up. There's so much underutilized space that already exists - just look at the "crisis" of empty office spaces since the pandemic - I don't understand why we need to encroach on protected habitats. Endangered, or even at-risk species, and their climates are so important to preserve, for history, for biodiversity, for the food chain, for the joy of living in the same world as them. Risking harm to a species, that could be gone FOREVER, because someone decided we need another Amazon warehouse just doesn't make sense to me. Short-term economic rewards will not erase the permanent damage done.

title: Comment from Petty, Traci

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Myrym Slosberg
132 South Padre Juan Ave
California

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

title: Comment from Hansen, Lois

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Holly Gant
92126
California

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Terri Burgess
93003
California

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Kristen Nelson
93401
California

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposed rule would undermine the ESA's requirement that critical habitat designations be based on "the best scientific data available." It would give undue weight to economic or non-biological criteria at the expense of the species' recovery.

In the United States, species proposed for listing such as the Monarch butterfly and the Bethany Beach firefly will need critical habitat protections. Science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.

text:
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the prosed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The ESA was passed in 1973 with bipartisan support . It remains extremely popular with the American people. It has been tremendously effective: 99% of protected species are still with us today. Our national bird, the Bald Eagle, was protected under the ESA in 1973. With the protections this provided it rebounded spectacularly from approximately 471 breeding pairs to around 71,000 breeding pairs in 2007 when it was delisted. We need to maintain a strong ESA. I do not support any of the prosed changes to it.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed change regarding critical habitat criteria. Habitat protection is key to species recovery. Designation of critical habitat should be based on species needs and science. To reestablish healthy and self sustaining populations, species will likely need to expand into habitat they occupied historically.. This revision would prioritize resource development over species protection, and is diametrically opposed to the intent of the ESA.

The Trump administration has said it wants to make these changes to the ESA to allow for the rapid development of domestic energy fields. Donald Trump accepted one billion dollars in campaign contributions from the fossil fuel companies to advance their interests, and said in his inaugural address he wants to “drill baby, drill”. The proposed changes to the ESA would open the way for oil and gas development which is exactly the kind of development we do not need if we are to address the climate crisis. To suppress the science of climate change and global warming and pretend these things do not exist does a grave injustice to the citizens of the United States of America, and of the world. We need our nation to be guided by science and not be hijacked by special interests. We need to maintain a strong ESA.

text:
I am a concerned U.S. citizen worried about the long-term impacts of repealing the Endangered Species Act's (ESA) Threatened Species Blanket Rule (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029). As a proud American, I believe it is our responsibility as a nation to protect wildlife for future generations. The legacy of the ESA has led to the protection and recovery of many species that were on the brink of extinction, including the bald eagle, our national symbol. Rolling back these protections would undermine this legacy and cause irreversible damage to our ecosystems.

The Blanket Rule serves an essential purpose: it automatically extends the robust protections afforded to endangered species to all newly listed threatened species, swiftly prohibiting harm, killing, or trade of these vulnerable creatures. If we were to rescind the Blanket Rule, we would be forced into a convoluted process of creating species-specific regulations, leading to frustrating delays and uncertainties at the most critical moments for these species’ survival. With the alarming increase in species facing threats each year, this is a risk our country simply cannot afford to take.

The Blanket Rule is crucial because it automatically extends the same protections granted to endangered species to all newly listed threatened species, quickly prohibiting harm, killing, or trade of these species. If the Blanket Rule is rescinded, we would need to create species-specific regulations, leading to procedural delays and uncertainty at the most critical times for these species' survival. With more species facing danger each year, this is a risk our country cannot afford to take.

It is imperative that we maintain our commitment to protecting endangered species and their habitats. I urge the Administration to withdraw all proposed changes to the ESA to ensure that our country's wildlife remains protected for generations to come.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly disagree with proposed revisions to the exclusion framework of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), section 4(b)(2). The ESA permits the Secretary of the Interior to exclude areas from critical habitat designation when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation. However, Congress intended narrow use of such exclusion and only when it would not result in species’ extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs. This means the Department of the Interior (the Agency) will be required to de facto prioritize economic impacts even if such impacts are speculative or secondary.

The proposed revisions also create an impermissibly high threshold for retaining habitat by stating that areas should be excluded unless the Agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This is inconsistent the ESA’s precautionary orientation with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have repeatedly held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule gives disproportionate weight to private industry and political entities whose obvious conflicting interests would minimize potential extinction risks and ignore species’ recovery. The habitat exclusion process would be transformed into a mechanism for conflicting interests to override scientific judgement — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures habitat exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species to recover and thrive.

To the Secretary of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

On behalf of the Klamath Irrigation District farmers and the agricultural communities of the Klamath Basin, we submit this letter to vigorously support the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations cited above.

Our support is grounded not only in the economic reality of our community but in a demand for unbiased science and a fair regulatory environment. For too long, the implementation of the ESA in the Klamath Basin has relied on flawed environmental baselines and outcome-oriented modeling that ignores the distinct biological needs of species like the SONCC Coho salmon.

We endorse the Department’s direction toward a more rigorous application of the "best scientific and commercial data available." We believe these proposed rules, particularly regarding the definition of the Environmental Baseline and the Critical Habitat exclusion analysis, are essential to restoring ecosystem health and ensuring that federal actions are evaluated against the true "but for" causes of species decline.

I. Support for Rigorous Exclusion Analysis (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)
We support reinstating the Secretary's discretion to exclude areas from Critical Habitat. While the economic cost to our district is immense, we emphasize that the "benefits of exclusion" must also account for the ecological benefits provided by the Klamath Reclamation Project—benefits that are lost when the Project is curtailed.

•Ecosystem Services as a Benefit of Exclusion: As detailed in our independent 2024 Biological Assessment provided to the Secretary, the Klamath Project effectively replicates the natural hydrologic cycle of the historic Upper Basin lakes and marshes. By filtering nutrient-rich water through agricultural application and returning it to the system, the Project often lowers nitrogen and phosphorus levels downstream (PacifiCorps, 2012). Excluding Project lands from critical habitat designation allows this beneficial cycle to continue, whereas restrictive designations that fallow land sever this natural ecological function.

•Consideration of "Other Relevant Impacts": We support the inclusion of "community interests" and "public health and safety." A fair ESA environment recognizes that food security is national security, and that the stability of our irrigation district creates the tax base for local schools and services.
II. Support for Accurate Listing and Baseline Definitions (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039)

We strongly support the revisions that ensure listing and Critical Habitat decisions are based on accurate data. Specifically, we endorse the move to clarify the Environmental Baseline, as this has been the primary source of conflict in the Klamath Basin.

•The "Two-Step" Process for Unoccupied Habitat: We endorse the reinstatement of the requirement to evaluate occupied areas first. This is scientifically vital for the Klamath Basin because, as the National Academy of Sciences (2004, 2008) and recent independent reviews confirm, the Critical Habitat for SONCC Coho is located in the tributaries, not the mainstem Klamath River where Project operations occur. Designating unoccupied mainstem river reaches or irrigation infrastructure as "essential" contradicts the species' biological preference for low-velocity tributary refugia (Lestelle, 2007).

III. Support for Reforms to Threatened Species Protections (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029)

•Tailored 4(d) Rules over Blanket Prohibitions: We support rescinding the "blanket rule." Species-specific rules allow for management based on actual biological needs rather than broad assumptions. For example, applying blanket "high flow" requirements intended for Chinook salmon to Threatened Coho salmon—which require low-velocity water—has historically harmed the very species the ESA intends to protect.

•Scientific Integrity in "Necessary and Advisable" Determinations: We support the requirement for rigorous analysis in 4(d) rules. This must include a review of whether the proposed protective regulations are actually supported by the species' life history, rather than relying on surrogates (e.g., using Chinook data for Coho).

text:
The Native Plant Society of New Mexico (NPSNM) respectfully submits these comments into the public record, strongly opposing the proposed changes to Section 4 (50 CFR part 17 section 4 (b)(2)) of the Endangered Species Act. The USFWS should retain the stronger 2024 rules to protect threatened and endangered species.

The NPSNM strives to educate the public about native plants by promoting knowledge of plant identification, ecology, and uses; fostering plant conservation and the preservation of natural habitats; supporting botanical research; and encouraging the appropriate use of native plants to conserve water, land, and wildlife. The society and its members have been actively involved in rare plant conservation efforts in New Mexico.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 Critical habitat exclusions (50 CFR part 17; section 4(b)(2)) This section identifies specific areas essential for the species' survival and recovery, with rules for excluding areas if benefits of exclusion outweigh inclusion, provided extinction is not jeopardized.

The purpose of critical habitat is to identify the areas that are essential to the listed species' conservation. The proposed changes to this section would allow disproportionate weight to be given to economic impacts of designating critical habitat over biological necessities for species protections. Critical habitat is costly to replace once lost. Restoration can take decades, and by then a species may be lost. With this proposed rule change, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting oil drilling or development of an industrial complex to be built where the species lives. This critical habitat often could not be replaced, likely leading to species’ extinction over time. Changing the rule would likely reduce the size and effectiveness of designated areas, increase habitat fragmentation, and shift decision-making away from science towards political and economic entities.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Many of New Mexico’s current threatened and endangered plant species occur in areas where oil drilling, data center development, ranching, infrastructure development, and other economic land uses threaten their continued existence. NPSNM urges the USFWS to reject this rollback and instead restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger science-based framework. Exclusions should remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Dear Director Nesvik and Acting Director Menashes,

I am writing in opposition to the four proposed rules regarding the Endangered Species Act found in the following dockets:

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

As someone concerned with the protection of birds across the United States, and someone who believes in the power and importance of the Endangered Species Act as a tool to boost recovery and prevent extinction, I request that these proposed rules be withdrawn and the current statutory language stay in place.

Species like the Hawaiian Coot, Nene, Marbled Murrelet, and Eastern Black Rail are facing high pressure from invasive species, habitat loss, and climate change. Threatened species such as the Florida Scrub-Jay have long escaped being designated as “endangered” because of crucial protections in the blanket 4(d) rule. Additionally, birds such as the Whooping Crane and Streaked Horned Lark could be harmed by federal projects from other agencies, making clear inter-agency communication important.

I believe that the proposed rules would weaken the Endangered Species Act for birds, making important tools such as critical habitat designations, inclusion of historical baselines in listing decisions, and blanket protections for threatened species inaccessible.

Please withdraw the proposed rules in dockets FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039. Given the ongoing declines of birds confirmed by scientific studies, now is not the time to weaken ESA protections. As a scientist who directly works to inform effective conservation and management strategies for animals protected by the Endangered Species Act, I must emphasize how important it is that the ESA remains unaltered. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Brendan Hobart

text: I strongly oppose reinstating the 2020 Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule under ESA Section 4(b)(2). This approach improperly elevates economic and political considerations over the biological needs of imperiled species, shifting decisions away from science and toward industry convenience. Critical habitat is often the only tool that protects the physical and biological features species need to survive and recover, and weakening it makes habitat loss—already the primary driver of extinction—even worse. A framework biased toward exclusion invites pressure from energy development, ranching, and other special interests, reduces the size and effectiveness of habitat designations, fragments landscapes, and undermines recovery planning. Taken together, this puts us on a path toward looking more like Europe, where much critical habitat and many species are already gone, denying Americans our unique natural heritage in the world so that a few special interests can benefit. The ESA was designed to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to trade them away based on speculative economic concerns. FWS should reject the 2020 rule and instead restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger, science‑forward framework that keeps conservation—not exclusion—at the center of critical habitat decisions.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I respectfully oppose the proposed revisions to critical habitat regulations in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001.

Critical habitat designations are a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act’s preventive conservation approach. The proposed rule would change how the Service evaluates whether the benefits of excluding an area from critical habitat outweigh the benefits of including it, and could allow economic considerations to outweigh ecological needs without equivalent valuation of ecosystem services. This risks excluding habitat vital to species’ survival and recovery, ultimately increasing the likelihood of extinction for imperiled species. Stripping strong critical habitat protections also jeopardizes water quality, climate resilience, and ecosystem services that benefit communities and the economy.

The ESA’s intent is to prevent species from becoming extinct or declining to the point of needing more drastic protections. Weakening critical habitat standards contradicts that goal and could lead to higher long-term ecological and economic costs.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to withdraw or substantially revise this proposal to ensure that critical habitat exclusions do not undermine species conservation objectives.

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Taylor Young

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent and undermines the original intent of Congress to advance science-based conservation.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. If applied loosely, at risk species could lose ESA protection before populations are truly stable and resilient.

The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Tisius , Blair

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Dennis Curry
5851 Silverado Place
California

title: Comment from Collins, Kinsey

text:
It's insane that we even have to try and convince anyone to save our precious wildlife but here we are again.

The species that are being protected (and those that are now threatened that will soon join the list) are important to the overall well-being of our country, and ultimately our planet. And that is extremely important to me.

Reject ANY changes to the Endangered Species Act.

I go on the record today in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation’s threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act’s original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

Don’t sell out our wildlife. Extinction is forever.

title: Comment from Strombotne, Carey

text:
The proposed Endangered Species Act (ESA) rulemakings will dramatically weaken
protections for the nation’s most vulnerable species. These changes undermine the ESA’s
core requirement that the designation of critical habitat be based on best available
science. Congress enacted the ESA to provide a comprehensive, science-based framework
for protecting imperiled species and the ecosystems they depend on. It is unacceptable to
prioritize economic interests over science when extinction is on the line. Habitat loss is
the leading driver of species declines worldwide. Habitat protection must be
strengthened and expanded, not restricted! The ESA’s greatest successes — the recovery
or down-listing of species like the bald eagle, peregrine falcon, and many others — have
come through strong habitat protection, restoration, and conservation, not merely
preventing direct killing. As habitat loss accelerates in the U.S. and globally, weakening
habitat protections will push more species toward extinction. I urge the agencies to
withdraw these changes and retain the science-based regulations that have helped
prevent extinctions for more than 50 years.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
We are loosing critically endangered species at an alarming rate. We need stronger habitat protections, not weaker protections.

I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
