title: Comment from Malone, Annie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to section 4, and specifically section 4(b)(2), of the Endangered Species Act. Human economic factors should not be allowed to outweigh the benefits of preserving an endangered species and natural habitats. The proposed changes to section 4(b)(2) will alter the considerations of natural versus economic benefits gained from any evaluated habitats. Re-evaluating the importance of economic and natural benefits enables businesses to remove habitats from critical protection if the economic benefits to humans is projected to be high, as summarized here by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, "...[section 4 (b)(2) of the Act] authorizes the exclusion of areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating it as critical habitat." The issue with this writing is that human economic growth has always been the justification for the loss of nature. And if the proposed changes are enacted that create more opportunities to disqualify habitats as critical, more species will be lost. All habitats provide fresh air, water, and climate stabilization. Habitats that also provide homes for endagered species should not have to contend with the promise of new economic growth when there are impoverished human areas that could be invested in for economic growth and urban/economic areas that already exist.

Any habitat that is destroyed or polluted in the name of economic growth will increase the amount of species at risk of extinction. Critical habitats should be determined only based on scientific data and species' needs. Humanity has the means to develop the economy without destroying or polluting habitats.

The Endangered Species Act successfully protects and focuses on the well being of plant and animal species. This is the purpose of the Act. Please, do not change the current version of the Endangered Species Act.
title: Comment from Hinchcliffe, Jocelyn

text: Critical habitat is critical. There should be no waffling about. If a scientist has deemed a piece of land critical to a species' survival, humanity can figure out an alternative. Who even makes a judgement as to how 'vital' a land is to economic interests? Anyone can craft an argument that it would be more profitable to open land up to development. This is not an area in which profit should be king. Animals need land to survive. This act is supposed to support diversity and prevent the loss of threatened species. So many species are suffering due to their habitat being split up and divided, leaving small 'patches' available where they might be able to manage in the short term, but in the long term decreases genetic variety and harms the environment. Profit has numbers attached, nature and wildlife is invaluable. I want our future generations to inherit a land still rich in natural beauty and diversity, not one that has been plundered for its natural resources. There is enough profit to be made in other places. This absolutely does not have my support.

text: Removing critical habitat designations may have considerable negative economic impact on areas that are economically dependent on tourism. Many rare and exotic birds, fish, reptiles, corals, plants, aquatic mammals, etc. attract domestic and international tourism. Habitat destruction negatively impacts the economic value of the immediate area, and the value of surrounding areas that are or may become ecologically linked. Destruction of a habitat may disrupt feeding and nesting areas for surrounding migratory animals, and may also cause invasive migration of displaced animals into neighboring areas, which with cause further unintended and unpredictable habitat destruction. Too many economical institutions are dependent on natural preservation to remove protections for the benefit of other economic sectors.

title: Comment from Howell, Cynthia

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Hartman, Kathleen

text:
Subject: OPPOSITION to Proposed Rules: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. I contend that these proposals are arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to the clear statutory mandate of the ESA.
My specific legal and logical objections are as follows:
1. Violation of Statutory Mandate (Section 4(b)(1)(A)):
You propose to allow the presentation of economic impacts in listing decisions. This violates the plain language of the ESA, which mandates that listing determinations be made "solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available." 
• The Flaw: Injecting economic data, even for "informational" purposes, creates a pretext for politicizing scientific decisions. Congress explicitly removed economic considerations from listing decisions in 1982 to prevent exactly this outcome. Reintroducing them contradicts Congressional intent and the "best available science" standard. 
2. Arbitrary Removal of the "Blanket Rule" (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029):
Rescinding the blanket Section 4(d) rule for threatened species is arbitrary and capricious because it creates an unjustified administrative burden that harms species recovery.
• The Flaw: You have failed to demonstrate how a case-by-case approach—which inherently delays protection for species already identified as "threatened"—serves the ESA’s conservation purpose. In a biodiversity crisis, the default should be protection. Removing the blanket rule creates a "protection gap" where species are listed but legally defenseless until a specific rule is finalized. This "death by bureaucratic delay" is a logical failure in a statute designed to prevent extinction.
3. Improper Definition of "Foreseeable Future":
The proposal to limit the definition of "foreseeable future" ignores the reality of climate change.
• The Flaw: Climate models are "best available science." By artificially shortening the timeline of what is "foreseeable," the Services are choosing to ignore scientific consensus on long-term habitat degradation. This is a failure of rational decision-making and renders the rules vulnerable to legal challenge.
4. Failure to Account for Cumulative Effects (NEPA Violation):
The proposed changes to "critical habitat" exclusions (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) allow for a piecemeal destruction of habitat.
• The Flaw: By allowing industries to externalize environmental costs and making it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat, the Services fail to account for the cumulative impact of these exclusions. A "death by a thousand cuts" approach violates the requirement to ensure species survival and recovery.
Conclusion:
These proposals prioritize short-term economic interests over the long-term, statutorily mandated goal of preventing extinction. They lack a rational basis in science and violate the text of the ESA. I urge you to withdraw these rules immediately. 
Sincerely,
Kynsie Brice

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from RUSHING, ALISA

text:
Let me explain the interaction of all species: The planet, in spite of extreme variations in weather, is part of an overall ecosystem. Every living creature contributes to the stability of the system. Some species are apex predators, such as big cats. They perform an essential function: keeping prey species in check.
What happens if the prey species is uncontrolled? They eat all the vegetation within reach, shoving out other creatures that rely on the vegetation to live. Well, that's the end of those creatures. And ultimately, the prey species group grow so large that they begin to die as a result of depleted resources.
You can ask, for example, what good is the little Pangolin? Well you actually don't know, do you? There is no way you can map all the species and their interactions, AI or no.
The planet is like a Jenga game, where everyone stacks little wooden rods, building a tower as high as possible. Then, someone pulls out an element and the entire tower collapses.
You have no idea which little log, or creature, will cause our entire ecosystem to collapse. With me so far?
The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.
I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.
title: Comment from Polk, Dionne

text: Economic considerations must not take precedence over protecting habitat critical to the survival and recovery of an imperiled species. Habitat first!

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Pronko, Colin

text:
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021) The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge.

Please do not make this rule change.

title: Comment from Donaldson, Stephen

text:
I urge you to keep the analysis method for determining critical habitat, habitat that are essential to species recovery
I am concerned this proposal will lead to extinctions. It will exclude too much area from critical habitat designations. Habitat loss is the top driver of species extinction.
In the United States, species proposed for listing, such as the Monarch butterfly and the Bethany Beach firefly, will need critical habitat protections. Science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.

Please help these species by keeping the analysis method for determining habitat.
Thank you.
title: Comment from Smith, Misty

text: Please do not weaken any regulations that help to keep our habitat healthy. These regulations are needed to keep our planet from having worse effects of climate change and to keep species from going extinct.
title: Comment from Barnhart, Sue

text:
Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I sincerely urge you to withdraw the proposed change to the Endangered Species Act which will rollback protection of habitats/ecosystems. The ESA has been essential in protecting and allowing species to recover from extinction for generations. We need to continue to protect these species and the habitats they live in.

We CANNOT prioritize profit over conservation.

Wildlife is easily disrupted by development-drilling, mining, building- in the surrounding landscapes. Not to mention the potential deadly interactions between humans and wildlife. We must continue to protect their habitats to avoid these occurrences from happening.

The proposed change will also eliminate the “blanket rule”, which gives newly threatened species the same baseline protection of endangered species. By eliminating this, future threatened species will lose the standard protections vital to recovery. Again, this change PRIORITIZES PROFIT OVER CONSERVATION. We must NOT allow any changes that prevent species-future and past- to recover. We must not weaken our commitment to protect the ecosystems for threatened species

For the sake of American wildlife, we must continue to conserve endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Habitat protection is important for giving threatened wildlife a chance of recovery.

title: Comment from Defelice, Monica

text:
Under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the federal government designates critical habitat to safeguard threatened and endangered wildlife. The proposed rule, however, would allow the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to place economic interests ahead of habitat conservation needs for newly listed species. This marks a serious step backward for wildlife that rely on large, connected landscapes that are highly vulnerable to fragmentation from development, drilling, and mining.

Over the 51 years since its enactment, the ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct. As a committed supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule, which departs from decades of legal precedent, disregards the best available science, and undermines Congress’s original intent by creating new loopholes that allow the exclusion of critical habitat essential for species recovery.

The ESA embodies our national commitment to protecting not only imperiled species, but also the ecosystems on which they depend—an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change would hasten species decline and erode the ESA’s core purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposal and reaffirm the ESA’s original mandate: to conserve endangered and threatened species and the habitats they need to survive and recover. Robust, science-based habitat protections are essential to giving imperiled wildlife a genuine chance at recovery.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: I’m writing to ask our government to oppose any efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act. This landmark law has protected Hawaiian monk seals, Guadalupe fur seals, southern sea otters and other animals and their ecosystems for more than 50 years. title: Comment from Dewitte, Anne

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from Z, Zach

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment. I have interest in the subject not only as one who benefits from the ecosystem services of species but also as someone who has worked directly in the implementation of the Act as a former federal employee spanning multiple administrations. Where I've use quotation marks are direct excerpts from the rule. My comments on the excerpt then follow.
An overarching comment I have is the amount of discretion added to a temporary role: a particular Secretary exercising his/her discretion is only appointed for a potentially 4-year term. Habitats supporting a listed species often take decades to develop. Exclusion based on temporary factors (e.g., a term of an Executive, changing economic market analyses, and/or changes to economic relevancy due to technological advances) can have irreversible outcomes (i.e., extinction).
"In contrast to the 2016 policy (see 81 FR 7226, at 7231, February 11, 2016), we now will consider the avoidance of the administrative or transactional costs associated with the consultation process as a benefit of exclusion of a particular area of Federal land. We did acknowledge then, and restate now, that we will also consider the extent to which consultation would produce an outcome that has economic or other impacts, such as by requiring project modifications and additional conservation measures by the Federal agency or other affected parties. While we acknowledge that Federal lands are important areas to the conservation of species habitat, we do not wish to foreclose the potential to exclude areas under Federal ownership." Comment: Administrative and transactional costs as a benefit of exclusion are short-sighted. This double counts the expertise of scientists who already work for the federal government and whose job it is to follow the law. It invites an air of distrust in the very people hired by the federal government as civil servants and undercuts their work in using best available science and gaining new information about a species or its habitat which may result in delisting. An outcome of this discretion to weigh administrative fees and transactional costs may be the bias on short-term economic factors instead of the Act’s purpose to conserve and recover the species.
"We propose to reinstate paragraph (e) as set forth in the 2020 rule and in the proposed regulation promulgation portion of this document. Proposed paragraph (e) describes that the Secretary would exercise the broad discretion given under section 4(b)(2) by establishing as a principle that the FWS will exclude areas whenever it determines that the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, as long as exclusion will not result in the extinction of the species." Comment: There needs to be more inclusion of the temporal benefits of each. The exact timeframe of extinction cannot be determined with temporary exclusions to Critical Habitat. Because extinction is forever, a conservative approach to benefits of inclusion would allow for the consideration of new information, technology, and conditions regarding both economic and biological factors.
"The Service is the only entity that is directly affected by this proposed regulation change at 50 CFR part 17 because changes to this section of the Code of Federal Regulations merely describe how we will designate critical habitat under the ESA. Since the only potential entities directly affected by this proposed regulation change are not small entities, including any small businesses, small organizations, or small governments, we certify that, if adopted as proposed, this rule would not have a significant economic effect on a substantial number of small entities." Comment: Lack of direct impacts does not conclude lack of significant economic impacts to substantial number of small entities. What of the indirect impacts or cumulative impacts? Does the benefit of exclusion benefit one industry over another? A large business entity over a small one? Is this up to the subjective discretion of the Secretary whose term is temporary?

In summary, I believe the proposed rule changes are unnecessary and rely on temporary, short-term indicators of which the existing rule already incorporates.
title: Comment from Webb, Barbara

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from LEUNG, PERRINE

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text: The original Endangered Species Act affirms a simple but essential moral truth: the value of living species cannot be reduced to a line item on a balance sheet. It recognizes that plants and animals have an inherent right to exist, and that human prosperity is ultimately inseparable from healthy ecosystems. When we allow short-term corporate profits to override the protection of endangered species, we trade irreplaceable lives and ecological stability for temporary financial gain. The Act stands as a commitment to stewardship, insisting that economic activity must respect the limits of the natural world and that preserving life—human and nonhuman alike—is a responsibility that transcends profit.

title: Comment from KEWAY BIBER, Nichole

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Richard, Isabelle

text:
The Port Gamble S’Klallam Tribe opposes the changes to the Endangered Species Act in – Docket Number: FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048. The Tribe opposes the two-step approach to habitat, where occupied habitat is considered before unoccupied habitat. Unoccupied habitat needs to be evaluated with occupied habitat, to best ensure species recovery. Many species rely on habitat protection that may not currently be occupied but may be used once a barrier is removed. Additionally, protected unoccupied habitat ensures that species may migrate, evade wildfire and drought conditions, seek elevation, and ensure healthy genetic populations. The focus on occupied habitat first focuses on what is convenient over what is biologically required and does not consider the realities of species recovery. Habitat may be restored to the level of service necessary to accommodate species survival with the anticipation of occupation after a barrier is removed or with the understanding of other environmental stressors. Restriction of access to these habitats harms species with small, degraded, or fragmented ranges. It also limits recovery for species like salmon, who need access to habitats which may not be currently occupied, but which may be used once fish passage barriers are removed.
The Tribe also opposes the rule changes that consider non-scientific considerations, privileging non-biological interests over conservation needs. Economic interests should not overweigh the interests of threatened and endangered species and their recovery, which is the purpose of the ESA. Critical habitat exclusions should not be normalized, especially for non-conservation reasons. Exclusion criteria that considers economic and homeland security impacts are not following best available science. Tribes consistently emphasize that decline in habitat is the decline of the resources themselves. Adding economic considerations puts costs on Tribes, whose lands, waters, and resources and disproportionately impacted by species decline and habitat degradation. This ruling does not anchor Tribal stewardship, nor is there a consistent mechanism to evaluate Tribal impacts in this consideration.
The Tribe also opposes the language that allows the Service to conclude that a designation is “not prudent”. The ESA is meant to service species recovery, not administrative or external convenience. This language opens the possibility of declining the designation of habitat when it is essential to recovery, simply because another regulatory level is limited. The ESA must place best available science and species recovery at the center of its actions, to preserve its purpose of species recovery. The Tribe notes that this has not gone through proper government-to-government consultation, which are necessary for changes that impact Tribal rights.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act has been extraordinarily successful, preventing extinction for 99% of the species it protects. As someone who cares deeply about America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule. It discards decades of legal precedent, disregards the best available science, and weakens Congress’s original intent by creating loopholes that allow critical habitat to be excluded for species still in recovery.
The ESA embodies our responsibility to protect not only vulnerable species, but also the ecosystems they rely on to survive. That responsibility should not be diminished. This proposed rule would undermine the Act’s core purpose and risk accelerating the decline of already imperiled wildlife.
I respectfully call on the Administration to withdraw this proposal and reaffirm its commitment to the ESA’s original mandate: protecting endangered species and the habitats they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are essential to ensuring wildlife have a genuine opportunity to recover.
title: Comment from Sit , Samantha

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021) The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge.
title: Comment from Brown, Mel

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed revisions to its regulations implementing section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) raise significant legal and conservation concerns. Although framed as an effort to increase transparency and certainty, the proposal risks undermining the ESA’s core purpose by expanding agency discretion to exclude areas from critical habitat designation in ways inconsistent with the statute’s protective mandate.

Section 4(b)(2) requires that critical habitat designations be based primarily on the “best scientific data available,” while allowing consideration of economic and other impacts only as a secondary step. Courts have consistently emphasized that exclusions under section 4(b)(2) are discretionary exceptions—not coequal considerations—and must not compromise the conservation value of critical habitat. By formalizing an exclusion analysis that elevates non-biological impacts and broadens the circumstances under which exclusions may occur, the proposed rule risks shifting the statutory balance away from science-driven conservation.

Moreover, increased emphasis on exclusion determinations invites arbitrary and capricious decision-making under the Administrative Procedure Act. The proposal provides limited substantive constraints on how benefits are weighed, potentially enabling inconsistent outcomes across species and regions and increasing susceptibility to political or economic pressure. Such outcomes would conflict with judicial precedent cautioning agencies against allowing economic considerations to eclipse the ESA’s conservation objectives.

Finally, critical habitat is a central tool for recovery planning and section 7 consultation. Systematic exclusions reduce regulatory clarity rather than enhance it, weakening habitat protections essential for species survival and recovery. The Services should retain a narrow, conservation-first approach to section 4(b)(2) exclusions to ensure fidelity to the ESA’s text, structure, and overarching purpose of preventing extinction.
title: Comment from hargrove, john

text:
Rule Change #1: Critical Habitat Designations

The economic impact of designating Critical Habitat should not carry the same weight as scientific research. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the methods of designating Critical Habitat under the ESA as they read now.

Rule Change #2: Removal of the “Blanket Rule”

Sea turtles need continued protection if they are downlisted under the ESA in the future. The “blanket rule” ensures that species are protected when they are at their most vulnerable – before they are considered “endangered” of becoming extinct. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the “blanket rule” under the ESA as it stands now.

Rule Change #3: Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat

One of the most pressing threats to all sea turtle species is impacts from climate change on land and at sea. This rule change will make listing species and habitat more difficult and make delisting easier, which will result in fewer protections. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep listing criteria under the ESA as it stands now.

Rule Change #4: Interagency Cooperation

Agencies must continue to coordinate and share information to reduce potential harm to wildlife. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep interagency cooperation requirements under the ESA as they stand now.

title: Comment from Cowan, Gerald

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Haginicolas, Nella

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As an Illinois resident, I see firsthand how habitat loss and fragmentation already strain wildlife and the natural systems that support our communities - as well as the positive result of long-term focus on sustainable solutions grounded in science (like the successful improvement of the Chicago River waterways!).

The proposed changes to the ESA’s Section 4(b)(2) exclusion rule are deeply concerning because they set an extremely low bar for justifying harm: as long as a project does not cause outright species extinction, economic justifications would be allowed to carry greater weight than the protection of essential habitat. This approach makes it far easier to exclude vital considerations needed for species recovery, even when science clearly shows those habitats are critical to long-term survival and ecosystem stability.

By prioritizing economic considerations and allowing ‘other’ inputs to not be considered, the rule grants the agency sweeping discretion that can be used to justify exclusions at the expense of conservation. If economic benefits are consistently allowed to outweigh biological need, essential habitat will be lost incrementally—placing not just individual species, but entire ecosystems, at risk, particularly in the face of accelerating climate change. The Endangered Species Act has succeeded because it centers science and the public interest, not political or industry pressure. Science tells us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These proposed changes undermine both, opening the door for politics and short-term economic interests to override science-based stewardship and weaken the very foundation of the ESA.

Thank you for your consideration.
title: Comment from Davidson, Kirk

text:
I urge you to keep the analysis method for determining critical habitat, habitat that are essential to species recovery
I am concerned this proposal will lead to extinctions. It will exclude too much area from critical habitat designations. Habitat loss is the top driver of species extinction.
In the United States, species proposed for listing, such as the Monarch butterfly and the Bethany Beach firefly, will need critical habitat protections. Science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.

text:

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Becker, Michael

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Melton, Emma

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Alisa Kempema
93010
California

text: I am strongly opposed to the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)).   The ESA requires that decisions be based on the best available science.   It has demonstrably been very successful and is extremely popular.  Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction and weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects.   Re-instituting the 2020 rule supports industry and elevates economic and political considerations over the environment.  It is antithetical to the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems and recover species.   I do not want to see economic and political considerations given priority over the environment.

The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Riedell, Faith

text:
Rule Change #1: Critical Habitat Designations

The economic impact of designating Critical Habitat should not carry the same weight as scientific research. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the methods of designating Critical Habitat under the ESA as they read now.

Rule Change #2: Removal of the “Blanket Rule”

Sea turtles need continued protection if they are downlisted under the ESA in the future. The “blanket rule” ensures that species are protected when they are at their most vulnerable – before they are considered “endangered” of becoming extinct. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the “blanket rule” under the ESA as it stands now.

One of the most pressing threats to all sea turtle species is impacts from climate change on land and at sea. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep listing criteria under the ESA as it stands now.

Agencies must continue to coordinate and share information to reduce potential harm to wildlife. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep interagency cooperation requirements under the ESA as they stand now.

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Jennifer Sherman
Mystic Aquarium

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Mary Brooks

California
