In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Robert Kvaas
6271 Parkhurst Dr
California
title: Comment from Kvaas, Robert

text:
As a wildlife researcher, I am appalled by the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, and I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. This proposed rule will destroy the government’s ability to designate critical habitat. If an endangered species doesn’t currently occupy an area, even if it historically lived there, even if it must return there for its recovery, this area will be ruled out. This is handing over a species’ ability to recovery to industry, and is absolutely counter to the intent of the ESA.

Congress intended the authority to exclude habitat to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

In addition, the rule would give private industry more weight than biological researchers by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This dangerous change to the ESA will allow corporations the ability to exclude areas that need habitat protections, including areas that already currently have protection as deemed by the USFWS as part of a species’ necessary recovery. This is absolutely not what the ESA was intended for.

I urge the Service to abandon this proposed rule and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

The threat to wildlife and habitat has not decreased since the introduction of the ESA; rather, it has increased due to habitat loss, destruction, and climate change. Weakening the ESA will only drive species further toward extinction. Not only that, but weakening the Act is counter to what most Americans want. Recent polls, such as the one conducted by Atomik Research before the 2024 election on behalf of the Indianapolis Zoological Society, showed that 87% of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, believe that the federal government should do more to strengthen the Endangered Species Act.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Ruthe Heimel

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has helped save some of the nation’s most imperiled species from extinction, including the bald eagle, shortnose sturgeon, and peregrine falcon in New York’s Hudson Valley. The law is a cornerstone of American conservation that provides essential protections to our nation’s wildlife and the habitat they depend for survival.

A major reason why the ESA has been so successful — with a track record of saving 99% of listed species — is that it does not allow decisions to protect species to be influenced by profit. The law also grounds decisions about which habitats to preserve in ecological data, limiting the voices of industry.

The proposed rulemaking would undermine the ESA by giving economic interests and profit greater sway in decisions about whether to protect threatened species and their homes — even when this is prohibited by law. The new framework also puts habitats at risk that animals need for their populations to stabilize and recover.

Prioritizing economic interests over conservation science has a dark history: It’s led to the destruction of essential habitat to make way for sprawl development and resource extraction, the use of harmful pesticides that have decimated wildlife populations, and the unsustainable exploitation of species for commercial trade.

I urge the Departments to reject the ESA rulemaking and any proposal that puts economic interests ahead of the lives of our nation’s most at-risk wildlife.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Cassandra

Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I strongly object to the proposed changes to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. Although the ESA allows the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat if the exclusion benefits surpass those of designation, Congress intended this power to be narrowly applied, ensuring exclusion doesn’t lead to extinction. The proposed rule improperly prioritizes economic factors over biological necessities, mandating the agency to favor economic impacts even when they are speculative or secondary.

Additionally, the rule sets an unreasonably high standard of proof for preserving habitat, suggesting areas should be excluded unless the agency can prove that exclusion would lead to extinction. This approach shifts away from the ESA’s precautionary nature and contradicts its protective purpose. Courts have consistently upheld that critical habitat should be designated with recovery in mind, not just to avoid extinction.

Furthermore, the rule seems to disproportionately prioritize non-biological actors, such as private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without demanding the same scientific rigor. This threatens to turn the exclusion process into a way for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — an outcome Congress specifically aimed to prevent when it removed economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to reject these revisions and retain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, well-justified, and fully secondary to the biological needs of the listed species.

text:
I am strongly opposed to the proposed revisions to Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regarding the exclusion of areas from critical habitat designations. While the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) frames these revisions as a move toward "transparency and certainty," the proposed changes create a dangerous shift toward discretionary exclusion that prioritizes short-term economic interests over the biological necessity of species recovery. I oppose these revisions based on the following concerns:
1. Prioritization of Economic Interests Over Biological Recovery
Section 4 of the ESA was designed to be driven by "the best scientific data available." By expanding the framework for exclusion analyses, the FWS risks allowing economic and "other relevant impacts" to supersede the Act's fundamental goal: preventing extinction. The proposed rule creates a loophole for industries to lobby for the exclusion of vital habitats, potentially fragmenting ecosystems essential to a species’ long-term survival.
2. Increased Subjectivity and Loss of Protections
The "benefits of exclusion" are often easily quantified in dollars (e.g., development revenue, resource extraction), whereas the "benefits of designation" (e.g., ecosystem services, genetic diversity, existence value) are harder to monetize. This inherent imbalance in the proposed analysis framework biases the outcome toward exclusion. Rather than providing "certainty," this rule creates an unpredictable landscape where habitat protection depends on the political or economic climate of the moment.
3. Erosion of Judicial and Scientific Oversight
By codifying a specific process for weighing these benefits, the Service may be attempting to shield its decisions from judicial review. If the FWS can more easily exclude areas based on non-scientific "relevant impacts," the rigorous scientific standards that have historically defined critical habitat designations will be diluted. This deviates from the Service’s primary mission of conservation.
4. Undermining Climate Resilience
In 2025, the primary threat to most endangered species is habitat loss compounded by climate change. Reducing the scope of critical habitat designations—especially in areas that may serve as future climate refuge—is a regressive step. Flexible exclusion policies ignore the reality that species need more protected space, not less, to adapt to shifting environments.
The proposed revisions do not serve the "intended effect" of aiding the public; instead, they serve to weaken the legal protections of the nation's most vulnerable wildlife. We urge the Service to withdraw these revisions and maintain a strict, science-first approach to critical habitat designation as mandated by the original spirit of the Endangered Species Act.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Jamie Michelle Thomas

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would severely undermine the ESA's capacity to prevent extinctions, aid species recovery, and protect critical ecosystems relied upon by both wildlife and humans.

1. Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)

The ESA was created to act before species reach critical endangerment. The long-established 4(d) rule is based on significant scientific evidence that early protections are cost-effective and critical for preventing further declines. Eliminating these default protections would lead to delays, necessitate individual rulemaking for typically automatic safeguards, and expose vulnerable species to unnecessary harm. This contradicts the ESA's preventive goals and will result in greater ecological and financial burdens over time.

2. Introducing Economic Considerations in Species Listing

The ESA mandates that listing decisions should rely solely on the best scientific data, excluding economic impacts. Including economic factors would contradict the ESA, compromise scientific integrity, and delay necessary protections. Ignoring projected or climate-driven threats disregards current conservation science, which identifies gradual pressures like habitat loss and climate change as significant risks. Weakening these criteria would increase preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline. Curtailing critical habitat designations undermines recovery planning. Narrowing "harm" definitions to exclude habitat degradation reverses legal and scientific precedents. Weakening these definitions disrupts effective inter-agency consultations, increasing biological risks and conflicting with the ESA's recovery goals.

4. Allowing Agencies to Bypass ESA Protections

Loopholes permitting agencies or committees to override ESA protections, even risking extinction, oppose the ESA's purpose. This approach encourages exemptions, reduces transparency, and prioritizes non-scientific decision-making. Vulnerable species like Florida panthers and gray wolves could face faster declines.

Cumulative Impact

These proposals would collectively weaken the scientific basis of the ESA, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, heighten extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and increase taxpayer recovery costs. The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction due to its scientific and precautionary principles. Diluting these principles weakens a crucial law at a pivotal time for global biodiversity.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of these proposed changes and the preservation of the existing, science-based regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering this comment.
title: Comment from Batten , Freyah

text:
To the US Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:

The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is a profoundly successful tool at achieving the bipartisan goal of preventing extinction of wildlife, fish and plant species and the destruction of their habitats. Akin to an emergency room, the ESA is an effective response to ecological crises that aids species on their road to recovery. That success, however, is predicated on strong implementing regulations. The four proposed changes to those regulations would undermine the law's efficacy. Each must be rejected.

I oppose any and all efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act and urge you to withdraw the proposed rule changes. The proposed rules:

Deprive species newly listed as “threatened” with extinction of protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” even when that take is amongst the greatest drivers of the species' decline. This makes no sense. We must address each of the threats that are causing imperilment.

Fail to protect important habitat that was historically occupied but is currently unoccupied by narrowing the definition of critical habitat. Protecting historical habitat is often vital to the recovery of imperiled species. The goal of the ESA is to get species out of the proverbial emergency room, which inherently necessitates increasing populations and restoring species to historic range. Failing to protect historically occupied habitat fundamentally undermines the effectiveness of the law. Holistic approaches to species recovery is essential in the face of climate change impacts to habitat.

Reduce cooperation between and amongst agencies tasked with implementing the ESA. This change would make it easier for agencies to green light destructive extractive proposals even when doing so will clearly further imperil listed species. Again, this proposed change undermines the letter and intent of the ESA.

Allow consideration of economics in decisions of whether to protect species the science clearly shows are at risk of extinction, in direct violation of the ESA. The ESA clearly states that preventing extinction is the priority, and the Supreme Court has agreed. This regulatory change flips that on its head and allows short term potential lost profits to trump species safeguards.

Each of these proposed changes undermines the letter and intent of the ESA, a law passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed by a Republican President who stated upon doing so: “[T]his legislation provides the Federal Government with needed authority to protect an irreplaceable part of our national heritage—threatened wildlife. Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed. This important measure grants the Government both the authority to make early identification of endangered species and the means to act quickly and thoroughly to save them from extinction.” - President Nixon.

It is a betrayal of this legacy to undermine the efficacy of the law by making these ill advised regulatory changes. We all should be proud of the effectiveness of the ESA. Take for example, the bald eagle, our national bird and symbol of the USA - without the ESA's protections, we likely would have lost this iconic species. Now, Americans across the country are able to see bald eagles flying free.

As we confront the dual biodiversity-loss and climate crises, weakening the ESA is not only short sighted, it is dangerous. Protecting species and their habitats benefits humans as well - the law safeguards forest habitats that clean the air, watersheds and wetlands that filter drinking water for millions of Americans, pollinators that support our food supply, and estuaries that mitigate flooding. Humans are not isolated from the impacts of increasingly severe weather events and damaged ecosystems that are the symptoms of a rapidly changing climate.

I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

The proposal to allow economic considerations in listing decisions reverses the ESA’s science-only standard, which has served our nation well for 50 years. Allowing economic costs to influence listings could delay or prevent the protection of species at the edge of extinction.

Species like the bald eagle, whooping crane, and American alligator recovered because they were listed based solely on science, not economic tradeoffs. America would be very different today if our proud and patriotic bird the American Bald eagle was only a memory. On the other hand, 21 species were recently declared extinct because protection came too late, often due to inaction or regulatory delay. (https://www.fws.gov/press-release/2023-10/21-species-delisted-endangered-species-act-due-extinction)

Critical habitat designations are essential for recovery. Species such as the northern spotted owl and the snail darter survived because their habitat received legal protection. Many species also depend on protected areas for safe nesting and breeding, and disruptions can cause immediate and severe harm. The Piping Plover and the Florida Scrub-Jay are clear examples where disturbance or loss of nesting habitat leads directly to nest failure and population decline. Even species that are not currently listed depend on these protections. Even species not in the Endangered Species Act such as the Horned Lark, for example, is experiencing steep declines due to habitat loss and benefits when natural areas are preserved. Weakening the habitat designation process, including allowing exclusions of unoccupied habitat, would remove the very places species need to survive, recover, and adapt to a changing climate.

My name is Dylan Harrell. I was born and raised in Eastern North Carolina. Growing up, I bore witness to the ecological wonder that was the Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, and within this, the establishment of the Red Wolf Center. Set up as a site that would provide health check ups and rehabilitation for injured wolves, this and other sites like it have proved crucial in mitigating the catastrophic past that this species has endured, from habitat loss, to encroachment and over-hunting by humanity. Though the countless efforts of those that have manned this center have been nothing short of heroic, still the red wolf remains as the most endangered wolf species in the United States and still teeters dangerously close to extinction in the wild. The reason I provide this is to better convey why wildlife conservation is so important to me. This is how I grew up, knowing my home was once home to an amazing species of wolf, unlike any that any other legion could lay claim to. The red wolf was our pride, our symbol of hope and identity in a town that is well below the poverty line in which industry does not exist, and has not existed for decades. Though the red wolf is so symbolic to us, we are still to blame for its low population, for the over-hunting, for the massacring of countless individuals. Now we must face the consequences and support every call to action that aids in establishing legislation that protects other species of wildlife.

I call upon you now to support scientific based evidence when voting in any matter regarding wildlife. The proper research based opinions of wildlife experts are the only true information we should base any legislation regarding wildlife on. The individuals who have dedicated their entire professional careers to better understanding the daily experiences of our natural wildlife, and the impact these experiences have on the natural order of the land around them, are who should be consulted when creating legislation. This goes hand in hand with the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA incorporates and pushes scientific research to the forefront of protections and legislation meant to shield wildlife from harm. The ESA is not based on personal or political gain, as no legislation regarding wildlife should ever be. It serves no ulterior motives, and therefore, must be upheld and protected within our democratic society. We are still a democracy, one in which the voices and beliefs of the people are carried and conveyed by those they elect to represent them. The people have spoken, and continue to voice their discontent with anti-wildlife and more recently anti-wolf and anti-predator legislation such as HR-845. The people want natural species protected on the federal level. Canceling acts such as the ESA will only cause turmoil and the fallout will be catastrophic for wildlife who have no political party affiliation, who have no voice in our human society, who cannot defend themselves in the Senate or in the woods against a hunter armed with an assault rifle.

I urge you to uphold the Endangered Species Act. Continue to fight misinformation with scientific based research. Protect species through proper educated analysis. Do not let wildlife fall victim to political greed. Vote against proposed anti-wolf and anti-predator legislation. Vote for the protection and conservation of natural habitats. Vote for the protection of newly-listed endangered species, so that recovery efforts may successfully take place. Vote for us, for the people, who only wish to see our wildlife prosper, free and wild, as they have always been and should continue to be. Thank you for your commitment to seeing these points upheld, and for your continued efforts to help protect wildlife in this country, The United States of America.
-Dylan Harrell

Testimony on the Proposed Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule (Docket: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)

Aloha,

I am submitting this testimony in strong opposition to the proposed rollback of critical habitat protections under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction, and reinstating the 2020 exclusion rule improperly prioritizes economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species. Critical habitat designations must be guided by science and recovery goals, not by pressures from industry or short-term economic interests. Weakening these protections directly undermines species recovery and the ESA’s core purpose: conserving ecosystems and preventing extinctions.

The 2020 rule elevates economic factors over biological necessity, creating a precedent where species survival takes a back seat to convenience. Exclusions from critical habitat must be based on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns. To ensure meaningful conservation outcomes, the Fish & Wildlife Service should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger, science-driven framework that fully protects essential habitat for threatened and endangered species.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to reject the proposed rollback and maintain robust, science-based critical habitat protections.

Mahalo for your consideration.

Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Sincerely,  

[undersigned] 



Please let me know if you need more information. Thank you for your attention to this matter.  



Sincerely,  



Swetha Pottam  

Digital Advocacy Associate, Earthjustice

Spottam@earthjustice.org

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Deepali Panjabi
93401
California

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text: The Endangered Species Act is vital for the health and stability of ecosystems, plants, and wildlife. With the help and research from biologists, botanists, ecologists, naturalists, zoologists, etc., the Endangered Species Act is able to monitor plant and wildlife populations, and find sustainable solutions for present and future care. Many populations, though, are already at risk due to human colonization, greed, industrialization, trophy hunting, urbanization—to name a few. If plants and wildlife are eliminated (go extinct) anywhere within the trophic level pyramid, whether they’re consumers or producers, the pyramid would break down with negative consequences. Though many are trying, you cannot reverse extinction. Regarding trophic levels, bears and gray wolves are top consumers. Recently the bill, H.R. 845, passed, stripping and blocking restoration protections for gray wolves nationwide, ahead of these four rule makings against the Endangered Species Act. Gray wolves were vanished from Yellowstone for decades because of colonization, farming, and human-wildlife conflicts. In other words, humans forgetting that we’re visitors to these natural spaces. During 1926-1995, elk populations grew over the park’s carrying capacity. As a result, overgrazing along streams where willows weep brought about erosion. Without the willow’s shade and additional vegetation for nesting, aquatic species and birds suffered. Coyote populations took advantage of the gray wolf’s absence by hunting small mammals, initial prey for foxes and raptors. Another unfavored outcome was that the park’s primary consumers experienced a logistic growth due to limited prey until gray wolves’ reintroduction in 1995. This reintroduction reduced elk populations, bringing Yellowstone’s carrying capacity back in balance as a whole. The last three decades of American bison restoration shows, too, how substantial these animals are for the continent’s prairies ecologically. Prairies are also home to the native and critically endangered Black-footed ferret. Similar to gray wolves and the American bison, the Sea otter is a keystone species for marine habitats along the west coast. We’ve already seen the devastating, ecological collapse of Sea otter populations because of the 19th-century global fur trade, mining, and oil spills (1969 Union Oil and 1989 Exxon Valdez). With all that said as informative reminders, the Endangered Species Act has done so much to make sure that the air we breathe; the water we drink; the food we eat; the majestic awe of the bear, big cat, bison, condor, elk and wolf; the cleverness of the Black-footed ferret and Sea otter; the elegance of the monarch butterfly; of native flowers blooming in spring; the hum of a bee; the wind’s whisper through a willow; the bird song we hear continues. As a studying naturalist, I encourage you to honor and protect the Endangered Species Act. With it and backed by scientists, we can continue to help in restoration and sustainability nationwide for generations to come. When we protect the Endangered Species Act, we’re saving what’s left of the continent’s natural spaces. Endangered Species Act protections give ecosystems, plants, and wildlife a supportive chance for survival.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Jenn Koski

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing to express concern regarding proposed revisions to critical habitat regulations, particularly where economic or other exclusions may outweigh biological necessity.

As a freshman who has just completed ten weeks studying fish, wildlife, and conservation law, I now understand that habitat protection is the single most effective tool for preventing extinction. Species rarely disappear because of one cause; they disappear because their habitat is incrementally degraded until reproduction and survival are no longer possible.

Critical habitat does not prohibit land use—it guides it. Excluding areas from designation may appear reasonable in isolation, but ecosystems do not function in isolated parcels. Watersheds, migration corridors, and breeding grounds are interconnected. Fragmentation weakens populations even when some habitat remains.

I learned that genetic diversity is essential to species survival. Wildlife corridors—such as green bridges over highways—allow animals to move, breed, and maintain healthy populations. When habitat is excluded for short-term economic reasons, genetic isolation increases and extinction will win.

Economic considerations matter, but they should not eclipse biological reality. A 2018 study found that wild mammals now occupy only about 4 percent of terrestrial land, compared to 60 percent for livestock and 36 percent for humans. Habitat is already scarce. Further exclusions should be treated as exceptional, not routine. We don't need less forest, we need more vegetarians!

Critical habitat also protects ecosystem services humans rely on. Bats, for example, save U.S. agriculture billions of dollars annually since they are a natural pest control for crops, reducing pesticide costs and use. First observed in 2006, the White-nose syndrome fungal disease affects these creatures and by 2018, over 90 percent of three bat species declined. Habitat protection is prevention—and prevention is cheaper than recovery.

Transparency is valuable, but certainty should not come at the cost of conservation outcomes. I urge U.S. Fish and Wildlife to ensure that exclusion analyses remain biologically grounded and precautionary, with the benefit of the species remaining paramount.

Respectfully,
Jennifer Puccio

title: Comment from Mahder, Debbie

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.
title: Comment from Grizzard Ekzarkhov, Jennifer

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to
urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.
The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium
works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine
wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through
education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation
programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and
coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these
remarkable species.

Working as an aquarium instructor, I see firsthand how different species spark joy in the hearts of children of all ages, inspiring kids to help their communities and grow in their understanding of the world around them. The thought of future children only knowing these species as parts of the past, is not only a major disservice to them, but also a startling look into what would happen if the protections under the ESA are weakened. Protecting wildlife protects us and our connection to our planet. We are not separate from these ecosystems, and a failure to protect species and their habitats will echo in our lives.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for
delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation
requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken
safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase
stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic
Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving
these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and
for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the
ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Jennifer Vela
Instructor, Mystic Aquarium
