title: Comment from Hamilton, Shyla

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.
title: Comment from Chacko, Chris

text:
Hello,

My name is Dr. Reilly Jackson and I am a wildlife research biologist that has trained and worked in the US for almost 15 years. I have worked on numerous studies involving species monitored under the Endangered Species Act, many of which have focused on habitat, or the areas in which specific species can live. Today, I am writing to express my opposition to the federal government’s proposal to revise regulations related to section 4(b)(2) of the ESA. These proposed revisions are antagonistic to the success and recovery of species listed under the ESA and allow for greater superfluous influences on actions necessary to successful recover listed species.

Habitat is one of the most important aspects of life history as organisms require habitat in order to survive and reproduce (Hall et al. 1997). Habitat loss is currently the most significant driving force behind decisions to list species under the ESA, and removing tools to address this factor will significantly impede recovery efforts (Smith-Hicks and Morrison 2021). In fact, the best available science demonstrates that recovery actions including designated critical habitat outside of a species current occupied area is an important factor affecting the likelihood of whether an Endangered species actually recovers (Langhammer et al. 2024).

The federal government’s proposal to allow considerations of economic and security impacts when designated critical habitat seems to stem from efforts to reduce restrictions associated with the ESA and help spur economic development within the US. Importantly, recent research shows that the ESA has not significantly impacted development projects, with 0 out of 88,290 projects with Section 7 consultations stopped or extensively altered due to ESA limitations (Malcolm and Li 2015). Similarly, older research from the US Fish and Wildlife Service reported that of 219,000 consultations conducted between 1998-2001, only 367 of those (less than 1%) were found to potentially jeopardize Endangered species (USFWS 2002, Ruhl 2003). Even then, the majority of these projects were allowed to continue.

Given the published science, considering economic and security interests when designating critical habitat is nonsensical as protecting critical habitat is unlikely to significantly jeopardize economic growth in the U.S. Instead, it is likely that including such considerations will reduce the amount of habitat designated as critical for listed species. Given the important role of habitat to recovery, this is destined to negatively affect recovery efforts.

Thank you for your time,
Reilly Jackson
title: Comment from Jackson, Reilly

Under the ESA, the government designates critical habitat to protect threatened and endangered wildlife. But a suggested rule change would allow the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to prioritize economic interests over habitat conservation needs for newly listed species. That’s a major setback for wildlife like wolverines, which depend on large, connected landscapes that are easily fragmented by development, drilling and mining.

Since its inception 51 kears ago, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to please withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text:
Public Comment (Oppose weakening; strengthen the ESA)

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

I’m submitting this comment regarding FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 to strongly oppose any weakening of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge the Service to maintain and strengthen its full protections.

The ESA remains one of our nation’s most effective, science-based conservation laws. It protects wildlife before extinction becomes inevitable, and it protects the habitat and ecological processes species need to survive and recover. Weakening the ESA shifts costs onto the public, future landowners, and future taxpayers—while increasing the risk of irreversible biodiversity loss.

I urge the Service to reject changes that reduce protections, including anything that would:
•Narrow or weaken the definition of “harm” or “take,” or make enforcement harder in practice
•Undercut critical habitat designations or make them optional, delayed, or overly restricted
•Create broad exemptions that weaken Section 7 consultation (the federal duty to avoid jeopardy and adverse modification)
•Allow political or economic pressure to override best available science in listing, delisting, or recovery decisions
•Reduce consideration of cumulative impacts (habitat fragmentation, development pressure, water withdrawals, pollution, invasive species, and climate-driven stressors)

Instead, the Service should strengthen implementation by:
1.Keeping decisions grounded in best available science and transparent, peer-informed analysis
2.Protecting habitat up front (because preventing habitat loss is cheaper and more effective than trying to rebuild populations later)
3.Ensuring consistent, enforceable standards across regions so protections do not depend on where a species lives
4.Improving recovery planning with measurable benchmarks, clear timelines, and robust monitoring
5.Investing in proactive conservation and partnerships (landowner incentives, habitat connectivity, watershed restoration), while maintaining strong backstop protections when voluntary measures aren’t enough
6.Strengthening capacity for timely consultation and permitting by adequately staffing field offices—so projects can move forward without sacrificing species survival

The ESA is not just about protecting individual species—it’s about protecting the natural systems that support clean water, healthy soils, flood protection, fisheries, outdoor recreation, and local economies. Once species and habitats are gone, we don’t get them back.

Please maintain the ESA’s full intent and authority and reject any proposal that weakens protections for listed species or their habitat. I respectfully urge the Service to move in the opposite direction: strengthen habitat safeguards, improve recovery outcomes, and ensure the Act remains durable, enforceable, and science-driven.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
Chris

text:
I oppose this action.

" Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law" are not legitimate reasons for changing America's bedrock environmental laws in this way. These proposed revisions strengthen certainty for commercial interests rather than wildlife, reduce burdens that are hypothetical, and uphold the law by applying the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo to situations that are not analogous.

There is no justification for these revisions of the Endangered Species Act. They act against recovery of species by reducing protection of critical habitat and promote commercial and economic considerations over science.

Changes to the fundamental building block of environmental regulation should come from agency scientists and public comment, not unqualified administrators.

These proposed regulation revisions are motivated by partisan, political considerations rather than sound scientific research and analysis. They lose sight of the purpose of ESA by emphasizing energy, agricultural and infrastructure priorities. Actions based on Executive Orders 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” and 14219, “Department of Government Efficiency,” along with Secretary’s Order 3418, are inherently flawed.

There is no energy emergency. The United States produced more crude oil than any nation at any time for the past six years in a row. The reason the US imports oil is because many refineries are old and configured for specific grades of oil not produced in the US. Increasing production will not make the US oil and gas independent or significantly lower the cost of gasoline. Demand for oil fluctuates and influences prices. Renewable solar and wind energy are cheaper to produce than fossil fuels and cause much less environmental damage. Recently, renewable energy supplied more than half of the United States’ electricity generation for an entire month.

Do not implement these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Catherine A Salisbury

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. As a long term educator, I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act, as are the scores of children I have taught over the course of 25 years. The ESA is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage. The sole mandate of the FWS is to conserve, protect, and enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people. Without an intact ESA, the FWS purpose, to protect the natural world so current and future generations can live with, live from, and find awe in lands, waters, and wildlife, is mute. Extinctions become unavoidable without the legal safeguards of the ESA and the FWS cannot achieve either its purpose or its vision: a future where people and nature thrive in an interconnected way and where every community feels part of and committed to the natural world around us.

I urge you to retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

I further urge you to keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
Dear Sirs,
As someone residing in California and frequently witnessing the repercussions of habitat loss, I am deeply concerned about the potential weakening of protections for endangered species. I firmly believe in the importance of science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in our country.
The Endangered Species Act stands as a testament to the effectiveness of a system that prioritizes science and the public interest over political pressure or economic influence. It empowers science to guide us in understanding the needs of species for survival, while values play a crucial role in determining whether we choose to protect them. However, the proposed changes to the rule would shift decision-making away from both science and values, potentially jeopardizing the survival of imperiled species.
One significant concern is the proposed classification rule (Section 4), which aims to remove automatic protections from newly listed species. This move places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even commence. Newly listed species could be left unprotected while recovery efforts are delayed, exacerbating their vulnerability.
Another concern lies in the proposed 4(d) rule (Section 4(d)), which seeks to eliminate the blanket rule for threatened species. This change would result in inconsistent protections and delays in recovery for imperiled wildlife, especially at a time when they require the fullest protection possible.
Furthermore, the proposed exclusion rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows the criteria for critical habitat exclusions. This could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, posing a threat to ecosystem health. If economic interests are given precedence over essential habitat, entire ecosystems, not just individual species, are at risk.
Lastly, the proposed consultation rule (Section 7) limits federal review of agency actions. This limitation would facilitate the progress of destructive projects without fully assessing their impacts on endangered wildlife.

In light of these concerns, it is crucial to emphasize the importance of the democratic process and accountability in environmental conservation. Federal oversight serves as a vital check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily influenced by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability, especially at a time when a significant portion of the American population supports stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review to ensure that the best interests of endangered species are prioritized.
I strongly urge the agency to rescind these proposed rules and uphold the ESA’s robust, science-based protections.
Please prioritize strengthening, rather than weakening, federal safeguards to ensure that states and industry are held accountable for protecting endangered wildlife.
I respectfully request that you adhere to the ESA’s original intent: to prevent extinction and guarantee that future generations will inherit thriving and resilient ecosystems.

PLEASE STOP THIS BILL FROM PASSING!!
Stephanie Holzner, Ph.D.

text:
m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.
The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.
Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.
The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

text:
I am strongly opposed to the changes to the ESA outlined in the ESA Amendments Act of 2025 (HR 1897). These changes collectively are a move in the wrong direction for our wildlife and the health of our ecosystems. They would significantly delay or make it impossible for new species to be listed, speed up the delisting process, fail to protect habitats, and shirk Federal responsibility to protect these species, shifting it to states.

Quoting WWF new article, Washington, DC (October 9, 2024) -"There has been a catastrophic 73% decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations* in just 50 years (1970-2020), according to World Wildlife Fund‘s (WWF) Living Planet Report 2024. The report warns that parts of our planet are approaching dangerous tipping points driven by the combination of nature loss and climate change which pose grave threats to humanity.

The Living Planet Index, provided by the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), tracks almost 35,000 vertebrate populations of 5,495 species from 1970-2020. The steepest decline is in freshwater populations (85%), followed by terrestrial (69%) and then marine (56%).

Habitat loss and degradation and overharvesting, driven primarily by our global food system are the dominant threats to wildlife populations around the world, followed by invasive species, disease and climate change." https://www.worldwildlife.org/news/press-releases/catastrophic-73-decline-in-the-average-size-of-global-wildlife-populations-in-just-50-years-reveals-a-system-in-peril/

Given that habitat loss is the primary driver in this massive loss of wildlife already underway, we need to be protecting MORE habitat, not creating impossible loopholes and criteria that developers can use to destroy more habitat, and make it more difficult for species to be listed and protected. In an interconnected ecosystem, it's unwise/self-defeating to destroy the life support system on which one's society depends, aside from the general morality of the issue. If we are "stewards" of this planet, then we have a responsibility to care for and protect life, not destroy it as it suites us for profit. The economic considerations should not be a factor in this case because there is an inherent flaw in the economic calculations- that is that they assume that infinite growth is possible and desirable in a finite and fragile planet. They also are not factoring the economic value that healthy ecosystems provide- more than I can list here- clean air, water, food, the web of life, you know. These changes must not be allowed, and the ESA should be strengthened instead, along with considering giving rights to nature, especially if our "leaders" won't take their responsibility to care for life seriously. The commons is not for corporations to destroy. The health of the soil in protected areas provides a healthy foundation for all of life, including us, and we need to keep soil disturbances to a minimum. Seeking and striving for balance is sustainable, smash, grab and hoard is not. We have a responsibility to future generations as well. Our wildlife is precious and so is the land- let's start acting and legislating that way. I have a degree in Environmental Studies and one in Anthropology, and the disaster of climate change is a clear and present danger, as is the loss of biodiversity. I believe those in charge are well aware, but foolishly place more value on short term gains. That needs to end, and the people are realizing it. Only valuing profit creates a sick culture and a sick planet. I would encourage our representatives to represent us, WE THE PEOPLE, NOT corporations. Protect our wildlife, and do not change or weaken the ESA. What is "unduly burdensome" is trying to explain to children why their leaders aren't looking out for their interests, and watching the animals you love suffer and disappear for greed, or trying to survive on an unhealthy, increasingly poisoned planet. 99% of species protected by the ESA are still living and with us- it works, and it could be better and stronger still. Let's start doing the right thing for a change, valuing and protecting what is precious and innocent instead of exploiting it? Thank you for your attention to this matter.

text:
The Endangered Species Act should not be changed at all.

The ESA is one of the most effective laws every passed by the United States. It has been a valuable law to help mitigate the affects of humans on the natural world.

Rule Change #1: Critical Habitat Designations
The economic impact of designating Critical Habitat should not carry the same weight as scientific research. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the methods of designating Critical Habitat under the ESA as they read now.

Rule Change #2: Removal of the “Blanket Rule”
Sea turtles need continued protection if they are downlisted under the ESA in the future. The “blanket rule” ensures that species are protected when they are at their most vulnerable – before they are considered “endangered” of becoming extinct. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the “blanket rule” under the ESA as it stands now.

Rule Change #3: Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat
One of the most pressing threats to all sea turtle species is impacts from climate change on land and at sea. This rule change will make listing species and habitat more difficult and make delisting easier, which will result in fewer protections. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep listing criteria under the ESA as it stands now.

Rule Change #4: Interagency Cooperation
Agencies must continue to coordinate and share information to reduce potential harm to wildlife. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep interagency cooperation requirements under the ESA as they stand now.

These resources belong to everyone and the USA should be doing everything possible to protect the ocean and the creatures that live there.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I have a degree in Zoology, and have worked in the field and teaching college biology since the 90s. Changing the definition of "harm" in the Endangered Species Act to not include habitat modification negates the entire purpose of the Endangered Species Act. The Act is intended to protect entire species, not individual organisms per se. If an entire species is endangered, it requires an environment to live, feed, and reproduce in. Most animal species require territories; most plant species have complex underground systems that stretch far beyond the individual plants.

Any species requires a healthy ecosystem to thrive. A healthy ecosystem is a complicated, interconnected web of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, soil, air, and water. If any of those components are disrupted, it destroys the system- which can't be easily replaced or fixed, like a building or legal system can. Any of those components rely on all the others to survive- an animal requires a place to live (shelter and habitat) and food, which is either other animals that eat plants or fungi that need a healthy soil system, or a plant or fungus that needs a healthy soil system. Some species are so sensitive to disturbance that footsteps compact the soil too much for that species to live.   Assuming the intent of the change in defnition is an economic one- to be able to go into these environments to extract lumber, oil/gas, or minerals, let me just say that healthy ecosystems provide an estimated 150 TRIllion dollars in "services" every year, for free. They provide flood and polllution control; keep our air and water clean; control our climate; provide recreation/tourism and economic support for the local businesses that come with that recreation/tourism; give us the oxygen we breathe; allow for pollination of food plants (with wild bees accounting for 190 billion dollars alone); increased property value; and that's just off the top of my head. These "services" are priceless, truly- we can't survive without them. Disrupting the health of our ecosystems any more than we have already threatens our health and well-being, leading to greater environmental and medical crises.

Our remaining wildlands, and the biodiversity (including endangered species) they support, are part of what make America special.

Endangered species can't be separated from their habitats. To protect endangered species, we need to protect their habitats.

Please don't make this change to the Endangered Species Act. It will allow our wildlands to be irrevocably harmed at the expense of our endangered species, all other species, and us.

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.
Undoubtedly, the best way to substantially improve the status of endangered species is through the protection of their habitat.
The stated intention of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 is not only to prevent extinction in the short term, but to recover species to the point where they no longer require federal protection. The Act explicitly recognizes this ecological reality by directing the federal government to conserve both listed species and “the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend” (Endangered Species Act, 16 U.S.C. §1531(b)). There is no conceivable way that species will ever be removed from the threatened and endangered lists without self-propagating conservation measures such as habitat protection.
Habitat conservation is also the most cost-effective approach to endangered species recovery. Protecting and restoring habitat delivers broad conservation benefits at lower cost than intensive, species-by-species management actions, while also supporting ecosystem services such as water filtration, carbon storage, and climate resilience (Evans et al., 2020). Once protected, intact habitat continues to provide benefits over time without the need for perpetual intervention, making it both economically efficient and ecologically durable .
Critically, the Endangered Species Act has been most effective on federal lands precisely because habitat protections are enforceable there. Habitat loss occurs more slowly on lands subject to ESA protections than on unprotected private lands (Eichenwald et al., 2020). Weakening or eliminating habitat protections would remove one of the few mechanisms that has slowed biodiversity loss in the United States. Such a change would be short-sighted and would undermine decades of conservation progress.
Removing habitat protections from the ESA contradicts both the intention of the statute and the best available science. Species do not exist independently of their environments, and conservation policy that ignores habitat is conservation policy destined to fail. If the goal of the Act is genuine recovery rather than permanent crisis management, habitat protection must remain central to its implementation.
For these reasons, I urge the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reject any regulatory changes that weaken or eliminate habitat protections under the Endangered Species Act. Maintaining strong habitat safeguards is essential to preventing extinctions, promoting species recovery, and ensuring that this landmark law continues to fulfill its original purpose.
title: Comment from Farmer, Quinn

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Gage, kyle

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is a profoundly successful tool at achieving the bipartisan goal of preventing extinction of wildlife, fish and plant species and the destruction of their habitats. Akin to an emergency room, the ESA is an effective response to ecological crises that aids species on their road to recovery. That success, however, is predicated on strong implementing regulations. The four proposed changes to those regulations would undermine the law's efficacy. Each must be rejected.

I oppose any and all efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act and urge you to withdraw the proposed rule changes. The proposed rules:

Deprive species newly listed as “threatened” with extinction of protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” even when that take is amongst the greatest drivers of the species' decline. This makes no sense. We must address each of the threats that are causing imperilment.

Fail to protect important habitat that was historically occupied but is currently unoccupied by narrowing the definition of critical habitat. Protecting historical habitat is often vital to the recovery of imperiled species. The goal of the ESA is to get species out of the proverbial emergency room, which inherently necessitates increasing populations and restoring species to historic range. Failing to protect historically occupied habitat fundamentally undermines the effectiveness of the law. Holistic approaches to species recovery is essential in the face of climate change impacts to habitat.

Reduce cooperation between and amongst agencies tasked with implementing the ESA. This change would make it easier for agencies to green light destructive extractive proposals even when doing so will clearly further imperil listed species. Again, this proposed change undermines the letter and intent of the ESA.

Allow consideration of economics in decisions of whether to protect species the science clearly shows are at risk of extinction, in direct violation of the ESA. The ESA clearly states that preventing extinction is the priority, and the Supreme Court has agreed. This regulatory change flips that on its head and allows short term potential lost profits to trump species safeguards.

Each of these proposed changes undermines the letter and intent of the ESA, a law passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed by a Republican President who stated upon doing so: “[T]his legislation provides the Federal Government with needed authority to protect an irreplaceable part of our national heritage—threatened wildlife. Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed. This important measure grants the Government both the authority to make early identification of endangered species and the means to act quickly and thoroughly to save them from extinction.” - President Nixon.

It is a betrayal of this legacy to undermine the efficacy of the law by making these ill advised regulatory changes. We all should be proud of the effectiveness of the ESA. Take for example, the bald eagle, our national bird and symbol of the USA - without the ESA's protections, we likely would have lost this iconic species. Now, Americans across the country are able to see bald eagles flying free.

As we confront the dual biodiversity-loss and climate crises, weakening the ESA is not only short sighted, it is dangerous. Protecting species and their habitats benefits humans as well - the law safeguards forest habitats that clean the air, watersheds and wetlands that filter drinking water for millions of Americans, pollinators that support our food supply, and estuaries that mitigate flooding. Humans are not isolated from the impacts of increasingly severe weather events and damaged ecosystems that are the symptoms of a rapidly changing climate.

Please rescind the four proposed rules (docket numbers: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039-0001) undermining the Endangered Species Act for the benefit of wildlife, fish, plants and humans alike.

Sincerely,
Michelle Casey

text:
I live in the Pacific Northwest, where the decline of Southern Resident killer whales is not abstract or theoretical. These whales are critically endangered, and their survival depends on strong, science-based protections under the Endangered Species Act. The ESA was designed to be preventative, not reactive. Rolling back protections until species are already in severe decline undermines recovery and increases the risk of extinction.

Habitat protection is essential to species recovery. Habitat loss is the leading cause of extinction, and critical habitat protections are among the most effective tools the ESA provides. Species are harmed by cumulative and indirect impacts over time, not just single actions viewed in isolation. Weakening protections for threatened species only increases the likelihood that they will become endangered.

Southern Resident killer whales rely almost entirely on healthy Chinook salmon populations. Weakening protections for threatened and endangered salmon stocks directly reduces prey availability and further jeopardizes the whales’ recovery. Federal actions that degrade salmon habitat, increase vessel disturbance, or fragment ecosystems may appear minor on their own, but collectively they undermine recovery efforts. As climate change continues to alter ocean conditions, river systems, and prey distribution, broad and forward-looking habitat protections are more important than ever.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective conservation laws in the world and has prevented extinction for the vast majority of species listed under it. Weakening its implementation would affect not only Southern Resident killer whales, but countless species across marine, freshwater, and terrestrial ecosystems, including salmon, pollinators, and other wildlife that Pacific Northwest communities depend on.

Healthy wildlife populations support clean water, fisheries, cultural heritage, recreation, and local economies throughout this region. When species disappear, ecosystems become less resilient and communities lose the natural systems they rely on for their health, livelihoods, and future. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Re: Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048 (RIN 1018–BI76) — Proposed Rule: “Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat” (ESA § 4(b)(2))

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

I am writing to oppose the Service’s proposed revisions to the regulations implementing ESA § 4(b)(2), especially the provisions that expand the role of economic considerations in excluding areas from critical habitat. While economic information can be useful in how conservation policies are carried out, this proposal risks allowing economic “impacts” to justify weaker habitat protections. That approach conflicts with both the structure of the Endangered Species Act and Congress’s original intent.

Congress intended economic considerations to play a limited role

The ESA was not designed as a cost-benefit statute. Congress passed the Act to prevent extinction and protect ecosystems based on biological need and the public interest, not on whether conservation is economically convenient. The proposed rule itself recognizes that identifying critical habitat must begin with biology and rely on the best scientific data available.

When Congress later allowed agencies to consider economic impacts during critical habitat designation, it did not authorize a formal balancing process that weighs conservation against profits or short-term employment numbers. As Amy Sinden explains, the statutory language reflects a deliberate decision to reject traditional cost-benefit analysis and to acknowledge that many values tied to endangered species cannot be meaningfully expressed in dollar terms. Put simply, § 4(b)(2) was meant to be a narrow and discretionary exception—not a routine mechanism for shrinking critical habitat whenever development would be costly.

Economic analysis tends to undervalue species and habitat

From an economic perspective, endangered species protection exists because markets do not work well in this context. Shogren and Hayward explain that markets often fail to account for the full benefits of biodiversity and habitat protection. Many ecological benefits are shared by everyone and cannot be easily bought or sold, which leads species and habitats to be valued less than extractive or development uses. The ESA was enacted in response to this kind of market failure.

This is especially important for § 4(b)(2) because the proposed rule places heavy emphasis on economic factors such as productivity, jobs, and opportunity costs. Quantifiable data like this is easier to measure than the benefits of a healthy ecosystem or the maintenance of the values Congress seeks to protect. As a result, available monetary analysis carries more weight in decision-making, while ecological benefits are
diminished or treated as uncertain.

This is not a neutral way to apply economic analysis. Instead, it risks reinforcing the same market failures the ESA was created to address.

The rule’s energy focus raises concerns about how discretion will be used

The preamble to the proposed rule links this rulemaking to Executive Order 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” and states that the Service is proposing to reinstate the 2020 rule in response to that directive.

Regardless of broader energy policy goals, regulations implementing the ESA must remain grounded in the Act’s conservation purpose and the framework Congress established. Section 4(b)(2) should not be used as a tool to advance energy development by making habitat exclusions more common or easier to justify.

Requested action

I urge the Service to take action by:

1. Clearly stating in the regulatory text that § 4(b)(2) is a limited, discretionary provision and not a general economic balancing test

2. Ensuring that economic considerations do not consistently favor excluding habitats that face intense development pressure

Thank you for your consideration.

References:

Shogren, J. F., & Hayward, P. H. (1997). Biological effectiveness and economic impacts of the Endangered Species Act. Land and Water Law Review, 32(2), 531–550.

Sinden, A. (2004). The economics of endangered species: Why less is more in the economic analysis of critical habitat designations. Harvard Environmental Law Review, 28(1), 129–214.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act. The ESA has proven to be a successful bipartisan piece of legislation that has saved hundreds of species from extinction and its current format provides optimum protections.

These proposed revisions would allow for critical habitat to be excluded if it would result in an “undue burden” on activities such as energy resource development and extraction.

In direct contrast to the intent of the Endangered Species Act, this revision would prioritize resource development over species protection.

Weakening the critical habitat designation procedure would make it easier to exclude key habitats and avoid the necessary requirement to mitigate impacts for activities that occur in these essential areas.

Habitat protection is key to species recovery.

Critical habitat designations should be based on science and not special interests.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change regarding critical habitat criteria.
title: Comment from Cummins, Shannon

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from West, Carolyn

text:
Maintain all critical habitat. This is important for our climate and species of flora and fauna.

The Endangered Species Act is designed to be preventative, not reactive. Delaying protections until species are already in severe decline undermines recovery and increases extinction risk.

ESA listing and habitat decisions must remain based on the best available science, as required by law.

Habitat protection is central to species recovery. Habitat loss is the leading cause of extinction, and critical habitat protections are among the ESA’s most effective tools.

Cumulative and indirect impacts matter. Many species are harmed by multiple stressors over time, not a single action in isolation.

Weakening protections for threatened species increases the likelihood that they will become endangered.

Southern Resident killer whales are critically endangered and depend on healthy Chinook salmon populations for survival and recovery.

Weakening protections for threatened and endangered salmon stocks directly impacts Southern Resident killer whales by reducing prey availability.

Broad, forward-looking habitat protections are essential as climate change alters prey distribution, ocean conditions, and ecosystem function.

Federal actions that degrade salmon habitat, increase vessel disturbance, or fragment ecosystems can collectively undermine recovery even when individual impacts appear small.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective wildlife conservation laws in the world, credited with preventing extinction for the vast majority of species listed under it.

These proposed changes would affect protections for many of the most iconic and beloved endangered species in the United States, including bald eagles, Florida manatees, sea turtles, gray wolves, grizzly bears, Pacific Right Whale, Hawaiian monk seals, whooping cranes, and numerous pollinators, freshwater fish, and native plants. Weakening ESA implementation will affect wildlife across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems nationwide.

The loss or decline of these species directly impacts the American people. Healthy wildlife populations support clean water, fisheries, agriculture, pollination, flood control, cultural heritage, recreation, and local economies. When species disappear, ecosystems become less stable and communities lose the natural services they rely on for health, livelihoods, and resilience in the face of climate change.

title: Comment from Clarke, Grace

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Habitat loss is the primary driver of species endangerment and extinction. The ESA recognizes this by allowing economic considerations in critical habitat decisions only where exclusions do not risk extinction (16 U.S.C. §1533(b)(2)).

The Act’s effectiveness—preventing extinction for nearly 99% of listed species—is closely linked to protecting sufficient, connected habitat. In contrast, global wildlife declines of nearly 70% since 1970 (WWF, Living Planet Report, 2024) are strongly associated with habitat fragmentation and short-term economic tradeoffs.

The proposed rule expands discretion to exclude areas from critical habitat based on economic factors, increasing the likelihood that essential habitat is lost. Such exclusions may reduce near-term costs but increase long-term economic liabilities through degraded ecosystems, reduced resilience to climate change, and higher recovery expenses.

I urge the Service to maintain stringent standards for habitat exclusions and ensure that economic considerations do not outweigh the biological requirements for species survival and long-term economic stability.

title: Comment from Bane, Rachael

text:
I strongly oppose proposals to weaken the Endangered Species Act by excluding habitat damage from the definition of “take” and by incorporating financial considerations into listing and protection decisions.

Habitat loss and degradation are the primary drivers of species decline and extinction worldwide. In the United States, the vast majority of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are threatened not primarily by direct killing, but by the destruction, fragmentation, or degradation of the habitats they require to survive and reproduce. Treating habitat damage as separate from harm to species ignores decades of ecological science and undermines the biological reality that species cannot persist without suitable habitat.

Redefining “take” to exclude habitat destruction would significantly weaken the Act’s core protective mechanism. It would allow activities that eliminate breeding grounds, migration corridors, food sources, and shelter to proceed unchecked, even when the foreseeable outcome is population decline or local extinction. This approach creates a loophole that permits indirect but inevitable harm while claiming compliance with the law’s intent.

I am also deeply concerned about proposals to factor financial or economic analysis into decisions about whether a species warrants protection. The Endangered Species Act was intentionally designed to be science-based. Its purpose is to prevent extinction, not to weigh the short-term economic convenience of human activities against a species’ right to exist. Introducing financial considerations at this stage shifts the Act away from objective biological assessment and toward subjective, politically influenced decision-making.

Short-term economic calculations consistently underestimate long-term costs. Healthy ecosystems provide essential services including clean water, pollination, flood mitigation, soil stability, and climate resilience. The loss of species and habitats ultimately imposes far greater economic and social costs than proactive conservation ever does. Once species are gone and ecosystems are degraded, restoration is often impossible.

Weakening habitat protections and prioritizing near-term financial interests represents poor stewardship of our shared natural heritage. It transfers irreversible environmental damage to future generations, who will bear the consequences without having had a voice in these decisions. Conservation laws exist precisely because markets and short-term incentives fail to account for long-term ecological stability.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective conservation tools in the world, preventing the extinction of the vast majority of species listed under it. Its success is rooted in its clear, science-driven mandate. Diluting that mandate by ignoring habitat loss and prioritizing economic considerations will erode its effectiveness and accelerate biodiversity loss at a time when ecosystems are already under unprecedented stress.

I urge decision-makers to uphold the original intent of the Endangered Species Act by maintaining strong habitat protections, preserving a science-based decision framework, and rejecting changes that would lead to short-sighted outcomes with irreversible environmental consequences.
title: Comment from Katanic, Gabrielle

text:
FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I oppose any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I oppose weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever.
