title: Comment from Noble, Scott

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

title: Comment from Maurer, Bobbi

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. title: Comment from MARION, ANDREA

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

Although I am not familiar with every legal term in the proposed rule, the core issue is clear: weakening or “deregulating” the Endangered Species Act (ESA) undermines the very purpose for which it was enacted. The ESA was designed to prevent the irreversible loss of species and to ensure that federal actions do not push vulnerable wildlife closer to extinction. That purpose has not changed, and the need for strong protections remains as urgent as ever.

Decades of research demonstrate that the ESA’s existing consultation and critical habitat requirements are effective. A quantitative analysis published in *BioScience* found that species with designated critical habitat for at least two years were **more than twice as likely to show improving population trends** compared to species without such protections. Additional reviews of ESA implementation show that many listed species experience measurable recovery when the law’s safeguards are fully applied, underscoring the importance of maintaining strong regulatory standards.

Weakening consultation requirements would reduce accountability, increase the risk of harm to already‑vulnerable species, and contradict the statute’s intent as established by Congress. The evidence consistently shows that strong, science‑based oversight is essential for species recovery.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw the proposed rule and maintain the current consultation standards to ensure continued compliance with the ESA and to uphold the expectations of the American public.

Sincerely,

Tina L. Turner

text:
Attn: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service MS: PRB/3W 5275 Leesburg Pike Falls Church, VA 22041-3803
Re: Support for ESA Regulatory Reforms to Restore Balance and Respect Local Rights
To the Secretary of the Interior and the U.S.
Fish and Wildlife Service:
My name is Lisa Mott, and I am writing to you from Siskiyou County, California. Our county is ground zero for the conflict between federal regulation and rural livelihoods. We live daily with the consequences of an Endangered Species Act (ESA) that has drifted far from its original intent, morphing into a tool for controlling land and water at the expense of the people who steward it.
I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations. These changes are a breath of fresh air. They signal a return to common sense, lawful governance, and a recognition that human communities are part of the environment, not an enemy to be removed from it.
Restoring the "Environmental Baseline" (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044)
For too long, federal agencies have treated every consultation as an opportunity to rewrite history. They act as if our farms, ranches, and infrastructure are new "impacts" that must be mitigated, rather than the established baseline of our community.
Respecting Existing Rights: I strongly endorse the proposal to clarify that the Environmental Baseline includes ongoing, non-discretionary activities and existing infrastructure. Our water rights and our presence on this land predate the ESA. We should not be forced to justify our existence in every new biological opinion. This change protects our property rights and restores the proper scope of federal review.
Prioritizing Reality Over Models
In Siskiyou County, we see the river and the land every day. We know when the fish are running and when the creeks are dry. Yet, we are constantly regulated by computer models from distant offices that contradict what we see with our own eyes.
Empirical Data: I support the move to prioritize empirical, on-the-ground data over theoretical modeling. If a model says a fish needs water in a place where nature never put it, the model is wrong, not the farmer. We need a regulatory system that values local knowledge and physical reality over outcome-oriented science.
Counting the Cost (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)
The federal government has a moral obligation to consider the human cost of its actions.
Economic Impacts: I applaud the proposal to mandate the consideration of economic impacts when designating Critical Habitat. When you designate vast swathes of our county as critical habitat, you aren't just drawing lines on a map; you are devaluing property, restricting land use, and strangling our local economy. It is time for the Service to weigh these costs honestly and to use its discretion to exclude areas where the economic damage outweighs the conservation benefit.
Conclusion
The people of Siskiyou County are tired of being treated as collateral damage in a federal regulatory experiment. We want healthy forests and rivers, but we also want a vibrant economy and a future for our children. These proposed rules offer a path to balance. They respect the law, they respect science, and most importantly, they respect the people who live here.
I urge you to finalize these rules immediately.
Sincerely,
Lisa Mott Siskiyou County, California
title: Comment from Mott, Lisa

Opening land to drilling, clear cutting and strip mining by considering potential economic losses without a science-based analysis of the ecosystem services these lands provide will not just result in the endangerment and potential elimination of several species, but it will also endanger human health with an increase in pollution, flooding and contamination of our water supply.

Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

This rule change would prioritize economic interests over habitat conservation needs for newly listed species, and I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

Public Comments Processing Attn: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service MS: PRB/3W 5275 Leesburg Pike Falls Church, VA 22041-3803
Re: Support for ESA Regulatory Reforms to Restore Balance and Respect Local Rights
To the Secretary of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:
My name is Lisa Mott, and I am writing to you from Siskiyou County, California. Our county is ground zero for the conflict between federal regulation and rural livelihoods. We live daily with the consequences of an Endangered Species Act (ESA) that has drifted far from its original intent, morphing into a tool for controlling land and water at the expense of the people who steward it.
I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations. These changes are a breath of fresh air. They signal a return to common sense, lawful governance, and a recognition that human communities are part of the environment, not an enemy to be removed from it.
Restoring the "Environmental Baseline" (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044)
For too long, federal agencies have treated every consultation as an opportunity to rewrite history. They act as if our farms, ranches, and infrastructure are new "impacts" that must be mitigated, rather than the established baseline of our community.
Respecting Existing Rights: I strongly endorse the proposal to clarify that the Environmental Baseline includes ongoing, non-discretionary activities and existing infrastructure. Our water rights and our presence on this land predate the ESA. We should not be forced to justify our existence in every new biological opinion. This change protects our property rights and restores the proper scope of federal review.
Prioritizing Reality Over Models
In Siskiyou County, we see the river and the land every day. We know when the fish are running and when the creeks are dry. Yet, we are constantly regulated by computer models from distant offices that contradict what we see with our own eyes.
Empirical Data: I support the move to prioritize empirical, on-the-ground data over theoretical modeling. If a model says a fish needs water in a place where nature never put it, the model is wrong, not the farmer. We need a regulatory system that values local knowledge and physical reality over outcome-oriented science.
Counting the Cost (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)
The federal government has a moral obligation to consider the human cost of its actions.
Economic Impacts: I applaud the proposal to mandate the consideration of economic impacts when designating Critical Habitat. When you designate vast swathes of our county as critical habitat, you aren't just drawing lines on a map; you are devaluing property, restricting land use, and strangling our local economy. It is time for the Service to weigh these costs honestly and to use its discretion to exclude areas where the economic damage outweighs the conservation benefit.
Conclusion
The people of Siskiyou County are tired of being treated as collateral damage in a federal regulatory experiment. We want healthy forests and rivers, but we also want a vibrant economy and a future for our children. These proposed rules offer a path to balance. They respect the law, they respect science, and most importantly, they respect the people who live here.
I urge you to finalize these rules immediately.
Sincerely,
Lisa Mott Siskiyou County, California

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

The proposed rule change would require the agency to give priority to economic needs over the needs of protected species, even if these economic needs are speculative and not fully backed up by data.

The proposed change would remove the ESA’s traditional precautionary orientation, a stance that has been upheld by the courts, that critical habitat needs to be designated with the intent on recovery for the species in question and not just the avoidance of extinction.

The change would give more weight to the wishes of regulated entities rather than relying on the sound judgement of science.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being considered. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, would significantly undermine the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinctions, support species recovery, and preserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species**

The ESA aims to act before species reach crisis levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule, backed by decades of scientific evidence, shows that early protective measures reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default protections for threatened species would cause unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm or death. This opposes the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Economic Considerations in Listing Species**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic considerations would contradict statutory language, undermine scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species are critically endangered. Ignoring projected or climate-driven threats disregards current conservation science and increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing Critical Habitat Protections**

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially climate-refugia necessary for long-term recovery, directly threatens recovery efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses longstanding legal and scientific precedent, weakening inter-agency consultations and increasing biological risks.

4. **Creating Loopholes for Agencies**

Allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, contradicts the ESA’s core purpose. Such loopholes invite project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analyses. This disproportionately affects species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, potentially accelerating their decline.

**Cumulative Impact**

Taken together, these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay species protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and escalate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers. As the ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, it's crucial to reinforce, not weaken, this successful law during a time of global biodiversity loss.

**Request**

Given the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing regulatory framework grounded in science and legal precedent.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I am a biologist and concerned US citizen and voter, writing to firmly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s 2025 proposed rule revising the regulations governing exclusions from critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As a photographer and outdoorswoman who cares deeply about our nation’s health and its children, I urge you to keep the ESA fully intact and functioning, so that future generations can enjoy the opportunity to experience our nation’s wild species, from bald eagles to polar bears.

Critical habitat designation is one of the ESA’s most important and effective conservation tools. The proposed rule would significantly weaken that tool by expanding discretion to exclude areas from designation, elevating non-biological considerations, and reducing the Service’s obligation to prioritize species conservation as Congress intended.

The ESA is one of the world’s most effective conservation laws, and it has protected 99% of the species listed under it. Our nation’s species are part of our national heritage and should be protected for future generations. This rule, plus the gutting of staff and budget at US Fish and Wildlife Service and other conservation agencies, is an attempt to allow our nation’s valuable natural resources to be plundered by already-wealthy corporations. In essence, it is selling off our future to the wealthy few.

The ESA requires that critical habitat exclusions occur only when the benefits of exclusion clearly outweigh the benefits of inclusion—and never where exclusion would result in extinction. The proposed rule distorts this standard by broadening the range of interests that may justify exclusion while narrowing the weight given to ecological necessity, recovery needs, and long-term species viability. This shift undermines the Act’s precautionary, conservation-first framework.

Of particular concern, the proposed rule appears to normalize exclusions based on speculative or short-term economic and administrative considerations, even where the habitat in question is demonstrably essential to species recovery. This short-sighted approach sells our country’s natural heritage to the highest bidder. Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction. Weakening protections at the designation stage virtually guarantees greater harm later, when recovery options are fewer, costlier, and less effective.

The proposal also reduces transparency and accountability. By allowing exclusions without clear, rigorous, and publicly reviewable justification, the rule makes it more difficult for the public to understand how conservation tradeoffs are evaluated and whether exclusions comply with statutory limits. This invites inconsistency, politicization, and increased litigation—outcomes that benefit neither species nor stakeholders.

Furthermore, the proposed rule fails to adequately account for climate change and cumulative impacts. As species’ ranges shift and suitable habitat becomes increasingly scarce, protecting all habitat essential for conservation—not just what is currently occupied or convenient to protect—is more important than ever. Expanded exclusion authority directly conflicts with this ecological reality.

Congress enacted the ESA to prevent extinction and promote recovery, not to maximize discretionary exemptions from habitat protection. A regulatory approach that prioritizes exclusions over conservation reverses that intent and weakens one of the law’s core safeguards.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw the 2025 proposed rule on critical habitat exclusions and to retain strong, narrowly applied exclusion standards that place species conservation first, as required by the Endangered Species Act.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
Carol Blaney, MA Botany, MS Resource Interpretation
United States

text:
Sea turtles play a vital role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems. They help balance ocean food webs by controlling jellyfish populations and supporting seagrass beds, which improve water quality and provide habitat for many marine species. Healthy seagrass meadows also store carbon, helping reduce the effects of climate change.

Sea turtles contribute to biodiversity and support coastal ecosystems that protect shorelines from erosion. Their nesting activities help transport nutrients from the ocean to beaches, benefiting plant life and other wildlife. In addition, sea turtles are an indicator species when their populations decline, it often signals broader environmental problems in the ocean.

Protecting sea turtles helps preserve ocean health, supports coastal communities, and ensures that future generations can benefit from diverse and balanced marine ecosystems. Their survival is closely connected to the overall well being of our planet.

I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Interior and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This bedrock law is the most important tool against the extinction crisis and provides the most significant protections for our nation's threatened animal and plant life.

We don’t survive unless all ecosystems and species survive.

Prioritizing economic potential over safeguarding critical habitat ignores the enormous economic impact that protecting public lands has on a community. Access to healthy public lands drives job growth, tourism, and boosts rural economies. The outdoor industry is also one of the fastest growing in the U.S.

Protecting critical habitat for threatened species is one of the most important strategies for their recovery. This proposal would instead place profit above the Endangered Species Act's original intention and severely set back efforts across the nation to bring species back from the brink. Furthermore, the proposed exclusion of climate impacts in determining critical habitat ignores the best science and will prevent the protection of climate refugia for threatened species. If we fail to safeguard the most suitable places for these species, we cannot expect to ensure their recovery and long-term survival.

The proposed abolition of the “blanket rule” that grants threatened species immediate protection under the Endangered Species Act is especially harmful. This change would require federal staff to individually develop regulations for each individual species. With the significant cuts to conservation programs and staffing, there could be immense delays in issuing protections for imperiled species. For some species, these delays could be the difference between survival and extinction.

Over 1,600 species are protected by the Endangered Species Act, and since its passage in 1973, it has contributed to outstanding recoveries including the bald eagle and the California condor. This legacy can continue, but we need to strengthen bedrock conservation laws, not weaken them.

I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act to truly give our iconic species the best chances of survival.

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Don Meehan
95124
California
title: Comment from Meehan, Don

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Gourdin, Bethany

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

text: I am strongly opposed to the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)).   The ESA requires that decisions be based on the best available science.   It has demonstrably been very successful and is extremely popular.  Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction and weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects.   Re-instituting the 2020 rule supports industry and elevates economic and political considerations over the environment.  It is antithetical to the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems and recover species.   I do not want to see economic and political considerations given priority over the environment.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text: Critical habitat that supports wide ranging threatened and endangered species must be fully included in management decisions. This is different from the pockets of habitat where the species are confined or shelter, which tends to be small compared with the actual range necessary for successful population management
title: Comment from Anonymous

text: Having lived in two different areas were once almost extinct species were brought back by the ESA, I strongly oppose any change that further erodes protection for endangered species. Here on Big Pine Key in the Florida Keys we have several endangered species including the Key deer and Marsh rabbit.  Due to economic pressures and being one of the last mostly native environments in the Lower Keys, there is already tremendous pressure on endangered species. Loss of habitat is the most pressing.  Sea level rise is also contributing to loss of habitat.  These species were once almost extinct in the 1950's due to poaching and other influences. In addition the only living reef in the United States has been severely impacted by loss of habitat on the land mass of the Keys. Please do the right thing and don't pass this new regulation.  Beth Fennell, Big Pine Key Florida.

title: Comment from Hart, Erin

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes, which largely seek to reinstate provisions from 2019, represent a significant and detrimental shift away from the law's core, science-based mission to prevent extinction.
The proposed changes to critical habitat rules (50 CFR part 424) will severely hinder species recovery. Raising the standard to designate unoccupied habitat and expanding the rationale for exclusions are particularly short-sighted and obstructive to responsible species management. Reacting to the increased pressures of climate change and habitat fragmentation, species must shift ranges to survive. Requiring a higher standard of proof that unoccupied areas are "essential for conservation" ignores this ecological reality, the reality of how species are managed on the ground, and jeopardizes the long-term recovery of listed species by locking them into their current, often shrinking, ranges.
Expanding the agency's discretion to exclude areas based on economic or other impacts prioritizes short-term, often private, interests over the public interest in conserving biodiversity. Critical habitat designation is a crucial tool that only affects activities with a federal nexus. It does not create refuges or halt development, but it ensures federal actions do not undermine a species' last chance for survival. Weakening this process trades irreplaceable public natural resources. These proposals, framed as regulatory clarity following the Supreme Court's Loper Bright decision, instead systematically weaken proven protections. I urge you to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the strong, science-forward implementation of the Endangered Species Act that has successfully prevented extinction for 99% of species under its care

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.
title: Comment from Strelioff, K

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed approach to Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048, particularly the expanded and discretionary use of critical habitat exclusions.

Critical habitat designation is one of the ESA’s most important and effective conservation tools. Section 4(b)(2) was intended to allow for limited, narrowly tailored exclusions when the benefits of exclusion clearly outweigh the benefits of inclusion—and only when exclusion will not result in extinction of a listed species. The proposal risks undermining that statutory balance by elevating short-term economic or political considerations over science-based conservation outcomes.

Broadening or normalizing exclusions under Section 4(b)(2) weakens the ESA in several key ways:

First, it erodes science-based decision-making. Critical habitat designations are meant to rely on the best available scientific data. Allowing exclusions based on speculative economic impacts, unenforceable conservation plans, or voluntary agreements reduces the role of objective science and increases vulnerability to external pressure.

Second, it creates inconsistency and uncertainty in species protection. Expansive discretion to exclude habitat invites uneven application across regions and species, resulting in fragmented protections that are difficult to enforce and defend. This uncertainty harms both conservation outcomes and responsible land-use planning.

Third, the proposal overvalues voluntary or nonbinding conservation measures. While partnerships and local efforts can complement the ESA, they should not replace legally enforceable protections. Excluding critical habitat based on assurances that lack permanence, monitoring, or accountability exposes species to long-term risk once priorities or funding change.

Fourth, weakening critical habitat protections increases extinction risk, even if extinction is not immediate. Habitat loss is the primary driver of species decline. Exclusions that chip away at habitat connectivity, recovery areas, or future climate resilience undermine recovery prospects and contradict the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species depend.

Finally, the proposed approach sets a dangerous precedent by shifting Section 4(b)(2) from a narrow exception into a routine policy tool. Congress did not intend for exclusions to become the default or to serve as a workaround to avoid protecting ecologically important areas.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to limit section 4(b)(2) exclusions to truly exceptional circumstances. Such as, require clear, transparent, and evidence-based justification for any exclusion. In addition, ensure that excluded areas are protected by durable, enforceable conservation mechanisms. Also, prioritize long-term species recovery and habitat resilience over short-term economic considerations.

The Endangered Species Act has been successful precisely because it places science, precaution, and ecosystem protection at its core. Weakening critical habitat protections through expanded exclusions undermines that success and puts vulnerable species at greater risk.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important matter.

Respectfully,

Kathleen Pease

text: Its a sad day when we take steps backward in wildlife protection. I, among with many, support a strong and effective Endangered Species Act that preserves robust protections for threatened and endangered species and their vital ecosystems, supports effective pathways for species recovery, and maintains federal agency cooperation. title: Comment from Nolin-Brown, Jusdina

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of our nation's most successful conservation laws, preventing extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection. In the Los Padres National Forest alone, at least 23 threatened and endangered species depend on these safeguards, including California condors, steelhead trout, California red-legged frogs, and arroyo toads.

The proposed changes would move decisions away from science and make it harder to protect wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Weakening protections for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat safeguards, and limiting how cumulative impacts are evaluated would make recovery more difficult and extinction more likely.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, grounded in the best available science and focused on preventing extinction and supporting recovery.

Sincerely,

Nicholas Solakian
10013
New York

title: Comment from E Gibbons, Thomas

text:
(1)I request that the public comment period be extended an additional 90 days, especially given that the proposed rule was published on the Friday before Thanksgiving with only the minimum 30-day public comment period provided. The series of regulation revisions is complicated and takes time to review and analyze.

(2)The proposed rule references the standards and procedures for exclusions of particular areas of critical habitat at 50 CFR 424.19. In 50 CFR 424.19(c), the statement is made that the Secretary “will not exclude any particular area if, based on the best scientific and commercial data available, the Secretary determines that the failure to designate that area as critical habitat will result in the extinction of the species concerned.” I acknowledge this, but argue that this statement is inconsistent with the best reading and intent of the ESA “to provide a means to conserve the ecosystems upon which endangered and threatened species (listed species) depend, to develop a program for the conservation of listed species, and to achieve the purposes of certain treaties and conventions (16 U.S.C. 1531(b)).” By making the standard “extinction of the species” when allowing for the exclusion of an area from critical habitat rather than the using the standard “essential to the listed species' conservation”, listed species could suffer additional declines that increase the risk of extinction over time and could contribute to species becoming endangered that had only been listed as threatened previously. The currently rulemaking should be used to revise the language in 50 CFR 424.19(c) to substitute the phrase “essential to the listed species' conservation” for the phrase “extinction of the species” with regard to a specific area being excluded from the critical habitat designation. This would make the regulation consistent with the statute language at 16 U.S.C. 1532(5)(A).

(3)The proposed paragraph (e) should be rephrased so that it establishes the principle that the FWS will exclude areas whenever it determines that the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, as long as excluded area is not essential to the listed species’ conservation. This give FWS the ability to refine the boundaries of the critical habitat designation with relevant new information provided based on the same set of population analysis tools developed in the process of proposing the critical habitat designation. This also provides for the proposed regulation to be consistent with the statute language at 16 U.S.C. 1532(5)(A).

The possibility of putting economic or national security priorities above those of species habitat opens to door to self-interested, misguided and short-sighted decisions which could have (and have had, in past experience) devastating and permanent consequences for species, ecosystems and human well-being.

There is a great sufficiency of other forces willing to put profit and politics ahead of preservation. Let the role of this agency remain that of protective, long-term responsible stewardship of the greatest riches of our nation and planet : the natural environment and its many, interdependent inhabitants. Giving over to any other path of action would be to abandon your mission and betray the trust placed in your office.
title: Comment from Christensen, Melanie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Niez, Mary

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Carson, Kerri

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am writing to urge you to strongly oppose the current proposal to revise 50 Code of Federal Regulations, Part 424 on the listing of endangered and threatened species and designating critical habitat.

This proposal would undermine the Endangered Species Act's original intent and expose at-risk wildlife to possible extinction in multiple ways:

This proposal prioritizes commercial and industrial interests over the needs of wildlife and the protection of their habitat. By removing language that restricts agencies from considering “possible economic or other impacts,” natural habitats on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development would yield greater economic benefits than protecting them for wildlife.

Eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special regulations for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule would place a greater burden on the agency, as it would be required to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered. This change undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. Rather than listening to scientific evidence, this proposal would rely on cost-benefit analyses, which risk politicizing the protection of our natural resources.

By limiting consideration of “unoccupied areas” when making decisions about critical habitat, the proposal would exclude places where a species historically lived or could live in the future because of natural migration or reintroduction and other factors necessary for recovery and survival. By narrowing the concept of “foreseeable future,” listing and protection decisions would ignore habitat destruction, climate change, and other threats that are expected to worsen over time.

The ESA was established to protect imperiled wildlife before they go extinct—and for more than 50 years, it has done just that, with 99% of listed species already saved or on the path to recovery. Moreover, climate change and development projects are threatening our environment, meaning we need strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival. I look forward to hearing your response on this important issue.

Sincerely,

Erica Davidson
Powell, Ohio
title: Comment from Davidson , Erica

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, would significantly weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, aid in species recovery, and conserve the ecosystems essential to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA was crafted to act before species reach critical levels. The enduring 4(d) rule is supported by decades of scientific proof showing that early, precautionary protections lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing automatic protections for threatened species would lead to unnecessary delays, require individual rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, and leave vulnerable species exposed to preventable harm or death. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive nature and will result in greater ecological and financial costs in the future.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA clearly states that listing decisions must be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations would contradict the law, undermine scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species are nearly extinct. Further, limiting the use of projected or climate-threat analysis ignores current conservation science, which indicates that slow pressures like habitat loss, temperature rises, and ocean acidification already threaten species long before population declines are visible. Weakening future-threat criteria diminishes the likelihood of timely listings and increases preventable extinction risks.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations—especially unoccupied or climate-refuge areas essential for recovery—undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” so that habitat degradation isn’t included would reverse decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often kills wildlife indirectly, and this has long been recognized by law. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations, elevate biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating or expanding mechanisms that allow agencies to override ESA protections—even when extinction is a foreseeable outcome—contradicts the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would encourage exemptions on a project-by-project basis, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact wide-ranging and imperiled species such as Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines in many species already under pressure.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

While concerning individually, these rules collectively would:
- weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- delay or block protections for species in need,
- reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- increase extinction risk for both domestic and internationally threatened species,
- undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, making it one of the most successful conservation laws in history, rooted in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes conflict with those principles.

At a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should be fortifying—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to retract all four proposed rule changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful application.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule because it will significantly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Preservation of biodiversity is not only ethical - it is critical for human health and prosperity as well.

Human Health: The "One Health" framework, which is acknowledged by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes that the health of people is closely connected to the health of animals and our shared environment. For example, ticks and tickborne diseases that afflict many Americans every year are closely correlated with deer population numbers; therefore, it is important that we protect animals that control deer populations. Some of these predator populations are critically threatened.

Human Prosperity: Ecosystem services are the 100% FREE benefits that nature provides to us, like clean air, fresh water, food, and climate regulation. Many species literally clean up the world FOR us. However, we only get to keep these free services if we preserve biodiversity.

Therefore, I oppose removing automatic protections for threatened species and limiting "critical habitat." These are disastrous measures that will immediately undermine biodiversity, and by proxy human health and prosperity. Habitat depletion is a leading harm to endangered species and also leads to a rise in issues like zoonotic diseases, which hurt humans too.

I oppose letting economic factors influence wildlife protection decisions. This is very short-sighted and again, neglects all the free services we get from wildlife.

Finally, I oppose reducing collaboration with state wildlife experts and weakening scientific standards used to evaluate habitat protections. All policy decisions should be made by conferring scientists and scientific data.
