text:
I'm extremely disappointed to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

We need to invest in the future. Biodiversity and the protection of habitat preserves more than just endangered species its preserved entire food webs. The collapse we could see in the United States because of these regulation changes could be devastating. Humans are a part of the natural world and will also be negatively impacted by these actions. This have the potential to increase the likelihood of disease spread (due to decreased biodiversity), collapse economies (food webs collapse and species we rely on for food disappear), and steal the joys of connecting with nature from future generations (children may never hear the sound of a chorus of frogs at night). This nation has been a leader for environmental change and protections in the past.

I stand with most Americans and conservationist around the world in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered and threatened animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately. Please stand up for our future.
title: Comment from Levy, Emma

title: Comment from H, Hannah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Strong, Lauren

text:
I am a PhD candidate studying how emerging pathogens contribute to the decline of America’s smallest rattlesnake (Sistrurus miliarius) in the southeastern United States. I strongly oppose expanding discretionary exclusions from critical habitat. This proposal would weaken habitat protections essential for species recovery by prioritizing economic, energy and infrastructure considerations over scientifically documented conservation needs, contrary to the purposes of the Endangered Species Act. Research on southeastern rattlesnakes demonstrates that protected habitats are vital for population resilience, buffering against invasive parasites and habitat degradation (Palmisano et al., 2025; Gibbons et al., 2000; Todd et al., 2010). Even relatively small or fragmented habitat patches can function as refugia, maintaining landscape connectivity, supporting genetic exchange, and reducing disease impacts. Excluding such areas based on non-biological considerations increases fragmentation and edge effects, further degrading habitat quality and accelerating population decline.
Critical habitat protections are also essential for enabling ongoing scientific research, including studies of disease dynamics, climate stressors, and adaptive management strategies. Weakening designation standards undermines not only immediate conservation outcomes, but also the scientific understanding necessary to guide effective recovery planning in the future. ESA critical habitat provisions are therefore central to maintaining long-term population viability under current and emerging threats.

By lowering the threshold for exclusions and treating avoided regulatory or consultation costs as a benefit, the proposed rule shifts ESA implementation away from conservation-centered decisionmaking. In practice, this approach is likely to favor short-term economic or development interests over long-term ecological sustainability. Such a framing risks portraying ESA compliance as a harm to be minimized rather than as a tool for safeguarding ecosystems that support both biodiversity and human well-being, including through interconnected “One Health” outcomes linking environmental integrity, wildlife health, and human health.

The proposal also undermines the longstanding principle that federal lands should function as conservation anchors, particularly for species recovery. Allowing broad exclusions on federal lands denies this role and increases the likelihood of piecemeal habitat loss that compromises recovery at landscape scales.
Additionally, the rule’s conclusion that it lacks significant Tribal implications appears underdeveloped. Changes to critical habitat exclusion standards can directly or indirectly affect Tribal lands, treaty resources, and co-management efforts. The proposal does not meaningfully strengthen Tribal consultation or reflect Tribal sovereignty, instead treating Tribal concerns as one factor among many in an exclusion analysis.

Finally, the proposal raises concerns about transparency and consistency in decision making. The rule does not clearly define thresholds for what constitutes “credible information” sufficient to justify exclusions, nor does it establish clear limits on when administrative costs alone may warrant exclusion. Given the presence of economically powerful stakeholders in many listing contexts, the absence of defined constraints increases the risk that exclusion decisions will systematically favor development interests over recovery needs. Moreover, the rule does not adequately explain how recovery—defined as long-term persistence, not mere survival-- will be weighed in determining the conservation value of habitat.

For these reasons, I urge the rejection of this proposal and to retain stronger, science-based standards for critical habitat designation. Robust habitat protections are essential to species recovery, ecological integrity, and the credibility of ESA implementation.

title: Comment from Perelman, Zander

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

I oppose the proposal to reinstate the 2020 “exclusion rule” for critical habitat.

Critical habitat is one of the ESA’s most important recovery tools because it protects the physical and biological features species need to survive and rebound—especially when populations are already squeezed into tiny, fragmented remnants. A rule that is structurally biased toward exclusion turns critical habitat into a bargaining chip: the places most essential for recovery become the first places negotiated away.

Reinstating the 2020 framework improperly elevates economic and political pressure over biology. Congress wrote the ESA to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to optimize convenience for energy development, ranching, or short-term private gain. When habitat is excluded because costs are emphasized and benefits are discounted, the result is predictable: smaller designations, more fragmentation, weaker recovery planning, and higher extinction risk. Habitat loss is already the dominant driver of imperilment; policies that make it easier to chip away at habitat protections are anti-recovery by design.

If the Service considers exclusions, that discretion must be exercised under a science-forward, transparent standard with a presumption in favor of designation where habitat is essential. Exclusions should require clear, evidence-based justification and should never be compelled by rigid procedural weighting that effectively forces the agency to trade away high-value habitat on the basis of speculative or inflated economic claims.

FWS should withdraw this proposal, reject the 2020 exclusion rule, and instead restore the more balanced 2016 approach or adopt a stronger framework that keeps biology and recovery outcomes at the center of critical habitat decisions.

e is Natalie Grant and I am a Restoration Ecologist. I work in land protection and stewardship, and as such manage land that has threatened and endangered plants and animals on it. I am firmly against these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The Endangered Species Act was put in place to protect threatened and endangered species, and it has been effective in doing so. To weaken the Endangered Species Act would put these already at-risk species in even more risk.

These proposed changes will:
- Slow the listing process for climate-affected species and limit consideration of future climate driven threats.
- Make it easier to avoid designating critical habitat and reduce the scope and strength of critical habitat protections.
- Make designation of unoccupied habitat more difficult.
- Reinstate a requirement to prove occupied habitat is inadequate before protecting additional areas.
- Remove clear language prohibiting economic considerations in listing decisions.
- Increase the likelihood of delisting species for non-biological reasons
- Limit consideration of ecological harm from federal activities
- Decrease default protections for threatened species.

These proposed changes would make it so the Endangered Species Act would no longer effectively protect threatened and endangered species. This would make a mockery of the original intentions of the act - to which we owe the current healthy population status of our very own national symbol, the bald eagle. The largest driving factor for these proposed changes is economic. In other words it aims to make it easier for developers to develop, loggers to log, and miners to mine where threatened and endangered species are present. I argue that developers, loggers, and miners can pivot and find alternative locations or vocations to work in. Threatened and endangered species cannot pivot. They cannot just find alternative locations to live. This is the reason why they are threatened or endangered. Therefore, according to the very principles in which this act was put in place - to help threatened and endangered species - these changes make no sense. The only species these changes will help is the human species - a decidedly non-threatened species - and only a very small subset of them.

I recommend that these changes not be made and the Endangered Species Act left in the state that it currently is.
